#1 — Highly Innovative (83)

TokTier

Zhenyu Zhang, Zhichao Cao · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TokTier, a stateful CPU+GPU tokenization service that incrementally repairs session continuations and exactly reproduces frozen reference tokenization for full-context requests. - Why it's important: Coding agents repeatedly resend long transcripts after small tool-result appends, so front-end tokenization can rescan far more data than the model actually prefills despite high KV-cache hit rates. - How it does it: TokTier stores token IDs and byte spans per session, re-tokenizes only an append plus a suffix window, accepts a splice only after a tokenizer-family-specific stable-boundary certificate, and uses a run-decomposed GPU pre-tokenizer plus GPU BPE for large state misses. - The good: Across 1.50 × 10^10 split checks, a 12.4 TB corpus, and more than 93,000 replayed agent steps, the evaluated configurations produced zero divergence from their frozen references while reducing vLLM TTFT by 16–34% in loaded regimes. - The missing: The shipped system does not yet provide GPU byte-span export, cross-worker state transfer, or complete normalization coverage, and its large capacity comparison mixes different CPU and GPU resources rather than isolating algorithmic efficiency. - Read it or not: Serving-systems researchers and practitioners working on long-context agent inference should read it for the correctness-aware state-reuse design; readers focused on general-purpose tokenization or non-agent workloads can defer it because the evidence is concentrated on coding-agent traffic.
Why this rank
Systems profile. Novelty (84) and Non-Obviousness (86) are high: correctness-certified incremental tokenization addresses a real mismatch between stateful agent sessions and downstream KV caching, while the exact GPU pre-tokenization design is technically distinctive. Rigor (86) is especially strong despite the preprint status, supported by theorem-guided checks, differential validation, adversarial testing, massive corpus sweeps, runtime shadow verification, and an identified public repository. Completeness (82) and Resilience (80) benefit from explicit coverage boundaries and candid discussion of unsupported tokenizer families, normalization failures, state replication, and non-equal-resource capacity comparisons. Impact (82) reflects a released Rust/CUDA artifact and measured 16–34% TTFT reductions, though deployment remains single-host and agent-focused. Weighted composite: 0.15*84 + 0.15*86 + 0.10*86 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*80 + 0.30*82 = 83.0, rounded to 83.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses front-end tokenization overhead in agentic LLM serving, particularly coding agents that repeatedly submit a growing transcript with a small appended tool result. Existing KV/prefix caching begins after text has already been converted to token IDs, so a stateless tokenizer still scans the complete context on every call. In the authors' traces, the median append is approximately 1.4 K characters against 86 K–123 K-token contexts, aggregate prompt-cache hit rate is 94.1%, and only 1.0–3.6% of calls lack a reusable prefix but those calls carry large contexts. The resulting mismatch creates O(N) tokenization work per turn and potentially O(N^2) work over a growing session. The gap is not merely performance: concatenating independently tokenized prefix and suffix text can change token boundaries and BPE merges, so approximate incremental reuse can silently alter model inputs and invalidate prefix-cache keys. Key Idea: The central insight is to separate tokenization reuse into two workload-specific modes while making correctness a hard acceptance condition. For continuations, a matched token/byte-span run is not trusted by itself; TokTier searches for a synchronizing, tokenizer-family-specific boundary at which the pre-tokenizer cannot depend on text to the left, and splices only after that certificate is found. For full requests, it observes that the studied GPT-family regex pre-tokenizers can be reformulated as parallel character-class runs, bounded lookback, run summaries, and per-character piece-start predicates, removing the apparent sequential regex dependency without changing the reference segmentation. Both mechanisms may fall back to more work, but neither is permitted to emit different token IDs. Methodology: TokTier registers immutable, content-addressed tokenizer configurations containing added-token rules, normalization, pre-tokenization, vocabulary, merge tables, and family-specific checks. A request first undergoes session-state lookup with session affinity. On a state hit, the service retains the previous token sequence and byte spans, retokenizes the new text plus a default 512-character suffix window, compares fresh and cached token records, and searches for a matched run containing at least two tokens, more normalized characters than the longest vocabulary token, and a certified stable boundary. Failed checks double the window up to five times and then invoke full reference tokenization. This protocol is justified by a splice theorem under explicit assumptions: the front end must factor into units whose BPE/WordPiece encoder is deterministic and independent across units, with no sequence-level post-processing during chunking. On state misses, small inputs and unsupported cases use the Hugging Face reference CPU path; large inputs use GPU UTF-8 decoding, character classification, maximal-run construction, prefix scans, regex-equivalent piece-start predicates, size-specialized BPE kernels, output compaction, and CUDA-graph dispatch. The main design decisions—family-specific certification rather than fixed overlap, in-place Rust session bookkeeping to preserve O(Δ + w) behavior, and GPU run decomposition rather than approximate chunking—are technically motivated and supported by theorem-plus-differential-testing evidence, although full normalization and span handling remain incomplete. Key Results: The evaluation runs on a dual-socket 32-core AMD EPYC 9115 host with RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, using version-pinned tokenizer artifacts and real or replayed agent traces. Incremental repair takes 0.5–1.1 ms P50 from 100 K to 3 M characters and is 7.2× faster than full fastokens retokenization from 300 K–1 M characters and 13× faster from 1–3 M characters. Against the fully prewarmed Gigatoken cache, repair is slower at 100 K characters (0.52 versus 0.14 ms) but 2.1× faster at 1 M, 3.0× at 2 M, and approximately 3.3–3.4× at 3–4.4 M characters. Of 56,052 replayed appends, 56,049 were accepted with the initial 512-character window, three widened once, and none fell back to full retokenization; adversarial inputs can force fallback. Full GPU tokenization reaches 3.8–4.7 GB/s on English, CJK, and templated corpora and encodes a 1 M-character request in 0.87 ms with array delivery, compared with 20.5 ms for one-core fastokens, 6.05 ms for empty-cache Gigatoken, 42.2 ms for the LoPT reproduction, and 360.3 ms for serial Hugging Face; Python-list delivery raises TokTier's 1 M-character result to 3.86 ms. At 4.4 M characters, Qwen3 normalization failures produce a 133.1 ms P90, while Llama 3.1 without normalization achieves a 3.28 ms P50 and 4.1 ms P90. In a measured request mixture, four repair cores plus one GPU sustain 1,821 requests/s under a 50 ms P99 objective, whereas 16 stateless CPU cores sustain 40 requests/s; this is a system-capacity comparison using different resource types, not an equal-hardware efficiency comparison. With vLLM 0.25, TTFT improves by 26% for 100 K-character Poisson traffic, 27% P50 and 23% P99 under recorded burst arrivals, 32% on 350 K-character contexts with gpt-oss-120B, and 16–34% in closed-loop regimes. The paper also reports no divergence in 1.50 × 10^10 split checks, 6.21 × 10^7 GPU end-to-end checks, 1.09 × 10^5 incremental-repair checks, a 12.4 TB real-text sweep, 93,000-plus agent replays, and sampled serving runs. The strongest counter-evidence is that Gigatoken remains preferable for short contexts or unusually large appends, and Qwen3 normalization creates a substantial tail. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION—the genuinely new contribution is the combination of correctness-certified cross-turn token-state repair with a reference-equivalent GPU implementation for GPT-family pre-tokenization, while the session workload characterization and runtime differential-validation methodology provide additional empirical contributions; the underlying BPE, overlap, CUDA-kernel, and prefix-cache techniques are individually established components. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is an arXiv preprint (v3, dated 6 August 2026), so the results have not been established here as peer-reviewed findings. Its strongest rigor feature is layered validation: a conditional splice theorem, per-request stable-boundary checks, version-pinned comparisons at both piece-boundary and final-ID levels, synthetic and adversarial tests, real-text corpus sweeps, replayed sessions, and a 5% runtime shadow verifier. The campaign found and fixed an o200k chunk-seam bug and a Unicode-version mismatch that synthetic tests missed; a separate history-dependent bug in an external Rust tokenizer was exposed by session-shaped runtime testing. No divergence was observed in the shipped configurations, but no confidence intervals or statistical tests accompany most tokenizer microbenchmarks; sample sizes are often n=20 or n=24, and the 1.50 × 10^10 split checks are not independent observations. The authors explicitly distinguish theorem coverage from implementation validation and state that the theorem does not formally verify the Rust, Python, or CUDA implementation. The code is publicly released at https://github.com/asuidi/toktier. The paper states that tokenizer artifacts, datasets, dependency versions, and manifests are frozen, but the private six-user trace is not released; public traces include length-preserving filler substitutions, limiting exact workload reproducibility. Evaluation primarily uses vLLM 0.25, frozen tokenizer snapshots, one host topology, and coding-agent workloads. The capacity headline is not a controlled equal-resource comparison, and some large-append routing prototypes have not passed the full certification battery. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the work implements a deployable Rust/CUDA tokenization service, integrates it with vLLM, and evaluates latency, tails, capacity, memory, power, and runtime verification. * Practical: The implementation runs on commercially available CPUs and GPUs, including an RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000, and integrates through vLLM's existing `prompt_token_ids` interface, but production deployment still requires state replication, admission control, worker-affinity management, and robust fallback handling. * Efficient: Repair reduces measured CPU time from 13.4 ms per request for fastokens to 2.3 ms over the same workload mixture, while GPU full tokenization reaches 3.8–4.7 GB/s; however, GPU span export, Python-list materialization, normalization, and session-state construction can dominate particular paths. * Effective: The evidence directly shows lower tokenizer latency, higher front-end capacity, and 16–34% TTFT reductions in loaded vLLM scenarios, while preserving reference token IDs; it does not measure downstream model quality because exact token equivalence is used as the proxy for semantic safety. * Scalable: The system is tested through contexts of roughly 8 M characters and up to about 1.14 M tokens, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger contexts, distributed state transfer, multi-node failure recovery, or fleet-scale contention; scalability beyond the tested host and session-retention policy is therefore claimed rather than demonstrated. The work delivers a public software artifact consisting of a Rust session store/service, CUDA tokenizer paths, validation machinery, and tokenizer manifests; it does not release the private production traces or a generally complete tokenizer implementation for all families. The GPU path is exact for the evaluated supported configurations, but two of 17 examined families do not satisfy the current repair predicate, WordPiece remains outside the current GPU path, one NFC normalizer remains CPU-based, and the GPU path initially returns IDs without byte spans. Strengths: - It identifies a specific systems mismatch—KV-cache reuse after a stateless full-text tokenizer—and supports its importance with multiple independent workload sources, including 153,951 private calls, provider metadata covering approximately 5.12 billion tokens, a 20,230-call public autonomous-agent trace, and TraceLab's 357,161 steps. - The stable-boundary certificate is a meaningful correctness improvement over fixed-window or length-only heuristics: it turns a potentially silent token-stream corruption problem into a checked fast path with widening and reference fallback, and the appendix states the assumptions needed for the splice theorem. - The GPU contribution addresses the difficult pre-tokenization stage rather than only parallelizing BPE, and the authors validate intermediate piece boundaries as well as final IDs, which exposed failures that ID-only testing could miss. - The evaluation measures more than isolated throughput: it includes burst tails, vLLM TTFT, capacity, host contention, memory retention, power, session lifetime, adversarial edits, and a history-dependent external tokenizer failure. The public GitHub artifact and explicit disclosure of failed fast paths strengthen reproducibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the GPU path is limited by the dependent BPE merge chain; two examined families fall back to full tokenization, WordPiece and some normalization/added-token operations remain on CPU, and GPU requests currently lack source byte spans. Session affinity is required because cross-worker state transfer is not implemented. Large appends of 30–100 K characters can exceed a 10 ms P99 target, although delta-aware routing is explored but not shipped. Qwen3 NFC normalization creates slow branches, including a 133 ms P90 at 4.4 M characters. The private workload is concentrated on six users and coding agents, and the authors caution that zero observed divergence covers only tested frozen artifacts, not future tokenizer versions. They also state that state replication, admission control, and state-lifetime policy remain necessary for production deployment, and that the large-append routing prototypes have not passed the shipped path's full certification battery. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The evaluation does not demonstrate a real production deployment with distributed routing, state loss, failover, replication overhead, or multi-tenant isolation, even though these mechanisms are central to a stateful serving tier. The main capacity result compares four CPU repair cores plus a GPU against 16 CPU cores and explicitly cannot separate the benefit of session reuse from the benefit of heterogeneous hardware; an equal-cost, equal-power, or equal-throughput resource-normalized comparison against GPU-only and cache-based alternatives would be more informative. The paper relies heavily on private traces from six users and public traces with redacted or filler text, so the claimed splice coverage may not generalize to multilingual, adversarial, privacy-transformed, or non-coding-agent traffic. The theorem depends on frozen tokenizer configurations and stateless per-unit encoding, while future tokenizer snapshots, custom normalizers, special-token behavior, and engine changes could invalidate the family-specific certificates. The shadow verifier samples rather than guarantees live correctness and reports detection latency only for injected faults, not a quantified operational risk under arbitrary correlated failures. Finally, the TTFT experiments show improvement for selected vLLM regimes but do not establish end-to-end cost or user-visible quality benefits across model sizes, batching policies, network placement, or competing serving engines. Bottom Line: This is a technically substantial and unusually careful systems paper that practitioners building long-context coding-agent infrastructure should read, but its strongest claims are bounded by frozen tokenizer families, single-host experiments, incomplete stateful deployment machinery, and a capacity comparison that does not isolate hardware cost from algorithmic benefit.

#2 — Highly Innovative (82)

Spend Bits Where Queries Look: KV Cache Vector Quantization with Attention-Preserving Transforms

S Fernández-Menduiña, A Ziashahabi, E Pavez… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces NOVA-KV, a serving-compatible 2-bit KV-cache compressor that combines a query-aware non-orthogonal key transform, fixed-size vector quantization, and volume-equalized coefficient grouping. - Why it's important: Long-context LLM decoding is often limited by repeatedly streaming the KV cache from memory, so reducing cache bytes can improve throughput, memory capacity, and supported batch size without retraining the model. - How it does it: It minimizes query-weighted key inner-product distortion, transforms that metric into ordinary MSE through a generalized Parseval relation, and uses small per-group codebooks whose groups balance transformed coefficient volumes. - The good: At approximately 2.22 bits per KV element, NOVA-KV reaches 75.4% versus 25.3% for OSCAR and 0% for QuaRot on Qwen3-8B at 128K RULER NIAH, while preserving 72.4 versus 76.5 BF16 mean accuracy on GPT-OSS-20B across five reasoning and coding benchmarks. - The missing: The central theory is asymptotic and assumes independent Gaussian transform coefficients, while the deployed operating point is only 2 bits per coordinate and the method is not evaluated across a broader range of models, hardware, and production traffic patterns. - Read it or not: Researchers and systems practitioners working on low-bit KV-cache inference should read it for the attention-aware transform and fixed-width VQ design, but readers seeking a general-purpose compression guarantee should treat the empirical scope as limited.
Why this rank
Empirical profile. Novelty (85) and Non-Obviousness (87) are strong because the method derives an attention-aware non-orthogonal key transform and combines it with fixed-width, volume-equalized vector quantization. Rigor (82) is supported by formal derivations, cross-model evaluation, confidence intervals, paired tests, and extensive ablations, although the deployed 2-bit regime exceeds the theory's assumptions and stochastic replication is limited. Completeness (82) and Resilience (77) are strengthened by candid treatment of Gaussian and high-resolution assumptions, protected BF16 regions, custom-kernel dependence, and incomplete joint key-value optimization. Impact (80) reflects open-source calibration and serving code plus substantial long-context throughput and quality results, while broader hardware and production validation remain missing. Weighted composite: 0.20*85 + 0.25*82 + 0.15*87 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*77 + 0.10*80 = 82.4, rounded to 82.

Problem & Motivation: Long-context autoregressive decoding repeatedly reads every cached key and value for every generated token, making KV-cache traffic and capacity a bottleneck at large context lengths and batch sizes. Existing 2-bit approaches use direct scalar quantization or random, Hadamard, or heuristic orthogonal transforms; these methods either optimize ordinary reconstruction error rather than attention products, flatten coefficient variances and discard energy-compaction benefits, or cannot exploit vector quantization under a fixed-width cache layout. The practical problem is therefore to preserve the query-key logits and attention outputs with a fixed number of bits per token while keeping reconstruction on the read path to parallel table lookups rather than sequential entropy decoding or dense matrix multiplication. Key Idea: The key quantizer should allocate distortion according to the query covariance, not Euclidean key error. If \(M_q=Q^TQ\), key quantization error is measured by \((k-\hat{k})M_q(k-\hat{k})^T\); choosing a transform \(R_K\) satisfying \(R_KR_K^T=M_q\) converts this attention-weighted error exactly into transform-domain MSE. The remaining degrees of freedom are chosen to compact key energy using a query-weighted PCA. Because this transform produces unequal coefficient variances, the method groups coefficients into approximately equal-volume vectors so equal-size codebooks approximate variable-rate allocation while retaining fixed-width storage. The paper's central insight is thus a joint design principle: attention-aware stretching for the transform and volume balancing for fixed-rate vector quantization. Methodology: Offline calibration collects post-RoPE queries and keys per layer and KV head, computes the key mean, query second moment \(M_q=Q^TQ\), and centered key second moment \(S_{ek}\). It eigendecomposes \(M_q^{1/2}S_{ek}M_q^{1/2}=E\Lambda E^T\), sets the full-rank key transform to \(R_K=M_q^{1/2}E\), and folds a coefficient permutation into the transform. The permutation sorts transform-coordinate variances and distributes them cyclically across groups to approximately equalize the products of variances. Each four-dimensional key group is encoded by a 256-centroid k-means codebook, giving 2 bits per coordinate, with per-token RMS scaling; reconstruction is a codebook lookup and scale multiplication. The key mean is omitted from the read path because it shifts all token logits by a common amount and therefore cancels in softmax, except for a special correction for GPT-OSS learned sink logits. Values use the prior OSCAR-style orthogonal rotation and per-token affine INT2 scalar quantization rather than the paper's theoretically derived value transform, because value VQ produced little practical improvement and added complexity. At inference, a transformed query absorbs the inverse key transform once per step, while the fused kernel performs groupwise centroid lookup, scaling, attention accumulation, and split-KV reduction. The output-error analysis uses a softmax Lipschitz bound and decomposes error into key-logit and value-output terms, while the grouping theorem assumes independent Gaussian transform coefficients and high-resolution quantization. These design decisions are mathematically motivated for the transform and grouping, but the choice to retain the prior value codec is supported mainly by a small ablation rather than a joint optimization result. Key Results: The paper evaluates Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, and GPT-OSS-20B on RULER NIAH, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench v6, AIME25, MATH500, LongBench, and LooGLE. At 128K RULER NIAH, NOVA-KV scores 79.2 versus 34.7 for OSCAR on Qwen3-4B-Thinking, 75.4 versus 25.3 for OSCAR and 0 for QuaRot on Qwen3-8B, 63.3 versus 36.7 for OSCAR on Llama-3.1-8B, and 54.0 versus 0 for OSCAR and QuaRot on GPT-OSS-20B; BF16 references are 89.9, 83.4, 84.2, and 80.4, respectively. On the five generation benchmarks, NOVA-KV's mean scores are 73.7, 72.9, 29.0, and 72.4 for the four models, compared with BF16 means of 75.3, 74.7, 28.7, and 76.5; GPT-OSS is the most consequential case, where OSCAR scores 13.9 and TurboQuant 37.4. The method uses 2.22 BPE at 128K, versus 2.28 for OSCAR and 2.25 for QuaRot, including metadata and the 64-token sink plus 256-token recent BF16 band. On Qwen3-8B, NOVA-KV provides 1.6–3.1x BF16 decode throughput at batch sizes 1 and 4 over 30K–90K inputs, and on Qwen3-4B it provides 1.7–3.4x; throughput is within a few percent of OSCAR at matched rate, although the custom CUDA implementation is slower than OSCAR at some high-batch settings because VQ adds read and write overhead. The transform-quantizer ablation shows that both components matter: replacing OSCAR's scalar quantizer with VQ improves 128K Qwen3-8B NIAH from 25.3 to 62.7, while replacing OSCAR's transform with NOVA-KV under VQ raises it to 75.4. Volume-equalized grouping reaches 75.4 at 128K versus 74.4 for random grouping and 37.2 for variance-sorted grouping. The high-resolution empirical test finds rate exponents of 1.816–1.878 rather than the predicted 2 and preserves the predicted ordering of grouping schemes, but overpredicts distortion for variance-sorted groups by 81.5%. LongBench gives NOVA-KV 48.23 versus 47.53 for OSCAR and 48.86 for BF16 under the full protection band, while LooGLE gives 28.81 versus 26.38 for OSCAR and 31.50 for BF16. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely new contribution is the closed-form non-orthogonal key transform derived from attention-logit distortion together with a fixed-width, volume-equalized vector-quantization layout; the serving integration, k-means VQ, sink/recent protection, and much of the value-side codec combine established techniques, while the GPT-OSS result is a notable empirical finding showing that orthogonal scalar 2-bit codecs can fail on hybrid-attention MoE architectures. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes formal derivations for the attention-error decomposition, softmax perturbation bound, key transform, generalized Parseval relation, value transform, and variable-rate/fixed-rate grouping result, plus empirical tests of the high-resolution assumptions. It reports bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, paired McNemar tests, calibration ablations, transform-quantizer cross-ablation, grouping ablations, rate-scaling measurements, held-out coefficient tests, and additional LongBench/LooGLE evaluations. However, the primary stochastic evaluations use only 3 RULER rollouts or 5 samples per prompt, and compression parameters, k-means initialization, and partitions are fitted once rather than replicated across independent fitting seeds; confidence intervals therefore capture generation or item variability more than method-training variability. Calibration uses 198 GPQA-Diamond prompts and the main evaluations include GPQA, although MMLU and reduced-calibration ablations reduce concern about direct task leakage. Baselines include QuaRot, TurboQuant, and OSCAR at comparable rates, but the comparison is tied to the authors' serving configuration and reference settings; broader comparisons against token eviction, recent vector-quantization methods, or higher-rate scalar baselines are limited. The paper explicitly provides code at https://github.com/Amir-zsh/nova-kv and a project website at https://amir-zsh.github.io/nova-kv; model weights and datasets are not introduced, and the serving implementation is described as a research fork of SGLang rather than a merged production release. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS, because the paper runs implemented codecs and fused decoding kernels on A100 and H100 GPUs while measuring accuracy, throughput, and capacity. Practical: The method runs on commercially available NVIDIA A100/H100 hardware and uses offline calibration plus fixed-size codebook lookups, but it requires per-layer, per-KV-head transforms and codebooks and a custom serving-kernel integration. Efficient: It reduces the cache payload from BF16 to approximately 2.22 BPE and often gives 1.6–3.4x BF16 throughput at long contexts, but NOVA-KV's VQ read/write overhead makes it slightly slower than OSCAR in some high-batch profiles and can prevent speedups when cache traffic is not dominant. Effective: The evidence shows substantial preservation of long-context retrieval and general benchmark accuracy, especially on GPT-OSS-20B, but the measured task coverage does not establish equal performance for all LLM architectures or workloads. Scalable: Tests reach 128K context and batch sizes up to 16 for Qwen and 128 for GPT-OSS in profiling, but there is no experiment at 10x–100x larger contexts, model sizes, multi-node deployments, heterogeneous hardware, or sustained production traffic; scalability beyond the tested regime is a claim rather than measured evidence. The work delivers an open-source software artifact consisting of calibration/codebook tooling and research serving kernels, not a new dataset or trained model. Strengths: - The paper aligns the optimization criterion with the actual key-side failure mechanism—query-key logit distortion—rather than treating ordinary key MSE as a sufficient proxy. - The generalized Parseval construction gives a clear bridge from attention-aware distortion to standard transform-domain MSE, enabling reuse of vector-quantization theory and making the non-orthogonal transform analytically interpretable. - The fixed-width grouping argument addresses a real serving constraint rather than optimizing only an unconstrained rate-distortion objective; the transform/quantizer ablation demonstrates that both the energy-compacting transform and VQ are required. - The GPT-OSS-20B evaluation exposes an architecture-dependent failure mode of prior 2-bit orthogonal scalar codecs and shows that NOVA-KV remains functional across retrieval, reasoning, coding, summarization, and classification tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the high-resolution model is not guaranteed to hold at the deployed 2-bit rate and use it as a design guide rather than a finite-rate guarantee. They acknowledge that the independent-Gaussian assumption is violated, especially for variance-sorted groups, and that the theory overestimates their distortion. They explicitly note that the two-step key/value design is not jointly optimal, that the value branch remains scalar for read-path simplicity, and that joint key-value quantization is future work. The paper also documents the chunked-prefill dequantization leak and the extra memory needed to close it, and explains that GPT-OSS's sliding-window layers remain unquantized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The reported speed benefits depend on a custom kernel and carefully tuned per-cell configurations; the paper does not provide end-to-end latency including prefill, calibration, scheduler effects, energy, or multi-tenant production measurements. The main accuracy comparison uses a fixed 64-token sink and 256-token recent BF16 band, so the contribution of this uncompressed protection and the method's performance with no protected band are not fully isolated across all models. The learned GPT-OSS sink requires a special correction and illustrates that the theoretical softmax offset invariance does not directly cover all deployed attention variants, but the generality of the method to other hybrid mechanisms is not tested. The analysis assumes positive-definite query covariance and uses eigenvalue flooring without studying sensitivity to ill-conditioned or rank-deficient query statistics. Codebook storage, calibration time, k-means fitting cost, and transform application on the write path are reported only partially, and the paper does not compare against all recent vector-quantization or cache-eviction alternatives at matched memory, quality, and kernel maturity. Finally, the strongest GPT-OSS advantage may reflect a particularly unfavorable OSCAR failure mode; broader model-family replication is needed before treating the result as a general 2-bit superiority claim. Problem & Motivation: Coding-agent prompts specify not only a desired patch but also intermediate work such as exploring alternatives, reasoning deeply, verifying repeatedly, or inspecting an entire repository. Existing prompt-efficiency discussions often treat cost as a function of prompt length or model capability, leaving unclear how wording changes downstream reasoning, tool calls, turns, latency, and cost when task objective, acceptance criteria, model, harness, and evaluator remain fixed. The paper studies this problem for software-engineering agents operating on deterministic bug-fix tasks, with particular relevance to users and platform operators who pay for model tokens and tool-mediated execution. The targeted gap is a controlled, end-to-end account of how semantic instructions induce distinct work mechanisms and how harness design amplifies them. Key Idea: Prompt wording functions as a work-allocation policy rather than merely a textual description of the task. In particular, “develop several approaches” induces a token-heavy internal tournament of elaborated but discarded solution branches, whereas certainty language induces a tool-heavy verification loop that repeats tests and checks after the patch is already validated. A bounded-efficiency instruction avoids authorizing either mechanism while preserving diagnosis and final validation. The paper further argues that the harness determines how much an instruction propagates by controlling static context, tool availability, turn discipline, and replay of tool results. Methodology: The study uses 24 deterministic coding tasks—eight each at low, medium, and high complexity, spanning nine Python, nine JavaScript, and six Go tasks—with each task limited to at most four files, explicit acceptance criteria, visible tests, hidden deterministic tests, allowed and forbidden paths, and a per-task evaluator. Sixteen tasks form a development split and eight form a frozen holdout. Eighteen prompt variants manipulate semantically controlled instructions including multiple approaches, deep thinking, maximum certainty, exhaustive exploration, adjacent cleanup, autonomy, verbose repetition, and bounded efficiency; stress variants separately introduce ambiguity, conflicting constraints, irrelevant context, misleading architectural hints, missing criteria, and multi-turn splitting. The original experiment uses six open-weight reasoning models of at least 500B-class served through Together AI and two harnesses, PI.DEV and Claude Code; post-registration studies add Kimi-K3 and first-party claude-sonnet-5. Runs are paired within model–harness–task blocks, with five repetitions per selected holdout cell. Outcomes include provider-reported reasoning and output tokens, tool calls by type, turns, files inspected, duplicate reads and searches, repeated tests, time to first edit, wall-clock time, out-of-scope changes, visible/hidden-test success, cached cost, and estimated no-cache cost. A condition-blind judge annotates exposed reasoning traces for alternatives, discarded branches, unsupported assumptions, and redundant verification, while deterministic telemetry handles tool-layer metrics. The primary waste criterion requires a median reasoning ratio above 1.5, a task-clustered 95% confidence interval lower bound above 1.1, no material success gain, and replication across multiple tasks. The design decisions to freeze prompt variants before holdout evaluation, separate randomized prompt effects from observed mediator levels, and distinguish cached billing from logical no-cache work are well motivated. The reliance on provider-exposed reasoning text is appropriately restricted to observable traces, but trace-level semantic conclusions remain limited by incomplete and potentially unfaithful reasoning displays. Key Results: On the frozen eight-task holdout, the multiple-approaches instruction increased reasoning by 2.44× to 7.40× across all six original models, with no material success improvement. Deep thinking increased reasoning by 1.57× to 2.21× wherever selected and roughly doubled wall-clock time without adding observable functional units. Multiple approaches generated approximately 3.5 additional approaches, elaborated about three discarded branches, and implemented exactly one; the first discarded branch increased median no-cache cost by approximately 1.9× while median tool calls changed only from 7 to 8. Maximum-certainty prompts increased redundant verification on all six original models, adding a median 1.75 post-success calls, one test execution, and four seconds of latency; the highest observed verification level cost 18.25× the clean-run median, used 15 rather than 6 median tool calls, and took roughly 3× the wall-clock time, without a success gradient. Misleading architectural hints raised pre-first-edit deliberation 4.2×, produced the only annotated semantic marker negatively associated with success (Spearman ρ = −0.19), and increased reasoning 2.61× in the stress family; ambiguous scope yielded 83% success and 1.44× reasoning. Verbose repetition remained approximately neutral at 0.96–1.05× reasoning, while bounded-efficiency variants stayed at or below baseline and preserved diagnosis, edits, tests, and final validation. Harness differences were large: PI.DEV transmitted 1,147–1,642 static prefix tokens versus 15,983–20,330 for Claude Code, Claude Code used 2–7× more turns in matched comparisons, and its cost per success was 5–30× higher in the original open-model comparison. Claude Code devoted 52% of baseline tool calls to tests versus 22% for PI.DEV, while PI.DEV devoted 40% to reads versus 21% for Claude Code. The first-party Sonnet 5 study reproduced multiple-approaches inflation at 2.70× under PI.DEV and 2.52× under native Claude Code; maximum certainty reached 4.13× output tokens and 2.7× no-cache cost per success under native Claude Code. Kimi-K3 showed a 16.6× multiple-approaches and 14.8× deep-thinking ratio, partly because its baseline median reasoning was only 55 tokens, although its absolute waste remained at or below K2-generation levels. These results are measured on small, mostly high-success tasks rather than stress-scale repositories. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW BENCHMARK/MEASUREMENT FRAMEWORK, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely distinctive contribution is the controlled decomposition of prompt-induced agent waste into discarded reasoning branches and tool-mediated verification loops, while the benchmark infrastructure, paired experiments, and bounded-efficiency prompt are largely combinations of established experimental and agent-evaluation techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports preregistration of hypotheses, metric definitions, prompt templates, classification rules, holdout selections, expansion protocols, and analysis code before inspecting the relevant results; the holdout variants were frozen using development data only. It reports task-clustered bootstrap intervals, sign-flip permutation tests, p-values for selected tool effects, repeated runs, a frozen holdout, paraphrase tests, Kimi-K3 replication, and a first-party Sonnet 5 replication. Trace annotation achieved 98.9% valid JSON outputs, 91.1% evidence-backed nonzero counts, and researcher-blind agreement within ±1 on 84.9% of fields; agreement was weaker for some judge-sensitive measures, with overall cross-judge κ = 0.28 and κ = 0.55–0.68 on key branch and verification fields. The benchmark code, task fixtures, prompt variants, raw ledgers, and analysis are stated to be available at https://github.com/PointFiveLabs/prompt-efficiency-benchmark. The paper does not provide conventional model-training code or weights because it evaluates external models. Important concerns are disclosed: exposed reasoning may not represent hidden computation, mechanism levels are observed mediators rather than randomized treatments, exact tool-induced dollar cost is not identifiable, Claude Code arms are smaller, provider prices and cache behavior are time-specific, and several registered expansion arms remain incomplete. Baseline comparisons are internally strong for the causal question because they use the same tasks, models, and harnesses, although the work does not compare against a broad range of alternative agent controllers or stopping-policy algorithms. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a secondary systems-analysis component because it measures two executable agent harnesses but does not deliver a deployed controller. - Practical: The evaluated agents run through commercially available model-serving APIs and coding-agent CLIs; the paper’s bounded-efficiency prompt and telemetry methodology require no specialized hardware, although the evaluated models are expensive and include very large open-weight systems. - Efficient: The evidence shows substantial potential savings: multiple-approaches prompts increase reasoning 2.4–7.4×, high verification levels reach 18.25× median no-cache cost, and harness choice changes cost per success by 5–30×; exact savings from deploying the proposed bounded instruction are not reported as a standalone dollar reduction. - Effective: The method-level evidence supports avoiding measured waste while preserving diagnosis, edits, tests, validation, and success on the benchmark; it does not establish better correctness, maintainability, or production reliability beyond the tested proxy tasks. - Scalable: The study tests 24 small tasks and has not evaluated 10×–100× larger repositories, long-running validation, multi-agent workflows, or architectural changes; the authors explicitly state that new-task and long-validation expansion arms were still in progress. The work delivers a reusable benchmark, task fixtures, prompt corpus, raw ledgers, and analysis code, plus a practical prompt pattern, but not a general-purpose runtime controller, library, or automated stopping mechanism. Strengths: - The paired, semantically controlled design isolates instruction content from task objective, acceptance criteria, and test command more effectively than ordinary prompt-comparison studies. - The paper distinguishes two mechanisms with different observable cost carriers: discarded branches increase reasoning while leaving tool activity nearly flat, whereas redundant verification increases calls, latency, context growth, and cost together. - The frozen holdout, paraphrase tests, Kimi-K3 replication, and first-party Sonnet 5 study provide unusually strong evidence that the main effect is not confined to one model, one phrase, or one serving stack. - The instrumentation work is technically careful: it validates gateway function calling, captures both sides of a translation gateway, separates cached from no-cache cost, reconciles native billing, and explicitly attributes extreme permission-friction loops to the harness rather than the prompt. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that provider-exposed reasoning text is incomplete and may not be faithful; tasks are small and have high success ceilings; multiple approaches may be useful for repository-scale or architectural work; annotated mechanism levels are observational mediators; exact per-turn cost attribution is unavailable; Claude Code arms are smaller; prices and cache behavior are time-dependent; and new-task, long-validation, and other registered expansion arms remain incomplete. They also note missing per-call timing and local CPU, GPU, and memory telemetry, the unobservable timing of hidden-test success, heavy-tailed tool counts, and possible provider-side latency from undisclosed safety classifiers. The paper confronts these limitations directly and generally narrows its claims to observable behavior rather than hidden cognition. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central generalization claim remains narrow because all tasks involve at most four files, deterministic tests, explicit acceptance criteria, and high success rates; the paper does not yet show whether alternatives become beneficial on architectural, ambiguous, or repository-scale work. - The bounded-efficiency instruction is evaluated mainly as a prompt-level neutral control, not as a fully specified adaptive stopping policy with independent comparisons against tool guards, test deduplication, context compression, or cost-aware planners. - The harness comparison is confounded by substantial differences in system prompts, tool schemas, protocol translation, turn policy, and possibly model configuration; the measurements establish an operational cost gap but do not isolate which harness component causes each portion of the 5–30× difference. - The analysis reports no direct downstream measures of patch quality such as maintainability, regression resilience beyond hidden tests, reviewer preference, or behavior on unseen real-world repositories, so “no success gain” should not be read as “no quality gain” outside the benchmark. - The work is a time-sensitive August 2026 arXiv preprint and relies partly on vendor-controlled usage fields, prices, caching, and proprietary model behavior; independent replication across providers and stable production workloads remains necessary. Bottom Line: This is a strong and unusually well-instrumented empirical study that gives coding-agent researchers and operators a credible vocabulary and measurement protocol for prompt-induced waste, but its practical conclusions should remain limited to small deterministic tasks until the promised repository-scale and long-validation evaluations appear.

Problem & Motivation: Organizational analytics frequently requires finding and combining evidence distributed across CSV/JSON files, relational databases, long Markdown/PDF documents, and multimedia, sometimes with Chinese and English mixed across the question and artifacts. The relevant sources are not preselected, and the requested result may require schema and entity alignment, filtering, joins, aggregation, temporal reasoning, ranking, and complete table materialization. Prior benchmarks generally emphasize one of structured querying, retrieval and long-document understanding, multimodal question answering, or open-ended data analysis; they less often combine workspace discovery, heterogeneous evidence integration, cross-language inputs, document-to-record extraction, and deterministic evaluation of a complete table. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat a data-agent task as a workspace-solving problem with a fixed complete-table output contract, while constructing each heterogeneous workspace from an executable relational source whose answer semantics remain known. This enables the authors to introduce difficult representations—long documents, video-defined predicates, cross-language schemas, and distractor artifacts—without losing a deterministic gold answer. The contribution is therefore primarily a benchmark formulation and construction methodology rather than a new agent-learning algorithm. Methodology: DataSpace-Builder takes an English Text-to-SQL tuple consisting of a question, database, and executable SQL from EHRSQL or BULL. First, cross-language transformation jointly translates the question, database schema and values, and SQL, using table-, column-, and value-level replacement maps; linked fields are clustered through foreign keys, shared names, or value overlap, and the transformed SQL is parsed, executed, and checked against the translated source result. Second, constraint-aware relational sampling creates a task-local database by extracting predicate, boundary, target-entity, primary-key, foreign-key, and join safeguards from the SQL AST, retaining anchor rows, propagating relational closure, sampling remaining rows, materializing all schemas, and re-executing the query. Third, a seeded router renders tables as CSV, JSON, SQLite, Markdown, and/or PDF; document generation uses bounded fact-grounded blocks with repeated record anchors and cell-level validation; optional video generation extracts typed predicate or answer atoms from the SQL and candidate result, creates a storyboard, renders a video, and rewrites the question so the selected evidence is available only through the video. Fourth, two of 11 domain experts independently solve each candidate task blind, verify the gold result, author evaluation semantics, and trigger evidence-based repair and rechecking until consensus or removal. The evaluator canonicalizes text, dates, booleans, numeric units and precision, searches header-invariant one-to-one column alignments, and compares ordered row sequences or unordered row multisets. Critical design choices—execution-grounded construction, constraint-aware sampling, and expert review—are well motivated for preventing broken joins, corrupted artifacts, and ambiguous gold answers, but the paper does not isolate their individual effects experimentally. Key Results: DataSpace contains 410 tasks and 7,439 artifacts totaling 15.01 GB: 363 tasks originate from BULL and 47 from EHRSQL; 265 tasks (64.6%) are cross-language; domains include funds (158), stocks (120), macroeconomics (85), and healthcare (47). Workspaces span 25,384 PDF pages, 26.88 million Markdown characters, 189 videos totaling 5.49 hours, and reference answers totaling 126,409 rows; the largest answer has 12,962 rows and the widest has six columns. Required solution paths use multiple modalities in 134 tasks (32.7%), documents or video in 202 tasks (49.3%), joins in 113 tasks (27.6%), and a median of five nontrivial operation types per task. With the authors’ ReAct-style DataSpace-Agent fixed, Grok 4.5 reaches 66.34% (272/410), GPT-5.6 Sol 64.63% (265/410), Kimi K3 53.41%, MiMo-V2.5 39.27%, Claude Sonnet 5 32.93%, and MiniMax M3 28.54%; the best and worst differ by 37.80 percentage points. With MiMo-V2.5 fixed, harness accuracy ranges from 30.98% for Smolagents to 46.34% for Grok Build, a 15.36-point spread. GPT-5.6 Sol is 1.71 points below Grok 4.5 while using 74.2% fewer tokens, 50.3% fewer tool actions, and 39.2% less latency; reported mean API costs range from $0.011/task for MiMo-V2.5 to $0.235/task for Kimi K3. Multimodal tasks reduce accuracy for every backbone by 1.8–14.0 points, required joins reduce accuracy by 9.7–19.8 points, and 76 tasks are solved by none of the six backbones. In an audit of 136 Grok 4.5 failures, 71 (52.2%) are attributed to materialization, including 60 cases with missing or extra columns; 77 failures (56.6%) combine output-schema misunderstanding or faulty column projection. These comparisons are descriptive, not causal, and the paper does not report confidence intervals or significance tests. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW PROBLEM, NEW FORMULATION, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an engineering component in the benchmark-construction pipeline. The genuinely distinctive element is the unified task contract—agent-visible heterogeneous workspace, autonomous evidence discovery, complete tabular output, and deterministic semantics-aware scoring—rather than a new reasoning model; the construction uses standard Text-to-SQL sources, LLM translation and generation, relational sampling, ReAct, and multimodal rendering in a new benchmark setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The benchmark construction has several strong safeguards: deterministic decoding and replacement maps for transformations, SQL execution and round-trip renderer checks, SQL-AST-based sampling safeguards, typed document/video validation, two independent blind expert reviews, versioned repairs, and a deterministic evaluator that does not use an LLM judge at test time. The authors provide the code, evaluator, baseline implementations, configurations, documentation, and task inputs at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DataSpace, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HKUSTDial/DataSpace; both are stated to use the MIT License. All 410 task inputs are released, but reference answers and evaluation configurations are available locally for only 60 representative tasks, while 350 are withheld for official evaluation. No multiple-seed model runs, error bars, significance tests, or ablations of the construction stages are reported. The backbone comparison controls the agent harness, and the harness comparison controls MiMo-V2.5, but provider-default reasoning settings, proprietary model endpoints, and native harness differences limit reproducibility and causal interpretation. The benchmark is derived largely from BULL (88.5%) and uses LLM-generated translations, documents, and videos whose quality is filtered by automated checks and expert review; this creates potential distributional and construction-model biases that are not fully quantified. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper primarily reports benchmark construction and experiments running multiple agent systems, although it also releases a usable benchmark and evaluator. * Practical: The evaluated agents run on commercially accessible CPU resources for local file processing—4 CPUs and 16 GiB memory in the controlled comparison—but inference depends on external model APIs and multimodal tooling, so deployment requires provider access and handling of potentially sensitive workspace data. * Efficient: Resource use varies substantially: GPT-5.6 Sol averages 77.8K tokens, 9.0 actions, and 49.2 seconds per task versus Grok 4.5 at 301.9K tokens, 18.1 actions, and 80.9 seconds; reported costs range from $0.011 to $0.235 per task, but these are provider prices rather than end-to-end infrastructure costs. * Effective: The evidence shows that current agents solve only 28.54–66.34% of the benchmark under exact complete-table scoring, with consistent degradation on multimodal and join-heavy tasks; this demonstrates a substantial reliability gap on the benchmark but does not establish performance on real organizational workspaces. * Scalable: The benchmark includes workspaces up to 74.18 MB at the 90th percentile, 36 PDF pages per PDF at the 90th percentile, videos up to 158.3 seconds, and answers up to 12,962 rows, but it does not test 10×–100× larger workspaces, longer videos, larger databases, or sustained production throughput. The work delivers a reusable dataset, evaluator, baseline agent, construction code, configurations, and documentation. It does not deliver a generally deployable production data-agent system or trained model; its principal artifact is the benchmark and its supporting generation and validation infrastructure. Strengths: - The benchmark fixes a meaningful and operationally precise output contract: a complete typed table, with missing or extra rows and columns counted as incorrect, while allowing equivalent column order, numeric formats, dates, booleans, and unordered row representations where appropriate. - DataSpace-Builder addresses several difficult dataset-construction failure modes explicitly. Joint translation preserves equality and join semantics; SQL-derived safeguards prevent sampling from deleting required predicates or join paths; renderer round trips and cell-level validation reduce artifact corruption. - The benchmark exposes failure modes that aggregate accuracy alone would hide. The oracle union of six backbones solves 334 tasks (81.46%), while 76 are solved by none; the trace audit shows that exact output materialization, rather than only evidence retrieval or arithmetic, is a major bottleneck. - The release is unusually useful for replication: it includes the full task inputs, official evaluator, construction code, baseline configurations, traces and validated predictions according to the paper, and local references for 60 tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly states that stratified performance analyses are descriptive rather than causal. It acknowledges that specialized systems such as DeepAnalyze and AgenticData cannot be included faithfully because of incompatible interfaces or unavailable implementations, and that the controlled experiments use a lightweight ReAct agent rather than task-specialized source selection or reasoning components. It also distinguishes the public 60-task local-evaluation subset from the 350 tasks whose references are withheld for official evaluation. The paper does not present a consolidated limitations section or quantify the impact of these scope boundaries on conclusions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The benchmark is mostly inherited from two English Text-to-SQL datasets, with 363/410 tasks from BULL and 47/410 from EHRSQL; the resulting domain, schema, query, and difficulty distribution may not represent general enterprise analytics, despite the heterogeneous presentation layer. - The paper does not compare against the strongest compatible specialized data-agent systems, human analysts, oracle artifact selection, modality-specific pipelines, or retrieval/SQL baselines, so it is difficult to separate workspace-discovery difficulty from multimodal reasoning and output-formatting difficulty. - There are no ablations for cross-language transformation, document rendering, video augmentation, distractor artifacts, relational sampling, expert repair, or evaluator semantics. The claim that multimodal integration and joins cause degradation is descriptive and may be confounded by task complexity, workspace size, answer size, or domain composition. - Construction uses LLM-generated translations, documents, videos, and an LLM-based question–SQL semantic judge. Although 11 experts review accepted tasks, the paper does not report rejection rates, repair counts, inter-reviewer agreement before adjudication, reviewer identities or expertise distribution, or error rates of the construction models. - The reported model results rely on newly released and partly proprietary endpoints accessed through provider defaults in July 2026. The paper does not report repeated runs across stochastic configurations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, and native harness differences make the 15.36-point harness spread difficult to attribute to specific design choices. - Binary whole-task accuracy gives no partial credit and may overemphasize output serialization relative to analytical correctness; the failure audit shows that 56.6% of audited failures involve output-schema or projection problems, but the paper does not report complementary metrics such as cell, row, column, or intermediate-query accuracy. - The dataset contains financial and healthcare-derived source domains, yet the paper does not provide a detailed leakage, memorization, privacy, or contamination analysis for models and construction resources. Bottom Line: DataSpace is a useful and technically careful benchmark release that raises the evaluation bar for heterogeneous data agents, but its strongest contribution is benchmark engineering and empirical diagnosis rather than a new agent method, and its conclusions should be treated as benchmark-specific until validated on independently collected real-world workspaces.

Problem & Motivation Agentic applications in coding, research, question answering, and customer service generate dynamic execution graphs containing dependent and parallel LLM calls interleaved with tool calls. Because LLM decoding is nondeterministic, identical user requests can produce substantially different call counts, token lengths, dependency structures, and queueing behavior. In the paper's mini-SWE-agent example, two runs with the same requests and fixed random seed differ by an average of 12.9 LLM calls per request, corresponding to 76% of the average call count; one run has 65% more cumulative queuing delay, 25% higher mean end-to-end latency, and 30% higher P95 latency. Existing agent evaluation harnesses emphasize task success and lack load generation and serving metrics, while conventional LLM-serving benchmarks use independent or conversational calls rather than interdependent agent workloads. AA-AgentPerf is described as using proprietary coding traces and providing a closed ranking service. The resulting gap is reproducible, configurable, application-diverse benchmarking of the LLM-serving layer under realistic agent execution patterns. Key Idea The central insight is to treat a recorded agent request as a dependency-preserving execution DAG rather than as a fixed timestamped sequence of calls. XPerf separates workload structure from the nondeterministic behavior that originally generated it: it records the exact input/output token sequences, infers causal ordering from nested time spans, and replays the same graph under new serving systems and arrival patterns. This makes system comparisons more controlled while preserving agent-specific parallelism, sequential dependencies, prompt prefixes, and tool-induced delays. Methodology XPerf has four main stages. First, its tracing module instruments LLM APIs through library interposition and traces tool calls through LangChain/LangGraph interposition or single-line annotations for custom Python applications. OpenTelemetry records request identity, parent spans, start/end times, and for LLM calls the input and output token IDs. Second, it constructs a time-span tree and recursively converts each request into a DAG. Leaf spans are LLM or tool calls; sibling spans are ordered when one completes before the other starts; transitive reduction removes redundant edges; graph boundaries are connected through sink/source nodes. The authors report construction time below 200 ms for traces containing at most 1,000 calls per request on one CPU thread. Third, the workload synthesizer replays graphs at recorded arrival times or generates Poisson online traffic, offline batches, fixed-concurrency workloads, or user-defined arrival schedules. Tool calls are replayed as sleeps for recorded durations, with duration optionally configured. Fourth, the replayer asynchronously executes DAG nodes when predecessors finish. It sends recorded input token IDs to preserve prefix-cache behavior and either decodes to the recorded output length or forces the exact recorded output sequence; the latter requires modifications to vLLM and supports effects such as mixture-of-experts routing and sparse attention. A profiler samples serving metrics through HTTP endpoints at 1-second intervals and GPU metrics through CUPTI at 20-ms intervals, including running/queued calls, KV-cache use, prefix-cache hit rate, token throughput, tensor-core utilization, SM utilization, and memory-bandwidth utilization. Important design decisions are technically appropriate but incompletely validated: time-span hierarchy reduces false dependencies in parallel workflows, exact token replay improves determinism but may not represent a fresh model execution, and treating tool duration as load-independent isolates serving performance but excludes host-side feedback effects. Key Results The evaluation uses eight applications—Open Deep Research, DeerFlow, mini-SWE-agent, LATS, LLMCompiler, Tau-Bench, CUGA, and MagenticOne—covering deep research, coding, Q&A, and general assistance. Per-request LLM-call averages range from 2.4 for LLMCompiler to 69.6 for Open Deep Research, with P95 counts up to 143.8. The primary testbed uses gpt-oss-120b and vLLM v0.19.0 on H100 NVL GPUs; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is used for some workload and scale-out experiments. Replayed isolated-request end-to-end latency has mean absolute percentage error below 3% for all eight applications; 4.6% of Open Deep Research individual calls exceed 3% relative error, but this does not materially affect end-to-end replay. In a two-hour concurrent replay, mean absolute errors in running and queued LLM-call counts are 1.4 and 1.6, cumulative queuing-time error is 2.9%, and request-latency MAPE is 1.9%. Across workloads, decoding contributes 60%–98% of end-to-end latency under unsaturated load; prefill is below 23% for DeerFlow and averages 4% for the other applications, while queueing reaches 69% under the heaviest tested loads. P95 latency can reach 6.60 times P50, mainly when agents fail to converge and continue issuing calls. Prefix-cache hit rates range from 41% to 91% at low load for most applications, but mini-SWE-agent falls from 91% to below 4% under pressure; DeerFlow remains below 1% because a timestamp invalidates its prompt prefix, and removing it raises the low-load hit rate to about 30%. In mini-SWE-agent, increasing request rate from 3.38 to 4.5 requests/minute increases running calls by 83% but output-token throughput by only 11%, while input-token throughput drops by up to 12%. Offline mini-SWE-agent throughput decreases 38% as requests grow from 25 to 200, whereas DeerFlow throughput increases 35% from 10 to 80 requests. Under fixed concurrency, mini-SWE-agent throughput decreases 35% from 10 to 50 concurrent requests, while DeerFlow throughput rises from 0.64 to 0.95 requests/minute from 4 to 36 concurrent requests. In a four-engine Qwen3.6-35B-A3B deployment, round-robin routing reaches only 2.26x single-engine output-token throughput, compared with 3.61x for cache-aware routing; at two engines the corresponding gains are 1.41x and 1.88x. The scheduling case study finds request-level FCFS comparable to or less than 8% better than call-level FCFS on matched traces, while mismatched traces could falsely suggest a 12% benefit. These are useful empirical observations, but the baselines are primarily vLLM policies and the paper does not present a head-to-head quantitative evaluation against alternative serving systems or benchmark frameworks. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The main novelty is an integrated trace-to-DAG-to-replay pipeline for reproducible agentic serving benchmarks, including token-level replay and full-stack profiling; the individual components—distributed tracing, DAG scheduling, configurable arrival processes, and GPU monitoring—are established techniques, while the empirical findings on prefix-cache thrashing, routing locality, and run-to-run variance are new measurements in this benchmark setting rather than a new serving algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides an algorithm for graph construction and reports replay accuracy, graph-construction cost, tracing overhead, profiler overhead, multiple workload types, eight applications, two models, and one- to four-engine deployments. It does not report error bars, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or a systematic multi-seed study beyond comparing several traces in the scheduling case study. Ablations are limited: the paper shows the effect of removing DeerFlow's timestamp on prefix-cache hit rate and contrasts routing/scheduling policies, but it does not isolate all tracing, graph-construction, token-replay, and profiling components. The authors state that XPerf will be open-sourced on GitHub, but no repository URL or evidence of an available release appears in the provided text. The implementation depends on modified vLLM for output-token enforcement and CPU prefix caching. Evaluation is concentrated on vLLM, H100 hardware, two model families, and the authors' eight instrumented applications, so portability claims to other engines, accelerators, APIs, and agent frameworks remain only partly demonstrated. Exact token replay also evaluates a controlled workload rather than the serving system's behavior under independently sampled outputs, and the treatment of tool calls as fixed-duration sleeps omits host-side contention and argument-dependent behavior. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper delivers and evaluates a built benchmarking and profiling framework rather than only proposing a conceptual methodology. Practical: XPerf runs on commercially available Python/OpenTelemetry infrastructure and NVIDIA GPUs, but integration is frictionless only for selected frameworks; custom applications require annotations, and exact output-token replay requires serving-engine changes. Efficient: Reported overhead is low—0.1% added end-to-end latency during tracing, less than 0.1% replay profiling interference, 16 KB/s PCIe traffic for GPU monitoring, and less than 5% of one CPU core for the trace backend—but trace storage is substantial at 4.6 MB per request on average and up to 27.46 MB for DeerFlow traces. Effective: The evidence shows that XPerf reproduces serving-system timing and exposes actionable causes such as prefix-cache thrashing, queue growth, and routing-locality loss; it does not show that using XPerf itself improves production latency or throughput. Scalable: XPerf scales from single-engine to four-engine experiments across two servers and uses streaming buffers so memory depends on concurrent rather than total requests, but the paper does not test 10x–100x larger deployments, longer traces, higher request rates, more diverse accelerators, or trace-storage/collection behavior at production fleet scale. The work delivers a software artifact consisting of tracing, graph construction, workload synthesis, replay, profiling modules, eight containerized applications, and a prototype vLLM integration; the promised public repository is not identified in the supplied paper text. Strengths - It identifies and quantifies a real evaluation pathology: agentic nondeterminism can change call counts and queueing enough to reverse or inflate conclusions about serving optimizations. - The time-span-tree-to-DAG construction is a concrete mechanism for preserving parallelism and dependencies while allowing replay on hardware with different execution speeds; the paper explicitly explains how it avoids false cross-task dependencies. - The framework combines workload control with cross-layer observability, linking request latency to queueing, KV-cache occupancy, prefix-cache hits, token throughput, and GPU utilization rather than reporting only aggregate latency. - The evaluation produces non-obvious systems findings: adding concurrency can reduce throughput through prefix-cache thrashing, tensor-core utilization can rise while memory-bandwidth utilization falls because of wasted recomputation, and cache-aware routing is essential for multi-engine scale-out. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly scope XPerf to the LLM-serving layer and exclude the application host, control logic, and tool execution environments. They acknowledge that tool interfaces and environments vary and that faithfully replaying host behavior is a separate problem. They also state that tool-call arguments are not currently captured and identify serializable RPC and shell-command arguments as future extensions. This is a direct and credible scope statement, but it means the current artifact cannot reproduce argument-dependent tool behavior or support faithful host-side benchmarking. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not quantitatively compare XPerf with AA-AgentPerf or other available agent-serving benchmarks under the same workloads, so its practical advantage over alternatives is inferred from feature comparisons rather than measured. - The evaluation is dominated by a single serving engine, vLLM, and uses modified engine code; claims of serving-system portability are therefore not established across SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, Triton, or commercial APIs. - The replay protocol can force recorded output tokens, which guarantees determinism but may hide serving-engine behaviors that depend on newly sampled outputs, dynamic stopping, speculative-decoding variation, or model-specific control flow. - The graph-inference algorithm assumes that temporal ordering within traced orchestration spans reliably represents causal dependencies; the paper does not evaluate incorrect or incomplete instrumentation, clock skew, asynchronous callbacks, retries, cancellations, streaming calls, or calls whose dependency is data-based but not reflected by span nesting. - No trace-level sample counts, workload split details, seed distributions, confidence intervals, or repeated-run variance for the reported application results are provided, limiting confidence in the precision of several headline percentages. - The workload suite is diverse in application type but narrow in infrastructure and hardware scale, and the paper does not assess trace privacy, token-sensitive logging, storage cost at fleet scale, or the effect of trace collection on distributed deployments. Bottom Line XPerf is a useful and technically credible benchmarking tool whose reproducible agent-DAG replay and cross-layer profiling fill a genuine gap, but its research impact would be stronger with public artifact evidence, broader engine/hardware validation, statistical rigor, and direct comparison against competing agent-serving benchmarks.

#6 — Highly Innovative (81)

Agentic Commerce World: An Auditable and Verifiable Environment for Vibe Commerce

S Fan, M Yang, D Wang, C Chen, Y Zhang, H Wei, M Li… · arxiv.org · Julian McAuley - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Agentic Commerce World (ACWORLD), a persistent two-sided commerce environment, Vibe Commerce Protocol (VCP), and deterministic benchmark for evaluating independently controlled Buyer and Merchant agents. - Why it's important: Agentic transactions require more than a successful final purchase: evaluators must determine which agent made each decision, whether it was authorized, what evidence supported it, and what state change followed. - How it does it: ACWORLD separates model proposals from state-changing authority through VCP binding, platform validation, atomic World commits, execution traces, and predicate-based rescoring. - The good: Across 2,000 capability-coverage runs, 99 incomplete runs (11.5%) shared the final World state of a full-credit run, while full lineage eliminated these collisions and enabled deterministic attribution. - The missing: The benchmark uses fixed counterparties, deterministic task worlds, public tasks, and a static catalog; it does not evaluate open-market strategy, live commerce, policy learning from process rewards, or production security. - Read it or not: Researchers building agent benchmarks, tool-use environments, or verifiable process evaluation should read it for its evaluation-boundary design; readers seeking evidence about real-world agentic-commerce performance can defer because external validity is limited.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (84) are strong because the proposal-to-authority-to-effect separation and lineage-based rescoring provide a distinctive formulation for auditable multi-agent transactions. Rigor (78) is supported by deterministic execution, reconstruction tests, mutation suites, integrity checks, extensive task coverage, and released code, though the lack of seeds, uncertainty estimates, external benchmark comparisons, and semantic validation prevents a higher score. Completeness (84) is particularly strong because the authors directly acknowledge fixed counterparties, public tasks, limited security evidence, and weak external validity; Resilience (76) remains lower because the taxonomy, weights, and controlled market assumptions are not independently validated. Impact (88) reflects a substantial released benchmark and environment artifact, although production commerce applicability is not demonstrated. Weighted composite: 0.20*82 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*84 + 0.15*84 + 0.15*76 + 0.10*88 = 81.3, rounded to 81.
