Problem & Motivation The work addresses evaluation of autonomous commerce in which independently controlled Buyer and Merchant agents pursue private mandates, negotiate with one another, and alter shared transaction state. Existing commerce protocols such as ACP, UCP, and AP2 coordinate deployment workflows, while shopping and market benchmarks generally fix the counterparty, website, or market dynamics. This leaves a gap in attributing a transaction outcome to each actor's decision, authorization status, supporting evidence, and downstream effects in a persistent many-to-many market. The paper targets researchers evaluating negotiation, product discovery, grounding, fulfillment, governance, adversarial robustness, and transaction integrity rather than operators measuring deployed commerce success. Key Idea The core insight is to make the authority to change shared state separate from the agent's proposed business decision. VCP binds each typed action to an authenticated Buyer or Merchant, the Commerce Intelligence Platform validates it against actor, protocol, policy, and World state, and only the World commits authorized effects. The resulting lineage connects actor decision, validation, execution evidence, and state delta. This allows an evaluator to distinguish a commercially poor but authorized action from an invalid action, reconstruct state without rerunning the model, and rescore intermediate process predicates rather than observing only the terminal transaction. Methodology ACWORLD presents each evaluated policy with a role-specific private mandate, scoped market observations, messages, and typed business tools. The policy emits a business decision such as search, offer, counteroffer, accept, reject, fulfillment, refund, or abstention. VCP authenticates and structures the proposal, including actor identity, counterparties, negotiation identifiers, reply links, rounds, and public payloads. The Commerce Intelligence Platform applies applicable rules and either rejects the proposal or emits an accepted validation. The World then applies the deterministic transition W_{j+1}=F(W_j,u_j) through an atomic commit, updating inventory, payment, order, fulfillment, and trust records. Ordered commits and event digests support reconstruction from the initial state; the stored lineage L_t=(a_t,d_t,v_t,E_t,Delta W_t) supports rescoring without another model call. The benchmark has a 200-task capability-coverage track with 10 families and 80 capabilities, and a 60-task large-catalog track over 785,022 transactable listings. Scores aggregate Boolean or fractional predicates as S=sum_i w_i c_i / sum_i w_i, with predicates checking decisions, evidence, validation, World effects, and transaction outcomes. Critical design decisions are the separation of proposal from authority, deterministic evidence-linked scoring without an LLM judge, and fixed counterparty policies. The paper justifies these decisions through reconstruction tests, targeted mutations, transport-parity checks, and restricted-view collision analyses, but does not establish that its policy taxonomy or predicate weights reflect real-world prevalence or utility. Key Results The capability-coverage track evaluates 10 models on 200 tasks each, producing 2,000 runs. Mean scores range from 65.9% to 85.6%; GPT-5.6 Sol leads overall at 85.6%, followed by Gemini 3.6 Flash at 85.0% and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 83.7%. The track produces 1,139 full-credit, 757 partial-credit, and 104 zero-credit runs. Inventory and Lifecycle are the strongest averaged families at 93.3% and 90.3%, while Timing and Discovery are weakest at 40.3% and 65.9%. Among 861 runs without full credit, 314 have Evidence as the dominant lost-credit source, 159 Choice, 208 Execution, 122 Authority, and 58 an exact tie. The large-catalog track evaluates 600 runs over 60 tasks and 785,022 listings. Mean scores range from 56.10% to 91.36%; Gemini 3.5 Flash scores 91.36%, Gemini 3.6 Flash 91.35%, and GPT-5.6 Sol 89.11%. It yields 365 full-credit, 206 partial-credit, and 29 zero-credit runs. Mean stage scores across models are 76.11% for Search, 86.75% for Evidence, 73.67% for Decision, and 94.17% for Validation, indicating that finding and selecting globally appropriate listings are harder than producing well-formed authorized actions. In the restricted-view analysis, 99 of 861 incomplete capability-track runs (11.5%) collide with an accepted full-credit run under final World state, 54 (6.3%) under the final VCP action, and 45 (5.2%) under the public VCP action sequence; the full trace has zero collisions by construction. A 95-case injected-mutation suite detects 78 errors from final state, 83 from final action, 92 from action trace, and 95 from full lineage. Incomplete runs retain at least one positive predicate signal in 757 cases (87.9%) and pass 1.88 of 3.49 predicates on average, but the paper does not measure whether these signals improve training. A fixed 5x5 multiagent study settles five trades at 97.8% of global optimum, but the authors correctly state that one market, model family, and seed cannot support strategic comparisons. The auxiliary World-only probe reaches 1,000 Buyers, 1,000 Merchants, 5,000 materialized candidate edges, and 1,000 sequential settlements, excluding model inference, concurrency, contention, VCP routing, and platform mechanisms. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW BENCHMARK, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the main contribution is a research environment that formalizes bilateral agent authority, persistent state, reconstruction, and evidence-linked scoring in one contract; the benchmark combines known ideas from tool-use environments, transaction simulators, typed protocols, and deterministic evaluation, while the restricted-view collision measurements provide a new empirical demonstration of why terminal-state evaluation can be insufficient in this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides a substantial validation suite: all 2,000 capability-track traces reconstruct and rescore consistently; all 60 large-catalog reference tasks receive full credit; 95 capability mutations and 374 large-catalog mutations lower intended predicates; 18 HTTP parity episodes are reported; all 60 large-catalog traces rescore identically; and ten integrity cases covering rollback, retry, authority, stale events, tampering, and reopening pass. Equalizing predicate weights changes model means by at most 1.7 percentage points and preserves ordering. The evaluation uses deterministic programmatic predicates rather than an LLM judge, and the repository is stated as https://github.com/shichengf/ACWorld. The paper does not report multiple model-inference seeds, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or controlled comparisons against alternative benchmarks/scoring schemes. Models use provider-default decoding and a 240-second timeout, which reduces experimental control. The task catalog and many tasks are public, enabling direct optimization or memorization; the authors acknowledge the need for held-out tasks. Mutation sensitivity validates implementation and oracle behavior, not semantic correctness of the task definitions, data provenance, or the claimed real-world importance of each capability. Several comparisons in Table 1 are categorical and author-defined, with no independent protocol audit. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a released systems artifact rather than a deployment evaluation. Practical: The environment uses SQLite, typed interfaces, and commercially available compute, and the reported catalog build uses 177 MB peak memory, but model-serving and full-system deployment requirements are not quantified. Efficient: The large-catalog database is 1.94 GB, builds in 33.88 seconds, and indexed queries take 0.52 ms median and 1.15 ms at p95 on the test machine; end-to-end cost, model latency, concurrent throughput, and comparison with production commerce infrastructure are not evaluated. Effective: The evidence shows reliable deterministic execution, reconstruction, and diagnostic scoring under the declared synthetic/controlled contract, but does not show improved agent behavior, better policy learning, higher transaction welfare across varied strategies, or safer deployed commerce. Scalable: A World-only sequential probe reaches 1,000-by-1,000 populations with 5,000 candidate edges, but excludes inference, concurrency, contention, VCP routing, and platform validation; therefore 10x-100x scalability of the complete environment remains untested. The work delivers a public environment, benchmark, skill manifests, typed tools, catalog database construction, scoring and reconstruction machinery through the repository; it does not deliver a production payment or security system, and its claimed verifiability means reproducibility under the declared contract rather than proof of semantic correctness or production security. Strengths - The proposal-to-authority-to-effect separation gives a clear evaluation boundary and prevents agent text or malformed requests from directly mutating shared commerce state. - The lineage representation and deterministic reconstruction make partial credit and failure attribution substantially more informative than terminal transaction success, with concrete collision rates and mutation evidence rather than only architectural claims. - The benchmark covers both breadth and catalog scale: 200 tasks across 10 families and 80 capabilities, plus 60 tasks over 785,022 listings, using a common execution and scoring path. - The authors explicitly separate infrastructure validity, authorization, commercial quality, and World consequences, and they avoid presenting the small multiagent study or component-scale probe as evidence of open-market strategy or full-system throughput. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that each task evaluates one policy against deterministic counterparties and that neither the model scores nor the fixed 5x5 study measure open-market strategy. They acknowledge that the catalogs lack independent audit, are not representative samples of deployed commerce, and do not model live inventory or demand. They state that reconstruction verifies consistency under the declared transition and scorer, not independent semantic correctness; ten integrity cases do not constitute a security proof; and public tasks may invite direct optimization or memorization. They also acknowledge that process signals are only candidate rewards because their utility for policy learning is not evaluated, and that the ten-model results characterize the benchmark tracks rather than provide a general model ranking. These limitations are confronted directly in the discussion and generally constrain, rather than inflate, the claims. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central scoring rubric, capability taxonomy, task distribution, and predicate weights are authored by the benchmark creators; practitioner review by four individuals improves plausibility but does not establish inter-rater reliability, external validity, or independence from benchmark design. - There is no external baseline environment evaluated under the same models, so the paper does not show whether ACWORLD produces more reliable conclusions or better diagnostic resolution than existing shopping, negotiation, or stateful tool-use benchmarks. - The fixed counterparty policy and deterministic market remove strategic adaptation, repeated-game effects, collusion dynamics, adversarial counterparties, and equilibrium behavior, despite the paper's two-sided-market framing. - The benchmark relies on public product snapshots and deterministic completion rules for missing fields; no sensitivity analysis examines how synthetic inventory, delivery, review, preference, or transaction assumptions affect model rankings. - Default provider decoding, absent seeds and error bars, and potentially changing pre-release model APIs weaken the statistical and temporal comparability of the ten-model panel. - The paper demonstrates that traces can support candidate process rewards but does not test training, fine-tuning, reranking, or evaluator-guided improvement using those rewards, leaving a major practical motivation unevaluated. - The security boundary is tested only against a small finite suite; there is no threat model, adversarial red-team study, cryptographic authentication analysis, concurrency stress test, or proof that private mandates cannot leak through all available interfaces. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically disciplined benchmark/environment paper for researchers studying auditable agent execution and process-level evaluation, but its contribution is primarily infrastructure and measurement methodology rather than evidence that autonomous commerce works in open or production markets.

#7 — Highly Innovative (81)

Relevant but Incomplete: Referential Dangling as a Paradigm-Level Failure Mode in Hard Prompt Compression (8 ▲ )

Zhengpei Hu, Kai Li, Dapeng Fu, Xuechao Zou, Yuanhao Tang, Yue Li, Tengfei Cao, Jianqiang Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the referential-dangling failure mode for extractive hard prompt compression, measures its prevalence across compressors and QA datasets, and evaluates fixed-budget and automatic restoration strategies. - Why it's important: A compressor can preserve an answer string or relevant-looking sentence while deleting the definition or bridge fact needed to derive or interpret the answer, causing downstream reasoning failures despite meeting the token budget. - How it does it: It diagnoses broken dependency pairs using content-word coverage, replaces omitted supporting paragraphs under a fixed budget, and trains a BERT sentence-pair classifier to restore omitted sentences. - The good: At a 0.30 compression ratio, six compressors exhibit dangling rates of 32.1%–59.8% on a shared HotpotQA set, and oracle-like fixed-budget reselection improves Qwen3-8B accuracy by 28.8–34.3 percentage points on affected examples. - The missing: The central dangling metric is an annotation- and overlap-based proxy rather than an exact measurement of referential completeness, and the automatic restoration advantage over random insertion is not statistically significant at the reported sample size. - Read it or not: Researchers working on prompt compression, extractive summarization, retrieval, or long-context QA should read it for the failure-mode diagnosis; practitioners seeking a deployable compressor should treat the restoration method as preliminary because transfer beyond Beaver and HotpotQA remains unresolved.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (84) and Non-Obviousness (82) are high because the paper introduces a clear dependency-completeness failure mode and formalizes why additive selection can preserve answers while destroying inference paths. Rigor (84) is strong, supported by multiple datasets, six compressors, downstream models, statistical tests, robustness checks, manual auditing, and released code, while Completeness (82) benefits from explicit acknowledgment that the operational metric is only a proxy. Resilience (78) is good but limited by incomplete support annotations, small cross-compressor comparisons, oracle reselection, and the nonsignificant advantage over random insertion for the automatic remedy. Impact (70) reflects a released diagnostic and model rather than a mature, compressor-agnostic production system. Weighted composite: 0.20*84 + 0.25*84 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*70 = 81.1, rounded to 81.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Hard prompt compression reduces long-context inference cost by independently ranking and retaining tokens, sentences, chunks, or parse fragments under a budget. The paper argues that relevance or salience is insufficient when retained text depends on an antecedent, entity definition, or multi-hop bridge fact that is independently deleted. The affected domain is long-context question answering, especially multi-hop QA and document understanding, where evidence is distributed across paragraphs or sections. The gap in prior work is the lack of an explicit objective or evaluation criterion for preserving the joint interpretability of retained fragments; the paper distinguishes this from ordinary relevance preservation, source-level coreference resolution, and faithfulness of generated summaries. Key Idea: The core insight is that hard selection should preserve dependency-complete evidence units rather than score evidence fragments independently. A retained sentence can be relevant and even contain the answer string while remaining unusable because the context no longer contains any sufficient support path for interpreting it or connecting it to the query. The paper formalizes this as referential dangling and shows constructively that an additive modular knapsack objective provides no guarantee of dependency completeness even when a complete selection fits the same budget. Methodology: The formal analysis models a context C, query Q, token budget, retained source positions, task-relevant sentences, and the family of inclusion-minimal sufficient support sets for each relevant sentence. A compressed context dangles when it retains a relevant sentence but no sufficient support set. For additive fragment selection, utilities are summed under a cost constraint; Proposition 1 demonstrates that selecting the two highest-utility fragments can omit the sole support fragment despite a complete alternative having equal cost. Empirically, the authors first run the official Beaver compressor, which segments documents into 64-token pages, scores pages using query similarity from Qwen3-0.6B embeddings, and selects pages to a target ratio. They evaluate HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue using a directional content-word coverage predicate at threshold 0.5, paired answer/definition units, annotated evidence retention, a manual audit, and a separate first-mention diagnostic on 80 LongBench-v2 Single-Document QA documents. They then compare Beaver, PartPrompt, Selective-Context, LLMLingua-2, DAC, and LongLLMLingua at ratio 0.30. For causal impact, they perform annotation-guided reselection: reinsert an omitted supporting paragraph and remove at least as many tokens from non-supporting paragraphs, comparing against the original compressed context and a full-support reference. Finally, they train a roughly 110M-parameter bert-base-uncased binary classifier on retained sentence, candidate sentence, and question pairs. Positive pairs are omitted annotated-support sentences sharing an entity; hard negatives share an entity without satisfying the positive rule; easy negatives share no entity. The classifier ranks candidates from omitted text, and the top three are inserted at inference. The dependency formalization is clear, but the main measurement is only an approximation because it does not enumerate alternative support paths. The annotation-guided reselection is useful for isolating content choice but relies on oracle support annotations and is not itself a deployable compressor. The automatic pipeline is reproducibly specified, but candidate generation, compressor-specific integration, and the choice K=3 are only partially justified. Key Results: With Beaver at compression ratio 0.30, answer-path dangling occurs in 34.2% of HotpotQA bridge examples, 53.5% of 2WikiMultiHopQA examples, and 54.2% of MuSiQue examples; complete annotated-evidence retention is 61.0%, 30.7%, and 27.0%, respectively. A 40-example manual audit confirms the omitted paragraph was required in 38 cases, giving 95% precision for the diagnostic. On a shared 184-example HotpotQA set, dangling rates are 32.1% for Beaver, 47.8% for PartPrompt, 51.6% for Selective-Context, 56.0% for LLMLingua-2, 58.7% for DAC, and 59.8% for LongLLMLingua. The Beaver rate rises from 6.3% at ratio 0.70 to 53.5% at ratio 0.20 on a broader HotpotQA sample. On LongBench-v2, all 80 documents contain at least one first-mention dangling reference, with a macro-averaged per-document rate of 30.5%. On dangling subsets evaluated with Qwen3-8B, fixed-budget reselection raises accuracy from 28.7% to 57.5% on HotpotQA, 9.7% to 40.3% on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and 14.7% to 49.0% on MuSiQue; the gains are 28.8–34.3 points with McNemar p-values between 3.1 × 10^-8 and 1.6 × 10^-6. Full support improves Qwen3-8B accuracy by 8.0 points on a separate 200-example HotpotQA set, with comparable gains for Qwen3-4B (+8.5), Llama-3.1-8B (+8.5), and Mistral-7B (+9.0). Full support improves GPT-5.5 by 8.8 points on MuSiQue and GLM-5.2 by 24.2 points, while GPT-5.5 shows no aggregate change on HotpotQA. Automatic restoration with three candidates improves Qwen3-8B from 56.7% to 61.3% on 300 HotpotQA examples (+4.7 points, p=0.022) and Mistral-7B by 6.5 points; the Llama-3.1-8B gain is 1.3 points and not significant. Random insertion of the same number of sentences gives +2.0 points versus +4.7 for targeted restoration, but the direct contrast is not significant (p=0.15). Transfer to PartPrompt, Selective-Context, and LLMLingua-2 yields +3.2, +1.0, and +1.0 points, none significant. These results support a substantial diagnostic failure and the value of oracle content replacement, but they do not yet establish a robust, compressor-agnostic restoration system. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and a preliminary ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new contribution is the explicit referential-dangling framing and formal dependency-completeness criterion for hard prompt compression, while the restoration classifier combines standard sentence-pair BERT classification and extractive reinsertion with an existing compression pipeline. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports multiple datasets, six compressor implementations, several downstream models, bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for diagnostic rates, McNemar tests for paired accuracy comparisons, Holm correction for a subset of comparisons, threshold and compression-ratio sweeps, a manual audit, salience analysis, and matched random-addition controls. The diagnostic is robust to replacing Qwen3-0.6B embeddings with GPT-2, with at most a 0.9-point change, and remains substantial across overlap thresholds from 0.3 to 0.7. Training/evaluation example IDs are separated for the restoration classifier, and the authors state that source contexts are disjoint between classifier development and downstream evaluation. Code, individual-example results, and the trained model are released at https://cslikai.cn/Referential-Dangling/; cited repositories include github.com/JusperLee/BEAVER and https://github.com/microsoft/LLMLingua. Important concerns remain: the main dangling measure uses directional content-word overlap rather than the exact formal definition; the bridge and LongBench diagnostics depend on incomplete annotations or heuristic first mentions; the fixed-budget reselection uses answer-support annotations unavailable at inference; the downstream model evaluation uses relatively small subsets; and automatic restoration is tuned around Beaver outputs and HotpotQA. The use of GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.2 relies on vendor APIs and reported model identifiers, so those results are less reproducible than the open-weight evaluations. No end-to-end latency, memory, or monetary-cost measurements are reported for restoration. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems-oriented compression and restoration pipeline. Practical: The compressors and the BERT restoration classifier can run on commercially available GPUs, but the paper does not report latency, throughput, memory, or deployment cost for the complete pipeline. Efficient: Restoration adds approximately 1.8 sentences or 40 tokens on average, changing the ratio from 0.30 to 0.31, but the additional classifier and candidate-generation compute is not compared against the savings from compression. Effective: Fixed-budget oracle reselection produces large gains on dangling subsets, while automatic restoration produces a 4.7-point Qwen3-8B gain and a nonsignificant advantage over matched random insertion, so evidence for a deployable solution is weaker than evidence for the failure diagnosis. Scalable: The study includes contexts of roughly 5.7k tokens, 20-paragraph MuSiQue contexts, and LongBench documents, but it does not test 10×–100× larger contexts or establish transfer across compression ratios, domains, languages, or production workloads. The work delivers code, results, and a trained restoration model rather than a complete dependency-preserving compressor or production library. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete failure mode that is distinct from generic information loss: the answer or relevant fragment can remain visible while the inference path becomes unusable. - The formal definition and additive-selection proposition clarify why independent scoring cannot guarantee completeness, without incorrectly claiming that every additive compressor must fail on every context. - The empirical diagnosis spans three multi-hop QA datasets, six substantially different hard compressors, a long-document benchmark, multiple downstream models, compression ratios, and overlap thresholds; the affected-example overlap analysis also shows that the phenomenon is not confined to one fixed subset. - The fixed-budget reselection experiment connects the diagnostic to downstream utility: on affected examples, replacing non-supporting content with missing support yields 28.8–34.3-point accuracy gains without increasing the nominal budget. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that support annotations are incomplete, so the operational overlap metric approximates the formal definition and does not enumerate alternative support paths. They limit the automatic restoration study to Beaver because token-level outputs are fragmented and difficult to modify comparably. They acknowledge that candidate construction limits performance, that the current restoration configuration is calibrated on Beaver and HotpotQA, and that transfer to other compressors is unresolved. They also describe the restoration pipeline as a diagnostic rather than a complete compression system and note that fixed-budget reselection relies on annotated support paragraphs. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central prevalence claims may overstate semantic referential failure because content-word overlap can conflate lexical similarity with support and can miss valid paraphrased or structurally distributed support; the paper should compare the heuristic against independent human judgments on a larger stratified sample and report inter-annotator agreement. The cross-compressor comparison uses one small, 184-example HotpotQA bridge set and a diagnostic denominator that differs from the main prevalence analysis, limiting generality. The oracle reselection experiment changes which non-supporting paragraphs are removed and sometimes produces contexts 1.5%–9.6% shorter, so its large gains cannot be attributed solely to restoring the missing bridge. The automatic method is trained using annotated supporting sentences and evaluated mainly on Beaver/HotpotQA, with no strong evidence that it beats random insertion after adequate statistical power or that it works on token-level compressors. The study does not evaluate actual compression latency, end-to-end cost, answer faithfulness, or behavior when annotations are noisy, multiple support paths exist, or restoration introduces distractors. Claims about a paradigm-level property would be stronger with an independently trained dependency-preserving compressor compared directly against current compressors at equal wall-clock cost and equal effective token budget. Bottom Line: This is a valuable diagnosis paper with unusually clear evidence that hard compression can break reasoning dependencies, but its automatic remedy is not yet a convincing general solution, so researchers in prompt compression and long-context QA should read it while practitioners should wait for compressor-agnostic, cost-controlled validation.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TextCall, a training- and inference-time carrier swap that preserves visual tool-call text while replacing returned images with the fixed placeholder `[Image output skipped]`. - Why it's important: Removing returned pixels can eliminate tool-execution overhead and reduce measured end-to-end latency by 29–46% without reducing accuracy on the evaluated perception-heavy benchmarks. - How it does it: It retains the model-generated reasoning text, tool names, spatial coordinates, and call intent, but withholds the post-call image during both fine-tuning and inference. - The good: Across 9.5K LoRA and 65K full-fine-tuning settings, TextCall matches or exceeds thinking-with-images, with a +1.39 percentage-point mean advantage on six core benchmarks at the 65K scale. - The missing: The central claim is tested on one 7B backbone, one cold-start corpus, one primary benchmark regime, one seed for the main experiments, and tasks selected where returned pixels may already be verbally recoverable; genuinely pixel-dependent tasks are not evaluated. - Read it or not: Researchers studying multimodal agents, tool-use attribution, or efficient VLM inference should read it for the controlled training-time ablation, but practitioners should not generalize TextCall as a universal replacement for visual feedback.

Problem & Motivation: Tool-augmented vision-language models commonly interleave language reasoning, crop/zoom or code calls, returned image observations, and final answers. The unresolved issue is whether the returned pixels cause the observed gains or whether the model benefits mainly from the structured text emitted before the return: the tool choice, target description, coordinates, and intent. This matters because image returns add vision-token prefill, latency, memory traffic, and tool-execution cost. The paper targets perception-heavy visual question answering, high-resolution understanding, spatial reasoning, counting, and related multimodal benchmarks. Prior inference-time image-removal, noise-replacement, attention, and gain-decomposition studies suggested pixel redundancy but were confounded by train–test mismatch or did not isolate the pre-return scaffold during training. The paper addresses that causal and engineering gap with a training-aligned comparison. Key Idea: The core insight is a controlled carrier swap: the tool call is treated as a structured textual thought primitive whose information can survive even when the observation it triggers is removed. TextCall hypothesizes that the scaffold carries much of the useful signal because it verbalizes the target and spatial region, while the returned image is often a redundant carrier under the training distribution. The component studies further suggest that textual reasoning supplies task intent and target description, whereas code supplies a structured spatial/procedural cue; the exact numeric coordinate values appear largely unnecessary during post-training. Methodology: The main pipeline starts from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and DeepEyes V2 cold-start trajectories. In the thinking-with-images condition, the model emits reasoning and executable crop/zoom code, receives the returned image, and continues reasoning. In TextCall, the same post-call image slot is replaced by the fixed text sentinel `[Image output skipped]` during both SFT and inference; no caption or oracle answer is provided. The authors train 9.5K-example LoRA models and 65K-example full-fine-tuned models, then apply matched GRPO post-training to the 65K checkpoints. They evaluate using an Agent Mode runner on six core benchmarks—V*Bench, HR-Bench-4K, HR-Bench-8K, MMStar, CV-Bench-2D, and CV-Bench-3D—and five additional benchmarks. A 1,000-sample factorial audit gives a judge the question, image, scaffold, or image-plus-scaffold; a scaffold decomposition trains variants with full reasoning plus code, reasoning only, or code only. Additional ablations test a 50-sample visual-jigsaw tool family and coordinate correctness by comparing verified versus shuffled coordinates. Critical design decisions are: applying the carrier swap during training to avoid distribution shift, preserving the complete scaffold rather than supplying an answer-bearing caption, and separating scaffold content from the returned carrier. The training alignment is well motivated; the use of a single fixed sentinel and the dependence on generated training traces leave open whether richer visual summaries or independently generated scaffolds would change the result. Key Results: At 9.5K LoRA SFT, TextCall scores 76.96% on VBench versus 71.73% for thinking-with-images, a +5.23-point difference. At 65K full fine-tuning, TextCall scores 78.01 versus 78.53 on VBench and has a six-benchmark mean of 71.23 versus 69.84, a +1.39-point difference; it wins on four of six benchmarks and loses by at most 1.05 points on the two reversals. On the extended suite, the 65K TextCall model reports 72.32 on CV-Bench-2D, 73.67 on CV-Bench-3D, 55.04 on PixmoCount, 65.53 on MMStar, 45.98 on BLINK, 85.20 on ChartQA, 29.30 on CharXiv, and 67.32 on MME-RealWorld as displayed in the table, though the table formatting indicates the extended-benchmark columns should be checked carefully before reuse. The 1,000-sample audit gives 73.10% accuracy for scaffold-only versus 73.50% for image-only, with a difference of −0.40 points and 95% CI [−3.20, +2.40], satisfying a stated 5-point non-inferiority margin; image plus scaffold reaches 79.40%. Full scaffold accuracy in the component study is 73.13% mean across VBench, HR-4K, and CV-2D, versus 66.32% for reasoning-only and 61.83% for code-only. Removing reasoning causes an 11.30-point drop, while removing code causes a 6.81-point drop; reasoning-only is slightly better than full scaffold on HR-4K but worse on VBench and CV-2D. At 65K, measured V*Bench latency is 2.91 seconds for TextCall versus 4.12 seconds for thinking-with-images, with 0 versus 1.8 returned-image API calls per sample and 2.3 versus 2.8 turns; the reported savings are 29% in the sandbox deployment and 46% in the no-execution latency reference. In matched GRPO, thinking-with-images tool-call rate falls to 0% at steps 800–900, while TextCall reaches 75.2% mean tool-call rate at step 800 after a transient collapse at step 200. In a small visual-jigsaw probe, trajectory-mean accuracy is 41.1% for placeholder returns and 41.2% for real-tool returns, but the n=50 confidence intervals are wide. Coordinate correctness has little detected effect: on a separate Qwen3-VL-8B experiment, correct versus shuffled coordinates differ by −0.11 points across 14,806 paired predictions with a 90% CI of [−0.74, +0.51], while the presence of code itself produces a much larger effect. The strongest evidence is therefore parity under aligned training/evaluation, not absolute state-of-the-art performance; comparisons are primarily against the authors' matched thinking-with-images model and DeepEyes V2 references rather than a broad set of current, independently trained agentic baselines. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the main novelty is the training-time carrier-swap formulation and the empirical finding that structured pre-return text can substitute for returned pixels in this regime, while TextCall is a relatively simple implementation of replacing image returns with a sentinel rather than a fundamentally new model architecture or learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes matched SFT comparisons, a training-time intervention, a factorial audit with paired bootstrap uncertainty, scaffold component ablations, a coordinate-shuffling test with three seeds in one experiment, latency measurements, RL dynamics, and an explicit separation of causal results from supporting diagnostics. It reports a single primary seed for the main SFT experiments and one GRPO epoch; most main results lack error bars, multiple-seed replication, or conventional significance testing. The audit uses a Gemini-3-Flash judge at temperature 0, and the jigsaw probe relies heavily on synthetic, API-generated trajectories and only 50 samples. The main intervention is not fully independent of the DeepEyes V2 data distribution: training traces already contain textual descriptions and spatial plans that may encode the answer-relevant information. The paper states a project page at `textcall.github.io`, but the parsed text does not establish that code, processed data, checkpoints, or weights are publicly released; no repository URL or release status is stated. Baselines include the base Qwen2.5-VL model and DeepEyes V2 official-checkpoint re-evaluations, but do not include a broad set of independently reproduced current tool-use systems under the same data and compute budget. The authors appropriately disclose that the thinking-with-images RL collapse depends on the 65K corpus, GRPO recipe, reward design, and absence of Long-CoT data, and do not claim it reproduces larger-scale published results. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper delivers and evaluates an inference/training protocol and agent-loop modification rather than only a theoretical result. * Practical: TextCall can run on commercially available GPUs; the experiments use Qwen2.5-VL-7B and NVIDIA H20 hardware, although the reported setup still requires multi-GPU fine-tuning and an agent runner. Efficient: It removes returned-image API calls and measured 2.91-second versus 4.12-second mean latency on VBench, but the advantage depends on sandbox implementation, sequential execution, decode speed, and whether tool calls are still executed for protocol compatibility. * Effective: The evidence shows parity or modest gains on the six core perception-heavy benchmarks and scaffold-only accuracy equivalent to image-only accuracy in a 1,000-sample audit, but it does not establish effectiveness on tasks where visual feedback contains information not already encoded in the scaffold or pretrained model. * Scalable: The paper tests 7B-scale models and 9.5K/65K training data, plus a limited Qwen3-VL-8B coordinate experiment, but does not test 10×–100× model, data, concurrency, or deployment scale; larger-scale behavior is explicitly left open. The work delivers the TextCall protocol and associated training/evaluation intervention, but the parsed paper does not confirm release of a software library, CLI, dataset, or trained model weights. Strengths: - The training-aligned carrier swap directly addresses the principal confound in earlier inference-only pixel-removal studies: models are trained and evaluated under the same return policy. - The evidence triangulates the claim across SFT scale, full fine-tuning, RL dynamics, factorial information audits, scaffold-content ablations, coordinate shuffling, latency measurement, and a different tool family. - The scaffold decomposition produces a useful mechanistic distinction: reasoning text and code both matter, while code syntax appears more important than coordinate numerical correctness in post-training. - The paper is unusually explicit about scope, including the difference between an internally matched RL collapse and general claims about thinking-with-images RL, and it reports a concrete operational benefit rather than only an attribution result. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict the conclusion to one Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, one DeepEyes V2 cold-start corpus, one perception-heavy benchmark suite, one main seed, and one GRPO epoch. They acknowledge that returned pixels may be load-bearing under representational bottlenecks, fine-grained visual comparisons, visual simulation, or visual-prior gaps; these regimes are proposed but not evaluated. They also acknowledge the transient TextCall RL collapse, the possibility that the thinking-with-images collapse is caused partly by reward design, the mismatch with larger DeepEyes V2 RL training using unreleased Long-CoT data, and the inability of the fixed placeholder intervention to assess richer captions or oracle visual hints. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, which improves the credibility of the scoped claim. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The main causal conclusion may be specific to a corpus whose generated reasoning and crop coordinates already verbalize answer-relevant content; an evaluation using independently generated, noisy, incorrect, or less descriptive scaffolds would test whether TextCall works beyond data artifacts. - The paper does not systematically construct adversarial or naturally occurring tasks where the returned crop contains novel object identity, unreadable text, subtle texture, occlusion resolution, or information absent from the scaffold, so the boundary between redundant and load-bearing pixels remains asserted rather than measured. - Main results rely on one backbone and mostly one seed, while the strongest coordinate study changes to Qwen3-VL-8B and a different evaluation protocol, weakening direct generalization from the auxiliary evidence to the main claim. - The principal comparison is against a matched author-trained thinking-with-images model; stronger independently trained baselines, larger backbones, multiple RL recipes, tool-use rewards, and current agentic systems are not comprehensively controlled. - The latency study uses sequential V*Bench evaluation and extrapolated decode-speed curves; throughput under batching, asynchronous tool execution, network/API variability, and production concurrency is not measured. - The scaffold-only model can exploit pretrained visual knowledge and the original full-resolution input available at the initial turn, so the experiments demonstrate that returned pixels are unnecessary after the call in this setup, not that the text scaffold alone contains all visual information. Bottom Line: This is a valuable and technically well-targeted preprint for researchers evaluating what visual tool use actually contributes, with credible evidence that returned pixels are redundant in the tested post-training regime, but its practical recommendation should remain conditional until it is validated on deliberately pixel-load-bearing tasks, more backbones, and replicated large-scale deployments.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses adaptation of real-time object detectors to new classes, domains, sensors, and deployment environments when full fine-tuning is expensive and generic PEFT interfaces select modules only by names or types. The relevant domain is heterogeneous detection architectures, including convolutional YOLO variants, attention-centric YOLO12, text-fusion YOLO-World, RT-DETR, and an MoE detector. The specific gap is the absence of a pre-training feasibility check that jointly accounts for convolution structure, depthwise/grouped operators, detection-head semantics such as DFL and geometry-sensitive regression, graph interfaces, backend/export compatibility, and architecture-conditioned failure risk. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat adapter placement as an auditable constrained-planning problem over a typed detector graph rather than as a generic module-name substitution. A target must be simultaneously operator-valid, semantically safe for detection, graph-interface preserving, budget-feasible, deployment-compatible, and—within calibrated coverage—above a catastrophic-performance-risk threshold; otherwise the system returns Refuse and can fall back to Full-SFT. Methodology: YOLO-PEFT first represents a detector as a directed acyclic computation graph and assigns each module independent operator and semantic roles, augmented with graph-interface and deployment metadata. It then filters candidates in a fixed order: operator validity, detection-semantic safety, family-specific policies, budgeted rank assignment, and reliability calibration. The placement is formalized as π(i) ∈ {0} ∪ K, with adapter costs constrained by Σ_i c_i(r_i) ≤ B; the rank solver maximizes a utility over operator, semantic, range, rank, and cost terms. The reliability model estimates ΔmAP using a linear function of architecture features such as attention, text-fusion, depthwise-convolution, and MoE ratios, but only within observed calibration coverage. The runtime freezes the base detector, trains sidecar adapters, saves adapter-only state and metadata, merges updates into ordinary YOLO modules, and exports the merged graph. Critical design decisions include excluding depthwise convolutions, fixed DFL projections, MoE routers, and geometry-sensitive paths; using group-local factors with r divisible by the number of groups; and applying family-scoped attention, text-fusion, and RT-DETR decoder guards. The exclusions are technically motivated by operator and detection semantics, but the utility function, architecture fingerprints, and refusal thresholds are empirically calibrated rather than derived from a formal safety guarantee. Optional optimization strategies include RS-LoRA, layer-wise learning-rate decay with ρ = 0.85, alpha warmup, orthogonal regularization with λ = 0.5, and dynamic dropout up to 0.15. Key Results: On the official VOC07+12 trainval set of 16,551 images evaluated on the 4,952-image VOC2007 test set, YOLO11s Full-SFT obtains 0.6428 mAP50:95, while planner-selected RS-LoRA obtains 0.7138 (+0.0710); YOLO12s Full-SFT obtains 0.6662, while planner-selected RS-LoRA at rank 16 obtains 0.7307 (+0.0645). The best reported PEFT configurations are HRA, reaching 0.7276 on YOLO11s and 0.7453 on YOLO12s, although HRA is not the headline planner-selected RS-LoRA configuration. On YOLO12s, rank 8/16/32 produces 0.7288/0.7307/0.7363 mAP50:95, with total parameters 9.66M/10.06M/10.85M and merged inference cost 23.6/25.6/29.6 GFLOPs. The constraint ablation increases YOLO12s mAP50:95 from 0.6900 with no constraints to 0.7094 after operator filtering and 0.7307 after detection-head semantic filtering. In the 300-epoch, 320-resolution diagnostic sweep, catastrophic degradation (Δ < −0.05) occurs in 6/7 YOLO12n and 7/7 RT-DETR-L LoRA-family trials, versus 0/10 YOLO11n trials; RT-DETR-L therefore refuses the evaluated LoRA-family requests and falls back to Full-SFT. Leave-one-variant-out calibration on five known architectures reports 86.7% accuracy and F1 = 0.850, but this is not held-out-family validation. In a controlled YOLO11 audit, LoRA reduces peak VRAM from 28.57 GB to 16.03 GB (43.9%) but increases training time from 118.2 s to 203.8 s (1.72×). Merged YOLO11s improves measured deployment throughput from 36.076 to 55.763 images/s and reduces latency from 27.719 to 17.933 ms; merged YOLO12s improves throughput from 28.494 to 40.191 images/s and reduces latency from 35.095 to 24.881 ms. The MoE stress test is limited to ordinary eligible hosts with router, expert, attention, and head targeting disabled; HRA reaches 0.7454 versus logged Full-SFT at 0.6891, while BOFT and OFT fail before evaluation. Baselines are primarily Full-SFT, generic PEFT variants, and naive placement; the paper does not provide direct comparisons against several detector-specific adaptation methods under matched protocols. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper’s genuine contribution is the typed-graph, constraint-and-refusal formulation plus an integrated train-save-merge-export runtime and evidence that PEFT rankings and failure modes vary sharply by detector architecture, while the underlying adapters and most optimization techniques are existing methods combined with detector-specific rules. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides operator, semantic, runtime, rank, and variant ablations, including a useful separation between hard constraints and counterfactual diagnostics; it also reports three seeds for selected core comparisons, with maximum within-configuration sample SD ≤ 0.006 mAP50:95 and unchanged rankings. It reports merge-equivalence reasoning and ONNX/TensorRT checks, including ONNX opset 18 and maximum absolute error below 1.24 × 10^-3 relative to PyTorch, but the evidence for some deployment claims is a smoke-test audit rather than broad hardware evaluation. No significance tests are reported, and most of the 14-variant-by-five-architecture sweep is seed-0 only. The paper states a project page at github.com/Tencent/YOLO-Master, but the parsed text does not establish that the YOLO-PEFT code, calibration data, trained weights, or complete experiment scripts are publicly released. The calibration model is trained and evaluated on the same small architecture matrix, with no detector family held out; the VOC2007 test set participates in common best-checkpoint selection, so absolute test scores are not blind estimates. The core benchmark is a single dataset and adaptation regime, and the principal comparisons omit matched evaluations of detector-specific PEFT and domain-adaptation systems. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS with substantial empirical evaluation, because the paper delivers a detector adaptation planner and runtime rather than only an algorithmic claim. * Practical: The system targets commercially available accelerator environments and supports ordinary YOLO training, adapter checkpoints, merging, ONNX, and TensorRT, but the exact hardware, software versions, and public installation path are not fully specified in the parsed paper. * Efficient: It reduces controlled YOLO11 LoRA peak training VRAM by 43.9% and trainable parameters to roughly 10.9% of Full-SFT, but increases training time by 1.72×; unmerged adapters also increase inference GFLOPs and latency, whereas merging restores near-base operator cost. * Effective: Evidence supports improved VOC mAP for YOLO11s and YOLO12s and avoidance of the seven observed RT-DETR-L catastrophic trials, but it does not establish effectiveness for COCO, domain shift, few-shot adaptation, unseen detector families, or expert-aware MoE adaptation. * Scalable: The largest main experiments use small YOLO models and a single mid-scale VOC dataset; no 10×–100× model, dataset, or deployment-scale test is reported, and scalability beyond the evaluated families is explicitly unvalidated. The work delivers a software-oriented planner/runtime, adapter-only checkpoints and manifests, merge support, and ONNX/TensorRT export paths; the parsed text identifies a project page but does not verify a dedicated public repository or released model artifacts. Strengths: - It identifies a real failure mode in generic PEFT tooling—syntactically valid but detection-semantically unsafe insertion—and converts it into inspectable rejection rules with per-module reason codes. - The operator/semantic separation is technically useful: the framework distinguishes dense, grouped, and depthwise convolution contracts from DFL, regression, router, decoder, and fusion semantics instead of relying on module type alone. - The ablations provide evidence that semantic filtering, not merely parameter reduction, drives the largest observed YOLO12s improvement: 0.7094 after operator filtering versus 0.7307 after adding head-semantic exclusions. - The runtime contract connects training decisions to checkpointing, merging, and export, and the paper explicitly reports the practical trade-off of lower VRAM but longer training rather than presenting PEFT as uniformly cheaper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit claims to VOC and the evaluated detector families, do not claim held-out-family safety, COCO or domain-shift generalization, few-shot performance, or expert-aware MoE planning, and state that refusal calibration is not validated on an unseen architecture. They also acknowledge that the MoE test disables planner, router, expert, attention, and head targeting; that the deployment audit is controlled and excludes external storage/distribution estimates; that VOC test participation in checkpoint selection prevents interpreting scores as blind test estimates; and that stronger base-checkpoint, class-vocabulary, model-YAML, and architecture-hash checks remain future deployment extensions. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, although they substantially narrow the practical scope of the refusal claims. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The refusal threshold and linear reliability model are calibrated on the same five-family matrix used for evaluation, so the reported 86.7% accuracy and F1 = 0.850 do not measure generalization to new detector families; a held-out-family protocol is essential for the paper’s central safety claim. - The evaluation lacks matched comparisons with detector-specific methods such as YOLO-IOD, SpotPatch, LoRA-Det, domain-adaptive PEFT, or carefully tuned full/partial-head fine-tuning, making it unclear whether the planner itself, rather than favorable adapter choices, drives the gains. - All primary results use VOC and ordinary supervised adaptation; the paper does not test the motivating settings of domain shift, new sensors, incremental classes, open-vocabulary adaptation, or large-scale deployment. - The high gains over Full-SFT may depend on the small VOC regime and checkpoint-selection protocol; evaluation on a held-out validation/test design with fixed hyperparameters and no test-based model selection would strengthen the claims. - The framework conservatively excludes many potentially important modules, but the paper does not quantify the resulting false-refusal rate or compare against safe partial fine-tuning, adapter insertion at residual interfaces, or alternative channel-preserving depthwise/attention adaptations. - Public reproducibility is uncertain because the cited project page is not shown to contain the planner implementation, calibration artifacts, exact environment, and all W&B exports required to reproduce the tables. Bottom Line: The paper offers a useful detector-specific systems abstraction and a credible warning against blindly transferring language-model PEFT, but its strongest contribution is a well-executed, family-scoped planning and deployment framework rather than a validated general safety mechanism; read it for the formulation and engineering contract, not as evidence that refusal or PEFT selection generalizes beyond its VOC-centered calibration set.

Modular TTT: Rethinking Test-Time Training as Composable Modules (6 ▲ )

Bohao Tang, Zhen Qin, Yuqi Pan, Zheng Li, Pengfei Liu, Ya Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Modular TTT, a framework that represents test-time-training inner learners as directed acyclic graphs of composable primitives and automatically derives their train-forward, train-backward, causal-query, and fast-weight state-update computations. - Why it's important: Existing TTT variants couple architecture, loss, update, normalization, and implementation choices, making them difficult to extend, compare, and diagnose; modularization could reduce both research and implementation cost for efficient long-context sequence models. - How it does it: It assigns each primitive explicit train-view forward, train-view backward, and query-view rules, then composes those local rules in topological order across a learner graph. - The good: Controlled ablations identify robust effects—small initial inner learning rates, scalar decay, and a shallow pointwise nonlinearity improve validation loss—while five-seed runs support the Linear-SiLU gain at 160M and 410M scales. - The missing: The central modularity and efficiency claims are not evaluated against a broad set of independently reimplemented contemporary TTT systems or at substantially larger than 1.45B scale, and inference is slower than Gated DeltaNet in the reported measurements. - Read it or not: Researchers working on TTT, linear sequence models, or efficient model kernels should read it for the framework and controlled ablations; readers seeking a better long-context language model can likely skip it because retrieval and containment results remain below LLaMA and no clear quality or inference advantage over GDN is shown.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) are strong because the DAG-level formulation exposes train, backward, query, and state-update semantics as composable objects rather than introducing another coupled TTT variant. Rigor (84) is the main strength: matched ablations, five-seed results, analytic update rules, efficiency measurements, and evaluation through 1.45B parameters provide credible evidence, despite recipe-mismatched baselines and limited scale. Completeness (82) and Resilience (78) benefit from openly reporting failures on retrieval and the fact that GDN is faster at inference, while Impact (72) reflects released code and useful infrastructure without a demonstrated end-to-end quality or serving advantage. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*84 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*72 = 79.5, rounded to 80.

Problem & Motivation: Test-time training applies online optimization to fast weights while processing sequences, offering a flexible alternative to fixed recurrent states, linear-attention accumulators, and explicit caches. The problem is that published TTT variants typically hard-code several choices simultaneously—fast-weight topology, self-supervised loss, learning-rate parameterization, decay, normalization, and causal update implementation—so researchers cannot cleanly attribute gains or failures to individual components, and modifying a learner requires deriving and implementing a new global update. The target domain is autoregressive language modeling with efficient, approximately linear-time sequence processing and long-context memory. Key Idea: Treat the TTT inner learner as a directed acyclic computation graph whose primitives carry three semantics: ordinary train-view forward computation, train-view backward computation that produces local gradients and fast-weight updates, and causal query-view computation that reads the updated state. The key insight is that global graph-level TTT updates can be assembled from registered local rules, allowing topology, loss, learning-rate, decay, and normalization choices to vary independently rather than being encoded in separate model-specific derivations. Methodology: For each sequence chunk, the model first projects the backbone hidden states into keys K, queries Q, and targets V. Pass 1 executes the learner DAG on K in topological order, producing a predicted target V-hat and retaining intermediate activations. Pass 2 evaluates an inner loss—inner product, MSE, L1, or RMSE—and propagates analytic local backward rules in reverse topological order to obtain gradients and updates for fast linear or gated weights. Pass 3 executes the same graph on Q, using the retained train activations, gradients, and parameter updates to produce causal outputs and the end-of-chunk fast state. Linear fast weights use a chunkwise dual update of the form W_end = W_start - K-hat^T dV-hat, with lower-triangular causal readout; scalar or vector decay modifies prior-state and within-chunk contributions. The outer model uses a pre-normalized LLaMA-style residual backbone with RMSNorm and a SiLU GLU channel mixer; Modular TTT is used as the token mixer. Critical design decisions are: a DAG with registered primitive rules, which is technically well specified but does not support arbitrary operations without new query/update rules; small learning-rate initialization at approximately 10^-3 without fixed mean scaling, justified by chunk-update scale and MSE spectral stability analyses; and scalar decay as the quality-efficiency operating point, justified by its near-vector-decay loss with much higher throughput. Experiments use chunk size 256, 2K contexts for 10B-token ablations, and 4K contexts for 100B-token scale-up runs. Key Results: At 160M and 410M parameters after 10B tokens, MSE validation loss is 3.0380 and 2.7949 for the shallow Linear learner with small learning-rate initialization and scalar decay; adding SiLU gives 3.0205 and 2.7849. Inner-product loss is nearly tied with MSE at 3.0383 and 2.7938 for Linear, and 3.0242 and 2.7838 for Linear-SiLU. Standard learning-rate initialization near 1 is substantially worse—for example, MSE with scalar decay is 3.3035 versus 3.0380 at 160M and 3.0820 versus 2.7949 at 410M. Vector decay reaches lower loss than scalar decay, 3.0038 versus 3.0380 at 160M and 2.7821 versus 2.7949 at 410M for MSE, but reduces throughput by roughly 25% and increases memory by about 3 GB. Deeper learners perform worse: the best reported deeper configuration, Linear-SiLU-Linear-Norm, has loss 3.1144 at 160M, versus 3.0205 for shallow Linear-SiLU. Analytic primitive backward operators provide 1.65x speedup for Linear and 2.62x for Norm over torch.autograd references; end-to-end training throughput is 2.2x higher for TTT-Linear and 3.3x higher for TTT-MLP than the official TTT implementation at 160M. At 410M and 1.45B trained for approximately 100B tokens, Modular TTT reaches average multiple-choice accuracies of 50.99% for MSE Linear-SiLU and 56.44% for inner-product Linear, respectively; GDN reports 50.45% and 56.30%, while LLaMA reports 50.63% and 55.67%. However, average containment accuracy is much lower for Modular TTT than LLaMA: at 1.45B, the best Modular TTT value is 35.46% versus 65.20% for LLaMA, and RULER single-needle accuracy at 8K is 21.07% for the best Modular TTT variant versus 92.13% for LLaMA. Inference measurements show GDN is faster: at 410M, GDN achieves 227,305 prefill tokens/s and 400.70 decode tokens/s, compared with 130,244 and 219.67 for Modular TTT Linear MSE; Modular TTT uses less peak memory than both GDN and LaCT in the reported setup. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the genuinely new contribution is the explicit DAG-level formalization and implementation of composable train/backward/query semantics for TTT, while the individual primitives, chunkwise dual updates, decay, nonlinearities, and fast-weight learners largely combine or generalize existing ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides extensive matched ablations across 160M and 410M models, includes five-seed results for key comparisons, reports throughput and memory, gives analytic update equations and proofs for chunk-scale, spectral, and factor-coupling claims, and evaluates 410M and 1.45B models on perplexity, multiple-choice, containment, and RULER retrieval tasks. The five-seed standard deviations are small—for example, Linear MSE is 3.0381 ± 0.0033 at 160M and 2.7954 ± 0.0023 at 410M—although no significance tests are reported. The code is stated to be available at https://github.com/ByteDance-Seed/Modular-TTT; dataset and model-weight release details are not stated. The strongest baseline comparisons are partly confounded: official TTT results use a different reconstruction target, normalization, update implementation, and decay recipe, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that these are not component-matched controls. External comparisons use LLaMA, GDN, and LaCT, but the paper does not establish identical data, tokenizer, training implementation, or tuning conditions for every baseline. The ablation study is conducted on one large-scale English corpus and a restricted primitive set, so its conclusions may be specific to the chosen backbone, chunk size, optimizer, one-step update, and training regime. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the paper runs language-model training and inference experiments and releases an implementation. Practical: The method runs on commercially available GPUs using PyTorch, BF16, FSDP, analytic kernels, and standard model sizes up to 1.45B parameters, although hardware requirements for the full 100B-token training runs are substantial. Efficient: Analytic backward rules improve primitive latency by 1.65x–2.62x and training throughput over official TTT by 2.2x–3.3x, but GDN is faster in both prefill and decode, and vector decay costs about 25% throughput and 3 GB memory. Effective: The evidence shows comparable aggregate language-model loss and multiple-choice accuracy to GDN, but it does not show superior exact retrieval or containment; at 1.45B, 8K single-needle retrieval reaches at most 21.07% versus 92.13% for LLaMA. Scalable: The method is tested at 160M, 410M, and 1.45B parameters and 2K–8K evaluation contexts, but no 10x–100x scale experiment beyond 1.45B or substantially longer training context is reported, so larger-scale behavior is not established. The work delivers a public software implementation and a reusable graph-level update framework, but trained model weights are not stated to be released. Strengths: - The DAG abstraction exposes topology, loss, learning-rate initialization, decay, and normalization as separable axes, directly addressing a real reproducibility and attribution problem in TTT research. - The three-pass formulation is algorithmically explicit and supports analytic local backward rules, enabling both automatic composition and measurable kernel-level efficiency gains. - The ablations produce concrete, actionable findings: small initial inner learning rates and decay matter substantially; a shallow SiLU extension gives consistent but modest gains; deeper, normalized, residual, and gated memories fail to improve under the tested one-step regime. - The paper does not hide negative results: it reports that GDN is faster at inference and that Modular TTT is substantially weaker than LLaMA on containment and exact long-context retrieval, which makes the empirical conclusions more credible. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the study covers only autoregressive language modeling, the reported scales and training budgets, and a limited set of learner primitives and update schedules. They note that deeper and gated learners could behave differently with other update rules, chunk sizes, optimizers, or hybrid attention designs; that LaCT-specific refinements such as Muon-style update normalization and momentum are not integrated into the current fused graph implementation; and that shallow Modular TTT remains weaker than LLaMA on containment and explicit long-context retrieval. These limitations are confronted directly and motivate future work on richer update schedules, retrieval-oriented memory, and broader domains. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not provide a clean, independently controlled comparison against the strongest contemporary TTT implementations under matched tokenizer, data, optimizer, update objective, and kernel conditions; its official-TTT speed and quality comparisons are explicitly recipe-mismatched. The modular framework's claimed generality is demonstrated only for a small registered primitive set and DAGs whose causal query/update semantics can be manually specified; the cost and correctness burden of adding more complex primitives is not measured. The study reports no wall-clock training cost, energy, or total hardware accounting, and it does not evaluate multi-step inner optimization, adaptive chunk sizes, larger chunks, sequence lengths far beyond 8K, or scales beyond 1.45B. The conclusion that depth and gating are unhelpful may therefore be specific to one-step Gaussian-initialized fast-weight updates and the chosen backbone rather than a general property of TTT. Finally, the paper does not report formal statistical testing for downstream benchmarks or disclose whether baseline models were trained on identical data and budgets. Bottom Line: This is a useful framework and ablation reference for researchers building TTT systems, but it is not a demonstrated improvement over GDN or LLaMA in end-to-end quality or inference efficiency, so its main value is methodological infrastructure and negative empirical evidence rather than a superior deployable language-model architecture.

Bole: Efficient Tree Speculation for Hybrid-Attention Language Models

L Wang, Y Su, X Wu, C You, Y Liu, Z Qiu, J Zhang… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Bole, a kernel–runtime system for exact tree speculative decoding in hybrid-attention LLMs with recurrent gated linear-attention layers. - Why it's important: Hybrid models reduce long-context costs, but naïve tree verification can become memory- and latency-bound, limiting batching and increasing agent-serving latency. - How it does it: Bole rewrites the gated-delta recurrence as an ancestor-structured closed form, solves all tree nodes with a value-tiled GPU kernel, stores branch updates as token-level factors, and calibrates a batch-wide verification budget per hardware configuration. - The good: Across four Qwen3.5 models and two platforms, Bole reports up to 7.7× faster per-layer recurrent tree verification, 82–99× lower transient state memory, and up to 2.03× higher throughput than the strongest tree-speculative baseline. - The missing: The evaluation is restricted to one model family and one native MTP drafter, with no reported error bars, multiple-run variance, public Bole implementation or model release, or comparison against a broader set of hybrid-model and speculative-decoding systems. - Read it or not: Systems researchers and LLM-serving practitioners working on recurrent or hybrid architectures should read it for the recurrence factorization and state-lifecycle design; readers interested only in general speculative decoding can likely skip it.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (88) and Non-Obviousness (90) are excellent: the exact ancestor-structured factorization and factorized recurrent-state lifecycle address a genuine mismatch between tree speculation and recurrent hybrid attention. Rigor (78) is strong due to formal equivalence results, component ablations, two hardware platforms, multiple model sizes, isolated kernels, and online agent replay, though the preprint status, lack of variance, narrow Qwen3.5 coverage, and unverified finite-precision equivalence reduce confidence. Completeness (76) and Resilience (76) are good but not exceptional because baseline fairness, quantization, workload diversity, profiler overhead, and broader architecture generality remain insufficiently tested. Impact (78) is high given the integrated SGLang runtime, substantial throughput and memory gains, and online serving improvements, although no public Bole repository or standalone artifact is stated.
