Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses inference serving for hybrid-attention LLMs that interleave full attention with recurrent linear attention, particularly in long-context and multi-turn agent workloads. Full-attention layers retain KV caches, while gated linear-attention layers maintain fixed-size recurrent states; this reduces some context-dependent costs but makes tree speculation difficult because each proposal node depends on its parent’s recurrent state. Existing tree-speculation systems designed for append-only KV caches either execute recurrent branches serially or materialize a full recurrent-state snapshot per proposal node. The resulting latency and transient memory grow with tree size and batch size, displacing reusable KV-cache capacity. A further problem is that the efficient number of verification tokens depends jointly on GPU architecture, batch composition, KV lengths, tree depth, and the mixture of full-attention, recurrent, and dense operators, so a fixed per-request budget is inadequate. Key Idea: The central insight is that gated-delta recurrence over a proposal tree can be represented exactly as an ancestor-masked, strictly lower-triangular linear system whose inverse is a finite Neumann polynomial bounded by tree depth. This removes the parent-to-child execution dependency at the implementation level without changing the recurrence. The same path-factorization identity also permits Bole to retain one committed state plus compact per-token factors and reconstruct only the state on the sampled accepted path. Methodology: Bole operates as a speculative-serving loop integrated into SGLang. First, a native MTP drafter creates a candidate tree for each active request. A profiler precomputes, for model/GPU/parallelism, batch-size, KV-length, and tree-template buckets, the largest total verification-node count whose complete hybrid forward remains within a latency allowance: Bole selects the maximum budget satisfying T_ver(N|c) <= (1+epsilon)T_dec(c). At runtime, candidate nodes are globally ranked by cumulative draft-path probability and selected across requests under this batch-wide budget; monotonic path probabilities preserve prefix-connected trees. The target model then processes full-attention layers with tree masks and recurrent layers with Bole’s solver. For each gated-delta head, the method forms decay products P, ancestor interaction matrix G, readout matrix C, and local correction matrix R, then computes U = (I+G)^(-1)R = sum_{m=0}^d (-G)^m R and outputs O = D_P Q S_pre + C U. The GPU implementation uses value tiling, key-dimension chunking, tensor-core operations, on-chip finite-Neumann propagation, and fused convolution/gating, factor construction, solve, and readout stages. For state management, Bole stores the canonical pre-tree state and token-scale factors P, K, and U; after sampling selects a terminal node, it reconstructs the accepted state with one batched matrix multiplication, S_new = P_a S_pre + (D_a K_a)^T U_a, and commits it across recurrent layers. The runtime packs request trees into a device-resident flat-ragged forest, performs selection, sampling, compaction, and state commit on the GPU, and uses CUDA Graph capacity buckets. The closed-form derivation is mathematically justified through path-state factorization, an ancestor-masked correction system, and depth-bounded nilpotency. The value-tile choices and hardware budget are motivated by resource constraints and profiling, although the paper gives limited sensitivity analysis for kernel tile parameters and profiling overhead. Key Results: The paper is an arXiv preprint (version 1 dated August 3, 2026) and reports experiments on Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, 27B, and 122B-A10B, using unquantized weights and the models’ native MTP head, on one NVIDIA A100 80 GB, four NVLink-connected A100s for the 122B model, and an NVIDIA GB10 system with 128 GB LPDDR5x. Compared with SGLang autoregressive decoding, SGLang tree speculation, and a ported/optimized AdaServe implementation, Bole achieves a geometric-mean offline throughput speedup of 2.74× over autoregressive decoding and 1.26× over the strongest speculative baseline across 28 model/platform/batch configurations. Peak speedups are 3.62× over autoregressive decoding and 1.41× over the strongest speculative baseline on A100, and 4.72× and 2.03× respectively on GB10. On MBPP, mean accepted tokens range from 6.38 to 6.88 for Bole across the four models, compared with 6.29–6.82 for SGLang-Tree and 6.35–6.82 for AdaServe. Across MBPP, GSM8K, ShareGPT, and CNN/DailyMail at batch size 4 for Qwen3.5-27B, Bole’s speedups over autoregressive decoding are 1.98×–3.36× on A100 and 2.85×–4.12× on GB10; over the faster speculative baseline they are 1.15×–1.20× and 1.38×–1.45×. The isolated recurrent verification core improves by 3.4× and 7.5× on A100 at batch sizes 1 and 16, and by 5.0× and 7.7× on GB10. At batch size 16, per-layer writes fall from 824 MB to 9.8 MB. Transient state memory is reduced by 82–99× relative to full snapshots in the analytical examples and by 74.0–88.5% relative to AdaServe in measured A100 speculation overhead. In online Open-SWE-Traces agent replay, Bole reduces mean TTFT by 61.3%–73.3% and mean TPOT by 28.9%–49.9% relative to AdaServe; compared with SGLang-Tree, reductions are 63.5%–67.6% for TTFT and 33.8%–50.3% for TPOT. The budget sensitivity test finds optimal total verification budgets of 128 tokens on A100 and 256 on GB10, demonstrating hardware dependence. The results are strong at standard serving scale, but they do not establish behavior at 10×–100× larger batches, longer trees, more diverse hybrid architectures, or larger heterogeneous GPU clusters. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION apply: the genuinely new contribution is the exact ancestor-structured factorization and its GPU realization for gated-delta tree verification, combined with factorized recurrent-state storage and hardware-aware batch scheduling, while speculative decoding, tree proposal, tensor-core tiling, CUDA Graphs, and SGLang integration are established techniques adapted to this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides formal lemmas and a theorem claiming exact equivalence between sequential gated-delta execution and the closed-form solver, including the assumptions of parent-before-child ordering, positive decay gates, and finite maximum tree depth. It includes component ablations: hardware-aware budgeting contributes 5.3% on A100 and 10.7% on GB10, adding the parallel solver raises cumulative normalized throughput to 1.21× and 1.30×, and factorized state management raises it to 1.59× and 2.23× over SGLang-Tree. It also includes isolated kernel measurements, memory measurements, cross-workload experiments, two platforms, multiple model sizes, and online replay. However, no error bars, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-trial variance are reported. The strongest baseline, AdaServe, does not natively support the evaluated hybrid models; the authors port and optimize it, which improves applicability but makes independent reproduction and fairness harder to assess. The evaluation uses only Qwen3.5 and its native MTP drafter, and does not compare with EAGLE-based drafting, STree on a supported recurrent model, or other hybrid-serving implementations. The paper mentions the SGLang repository at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/release/v0.5.12, but does not state that Bole’s code, kernels, profiler, configuration files, traces, or modified AdaServe implementation are publicly released. The exactness claim is algebraically supported, but the paper does not report numerical equivalence tests or finite-precision error bounds between sequential and parallel implementations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS. Practical: The system runs on commercially available NVIDIA A100 GPUs and a GB10 platform and is integrated into SGLang, but it currently targets the specific gated-delta and hybrid execution paths supported by the evaluated model family. Efficient: It reduces isolated recurrent verification latency by 3.4–7.7×, reduces measured transient speculation overhead by 74.0–88.5% relative to AdaServe, and adds an accepted-path commit costing less than 0.5% of a target forward; total cost still includes profiling, factor construction, GPU scratch, and the unquantized target model. Effective: The evidence shows improvements in accepted-token throughput, TTFT, TPOT, prefix-cache hit rate, and OOM feasibility rather than only a proxy; Bole reaches 90.8%/92.6% prefix-cache hit rates on the two online platforms versus 69.3%–69.7% and 58.3%–59.8% for speculative baselines. Scalable: It supports batch sizes up to 8 in end-to-end experiments, tree budgets up to at least 256 total nodes in sensitivity tests, four model sizes, and TP4 for the 122B model, but behavior at 10×–100× scale, longer contexts, larger distributed deployments, deeper or wider trees, and changing workloads is not evaluated. The work delivers an integrated SGLang implementation and GPU kernels; a standalone reusable library, public Bole repository, or released benchmark artifact is not stated. Strengths: - The recurrence-to-linear-system derivation addresses a genuine architectural mismatch between KV-oriented tree speculation and gated recurrent attention, rather than merely combining existing speculation heuristics. - The factorized state lifecycle converts an apparently branch-sized recurrent-state requirement into one persistent state plus token-scale factors, with both asymptotic analysis and measurements showing large memory reductions. - The kernel and runtime are co-designed: value tiling, on-chip finite-Neumann propagation, device-resident forest packing, CUDA Graph buckets, and cross-layer commit address separate bottlenecks that would otherwise limit end-to-end gains. - The evaluation isolates the contributions of budgeting, parallel verification, and state factorization and demonstrates improvements across offline, multi-workload, and online agent-serving settings on two substantially different memory/compute platforms. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly limits its design to gated-delta-style recurrent linear attention and distinguishes it from diagonal SSM transitions supported by STree. It acknowledges that verification capacity depends on GPU architecture, batch properties, KV lengths, and tree composition, motivating offline configuration profiling rather than a universal budget. It also recognizes that the finite-polynomial solver is bounded by the maximum tree depth and that additional proposal tokens cease to be near-free after a hardware-dependent threshold. Broader limitations concerning model-family coverage, profiling adaptation under workload drift, numerical precision, and external reproducibility are not explicitly discussed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The evaluation’s external validity is narrow: every end-to-end result uses Qwen3.5, one gated-delta implementation, one native MTP drafter, unquantized weights, and only two hardware platforms. The paper does not test quantization, alternative recurrent architectures such as Mamba-like or other non-diagonal state-space models, EAGLE or learned tree drafters, longer and more variable contexts, larger distributed serving clusters, or dynamic hardware/workload changes after calibration. Baseline fairness deserves scrutiny because AdaServe is ported and optimized by the authors and no ablation reports the effect of its port relative to an independently validated hybrid baseline. The online workload uses one coding-agent trace family, so the reported cache-hit and latency benefits may depend strongly on repeated long prefixes. The paper reports headline speedups and cumulative ablations but omits variance and statistical methodology, making the reliability of small gains such as 1.15×–1.20× harder to judge. It also does not quantify profiler cost, memory consumed by G/C scratch and topology metadata at larger trees, numerical discrepancies under BF16/FP16, or performance when trees have highly irregular depths and widths. Finally, the paper claims production integration but does not provide a public Bole artifact or sufficient implementation details to independently reproduce the reported end-to-end numbers. Bottom Line: This is a technically substantial and practically relevant systems paper whose exact recurrent-tree factorization and state compression merit attention from hybrid-LLM serving researchers, although its strong performance claims should be discounted until they are reproduced across model families, drafters, precisions, workloads, and publicly released implementations.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EcoAgent-Bench, a 304-task benchmark that evaluates whether LLM agents select tools, model tiers, escalation, and abstention actions correctly under explicit budgets. - Why it's important: Deployed agents can achieve task completion while wasting API, compute, or human-review resources, so correctness alone does not measure operational quality. - How it does it: It transforms real-derived QA and information-seeking seeds into frozen environments with priced actions, evidence-conditioned canonical decisions, contrasting high-regret traces, and strict budgeted scoring. - The good: The benchmark exposes a substantial gap between completion and conditional resource selection: tool-API agents achieve only 3.9–24.0% micro strict success and 3.6–7.3% economic consistency, while budget increases often produce little or misdirected escalation. - The missing: The evaluation relies on author-constructed cost schedules and small or weakly validated subsets for stop-loss and realism assessment, and it does not establish that benchmark decisions transfer to real provider prices or production workloads. - Read it or not: Researchers building cost-aware tool routers, abstention policies, or agent benchmarks should read it for its diagnostic task structure and failure analysis, while readers seeking a deployable routing method can skip it because the paper does not propose or evaluate such a controller.

Problem & Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks primarily score whether an agent completes a task and treat resource consumption as a secondary statistic. This misses a deployment problem faced by API-based assistants, research agents, coding agents, and human-in-the-loop systems: the agent must decide whether local evidence is sufficient, whether to purchase broader retrieval, whether to use a stronger model, and whether to stop when the premise is unsupported, all while respecting a stated budget. Prior benchmarks such as GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, AgentBench, and τ-bench generally do not make the price of each action and the remaining budget part of the task objective. The paper targets the resulting gap between accurate-but-wasteful behavior, cheap-but-insufficient behavior, and genuinely conditional economic decision-making. Key Idea: The central insight is to make the same broad agent capability—answering a question—appear in paired economic regimes where the correct action differs because evidence sufficiency differs. Cheap-QA tasks reward avoiding deep research, escalation-QA tasks require it, model-upgrade tasks reverse whether a cheap or frontier model is sufficient, and stop-loss tasks reward evidence-backed abstention. This lets the benchmark detect one-sided policies such as always escalating or always stopping, which ordinary micro-accuracy and mean-cost metrics can conceal. The economic-consistency score, defined as the minimum of strict accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups, is the paper's main diagnostic rather than a learned decision rule. Methodology: The transformation pipeline starts from licensed or traceable real-derived seeds from HotpotQA, MuSiQue, GAIA, and related sources; deterministically selects items; freezes evidence; adds a priced action set and tight, medium, and loose budgets; separates the agent-visible environment from evaluator-only oracle material; and packages canonical budget-compliant and contrasting high-regret traces. Shared retrieval actions include inspect_tool (4 units), search_tools (8), local_keyword_search (18), read_document (22), web_search_snapshot (70), deep_research_agent (260), and page_human_oncall (520), with model-tier prices defined on a separate 1:8 scale. The five families contain 72 cheap-QA, 115 escalation-QA, 100 model-upgrade, 7 frozen-information, and 10 stop-loss tasks. An episode is a strict success only when the answer is correct, the required evidence-access or grounding condition holds, and total cost is at most budget. The paper formalizes utility as R minus λ times normalized cost for correct or incorrect budget-feasible trajectories, with budget violations assigned negative infinity, and also reports cost per strict success and Pareto frontiers. Seven LLM agents are tested in tool-API and workspace-CLI tracks, alongside four oracle scripted controls; the main tool-API runs use one episode per task, while GPT-5.4 receives a three-budget sweep. The action prices are stress-tested by independently perturbing costs: canonical versus high-regret ordering is preserved in 100% of 50,000 draws at perturbation range R=2 and at least 99.90% at R=3. Critical design decisions—the frozen agent/evaluator separation, deterministic transformation and integrity checks, and paired save-versus-upgrade regimes—are operationally well motivated, although the paper does not empirically justify that its abstract prices match real deployment utility or that its family labels capture all relevant evidence uncertainty. Key Results: On the 304-task bundle, tool-API agents perform poorly: Sonnet reaches 24.0% micro strict success and 7.3% economic consistency at mean ledger cost 207; Gemini 2.5 Pro reaches 17.4% and 6.1% at cost 268; and GPT-5.4 reaches only 3.9% and 3.6% at cost 97. Workspace agents obtain higher completion-oriented results, led by Claude Code with Opus 4.8 at 65.1% micro success, 54% upgrade-group accuracy, 96% save-group accuracy, and 53.6% economic consistency; Codex GPT-5.5 reaches 56.2% micro and 49.5% consistency, while Haiku reaches 56.9% micro and 44.6% consistency. These workspace resource numbers use a post-hoc execution proxy rather than the shared action ledger and are not directly comparable to tool-API costs. Oracle controls illustrate the metric issue: CopilotFirst obtains 76.3% micro success but only 12.2% economic consistency and 12% save accuracy, while RetryLoop obtains 73.0% micro success, 100% upgrade accuracy, and 0% save accuracy. Tool-API failures include excessive spending on cheap-QA—Sonnet and Gemini exceed budget on 74% and 99% of those tasks—and premature stopping: GPT-5.4 abstains on 45/115 escalation-required tasks and invokes deep research on none of them. In the GPT-5.4 escalation budget sweep, deep-research use rises only from 0/115 at budget 202 to 1/115 at 370 and 3/115 at 644, despite the latter budgets exceeding the approximately 322-unit escalation path. On cheap-QA, mean cost rises with budget from 34 to 90 for GPT-5.4, 122 to 191 for Sonnet, and 116 to 248 for Gemini; Gemini's unnecessary deep-research rate reaches 19.4% at the loose budget. The findings are diagnostic rather than causal because the regimes use different questions and sources rather than item-level counterfactual pairs. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuine contribution is a reproducible benchmark formulation that makes evidence-conditioned action choice and budget feasibility first-class evaluation targets, plus the economic-consistency diagnostic and empirical evidence that current agents conflate budget compliance with budget conditioning; the underlying QA sources, tool use, model routing, abstention, and cost-sensitive evaluation components are established ideas recombined in a new benchmark setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides several meaningful validity controls: salted stable-hash selection, provenance and licensing metadata, agent/evaluator view separation, leakage checks, answer-availability checks, escalation verification, three-attempt offline model-tier verification, independently checked false-premise tasks, expected-fail smoke tests, and SHA256-bound result artifacts. It reports a 50,000-draw cost perturbation analysis per seven family/decision strata, but this tests robustness of relative trace ordering rather than price realism. Evaluation uses one temperature-zero episode per main task and does not report multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. A judge scores open-ended answers with a fixed rubric; one reviewer relabeled 96 responses, obtaining 91.7% agreement and κ=0.833, but the study does not measure human-human agreement and all eight disagreements were judge false positives. Grounding is coarse for several QA families because evidence access is checked rather than entailment from cited spans. The task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen environments, and integrity-bound artifacts are stated to be released, but no URL or repository is provided in the paper text. The benchmark is partly constructed from existing datasets and offline model-capability labels, which creates risks that transformations or labels encode the intended decision and that the benchmark measures constructor-defined action classes more than open-ended deployment economics. Baselines are useful for construct validity but the scripted controls have oracle answer access and are explicitly not information-fair competitors; the paper does not compare against a learned cost-aware router or a strong generic agent with explicit utility optimization. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a benchmark/data-and-evaluation artifact rather than a deployed production system. Practical: The evaluated tool-API agents can run with commercially available LLM and retrieval APIs, and the benchmark provides frozen environments, but the paper does not report hardware, wall-clock, or dollar costs for the main ledger track. Efficient: The benchmark measures abstract action cost and shows large cost differences—such as 22 units for document reading versus 260 for deep research—but it does not establish memory, latency, or real billing advantages relative to alternatives; workspace proxy units are not comparable. Effective: The evidence supports the narrower claim that current agents often fail conditional economic decisions, with tool-API economic consistency only 3.6–7.3%, but it does not show that the benchmark improves deployed agent outcomes because no new controller or intervention is evaluated. Scalable: The task bundle has 304 tasks and tool loops allow up to 10 turns, but there is no experiment at 10×–100× scale, with longer trajectories, larger tool catalogs, or production traffic; scalability is therefore not demonstrated. The work delivers a reusable task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and result artifacts; a public URL is not stated, and it does not deliver a trained router or production library. Strengths: - It identifies a real evaluation failure mode: micro-averaged success can reward always-escalate policies, while low cost can reward premature termination, and it supplies a compact worst-regime diagnostic plus the underlying family matrix. - The five-family design isolates four distinct decisions—avoid escalation, warranted escalation, model-tier routing, and stop-loss behavior—rather than appending a cost column to a conventional completion benchmark. - The transformation and packaging protocol is unusually explicit about leakage, provenance, frozen evidence, evaluator-only information, budget validation, and integrity-bound result reproduction. - The budget sweep produces a substantive empirical finding beyond a static leaderboard: GPT-5.4 barely responds when escalation becomes affordable, whereas Gemini increases unnecessary escalation when more budget is available. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that realism review covers only 45/304 tasks, main LLM runs are single-shot at temperature zero, judge calibration uses one human reviewer, and grounding is often evidence access rather than answer entailment. They acknowledge that costs are abstract rather than dollar estimates, workspace execution proxies do not implement the shared ledger, workspace templates may cue the action class, and workspace results cannot support cross-track tool-economy or cost comparisons. They also note that the main tool-API leaderboard uses one balanced-prompt episode per task and that budget sweeps use family-specific grids, limiting claims about absolute cost, prompt robustness, and cross-interface comparisons. The paper confronts these limitations directly and narrows its conclusions accordingly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The benchmark's canonical decisions and model-tier labels are partly author-defined, so the paper does not establish inter-annotator reliability or independent external validation for most of the 304 task labels. Only 10 stop-loss items and 7 frozen-information items make those regimes statistically fragile, and no uncertainty intervals are provided for differences between agents. The evaluation lacks a learned or optimization-based cost-aware routing baseline, human or expert policy baseline without oracle answer access, and ablations showing whether paired regimes, high-regret traces, budget prompts, or evidence-access checks drive observed behavior. The coarse grounding check may overstate answer quality, while one temperature-zero episode cannot characterize stochastic policy reliability. The abstract cost schedule is robust under perturbation but remains disconnected from actual provider prices, latency, failure rates, tool quality, and changing budget objectives. Finally, the benchmark evaluates mostly QA-like information seeking rather than coding, database, transactional, or multi-agent workloads where economic decisions may involve irreversible actions and non-answer rewards. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile benchmark paper for researchers studying cost-aware agent control because its regime-balanced design and budget-sweep evidence reveal failures that standard completion metrics miss, but its conclusions should be treated as benchmark-specific until independent labels, stronger routing baselines, larger decision families, and real deployment-cost validation are added.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a lightweight expert-pruning criterion that fine-tunes an MoE briefly with a parameter-efficient adapter, ranks experts by router or router-logit sensitivity, and removes the least-sensitive experts without retraining. - Why it's important: MoE deployment retains all expert parameters in memory even though only a few experts execute per token, so reliable pruning can reduce memory and latency without requiring full-model fine-tuning. - How it does it: It treats PEFT as a task-conditioned measurement instrument, using per-layer changes in router-weight norms—or held-out router-logit shifts when the router is frozen—to rank experts for one-shot deletion. - The good: On Mixtral-8×7B-Instruct, router-only rank-8 LoRA trains about 0.0022% of parameters and retains 27.54% MMLU-Pro accuracy after removing half the experts per layer, versus 15.88% for magnitude pruning and 16.31% for random pruning; rank 16 reaches 28.76%. - The missing: The main comparison against modern activation- and optimization-based pruning methods is cross-paper rather than controlled on the same checkpoint, calibration data, evaluation harness, and compute budget, and the strongest adaptation-geometry comparisons use unmatched training budgets. - Read it or not: MoE compression researchers and practitioners who already perform PEFT should read it for the router-only instrumentation recipe and its careful analysis of task conditioning, while readers seeking broad evidence across current MoE architectures should treat it as an initial empirical study rather than a definitive benchmark.

Problem & Motivation MoE language models reduce per-token computation by activating only a subset of experts, but deployment still requires storing every expert, making memory—not arithmetic—the principal compression bottleneck. The problem affects practitioners deploying large sparse language models on constrained hardware, especially when a model has many expert parameters but only a few active experts. Existing expert-pruning criteria typically use frozen-checkpoint statistics such as weight magnitude, router usage, activation norms, reconstruction error, or search-based subset selection; these can miss task-specific functional importance. A prior theoretical criterion uses changes in router norms during full fine-tuning to identify experts that can be pruned with an accuracy guarantee, but full fine-tuning a 46.7B-parameter model is economically inconsistent with the goal of compression. The paper addresses the narrower gap of whether this task-conditioned router signal can be recovered using a much cheaper PEFT run and whether it transfers from simplified or vision MoEs to instruction-tuned language MoEs and reasoning benchmarks. Key Idea The central insight is to use fine-tuning not primarily to improve the deployed model, but as an instrument that exposes which experts the task causes the model to recruit or revise. An expert whose router treatment changes little under task pressure is treated as a pruning candidate. The paper further argues that the perturbation geometry matters: adaptation should be expressive enough to reveal task-induced routing changes but constrained enough not to solve the task by arbitrarily changing attention, expert computation, or representations. This explains why router-only LoRA and multiplicative IA3 produce better rankings than broad LoRA or unconstrained additive Houlsby adapters. The direction-agnostic absolute norm change used in the experiments is a modification of the prior signed theoretical criterion, so the empirical method is not identical to the formally guaranteed one. Methodology The model is a decoder-only Transformer with an MoE feed-forward block at each layer. For a router matrix W_g whose expert rows are w_e, the primary score is s_e = | ||w_e^(T)||_2 - ||w_e^(0)||_2 |, computed after a short PEFT run and ranked independently within each layer; the n lowest-scoring experts are structurally deleted from the original, not adapted, checkpoint, and the router rows are deleted correspondingly. When the router remains frozen, the paper computes a held-out-token logit score s_e^logit = ||L_adapt[:,e] - L_base[:,e]||_2 / sqrt(N). The main Mixtral pipeline uses 4-bit QLoRA, 500 steps of 8-bit AdamW, learning rate 2×10^-4, sequence length 1024, and a rank sweep over {2, 4, 8, 16}; the canonical configuration attaches LoRA only to router weights. Controlled experiments vary target modules, rank, and adaptation family, comparing router-only LoRA, all-module LoRA, IA3, and Houlsby adapters. Critical design decisions are mostly well-motivated: per-layer ranking follows the observed nonuniform sensitivity map; router-only attachment tests whether the measured decision mechanism is isolated; and discarding adapters and avoiding post-pruning repair isolates selection quality. However, the absolute-value score departs from the signed theoretical guarantee, the logit-based and weight-based scores are not always compared under matched training conditions, and IA3/Houlsby use a different data budget and schedule from the LoRA sweeps. Key Results On Mixtral-8×7B-Instruct-v0.1, the unpruned model scores 44.83% on MMLU-Pro at 46.7B parameters. Removing one, two, three, or four of eight experts per layer leaves 41.1B, 35.4B, 29.8B, or 24.2B parameters, respectively. Router-only rank-8 LoRA yields 40.18%, 35.78%, 31.37%, and 27.54% MMLU-Pro accuracy at these four pruning depths; all-module LoRA yields 39.87%, 34.86%, 30.04%, and 24.42%. At four experts removed, router-only selection exceeds magnitude pruning at 15.88% and random pruning at 16.31% by 11.66 and 11.23 points. Increasing router-only LoRA rank from 2 to 16 improves the four-expert-pruned score from 23.42% to 28.76%, with trainable parameters rising from 0.0006% to 0.0045% of the model. IA3 obtains 40.27%, 36.11%, 32.48%, and 28.04%, statistically interpreted by the authors as a tie with LoRA because the differences are within the approximately 2.2-point single-comparison resolution; Houlsby reaches 40.08%, 35.52%, 30.71%, and 25.39%. On additional Mixtral benchmarks, the generic-instruction selection retains 46.59% ARC-Challenge accuracy after four experts are removed, 36.04% or 33.25% BIG-Bench Hard depending on selection, 12.05% GSM8K, and 62.10% BoolQ; GSM8K therefore exhibits a capability cliff rather than quasi-linear degradation. On Qwen1.5-MoE evaluated over eleven mathematical benchmarks, router sensitivity retains 49.7% mean accuracy after removing 10 of 20 experts, versus 39.1% for magnitude and 4.4% for random pruning. Deployment measurements on one A100 with 4-bit weights show memory falling from 24.2GB to 12.3GB and per-token latency from 40.3ms to 25.2ms at four experts retained, corresponding to 49% lower memory, 37% lower latency, and 60% higher single-stream relative throughput. Comparisons with prior methods are competitive at 25% compression and on ARC at 50%, but weaker on GSM8K and BoolQ at 50%; these are cross-paper comparisons with differing pruning allocations, calibration regimes, and evaluation settings rather than head-to-head results. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper’s main new method is recovering a theoretically motivated router-sensitivity pruning signal with brief PEFT and extending it to router-logit shifts when the router is frozen; its empirical contributions are the first reported validation on Mixtral/Qwen language MoEs, the controlled evidence that router-only scope and adaptation geometry affect ranking quality, and the observation that IA3 can match direct router adaptation. The underlying sensitivity criterion, LoRA, IA3, Houlsby adapters, and structural expert deletion are existing ideas, so the novelty lies in repurposing PEFT as an instrument and characterizing the conditions under which that instrument yields useful rankings, not in inventing a fundamentally new pruning objective or MoE architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes controlled sweeps over module scope and LoRA rank, comparisons among three adaptation geometries, four independently configured Mixtral runs, and repeated runs for three rank settings. It explicitly estimates run variability: paired runs differ by 0.76 accuracy points on average and at most 2.24 points, leading the authors to use approximately 2.2 points as the resolution of a single comparison. The monotonic rank trend is supported by consistent ordering across twelve adjacent comparisons and replication, although individual adjacent differences are often below the stated resolution. Standard errors of 1.4 points are reported for GSM8K and ARC. The main limitations are the absence of a controlled same-checkpoint comparison against strong activation-norm, reconstruction, differentiable-search, and trajectory-based baselines; reliance on cross-paper retention numbers for much of the comparative claim; unmatched budgets between LoRA and IA3/Houlsby; and mostly single-run results for the controlled sweeps. The Qwen experiment is not a clean test on the original model because the 60-expert checkpoint was first reduced to 20 experts using router sensitivity under hardware constraints. Code, configurations, scoring/pruning/evaluation implementations, and pruned Mixtral checkpoints are released at https://github.com/ianKa1/MoE_pruning and https://huggingface.co/collections/Na0s/pruned-moes-mixtral-8x7b-instruct-v01. The manuscript is an arXiv preprint (v1, dated 8 August 2026 in the supplied text), not a peer-reviewed publication. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper provides and evaluates a structural pruning procedure and deployable checkpoints, while its evidence is primarily experimental. Practical: The method runs on commercially available NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, uses standard PEFT/QLoRA tooling, and produces ordinary pruned checkpoints without retaining adapter parameters, although the adaptation and serialization workflow still requires substantial infrastructure for a 46.7B-parameter model. Efficient: Router-only LoRA trains roughly 0.0022% of Mixtral parameters at rank 8, and four-expert pruning reduces 4-bit memory from 24.2GB to 12.3GB and latency from 40.3ms to 25.2ms per token; however, the paper does not report the wall-clock or energy cost of adaptation relative to calibration-only baselines. Effective: The method substantially outperforms magnitude and random pruning at severe Mixtral compression and retains 49.7% mean accuracy on the Qwen mathematics suite at 50% expert removal, but effectiveness is capability-dependent: GSM8K falls from 51.25% to 12.05% at maximal Mixtral pruning, so the method does not preserve all downstream tasks uniformly. Scalable: The experiments cover Mixtral with eight experts per layer and a Qwen-derived 20-expert checkpoint, not 10×–100× larger models or substantially different MoE designs; the paper claims broader transfer but directly tests only two model families and does not measure behavior at frontier-scale deployment loads or multi-request serving. The work delivers a reusable software artifact, released pruning and scoring code, configurations, and pruned Mixtral checkpoints; it does not deliver a new general-purpose library or a formal proof extending the prior guarantee. Strengths - It identifies a practically meaningful use of PEFT: a tiny router-only adaptation can serve as a task-conditioned measurement phase, after which the adapter is discarded and the deployed artifact contains no additional parameters. - The controlled module and rank sweeps support a specific mechanistic explanation rather than only reporting a pruning curve: broader adaptation dilutes router changes, while insufficient rank produces misleading rankings, especially at high compression. - The paper distinguishes evidence from resolution unusually clearly, reporting replication variability and refusing to interpret many sub-two-point differences as meaningful. - It measures deployment consequences directly on hardware, showing near-linear memory and latency reductions rather than inferring them only from parameter counts, and exposes an important failure mode in which generic adaptation preserves broad capabilities but fails on GSM8K-style arithmetic. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that the theory guarantees the signed norm-change criterion, whereas experiments use the absolute change; that controlled sweeps focus primarily on one coarse-grained MoE family; that IA3 and Houlsby comparisons use unmatched budgets; that the cross-paper baseline comparison is confounded by different datasets, allocations, and harnesses; that results are one-shot and omit router calibration, distillation, or retraining; that configuration selection is keyed to MMLU-Pro; that the Qwen experiment begins from a sensitivity-selected 20-expert checkpoint rather than the original 60-expert model; and that attention-only and expert-only adaptation under the logit score, sign-based reranking, and constrained-adaptation theory remain open. The paper confronts these limitations directly and proposes corresponding experiments rather than presenting the claims as universal. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The strongest practical claim—competitiveness with modern pruning methods—is not established by a controlled head-to-head study using the same checkpoint, calibration/adaptation corpus, sample count, pruning allocation, repair policy, and evaluation harness; cross-paper normalized retention can hide substantial confounds. - The paper does not quantify the absolute compute, wall-clock time, memory peak, or energy required for the PEFT measurement phase, so the claimed economic advantage over calibration-only criteria is not fully costed. - The central mechanism is plausible but not causally isolated: the module ladder is incomplete under the logit score, and the IA3/Houlsby comparisons vary training budget, sequence length, and optimization settings in addition to perturbation geometry. - The use of uniform pruning across layers is convenient but leaves open whether sensitivity-guided nonuniform allocation would yield materially better accuracy at the same parameter budget, especially compared with baselines that learn layer-specific sparsity. - The evaluation lacks end-to-end generative quality, safety, calibration, long-context, throughput-under-concurrency, and memory-fragmentation measurements, which limits conclusions about production deployment beyond single-stream A100 decoding. - The Qwen transfer result is informative but partially circular because the evaluated 20-expert checkpoint was itself created with the proposed criterion; a clean evaluation on the original 60-expert model or an independently compressed starting point would provide stronger evidence of cross-family generalization. Bottom Line This is a useful and unusually disciplined empirical study for MoE compression: practitioners who already fine-tune Mixtral-like models can obtain a cheap, released pruning recipe with substantial memory and latency savings, but the paper should not yet displace strong activation-based or learned pruning methods because its comparative evidence is not controlled and its architectural coverage is narrow.

Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Align-RAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented forecasting method that amplitude- and phase-aligns retrieved past–future windows before presenting them as demonstrations to a frozen time-series foundation model. - Why it's important: It reduces the need for labeled data, per-domain fine-tuning, or learned fusion modules when adapting frozen forecasting models to new time-series distributions. - How it does it: It applies a regularized closed-form affine transformation and an integer-lag cross-correlation shift to each retrieved pair, then combines the frozen model's forecast with a distance-weighted retrieved-future prior and a second query-only pass. - The good: On the seven-dataset TS-RAG benchmark with frozen Chronos-Bolt, it improves MSE on all 7 datasets, averaging 3.75% relative reduction, while using no learned parameters; it also beats trained RAFT on all 8 reported ETT/horizon cells. - The missing: The strongest attribution claim is tested only on Chronos-Bolt, and the evaluation remains confined largely to univariate benchmark datasets without multivariate covariates, realistic deployment shifts, or broad comparisons against every competitive retrieval method. - Read it or not: Researchers working on retrieval-augmented time-series forecasting or in-context learning should read it for the alignment mechanism and behavioral analysis; practitioners seeking evidence on multivariate or production-scale forecasting can treat it as an informative but incomplete benchmark study.

Problem & Motivation: Frozen time-series foundation models can forecast unseen series without fine-tuning, but their performance may degrade when the target distribution differs from pretraining data. Retrieval-augmented forecasting addresses this gap by supplying past–future examples from a reference corpus, yet recent TSFM methods generally train adapters, projection heads, retrievers, or fusion modules to make the backbone use those examples. The paper targets the more specific problem of whether retrieved demonstrations can be made useful to an unchanged TSFM through inference-time transformation alone, particularly when retrieved windows resemble the query structurally but differ in amplitude and temporal phase. The evaluated application domain is univariate forecasting across energy, weather, exchange-rate, and electricity datasets. Key Idea: The central insight is that retrievals need to be aligned to the query before entering the model, rather than fused after the frozen backbone has processed incompatible demonstrations. A per-example affine transformation matches the retrieved past's level and scale to the query, and a shared lag shift aligns temporal phase; applying the identical transformation to the future preserves the past–future relationship. This makes the demonstrations resemble regression examples in the query's coordinate system, allowing the frozen TSFM's in-context behavior to produce a ridge-like prediction update without learned fusion. Methodology: For each query past q of length S=512, the method retrieves 20 past–future pairs and selects K=10 using maximal marginal relevance with λ=0.3. For each selected pair, it estimates a regularized affine map with slope a_i = σ_q σ_{p_i}/(σ_{p_i}^2 + (σ_q/M)^2), intercept b_i = μ_q − a_i μ_{p_i}, and M=5; it applies this map to both past and future. It then selects an integer lag τ_i* within ±S/4=128 by maximizing normalized sample cross-correlation between the query and transformed retrieved past, applying the same lag to the future. The aligned examples are packed into a 2048-token Chronos-Bolt budget using two 256-step demonstrations and eight 32-step demonstrations, each retaining the full 64-step future. The frozen TSFM produces an in-context forecast fθ(C), which is blended with a distance-weighted retrieved-future prior using β=0.15 and temperature τ equal to one-fifth of the median retrieval distance. A second query-only pass is combined with the in-context prediction using α=0.60. The key design decisions—Wiener-style amplitude shrinkage, paired phase transfer, and tiered context packing—are operationally motivated by numerical stability and token limits, although the choices of M, β, α, and the layout are principally supported by ablations rather than a formal selection procedure. The paper also computes a closed-form ridge forecast, y_ridge = Qᵀ(PᵀP+λI)⁻¹PᵀF with λ=1, and compares its shift from zero-shot output with the model's demonstration-induced shift. Key Results: Against the released TS-RAG top-20 retrieval index and trained TS-RAG mixer on frozen Chronos-Bolt with S=512 and H=64, Align-RAG achieves MSE/MAE of 0.3434/0.3612 on ETTh1 versus 0.3556/0.3623, 0.2379/0.2964 on ETTh2 versus 0.2451/0.2981, 0.2671/0.3047 on ETTm1 versus 0.2904/0.3113, 0.1384/0.2188 on ETTm2 versus 0.1465/0.2230, 0.1372/0.1729 on Weather versus 0.1453/0.1770, 0.0620/0.1715 on Exchange versus 0.0624/0.1716, and 0.1119/0.2018 on Electricity versus 0.1120/0.2003. It wins 7/7 datasets in MSE, 6/7 in MAE, and averages −3.75% MSE and −0.93% MAE relative to TS-RAG; five of six small-dataset MSE comparisons have bootstrap intervals excluding zero, while the very large Electricity test set is not assigned a confidence interval. A retriever-by-alignment ablation shows that disabling alignment increases MSE by roughly 20–22% relative to zero-shot, whereas switching from ranked to random retrieval costs only 0.84 percentage points on average. Across Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.0, Moirai, and Toto, the method changes zero-shot MSE by −4.14%, −3.83%, −5.53%, −13.73%, and −2.45% respectively; however, Toto regresses on 4/7 datasets and TimesFM regresses on Exchange. At H=96 and H=192 on five datasets, it improves MSE in every cell by 1.20–6.59%. Against RAFT, it wins all 8 reported ETT/horizon cells with an average 4.5% MSE reduction. Mechanistically, the mean cosine similarity between model and ridge prediction shifts rises from 0.30 unaligned to 0.45 aligned, with the paired bootstrap excluding zero on all seven Chronos-Bolt datasets; future shuffling reverses the ETTm1 gain from −4.2% to +12.2%, supporting dependence on past–future pairing rather than simple future averaging. These are meaningful benchmark improvements, but the datasets are standard and mostly periodic, and the practical significance of 0.07% on Electricity or 0.69% on Exchange is small. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the genuinely new contribution is the use of closed-form, pair-preserving amplitude and phase alignment to elicit useful in-context behavior from frozen TSFMs without training, while MMR selection, token packing, retrieved-future blending, and consensus averaging are established or straightforward inference-time components. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes a retriever-by-alignment 2×2 ablation, cumulative and leave-one-out component ablations, multi-horizon evaluation, cross-backbone testing, a future-shuffle control, and sensitivity analysis for α. It reports paired moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals with block lengths of 24 or 20 and 2,000 resamples for several comparisons; deterministic Chronos-Bolt inference means test-window sampling is the relevant randomness, but the paper does not report multiple model seeds or conventional significance tests across all backbone and dataset results. The main head-to-head comparison reuses TS-RAG's released retrieval index and checkpoint, with reproduced TS-RAG numbers within 0.3% of its paper, which improves fairness but limits comparison to that implementation. The cross-backbone index is rebuilt from train splits with a stated leakage filter. Code, index-building scripts, and bootstrap seeds are released at https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag; the implementation is approximately 720 lines of Python, and no learned weights are required. Remaining concerns include substantial reliance on a single benchmark family, incomplete uncertainty reporting for large or cross-backbone tables, and possible benchmark-specific tuning of fixed hyperparameters and post-processing choices. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL with a systems-like inference pipeline. * Practical: The method runs on commercially available hardware; the authors report evaluating the seven Chronos-Bolt datasets on one H100 in under six hours, although CPU cost, retrieval-index construction time, and latency per query are not stated. * Efficient: It avoids adapter training and adds inexpensive affine/lag operations, but it uses retrieval search, ten demonstrations, a retrieved-future blend, and two frozen-model forward passes, so end-to-end inference cost relative to zero-shot forecasting or trained TS-RAG is not quantified. * Effective: The evidence shows lower MSE on the stated benchmark and consistent gains over zero-shot across most tested backbones, but it measures benchmark forecast error rather than operational outcomes such as calibration, decision quality, robustness to missing data, or real deployment shifts. * Scalable: The paper tests up to 1.67 million Electricity windows and reports H=64–192, but it does not test 10×–100× larger retrieval corpora, longer contexts, higher-dimensional multivariate inputs, distributed serving, or production throughput; scalability beyond the reported setup is therefore a claim rather than an established result. The work delivers a reusable software artifact and code repository, but not a new trained model, dataset, or general-purpose retrieval library. Strengths: - The method identifies a simple, parameter-free intervention that directly challenges the field's assumption that learned fusion is necessary, and the main comparison shows gains over a trained TS-RAG mixer rather than only over zero-shot baselines. - The retriever-by-alignment ablation isolates alignment as the dominant factor: removing alignment causes approximately 20–22% MSE degradation, while random retrieval with alignment remains competitive on four of seven datasets. - The future-shuffle control is a stronger mechanistic test than attention visualization alone: preserving the futures but breaking pair correspondence produces directional error changes consistent with regression on corrupted pairs. - The method transfers without per-backbone tuning to four additional TSFMs and to longer horizons, and the released code, retrieval scripts, and resampling seeds support reproduction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the mechanism evidence is correlational rather than a proof of ridge equivalence; the average aligned-versus-unaligned signature is 0.45 rather than 1. They acknowledge that evaluation uses a standard univariate TS-RAG benchmark, leaving multivariate covariates and distribution shifts open, and that the retriever-by-alignment attribution ablation is performed only on Chronos-Bolt. They also identify richer retrieval geometries and cross-backbone attribution studies as future work, confronting rather than hiding these boundaries. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not evaluate on real multivariate forecasting settings, exogenous covariates, nonstationary regime changes, missing or irregular observations, or operational metrics such as uncertainty calibration and decision utility. Although RAFT is included in an appendix comparison and TS-RAG is the principal head-to-head baseline, the main study does not provide a uniform, independently rerun comparison against all listed methods such as TimeRAF, RATD, TimeRAG, or TimesFM-ICF. The strongest causal attribution—that alignment rather than retrieval quality explains the gain—remains Chronos-Bolt-only, and the cross-backbone experiments change the retrieval index, making attribution less clean there. Some component effects are small or dataset-dependent: phase alignment is nearly irrelevant on ETTh1 in leave-one-out testing, Toto regresses on most datasets, and Exchange is near a zero-shot noise floor. The reported bootstrap treatment is incomplete for several tables, and there is no analysis of retrieval latency, memory footprint, index size, or the cost of the two-forward-pass configuration. Finally, fixed hyperparameters are reused across datasets but appear selected using the same benchmark family, so the paper does not fully rule out benchmark-level validation or hidden researcher degrees of freedom. Bottom Line: This is a strong and practically useful preprint for TSFM and retrieval-augmented forecasting researchers because it replaces a trained fusion baseline with a simple reproducible alignment procedure and supplies credible ablations plus a nontrivial mechanism probe, but its broader claims should remain limited until validated on multivariate, shifted, and independently curated forecasting workloads.

SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries (71 ▲ )

Xingyu Tan, Xiaoyang Wang, Qing Liu, Xiwei Xu, Xin Yuan, Liming Zhu, Wenjie Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SkillZip, a procedural-memory system that converts agent skill packages into typed section graphs, compresses recurring contract-compatible subgraphs into reversible macros, and hydrates task-specific executable contexts. - Why it's important: Large skill libraries can overwhelm agents with redundant or incomplete context, increasing prompt cost, retrieval ambiguity, tool errors, and verifier failures. - How it does it: Sec2Graph extracts source-grounded procedural sections and contracts, MotifZip performs typed graph-motif compression subject to boundary, dependency, and verifier checks, PathHydrate retrieves and progressively expands dependency-closed subgraphs, and ReZip updates macros using new skills and execution traces. - The good: Across SkillsBench and ALFWorld, two primary backbones, six additional backbones, and five repeated-run evaluations, SkillZip improves task performance while reducing context and trajectory cost; for example, it raises MiniMax-M2.7 performance over SkillDAG from 27.3 to 33.3 on SkillsBench and from 67.1% to 79.3% on ALFWorld. - The missing: The central contract representation is produced by model-assisted extraction, yet the paper does not establish that extracted contracts are semantically complete or that verifier reachability reliably predicts real execution correctness outside the evaluated benchmarks. - Read it or not: Researchers working on LLM-agent memory, skill retrieval, or context compilation should read it for the section-level contract abstraction and extensive systems evaluation, while readers seeking a formally verified compression method or evidence from production-scale skill ecosystems should wait for stronger external validation.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses context selection and procedural-memory management for LLM agents whose reusable knowledge is stored as editable skill packages containing instructions, tools, resources, execution steps, and verifiers. The affected domains include technical artifact construction and embodied household interaction. Existing systems generally retrieve whole skills, compress their text, or construct graphs only after retrieval; this creates a granularity mismatch that prevents reuse of shared internal routines, loads unrelated procedures, and can remove preconditions, dependencies, guards, or verification hooks. The specific research gap is persistent, source-grounded, cross-skill compression at the level of execution-complete subprocedures rather than whole packages or text spans, together with maintenance as skills and execution evidence evolve. Key Idea: The core insight is to make a contract-bearing section subgraph—not a skill package or text span—the common unit for retrieval, compression, execution, and maintenance. Repeated motifs are replaced only when their typed external interface, internal dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source expansion mapping remain valid, so compression becomes a reversible graph rewrite rather than a lossy textual summary. Methodology: Sec2Graph first segments each skill package using headings, lists, code blocks, warnings, tool references, and tests, optionally using an LLM-assisted parser to refine boundaries. It assigns each section one or more of nine execution roles—Intent, Trigger, Input, Precondition, Operation, Resource, Failure, Verifier, and Output—and extracts input/output signatures, resources, guards, effects, verifier hooks, dependencies, and source pointers. It then constructs occurrence-specific procedural subgraphs and links compatible occurrences to canonical prototypes. MotifZip buckets nodes by role, resource family, and I/O shape; grows typed candidate subgraphs; matches non-conflicting occurrences; builds a macro contract; and accepts a motif only if its boundary is clear, signatures are stable, dependencies are closed or exposed through ports, and every state-changing operation retains a reachable verifier. Accepted motifs are ranked by a description-length-style gain, reuse benefit, boundary-cut penalty, and risk penalty, then greedily rewritten as ported macros with reversible source maps. PathHydrate converts a query and executor profile into goals, outputs, capabilities, inputs, and subgoals; fuses dense section-level scores with skill-level rankings using reciprocal-rank fusion; searches for a compact connected subgraph; repairs missing input, precondition, resource, failure, verifier, and output scaffolding; and renders macros at name, contract, outline, or full-source granularity under a token budget. ReZip assimilates new skills through existing macros, buffers unmatched residuals, promotes recurring contract-valid residual motifs, and revises risky macros using expansion frequency, verifier failures, and downstream repair cost. The paper gives an explicit objective for context compilation and a compression-gain function, but many key operations—segmentation, role inference, contract extraction, seed construction, and graph search heuristics—remain implementation-level procedures rather than fully specified formal algorithms. The three main design choices—section-level units, hard contract checks, and progressive hydration—are supported by ablations; the weights and thresholds are reported, but their tuning methodology and sensitivity are only partially described. Key Results: On SkillsBench with MiniMax-M2.7, SkillZip obtains 33.3 reward versus 27.3 for SkillDAG, 18.7 for GoS, 10.4 for Vector Skills, and 17.2 for Vanilla Skills; on ALFWorld it obtains 79.3% success versus 67.1% for SkillDAG. With gpt-5.2-codex, SkillZip reaches 43.0 on SkillsBench versus 36.8 for SkillDAG and 96.4% on ALFWorld versus 93.6%. On the 1K-skill SkillsBench setting, it reports a 3.46x compression ratio, 1,941 average rendered tokens, 99.2% dependency preservation, 98.7% verifier reachability, and 14.8% query-level recovery compared with 6,716 tokens for the raw section graph. Relative to SkillDAG, it reduces rendered context from 3,103 to 1,941 tokens, online retrieval/hydration latency from 41.2 to 27.9 ms, total trajectory prompt tokens by 47.0%, tool calls by 21.7%, and task time from 429.7 to 339.0 seconds in the reported MiniMax-M2.7 setting. The main ablation shows that removing section-level units lowers reward from 33.3 to 27.9 and Ret@1 from 73.6 to 66.7; removing dependency closure lowers dependency preservation to 82.3%; removing verifier constraints lowers verifier reachability to 76.4%; and disabling adaptive hydration raises rendered tokens to 2,587. At 100K candidate skills, SkillZip reports 65.1 Ret@1, 12.4% similar-skill confusion, 248.3 ms online retrieval/hydration latency, 4.29x compression, and 178 seconds for local graph construction and MotifZip over 4.77 million cached section nodes. Contract extraction reaches 91.6 macro-F1 and 84.6 exact match on a human-annotated subset. Under synthetic corruption of 10% of contract fields, reward falls from 33.3 to 31.6 and verifier reachability from 98.7% to 95.1%; at 40% corruption, reward falls to 24.1 and verifier reachability to 77.2%. In streaming maintenance, ReZip reaches 3.64x compression, 33.2 reward, and 98.6% verifier reachability at 0.22x the normalized cost of periodic full recompression. Five matched runs yield statistically significant gains over SkillDAG in all four main backbone-benchmark combinations, with paired gains from 2.8 to 12.2 points and reported p-values from .031 to less than .001. These are substantial benchmark results, although the strongest comparisons are against recent but mostly arXiv-based systems and the 100K-scale experiment adds distractor skills rather than demonstrating a naturally occurring 100K-skill deployment. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING—the genuinely new element is the unified use of source-grounded section-level procedural graphs with contract-checked reversible macro rewriting and task-time hydration, while typed graph grammars, dense retrieval, reciprocal-rank fusion, progressive disclosure, and incremental graph maintenance are established techniques adapted to this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a strong ablation suite, structural-fidelity comparisons against exact-text deduplication, LLMLingua-2-style text compression, generic graph grammar, and unchecked SkillZip, controlled overlap experiments, library-scale retrieval tests, streaming-maintenance comparisons, failure attribution, cross-domain results, six-backbone evaluation, and five repeated matched runs with paired bootstrap confidence intervals and permutation tests. The ablations isolate the practical contribution of section-level units, dependency checks, verifier checks, global rescue, and adaptive hydration. The evaluation uses deterministic artifact verifiers on SkillsBench and fixed action budgets on ALFWorld, which is stronger than relying solely on LLM judgments. However, the method depends on LLM-generated segmentation, role labels, signatures, guards, and verifier hooks; the human-annotated extraction set and annotation protocol are not characterized in the supplied text sufficiently to assess coverage or inter-annotator agreement. The reported dependency-preservation and verifier-reachability metrics are partly aligned with the acceptance checks used to construct the representation, creating a possible circularity: the system defines and then measures preservation of recorded contracts, not necessarily preservation of the underlying procedure's semantics. The robustness study uses synthetic field corruption rather than naturally occurring extraction errors. The paper does not mention a released code repository, dataset, model weights, or artifact URL; therefore public reproducibility is not stated. Baseline policies are retained rather than strictly equalized by token budget, and SkillZip receives a structured task-anchoring stage whose quality and cost are excluded from online latency comparisons, although the same backbone performs anchoring for all methods where applicable. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile. Practical: The local graph pipeline runs on commercially available CPU hardware—the reported measurements use an Intel Xeon Gold 6248R with 512 GB RAM—and the agent interface targets existing OpenHands, Docker, text-action, and remote-LLM execution setups, but fresh LLM-based contract extraction adds provider-dependent deployment cost. Efficient: At 1K SkillsBench skills, SkillZip reduces active storage from 18.6 MB to 5.4 MB, renders 1,941 rather than 3,103 tokens versus SkillDAG, and takes 27.9 ms rather than 41.2 ms for local retrieval and rendering; the 112.4 MB source library must still remain available for expansion, and the paper excludes provider inference from the reported retrieval latency. Effective: The evidence shows improved benchmark reward, retrieval quality, tool-call count, task time, and structural metrics, including a 6.0-point SkillsBench gain and 12.2-point ALFWorld gain over SkillDAG in the main MiniMax-M2.7 setting, but it evaluates benchmark task success rather than production reliability or semantic correctness of arbitrary skills. Scalable: The implementation reaches 100K candidate skills and 4.77 million cached section nodes with 65.1 Ret@1, 248.3 ms online latency, and 178 seconds of local construction, but this is a fixed-query distractor-scaling experiment and excludes the fresh LLM extraction cost; behavior at 10x–100x beyond the tested scale, under continual high-rate updates, or with substantially more heterogeneous skill formats is not evaluated. The work delivers a procedural-memory software design and benchmark implementation, but no public software artifact or repository is stated. Strengths: - The section-level procedural unit addresses a concrete failure mode of whole-skill retrieval and is supported by a clear ablation: removing section-level nodes drops reward by 5.4 points and increases rendered context by 59.9%. - MotifZip distinguishes structural reversibility from semantic correctness and explicitly preserves ports, dependencies, verifier paths, occurrence identity, and source provenance; the comparison against unchecked compression shows that these checks materially affect reward, fallback, and downstream inflation. - The evaluation measures more than end-task reward: it reports retrieval ranking, context size, active storage, dependency preservation, verifier reachability, source fallback, trajectory tokens, tool calls, latency, maintenance cost, repeated-run confidence intervals, and failure attribution. - The 100K-library scaling experiment and ReZip streaming experiment extend beyond a single static benchmark snapshot, although both remain controlled evaluations rather than production deployments. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly states that the structural lifting proposition guarantees recovery of recorded interfaces, dependencies, verifier paths, and provenance but does not establish semantic equivalence of unrecorded behavior or correctness of the verifiers. It also acknowledges that MotifZip's conflict-aware greedy rewrite is tractable but not globally optimal, that contract extraction is a central requirement, and that extraction quality degrades under corruption. The failure analysis reports that SkillZip-controlled stages account for 58% of remaining failures: retrieval 26%, contract extraction 18%, and hydration 14%; it further identifies implicit preconditions, resource requirements, underspecified verifier hooks, tight budgets, and ambiguous anchors as failure sources. The authors distinguish cached-contract graph scaling from fresh LLM extraction and explicitly exclude provider inference from local latency measurements. They do not, in the supplied text, discuss the external validity of benchmark-generated skill libraries, possible circularity in structural metrics, or fairness implications of unequal baseline disclosure policies. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The primary gap is semantic validation: dependency preservation and verifier reachability measure graph bookkeeping and path availability, not whether extracted contracts, operations, guards, or verifiers faithfully represent the source procedure or produce correct outcomes under unseen conditions. The paper's hard checks may inherit errors from LLM extraction, yet the evaluation largely compares systems built from the same processed skill representations and uses only a limited annotated subset plus synthetic corruption. The main task results use 87 SkillsBench tasks and 140 ALFWorld episodes, while the 100K-scale test holds queries fixed and adds distractors, so the evidence does not establish performance on naturally evolving libraries with new task distributions or adversarially overlapping skills. The comparison is not fully cost-matched: SkillZip's structured task anchoring, offline extraction, and source-library retention are treated differently from baseline costs, and published baseline disclosure policies are preserved rather than normalized to one context and inference budget. The method's most important algorithmic components contain underspecified choices—model-assisted segmentation, embedding models and thresholds, candidate growth limits, subgraph search approximation, macro overlap policy, and risk-threshold calibration—making it difficult to know how sensitive results are to implementation tuning. Finally, no public code, artifact, or independent replication is identified, and the paper does not evaluate security failures such as malicious skill sections, incorrect verifier hooks, provenance tampering, or unsafe macro reuse. Bottom Line: This is a substantial and unusually well-instrumented systems paper whose section-level contract abstraction is worth reading for agent-memory and skill-retrieval researchers, but its strongest claims should be treated as benchmark evidence for structural context compilation rather than proof of semantic contract preservation or production-scale reliability.

ADIAS: Automated Design of Interactive Agentic Systems

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ADIAS, a full-code automated agent-design framework that maintains persistent issue states and uses them to select repair targets, parent agents, and revision directions across optimization rounds. - Why it's important: Automated improvement of interactive agents is expensive and failure feedback is sparse, so preserving which failures remain unresolved and which interventions worked can reduce wasted evaluations and regressions. - How it does it: A diagnostic agent converts trajectories into persistent issue records with identities, evidence, lifecycle states, and intervention histories, after which an issue manager guides focused code revisions. - The good: Across five interactive benchmarks, ADIAS reaches an average score of 78.4 versus 62.6 for the strongest reported baseline, DGM-H, a relative gain of 25.2%, with gains on every benchmark and four backbone models. - The missing: The method assumes accurate LLM-based failure diagnosis and issue association but does not measure their accuracy, attribution quality, or sensitivity to diagnostic errors. - Read it or not: Researchers working on automated agent evolution should read it for the issue-centric optimization formulation and ablations; readers seeking evidence for broad real-world deployment can defer because evaluation is limited to text-based benchmarks and small optimization budgets.
