Problem & Motivation: Tool-using LLM agents often fail because of the runtime surrounding the model rather than because of model weights alone: they lose state, misuse tools, violate interfaces, repeat actions, omit required task stages, or fail to recover from environment feedback. Existing approaches either update the target model or use fixed prompts, manually designed rules, search procedures, or fixed external models to modify isolated harness components. The unresolved problem is how to learn reusable, executable interventions across multiple runtime stages from observed target-agent failures, while preserving the target model and grounding edits in their actual downstream effect rather than their textual plausibility. Key Idea: The central insight is to make the harness editor—not the target task agent or only the resulting harness artifact—the reinforcement-learning policy. A failure-conditioned 9B engineer receives compact batches of failed trajectories, writes a constrained executable overlay around a frozen target, and is rewarded only when a fresh rerun of the same batch improves task outcomes. This turns runtime-harness construction into outcome-grounded policy learning over a lifecycle-wide edit space. Methodology: The pipeline first runs a frozen target agent on task batches, extracts only failed episodes, and compacts task constraints, action-observation excerpts, outcomes, and runtime state into a failure packet. A separate harness engineer consumes one packet and emits a serialized JSON patch containing Python hooks. The patch may intervene at episode initialization, before a model decision, before environment action execution, or after feedback; hooks can add context or hints, block or rewrite actions where supported, and trigger recovery behavior. The runtime validates and installs the patch, then reruns every task in the original batch, including tasks that initially succeeded. The engineer reward is the full-batch mean difference, r(B,P) = (1/n)Σ_i(R_i^P − R_i^0), with invalid, no-op, or incomplete patches assigned zero. Training begins with full-parameter SFT on 877 teacher-generated, executable, non-regressive examples produced by GPT-5.5 from a disjoint task split. Online training then samples K=8 patches per failure packet and applies group-relative policy optimization, normalizing each candidate's reward against the other candidates from the same packet; only engineer parameters are updated. Critical design choices are the constrained hook interface, same-batch outcome grounding, and separation of engineer and target updates. The interface improves executability and limits task-specific hard-coding, but the paper does not isolate the contribution of each constraint during training. Same-batch reruns provide a low-variance matched signal but make the objective transductive and potentially vulnerable to overfitting recurring task patterns. The SFT initialization is operationally sensible, although the benefit of SFT relative to alternative initialization and the influence of teacher filtering are only partially evaluated through a supervised-only comparison. Key Results: On 500 WebShop, 500 ALFWorld, and 300 DBBench test tasks, vanilla Qwen3.5-9B improves from 31.2% to 42.2% WebShop success, 40.6% to 53.2% ALFWorld success, and 61.0% to 65.3% DBBench success, yielding an equal-weight average increase from 44.3% to 53.6% (+9.3 points). The supervised-only engineer reaches 46.4%, while the strongest reported fixed frontier editor, GLM-5.2, reaches 48.8%; ReAct reaches 47.5%, and Self-Refine falls to 41.8%. Reflection reports 55.8% under a separate two-episode success@2 protocol and is explicitly not comparable to the single-episode rows. Direct SFT of the target raises the no-harness average to 59.2%, after which a target-specific Harness-R1 engineer reaches 64.2% (+5.0 points), with the largest improvements on ALFWorld. Across 20 unseen target configurations, target-specific patches generated from each model's own failures produce a mean +7.06-point gain; across 21 targets and three benchmarks, 56 of 63 target-benchmark combinations improve, four are unchanged, and three regress by at most 2.0 points. With only ten observed failures per benchmark, held-out success over 1,270 tasks improves by 8.9 ± 1.5 points over three seeds, compared with −4.3 ± 2.5 for Qwen3.5-397B and −0.4 ± 3.6 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro under the same sparse-evidence protocol. Lifecycle ablations on fixed patches show that removing pre-action mediation reduces average success by 3.9 points and removing post-feedback recovery by 3.3 points, while removing episode initialization and pre-decision hints costs 0.9 and 0.6 points. These results indicate meaningful gains and transfer, but the strongest generalization results use fresh failure traces from the evaluated target models, so they measure adaptive editor transfer rather than zero-shot deployment without target-specific evidence. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING—the paper formulates lifecycle-wide executable harness editing as RL over a dedicated editor and implements outcome-trained GRPO, while the individual ingredients of SFT, code generation, validation, and policy optimization are established techniques applied in a relatively new agent-runtime setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper uses disjoint SFT, RL, validation, and test task partitions, reports explicit task counts and training hyperparameters, compares against fixed prompting strategies, larger prompted models, and a supervised-only engineer, and includes held-out-task, cross-target, lifecycle-position, and qualitative analyses. Code is released at https://github.com/DeepExperience/Harness-R1, and models are released at https://huggingface.co/ShaoShuai0605/Harness-R1. However, the main benchmark results appear to use deterministic evaluation without confidence intervals, multiple evaluation seeds, or statistical significance tests; the only reported variability is across three sparse-failure evidence seeds. The SFT examples are generated and filtered using GPT-5.5, and the frontier-model comparisons depend on externally provided or vendor-described models whose prompting and implementation parity may be difficult to verify. The same-batch reward is deliberately transductive: it reruns the evidence batch and includes initially successful tasks for regression detection, but it can still optimize for recurring patterns in those batches. The held-out experiment mitigates this issue, though it uses only three seeds and one target backbone. The paper does not provide a full accounting of candidate-generation failures, wall-clock training cost, patch-generation cost, rerun cost, or inference overhead. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The engineer and target are 9B-scale models and the released runtime uses a constrained Python-hook interface, so execution is feasible on commercially available GPU hardware, although the reported training runs require a node with eight NVIDIA H800 GPUs. Efficient: The method is not shown to be efficient relative to alternatives because each GRPO group evaluates eight candidate patches through full target-agent reruns, and neither training compute nor added inference latency is quantified. Effective: Evidence on three interactive benchmarks, held-out tasks, unseen target models, and lifecycle ablations shows substantial success-rate gains over the unmodified target and several baselines, but the evaluation remains a proxy for real deployment reliability and does not measure safety, human impact, or long-term maintenance. Scalable: The paper tests up to 21 target configurations and 1,300 final benchmark tasks, but does not test 10×–100× larger task streams, persistent online adaptation, multi-round co-evolution, or patch accumulation under changing environments. The work delivers released code and trained engineer models plus a benchmark-specific executable patch interface; it is a reusable software artifact, but not yet a production-grade continual harness-management system. Strengths: - It identifies a meaningful learning target that is distinct from updating model weights or searching over isolated prompts: a policy that edits executable runtime behavior around an existing agent. - The reward is grounded in realized target-agent outcomes and includes initially successful tasks in the rerun, allowing the training signal to penalize regressions rather than rewarding merely plausible code. - The evaluation goes beyond one target and one benchmark: it reports transfer to 20 unseen target configurations, held-out-task generalization from only ten failures per benchmark, and an ablation showing that pre-action and post-feedback interventions account for much of the measured gain. - The constrained hook interface and qualitative traces make the mechanism inspectable; examples show narrow guards and stateful recovery policies rather than only prompt paraphrasing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that they study only one adaptation from a vanilla target to a directly fine-tuned target rather than repeated multi-round co-evolution. They acknowledge that same-batch rewards tie the training signal to the tasks used to mine failures and propose held-out performance as a future reward component. They also identify inference-efficiency terms as missing and suggest jointly optimizing utility, robustness, and cost. Qualitative analysis acknowledges residual failures, including imperfect two-object state tracking and loops in ALFWorld. These limitations are confronted directly, although the operational implications of compute cost and regression risk are not quantified in depth. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not report statistical tests or broad evaluation-seed variation for its principal gains, making it difficult to distinguish robust improvements from benchmark-specific variance. It does not compare against the strongest directly related learned-harness or executable-repair systems under matched interfaces, despite positioning Harness-R1 against several concurrent works. Cross-target evaluation gives the editor fresh failure traces from each evaluated model and therefore does not establish zero-shot transfer or deployment without test-time adaptation. The same-batch objective and teacher filtering may select patches that exploit recurring benchmark regularities, while the held-out study uses only three seeds and ten failures per benchmark. There is no systematic measurement of patch size, runtime overhead, failure-recovery latency, unsafe action suppression, or regression rates across much larger task streams. The paper also does not test whether patches remain valid as environments, tool schemas, or target models change, nor whether repeated patch installation creates conflicting or accumulating interventions. Bottom Line: This is a substantive and technically credible preprint for researchers studying self-improving agents, with strong evidence that outcome-trained executable harness editing can complement model fine-tuning, but its practical value remains unproven until compute cost, long-term robustness, matched learned-harness baselines, and statistically replicated deployment-scale evaluations are addressed.

#23 — Highly Innovative (77)

Grounding Foundation Models for Embodied Intelligence

CH Song · etd.ohiolink.edu · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This dissertation develops a research program for grounding foundation models in embodied agents through hierarchical planning, milestone-based execution monitoring, spatial-reasoning data, executable computer-use trajectories, and representation-level diagnostics. - Why it's important: Reliable long-horizon behavior requires agents to connect perception, reasoning, and action under partial observability, execution errors, changing environments, and limited interaction data. - How it does it: It combines structured subgoals and feedback with large-scale grounded supervision and analyses whether spatial concepts form coherent, disentangled directions in model representations. - The good: The strongest evidence is the combination of reusable artifacts and measurable gains across several settings, including a 3M-QA RoboSpatial dataset, 53,125 video-derived UI trajectories, a 4.6-point unseen-task success gain from M-Track, and a 28.9-point real-robot improvement for RoboSpatial-trained LLaVA-NeXT. - The missing: The dissertation does not evaluate a unified agent that jointly uses its planning, monitoring, data, and representation contributions, and most embodied experiments remain simulator- or proxy-based rather than open-world robotic deployments. - Read it or not: Read it for a broad, technically grounded view of planning, data generation, and spatial-representation failure modes in embodied and computer-use agents; skip it if you need one unified end-to-end embodied system rather than a portfolio of related studies.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: The dissertation addresses the gap between strong static benchmark performance of language and vision-language foundation models and reliable action in physical or digital environments. The target users are embodied-agent and robotics researchers building systems that must interpret partial visual observations, decompose long-horizon instructions, execute sequential navigation or manipulation actions, recover from errors, and generalize across environments. It identifies three linked deficiencies in prior work: open-loop or weakly structured planning allows errors to accumulate; static or manually annotated datasets provide insufficient grounded interaction supervision; and benchmark accuracy can conceal spatial shortcuts and poorly organized internal representations. The dissertation studies these issues separately through simulated household instruction following, robotic spatial reasoning, computer-use agents, and controlled VLM analysis. Key Idea: The central insight is that grounding requires explicit intermediate structure at three levels: subgoals regulate decisions over time, geometrically generated or interaction-derived data align model outputs with executable behavior, and representation geometry reveals whether spatial reasoning is systematic or shortcut-based. The dissertation’s most distinctive individual idea is to treat execution monitoring and representation quality as first-class components rather than relying solely on end-task success; however, the overall thesis is a synthesis of several individually published contributions rather than a single new unified architecture. Methodology: The dissertation contains five main technical contributions. LLM-Planner uses a hierarchical architecture in which a frozen GPT-3-style language model maps instructions to high-level action-object subgoals, while an existing low-level planner executes them. It retrieves up to nine similar examples using BERT embeddings, uses logit biases to favor allowed actions and observed objects, and re-prompts after failed actions or fixed step intervals with completed subgoals and detected objects. M-Track extracts navigation or interaction milestones from each ALFRED subinstruction using a BERT-CRF tagger, grounds targets with Mask R-CNN object detection and reachability prediction, matches language/object labels using WordNet similarity, and passively or proactively verifies milestone completion; its loss combines behavior cloning, object selection, and A2C reinforcement-learning terms. RoboSpatial procedurally converts RGB images, camera calibration, oriented 3D boxes, and scans into configuration, context, and compatibility questions across ego-, world-, and object-centric frames; its compatibility labels simulate object placement with a 10 cm margin, while context labels are projected 3D free-space samples. Watch & Learn (W&L) trains a vision-only inverse dynamics model on roughly 600,000 web-interaction transitions, predicting one of six UI primitives plus coordinates or typed text from consecutive screenshots, then applies it to filtered tutorial videos and uses the resulting trajectories for retrieval-time in-context learning or supervised fine-tuning. The representation study constructs swapped-order question pairs, subtracts intermediate hidden states to form relational delta vectors, and measures axis coherence and a vertical-distance entanglement index; SpatialTunnel renders objects at fixed depths while varying angular positions to decouple image height from depth. These design choices are generally motivated by the target failure modes, but several rely on benchmark-specific assumptions, heuristic thresholds, or generated labels whose validity is not independently established at comparable scale. Key Results: On ALFRED, LLM-Planner uses 100 instruction/high-level-plan pairs instead of 21,023 instruction/trajectory pairs. With step-by-step instructions and grounded replanning, it obtains 16.42% success on unseen test environments and 18.20% on seen environments, versus 15.83% and 17.87% for static planning; its HLP accuracy is 46.59% on unseen validation and 50.33% on seen validation. Its LOOCV ablation gives 40.59% HLP accuracy with the full design, 17.48% without nearest-neighbor retrieval, 38.10% without logit biases, and 13.43% without both. M-Track raises VLN-BERT-L unseen ALFRED success from 12.23% to 16.29% and seen success from 21.46% to 24.79%; for LSTM-L it raises unseen success from 8.70% to 13.28%. Its milestone builder reaches 90.16–90.62% navigation F1 and 96.85–97.17% interaction F1, while ablations show proactive checking outperforming passive checking. RoboSpatial contains approximately 3M spatial QA pairs from 1M images and 5,000 scans. Fine-tuning produces total average accuracy of 63.9% for VILA, 60.5% for LLaVA-NeXT, 65.7% for SpaceLLaVA, 70.6% for RoboPoint, 64.6% for 3D-LLM, and 71.9% for LEO on its held-out benchmark; RoboPoint improves from 38.9% to 70.6%. On out-of-domain evaluation, RoboPoint improves from 44.1% to 64.7%, and LLaVA-NeXT reaches 52.6% versus 23.7% in the reported real-robot success experiment. W&L produces 53,125 trajectories across 69 applications and three operating systems. On OSWorld, W&L improves Gemini 2.5 Flash from 19.0% to 22.0%, o3 from 21.8% to 24.3%, Claude 4 Sonnet from 43.9% to 45.5%, and UI-TARS-1.5-7B after SFT from 27.3% to 31.1%; Qwen 2.5-VL 7B improves from 1.9% to 13.0%. On WindowsAgentArena, UI-TARS improves from 18.1% to 24.0% with W&L, whereas TongUI-labeled data reduces it to 12.9%. The W&L IDM achieves 95.8% action-type accuracy and 91.7% full action accuracy on a 600-transition held-out test. The representation study finds large consistent-versus-counter depth gaps, including 60.9% versus 24.0% for Qwen2.5-VL fine-tuned on 2M samples and 77.6% versus 36.0% for base Qwen2.5-VL on SpatialTunnel; Qwen3-VL-235B reaches 90.8% overall SpatialTunnel accuracy with a 6.8-point gap, while RoboRefer reaches 59.7% counter accuracy on EmbSpatial-Bench with a 4.6-point gap. These results support the claims that explicit monitoring, targeted spatial data, accurate trajectory labels, and structured representations can improve measured robustness, but they do not establish that the contributions compose into a general-purpose embodied agent. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new elements are grounded LLM replanning with few paired examples, explicit milestone verification, robotics-oriented multi-frame spatial supervision, inverse-dynamics labeling of web videos, and quantitative diagnosis of vertical-distance entanglement, while the broader hierarchical planning, retrieval, reinforcement learning, procedural data generation, and contrastive probing components are combinations or adaptations of established ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: The dissertation includes meaningful ablations for LLM-Planner, M-Track, W&L, and representation scaling, including component removal, proactive versus passive checking, training/test placement, retrieval strategies, data scales, and representation metrics. It reports held-out splits, unseen environments, cross-dataset transfer, external benchmarks, a real-robot study, and action-label accuracy, but generally does not report confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, statistical significance tests, or variance across robot trials. RoboSpatial states that its data and generation code are publicly released, but no URL is given in the dissertation; LLM-Planner cites the HLSM repository at https://github.com/valtsblukis/hlsm and the FILM repository at https://github.com/soyeonm/FILM. W&L release details, model weights, and a repository are not stated. Important concerns include dependence on procedurally generated labels and a held-out benchmark derived from the same RoboSpatial generation process, use of ALFRED-specific detectors and simulator state, evaluation of W&L on tasks and platforms closely related to its retrieval/training distribution, and comparisons involving rapidly changing closed models and vendor-reported systems. The 2026 dissertation includes peer-reviewed source chapters from ICCV 2023, CVPR 2022, CVPR 2025, and CVPR 2026, but the representation chapter is explicitly listed as a 2026 preprint under submission, so confidence should be lower for that component. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the work primarily makes experimental claims across simulators, offline datasets, computer-use environments, and a limited physical robot setup. Practical: The methods can run on commercially available hardware in principle, but LLM-Planner depends on external GPT-3 API access, W&L uses large multimodal models and web-video retrieval, and RoboSpatial’s strongest 3D variants require RGB-D or point-cloud processing. Efficient: LLM-Planner is parameter-free at inference but incurs repeated LLM calls, M-Track adds detector and checking overhead, RoboSpatial fine-tuning consumes millions of generated examples, and W&L requires training an IDM and processing 53,125 videos; systematic latency, memory, and cost comparisons are not stated. Effective: The evidence shows substantial gains on ALFRED, spatial QA, UI-agent benchmarks, and one modular robot pipeline, but it mainly validates task proxies rather than robust open-world embodied intelligence. Scalable: The data pipelines scale from 1M images, 5,000 scans, 3M QAs, 600K transitions, and 53K videos, but agent behavior is not tested at 10×–100× the reported task horizon, model size, environmental diversity, or physical deployment scale. The work delivers datasets, benchmarks, code-generation/data-generation pipelines, trained components, and analysis metrics, although release status is incomplete for several artifacts; it does not deliver a unified general-purpose embodied-agent software stack. Strengths: - The dissertation identifies a useful decomposition of grounding failures into planning structure, execution verification, supervision quality, and representation geometry, providing a coherent research agenda rather than treating end-task accuracy as the only signal. - M-Track isolates an actionable source of long-horizon failure and demonstrates consistent gains across two different agent architectures, with ablations showing that proactive target checking contributes beyond a generic completion classifier. - RoboSpatial is a substantial, robotics-specific data and benchmark contribution: its three relation types and three reference frames target actionable spatial reasoning rather than generic visual question answering, and the physical experiment connects model predictions to manipulation outcomes. - W&L makes a technically nontrivial data-quality argument: the inverse-dynamics labeler reaches 91.7% full action accuracy and produces downstream gains where TongUI labels can harm performance, showing that scalable data quantity alone is insufficient without reliable action grounding. - The representation study provides a concrete, interpretable failure mode—vertical-distance entanglement—and combines natural-image analysis, controlled synthetic interventions, and embedding-space metrics instead of relying only on aggregate benchmark scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The dissertation explicitly acknowledges that M-Track assumes instructions expose an ordered, compositional milestone sequence; that environment-state checking cannot verify procedural or history-dependent instructions; and that hard milestone ordering can exclude valid alternative execution paths. It also notes that RoboSpatial’s generated validation data and the 2D-versus-3D comparison do not fully establish real-world superiority, that 3D model comparisons are confounded by pretraining overlap and modality differences, and that 2D-to-3D projection errors remain significant. The outlook further recognizes that the current contributions do not solve tool orchestration, uncertainty handling, predictive world modeling, or unified long-horizon control. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The dissertation’s central thesis concerns integration, but no experiment combines LLM-Planner, M-Track, RoboSpatial, W&L, and representation diagnostics in one agent or tests whether improvements in one pillar causally improve the others. - The strongest embodied claims rely heavily on ALFRED, a simulator with explicit object classes, calibrated reachability, declarative goals, and relatively structured instructions; transfer to unstructured language, noisy sensing, deformable objects, contact dynamics, and open-world environments is not evaluated. - RoboSpatial’s scale is largely obtained through deterministic geometric heuristics and source-dataset annotations, so improvements on its derived validation set may partly reflect learning the generation rules; human agreement, label-noise analysis, and broader physical-task evaluation are limited. - The representation analysis uses a single synthetic tunnel family and correlational relationships between coherence and counter accuracy; it does not demonstrate that changing the proposed representation metrics through training causes better embodied behavior. - The W&L pipeline assumes that tutorial videos contain sufficiently synchronized, visible, executable interactions; failures from skipped frames, hidden keyboard input, narration/action mismatch, application-version drift, licensing, and privacy are not quantified in the reported results. - Compute, monetary cost, latency, safety behavior, failure recovery quality, and performance under repeated physical deployment are not systematically measured, limiting practical conclusions. Bottom Line: This is a valuable dissertation and a strong collection of complementary contributions—especially RoboSpatial, W&L, M-Track, and the shortcut diagnosis—but practitioners should treat it as a toolkit and research agenda, not as evidence that a unified, robust general-purpose embodied agent has been solved.

#24 — Highly Innovative (77)

OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution (184 ▲ )

Yunhao Chen, Xin Wang, Yixu Wang, Yi Liu, Jie Li, Yan Teng, Xingjun Ma, Xia Hu, Yu-Gang Jiang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OpenART, a target-agnostic arena of more than 10K validated stateful scenarios and the EMHA black-box attack policy for evolving agent-visible environments during long-horizon safety evaluation. - Why it's important: Existing agent-safety benchmarks mostly use short, fixed environments and can miss failures caused by persistent state changes, delayed propagation, and interactions among tools, memory, plans, and publication sinks. - How it does it: It generates executable workflow graphs with fixed benign objectives and hidden safety contracts, projects them through runtime-specific adapters, and uses feedback-guided hypergraph search to mutate only authorized environment state. - The good: Across 75 agent–model configurations, EMHA reaches 85.0% pooled strict Attack Success Rate, with its advantage over instruction-only evolution increasing to 17.2–17.6 percentage points on the most complex scenarios. - The missing: The evaluation lacks comparisons against several strong adaptive long-horizon or environment-level red-team baselines and relies heavily on synthetic, LLM-generated scenarios whose realism and attack validity are only partially independently established. - Read it or not: Researchers working on agent safety, long-horizon evaluation, or runtime security should read it for its scenario abstraction and cross-runtime evaluation protocol, while practitioners should treat the absolute ASR values as benchmark-specific rather than direct estimates of production risk.

Problem & Motivation AI agents increasingly perform multi-step work through tools, memories, plans, files, and external services whose state persists across an execution. In this setting, a state change that looks harmless when first observed can alter later retrieval, planning, capability behavior, or publication decisions. The affected users include developers and deployers of tool-using coding, enterprise, productivity, and operations agents, as well as researchers evaluating agent safety. Prior benchmarks such as AgentDojo, ToolEmu, AgentHarm, Agent Security Bench, and DTap provide interactive or multi-surface testing, but generally evaluate fixed or resettable task instances and often couple scenarios to one benchmark-specific runtime. The claimed gap is therefore not the absence of interactive safety testing, but the lack of a shared protocol for evolving target-visible environment state while keeping the task objective and safety criterion fixed, especially over workflows substantially longer than prior safety benchmarks. Key Idea The central insight is to make the executable scenario—not the prompt—the invariant unit of red teaming. A scenario contains a benign objective, a persistent environment, a workflow and capability structure, and a hidden safety contract. The attacker may alter authorized representations of the environment, but may not change the objective or evaluator. This separates attacks caused by environmental evolution from attacks caused by rewriting the task and enables the same semantic scenario to be projected into heterogeneous agent runtimes. EMHA operationalizes this idea by representing coordinated state mutations as paths through an evolving hypergraph and using evaluator feedback, soft transition values, archive elites, and population updates to search for delayed failures. Methodology OpenART has three main stages. First, a planner LLM expands a domain seed and complexity profile, together with retrieved Tools, MCPs, and Skills from a corpus exceeding 500K entries, into a scenario specification, workflow DAG, workspace, protected resources, and deterministic evaluator. The compiler validates executable dependencies, safe and unsafe evaluator cases, workflow complexity, and capability availability; failed bundles are repaired and only accepted bundles enter the corpus. Second, a target-specific adapter maps the target-agnostic scenario into the native interfaces of each deployed agent, exposing a supported subset of eight surfaces: workspace, instructions, Skills, Tools, MCPs, short-term memory, plan state, and long-term memory. Third, the attacker proposes environment updates, the adapter applies only authorized and feasible changes, the target executes the unchanged benign task, and evaluator feedback updates the attacker state. EMHA freezes attacker and target model parameters, retrieves context, selects or evolves a hypergraph, samples a ready path, decodes the path into a batch of mutations, and optimizes the best attack found within a fixed round budget. Its transition policy uses softmax values over eligible hyperedges; delayed improvements are redistributed across selected edges, while MAP-Elites-style behavior cells retain diverse high-fitness attacks. The fixed-objective design is well motivated for causal isolation, and the adapter/projection design is important for cross-runtime comparison. However, the paper gives limited independent justification for the hypergraph representation, mutation space, archive descriptors, and attacker prompt design beyond ablation results, and it does not establish that the generated scenarios faithfully model production environments. Key Results The released arena contains over 10K validated scenarios across 50 domains and more than 500K candidate capabilities. Median scenario complexity is 97 tool calls, dependency depth 32, parallel width 12.5, 96.5 state objects, and 7.5 file formats, versus 1–15 tool calls and substantially smaller state structures in the compared prior benchmarks; these measurements are based on samples of up to 100 tasks per benchmark. Human experts judged 99.3% of evaluators correct in a separate 10% audit. The study evaluates 15 deployed agents paired with five foundation models—GPT-5.5, Claude Opus-4.8, GLM-5.2, Qwen-3.7-Max, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro—covering 75 configurations. Benign completion on the original scenarios ranges from 80.81% for Qwen-3.7-Max to 96.18% for Claude Opus-4.8, with Aider lowest among agents. EMHA obtains pooled strict ASR of 85.0%, where success requires agreement between a deterministic evaluator and a GLM-5.2 judge. Average ASR varies substantially by model, from 59.2% for Opus-4.8 to 94.7% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and by agent, from 59.1% for Aider to 90.3% for OpenCode. Under DeepSeek-V4-Pro, workspace-only evolution reaches 92.5% strict ASR, instruction-only evolution 81.6%, and full EMHA 94.7%; removing the archive lowers ASR to 90.8%, while removing credit redistribution lowers it to 92.1%. Across five rounds, cumulative ASR rises from 42.9% to 94.7%. Under GPT-5.5, EMHA's advantage over instruction-only evolution grows from 1.8–2.7 percentage points in the simplest complexity groups to 17.2–17.6 points in the most complex groups. Across 10,000 converted trajectories, the median distance between first use of evolved state and the first unsafe action is 37 target actions, with evolved state first consumed at 23% of execution and the unsafe action appearing at 64%. Adding target-agent identity to model and benign-completion controls explains an additional 7.6% of ASR variation, increasing explained variation from 91.3% to 98.9%; this is an association, not a demonstrated causal effect. The results support the claim that environmental evolution and runtime implementation expose failures missed by static tests, but they do not measure real-world harm, production incidents, or performance at 10x–100x the reported arena scale. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM; NEW FORMULATION; NEW METHOD; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the formulation of agent red teaming as feedback-guided evolution of a target-visible, persistent environment under invariant task and safety contracts, together with a cross-runtime scenario representation and OpenART implementation. EMHA combines established ideas from black-box search, hierarchical actions, soft value updates, delayed-reward credit assignment, and quality-diversity evolutionary search; its novelty is their application to coordinated environment-state attacks rather than a fundamentally new optimization principle. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes vector-restricted ablations, removal studies for the archive and credit redistribution, matched-budget instruction-only comparisons, five-round cumulative analysis, paired-bootstrap confidence intervals for complexity groups, evaluator truth-table validation, and a 10% human evaluator audit. These experiments provide useful evidence that workspace and multi-surface evolution matter, although the ablations are concentrated on DeepSeek-V4-Pro and do not isolate all planner, adapter, mutation, hypergraph, judge, and scenario-generation choices. The 75-cell matrix is broad, but the number of independent runs, random seeds, per-scenario sample counts, attack budgets, and uncertainty estimates for the main pooled ASR are not stated. The strict metric uses GLM-5.2 as the judge while GLM-5.2 is also one of the evaluated target models, creating a possible evaluator-model interaction that is not analyzed; the deterministic evaluator and LLM judge also derive from the same generated scenario contracts. The benchmark is built from LLM-generated synthetic workspaces and evaluators, and the human audit establishes evaluator correctness only on a 10% sample rather than ecological validity. Comparisons against prior benchmarks are primarily descriptive complexity comparisons, not matched red-team performance comparisons, and the paper does not report results against strong adaptive alternatives such as AgentLAB-style attacks or other environment-search methods under the same interface. The authors provide a GitHub link, https://github.com/AI45Lab/OpenART, and a project page, https://ai45lab.github.io/OpenART; the text indicates released manifests, task bundles, provenance, and source configurations, but does not explicitly confirm the availability of all model-access scripts, target-agent versions, execution logs, or model weights. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a substantial systems artifact in the form of a benchmark arena, runtime adapters, scenario bundles, evaluators, and an EMHA implementation. - Practical: The design uses Docker-separated attacker and target containers, local workspace/service emulation, and API access to commercial foundation models, so it appears runnable on commercially available hardware, but required hardware, model-access costs, wall-clock duration, and external-service dependencies are not stated. - Efficient: EMHA performs repeated long-horizon target executions and LLM-driven scenario and mutation generation over workflows with a median of 97 tool calls; the paper reports no latency, token, memory, dollar-cost, or throughput comparison against instruction-only evolution or other red-team systems. - Effective: The evidence shows that the protocol exposes evaluator-detected confidential-marker leakage in synthetic scenarios and that environmental evolution raises benchmark ASR, but it does not establish that these failures predict harmful behavior in deployed agents or that the resulting attacks improve defenses. - Scalable: The arena scales to 10K scenarios, 50 domains, and 75 agent–model configurations in the reported experiment, but no 10x–100x stress test, distributed execution analysis, or cost-growth curve is provided; “open-ended” evolution is a design claim rather than a demonstrated result beyond five evolution rounds. The work delivers a reusable software and dataset artifact—OpenART scenario bundles, manifests, evaluators, adapters, and EMHA code are linked at the stated GitHub repository—rather than stopping at a conceptual protocol. Strengths - It identifies a meaningful evaluation failure mode: static or prompt-centric tests can miss safety violations produced by persistent state changes whose effects appear many actions later. - The scenario abstraction cleanly separates benign task semantics, hidden safety contracts, runtime projection, and attacker-controlled state evolution, which is a useful interface for comparing heterogeneous agent implementations. - The empirical matrix spans 15 deployed agents, five models, eight attack surfaces, 50 domains, and long workflows, and the results show strong heterogeneity by runtime as well as by foundation model. - The propagation analysis and case studies go beyond reporting ASR by identifying recurring mechanisms—stale assumptions, propagated safety decisions, and compositional risk—which suggest concrete defense directions such as capability revalidation and repeated safety checks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper explicitly distinguishes the controlled MCP capability-rebinding example in Appendix E.6 from the empirical results and states that it is a future validation target rather than an included attack measurement. It also states that the target-agent identity analysis does not identify the underlying mechanism. Beyond these points, substantial limitations concerning synthetic scenario realism, judge dependence, baseline coverage, cost, and production transfer are not directly discussed in the provided text. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The benchmark's scenarios, safety contracts, protected markers, attack fixtures, and evaluators are largely generated and validated within the authors' pipeline, creating a risk that EMHA optimizes against artifacts of the generator or evaluator rather than general agent safety. - The main comparison is against instruction-only evolution; the paper does not provide matched-budget comparisons with strong adaptive long-horizon or environment-level red-team systems, nor does it compare against simpler search methods that would test whether EMHA's hypergraph and quality-diversity machinery is necessary. - Strict ASR is partly judged by GLM-5.2, which is also a target model, and no judge-swap, blinded human adjudication, inter-rater agreement, or evaluator-judge disagreement analysis is reported. - The reported 85.0% ASR is difficult to interpret without the number of attacks per scenario, seeds, attack budgets, repeated-run variance, and confidence intervals for the full matrix; high ASR may also reflect scenarios deliberately constructed around confidentiality leakage rather than a representative distribution of safety failures. - The cross-agent adapters may not preserve semantic equivalence in practice because supported surfaces, memory behavior, native instruction files, tool implementations, and failure handling differ across runtimes; the paper reports the adapter contract but does not provide an independent equivalence audit. - The association between runtime identity and ASR may be confounded by adapter coverage, enabled attack vectors, agent-specific tool availability, context limits, execution policies, and model-version differences. The variance decomposition does not establish that implementation itself causes the additional 7.6%. - The arena evaluates leakage of synthetic protected markers into public artifacts, a narrow proxy that omits availability, integrity, privilege escalation, destructive actions, financial loss, and real external side effects. - The most striking long-horizon findings use only five evolution rounds and selected case studies; the paper does not establish behavior under longer horizons, changing attack budgets, defense instrumentation, or realistic noisy service failures. Bottom Line OpenART is a valuable benchmark and protocol contribution for researchers studying long-horizon, stateful agent safety, but its headline ASR and runtime conclusions should not be treated as production-risk estimates until the community validates the scenarios externally and compares EMHA against stronger adaptive baselines with independent judges and repeated-run statistics.

Yutao Mou, Pengfei Yang, Zhe Yin, Zhangchi Xue, Xiaotian Luan, Dingyao Yu, Tong Zhang, Shikun Zhang, Wei Ye · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ToolHazard, an LLM-driven framework that synthesizes executable stateful tool environments, discovers task-reachable prompt-injection locations, generates adversarial tasks, and produces evaluation and alignment data. - Why it's important: Existing agent-security benchmarks are costly to expand, often use manually built environments or stochastic simulators, and therefore provide limited coverage of the long-horizon environment-side attacks relevant to deployed tool-using agents. - How it does it: It chains environment blueprint inference, Python program generation, automated testing, state-grounded task generation, read/write dependency analysis, trajectory-aware attack-point selection, payload planning, and programmatic terminal-state verification. - The good: On 28 held-out synthesized environments with 512 tools and 87 retained tasks, the framework exposes substantial vulnerabilities across seven current LLMs and improves Qwen3-8B from 36.10% to 18.06% ASR on ToolHazard-Bench and from 29.16% to 18.34% ASR on AgentDojo while increasing benign completion. - The missing: The paper does not establish that LLM-synthesized environments and six hand-specified payload wrappers predict naturally occurring attacks or production risk, and it reports no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed analysis for the main experiments. - Read it or not: Researchers building benchmarks or defenses for API-based tool-use agents should read it for the environment-synthesis pipeline and attack-position findings, while practitioners seeking production-risk estimates should treat the results as controlled stress tests rather than deployment evidence.

Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (75) are strong for turning adversarial-environment construction into a compositional synthesis and task-reachable attack-discovery problem. Rigor (72) is supported by disjoint environments, seven evaluated models, programmatic verification, human review, cross-benchmark testing, and released code, but circular LLM generation, absent uncertainty estimates, and weak matched baselines remain important concerns. systems Novelty 78 Rigor 72 Non-Obv 75 Completeness 72 Resilience 68 Impact 85
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses security evaluation and alignment for LLM agents that invoke API-based external tools over multiple steps. In this setting, an attacker who can modify writable environmental content—such as records, notes, emails, documents, or tool-returned text—may induce unsafe or unauthorized actions even when the user query is benign. Prior benchmarks generally depend on manually implemented or reused environments, simulated tools with stochastic feedback, and predefined injection locations; these choices limit domain coverage, reproducibility, long-horizon complexity, and automated discovery of propagation paths. The paper specifically excludes browser-based agents and webpage-level injections, focusing on environment-side attacks in API-oriented tool-use systems. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat adversarial-environment construction as a compositional synthesis problem rather than manually authoring attack scenarios. Given seed tool-use tasks, ToolHazard infers a stateful environment schema and operations, generates executable code, identifies free-text attributes with both attacker write paths and agent read paths, and filters these locations using observed benign trajectories. This makes the attack surface task-reachable and verifiable while allowing new environments to be added by supplying seed tasks and computation, although the attack wrappers themselves remain predefined. Methodology: The Environment Simulator first infers an environment type, entities, state variables, constraints, and query/state-changing operations from ToolACE and API-Bank seed tasks; it then generates an object-oriented Python environment and API documentation. A Testing Agent exercises generated tools using positive and negative cases, while a Checking Agent validates state transitions and constraint consistency; environments below a threshold are discarded. The User Simulator initializes valid states and generates read-then-write benign tasks. The Attacker Agent identifies free-text injectable attributes, uses LLM-based operation/source-code analysis to build read/write dependency graphs, retains attributes whose read paths occur in the benign trajectory, and selects a location and payload through plan-and-execute prompting. Six wrappers are used: basic combined, important template, multi-turn, decision hijacking, reasoning criteria, and tool selection. Generated condition decompositions and verifier functions evaluate terminal state snapshots, with score equal to the mean of binary condition checks. For alignment, 1,040 valid adversarial samples are split into 711 SFT and 329 RL examples; the RL reward is R(τ)=R_task(τ)-R_injected(τ), optimized with GRPO, while clean successful trajectories support SFT. Critical design choices—trajectory filtering, terminal-state verification, and the reward penalizing hijacking while requiring benign completion—are functionally motivated, but the paper provides limited sensitivity analysis for filtering thresholds, verifier generation, wrapper choice, and reward formulation. Key Results: ToolHazard-Bench retains 28 disjoint test environments, 87 long-horizon tasks, 512 tools, an average of 15.56 execution steps per task, and 18.75 candidate tools per task; the paper also reports 502 adversarial test cases in an appendix figure, which is not fully reconciled with the 87-task description. Across six attack types, GPT-5 reaches 51.49% ASR for important-template, 44.82% for decision hijacking, 44.96% for reasoning criteria, and 59.14% for tool selection, with benign rates of 80.59%, 72.28%, 76.61%, and 77.12%, respectively. Gemini-3.1-Pro reaches 63.20% ASR for reasoning criteria, while DeepSeek-V3.2 reaches 73.33% ASR for important-template, multi-turn, and tool-selection attacks; lower-capability Qwen3-4B has lower ASR in several settings but also much lower benign completion. In timing analysis, GPT-5 ASR is 67.2% for the earliest location, 52.1% for the second-earliest, and 57.5% for random; Gemini-3.1-Pro gives 45.7%, 30.4%, and 34.3%. For placement, GPT-5 produces 67.4%, 53.5%, and 57.6% ASR for the last field, second-last field, and random placement, while Gemini-3.1-Pro produces 44.2%, 41.5%, and 43.5%. Free-form tool outputs are substantially more vulnerable than JSON or YAML: for GPT-4.1, tool-selection ASR is 80.4% for free-form text, 62.0% for JSON, and 75.6% for YAML; the corresponding Gemini-3.1-Pro values are 77.7%, 40.5%, and 32.6%. ToolHazard-Align improves Qwen3-8B from 67.64% BR and 36.10% ASR to 75.94% BR and 18.06% ASR on ToolHazard-Bench, and from 43.05% BR and 29.16% ASR to 52.08% BR and 18.34% ASR on AgentDojo. For Qwen3-4B, it improves ToolHazard-Bench from 38.19% BR and 25.05% ASR to 70.68% BR and 22.76% ASR, and AgentDojo from 30.03% BR and 14.23% ASR to 41.73% BR and 7.17% ASR. In leave-strategy-out testing, training on three wrappers reduces Qwen3-8B ASR on three unseen wrappers from 37.19% to 26.92% while raising BR from 65.57% to 73.31%. The comparisons use contemporary named models, but the benchmark itself is authors' synthesized data and there is no direct comparison against alternative automated environment-generation or attack-discovery systems under matched conditions. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the main contribution is a new automated synthesis and attack-point-discovery pipeline plus its generated benchmark and alignment dataset, while its individual components—LLM code generation, dependency analysis, plan-and-execute prompting, SFT, and GRPO—are mostly standard techniques combined for environment-side agent security. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper uses disjoint training and test environments, evaluates seven current models, includes cross-attack and cross-benchmark tests, and computes BR and ASR programmatically from generated check functions rather than using an LLM judge at evaluation time. Three master's students reviewed all 28 test environments and 92 candidate tasks; all environments passed inspection, more than 99% of candidate tasks were judged solvable, check functions agreed with human judgments above 95%, and inter-annotator agreement exceeded 99%. The authors report synthesis cost—about $0.59 per environment, $0.03 per scenario, and $0.05 per attack instance under GPT-4.1/GPT-4.1-mini—and provide prompt templates, implementation details, code, and an anonymized repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ToolHazard-845F, as well as a GitHub link at https://github.com/MurrayTom/ToolHazard. However, the study reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, statistical significance tests, or attack-generation success rates before filtering. The benchmark, payloads, verifiers, and training data are all generated by related LLM pipelines, creating risks of generator artifacts, evaluator bias, and circularity. Human validation samples one trajectory per task for verifier checking, and the paper does not compare ToolHazard against strong automated synthesis or red-teaming baselines with matched compute and environment budgets. Deployability (4-property check): SYSTEMS profile, with empirical evaluation. Practical: The framework runs through commercial LLM APIs and Python environments on commercially available hardware; the reported training experiments use eight 80 GB NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while synthesis is API-cost driven. Efficient: Synthesis costs approximately $0.59 per environment plus $0.03 per scenario and $0.05 per attack instance, but the 1.86 million-token quality-inspection stage dominates per-environment cost and no end-to-end throughput comparison with manual construction or competing generators is provided. Effective: The evidence shows that the generated benchmark elicits environment-side hijacking and that ToolHazard-generated training data improves measured BR/ASR on ToolHazard-Bench and AgentDojo, but it does not show effectiveness against naturally occurring attacks or production systems. Scalable: The framework scales the authors' generated corpus to 191 initially valid environments and 88 retained train/test environments, but it has not demonstrated 10×–100× expansion, cross-provider robustness, or quality retention at substantially larger scale. The work delivers a software framework, benchmark, alignment dataset, executable environments, and prompt templates rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - It identifies a meaningful bottleneck—manual, non-expandable adversarial environment construction—and provides an end-to-end executable pipeline rather than only proposing another payload wrapper. - The attack-point discovery mechanism combines semantic free-text identification with operation-level read/write reachability and benign-trajectory filtering, reducing the chance of evaluating injections that the target agent never observes. - The benchmark measures both security and utility, and the alignment experiments include clean SFT, clean SFT+RL, ToolHazard alignment, an independent AgentDojo test, and a leave-strategy-out condition. - The timing, placement, and output-format analyses produce actionable hypotheses: early observations, tail-position content, and free-form outputs are associated with higher measured ASR. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that synthesized environments do not fully represent proprietary enterprise systems, deployment-specific interactions, or long-tail production failures, and that ToolHazard should be interpreted as reproducible stress testing rather than a direct estimate of production risk. They also acknowledge that the framework uses six predefined injection strategies and does not automatically discover new payload wrappers or naturally occurring attacks. These limitations are stated directly and accompanied by proposed future work on deployment-grounded environments and automated strategy discovery. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unacknowledged concern is evaluator and data-generation circularity: LLMs generate environment code, tasks, attacks, and verifiers, while the measured vulnerabilities may partly reflect artifacts of the same prompting conventions rather than general agent weaknesses. The paper does not report confidence intervals, per-environment variance, seed stability, or statistical tests, so differences such as the alignment gains cannot be separated from sampling noise. It lacks matched baselines for alternative scalable environment generators, automated red-teamers, structured-output defenses, and standard agent safeguards. The timing and placement studies appear to use small subsets and only two models, with no detailed sample counts or controls for attack-point semantics, trajectory length, or content difficulty. The use of terminal-state checkers may miss unsafe intermediate actions, privacy leakage, irreversible side effects, and attacks that do not map cleanly to a final state. Finally, the claim that stronger models are more susceptible is confounded by differences in benign task capability, model prompting, decoding, and attack success opportunities; it is not established as a causal scaling law. Bottom Line: This is a useful and reproducible systems contribution for generating controlled environment-side prompt-injection stress tests and alignment data, but its novelty and practical security claims should be discounted until independently generated environments, natural attacks, variance analysis, and matched synthesis baselines are evaluated.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Evoke, a three-step interactive video world model that combines bounded recurrent generation, an external camera-indexed geometric memory bank, and long-horizon teacher distillation. - Why it's important: Interactive world models need persistent scene memory, prompt responsiveness, and long sessions without allowing denoiser context, latency, or memory cost to grow with elapsed time. - How it does it: It separates spatial persistence from the denoiser using pose-addressed geometry retrieval and trains the few-step student with a 30-second self-forced distribution-matching objective from a sparse-attention teacher with per-chunk prompts. - The good: The released CFG-free student generates 1.5-second chunks in 2.11 seconds of diffusion time on one H200, maintains bounded per-step state over 65.5-minute rollouts, and obtains 80.8 on the WBench navigation split. - The missing: Evidence for hour-scale scene fidelity and general long-range consistency remains limited: the main quantitative stability analysis uses eight rollouts, memory retains only 90 seconds of geometry, and the teacher-horizon benefit is demonstrated primarily for photometric stability rather than content identity. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on interactive video/world models, recurrent diffusion, or external scene memory; skip it if you need evidence of real-time deployment, indefinite memory, dynamic-world modeling, or robust identity preservation.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive video world models must preserve previously observed scene structure, respond to camera and text interventions, and continue generating for minutes or hours. Existing systems either retain history in the denoiser context or key-value cache, causing per-step cost to grow or requiring eviction, or use few-step students whose behavior is limited by short-horizon and fixed-condition teacher supervision. Geometry-based memory can restore revisited views, but prior systems do not fully establish a bounded recurrent interface together with a teacher explicitly trained for long-horizon, time-varying interaction. The paper targets controllable visual world generation rather than a physical simulator; its setting assumes known camera trajectories and focuses primarily on static or slowly evolving scene structure. Key Idea: Evoke assigns different consistency problems to different mechanisms: long-horizon teacher supervision addresses temporal content and photometric drift, while an external camera-indexed geometry bank restores previously observed spatial content when the camera revisits it. The central design principle is therefore decoupling persistent spatial state from the deployed denoiser while redesigning the distillation teacher so that a three-step student observes long rollouts and prompt transitions during training. This is a system-level synthesis of geometric warp memory, sparse long-video attention, self-forcing, and distribution-matching distillation rather than a wholly new primitive. Methodology: At recurrent step k, the model reads a bounded local history h_k, a text condition c_k, a camera trajectory P_k, and a view-aligned render r_k = Read(M_k, P_k) from the external world-state bank; it samples a 1.5-second chunk x_k from p_theta(· | r_k, h_k, c_k), then writes the generated observation and camera pose into M_{k+1}. Each chunk contains 9 latent frames, equivalent to 36 pixel frames at 24 fps; the student retains 19 latent history frames, organized into 16 long-, 2 mid-, and 1 short-range frames. For geometric memory, a monocular depth model estimates depth for 12 generated frames, unprojects them using known camera intrinsics/extrinsics, and stores frame-level point-cloud observations. At read time, source views are ranked by target-view co-visibility, up to eight are rendered with batched projection and z-buffering, and a visibility mask suppresses unsupported regions; retained geometry is injected only at the coarsest stage of a three-stage 12x20, 24x40, and 48x80 latent pyramid. The teacher is based on the 14B Wan2.2 A14B diffusion transformer and uses chunk-wise sparse attention over nine-latent-frame chunks: a sink/first frame, local overlapping context, compressed nearby frames, selected distant frames, and a linear-attention global state. It assigns independent text conditions to chunks, with training captions segmented at 12-second intervals. Long distillation starts from one ground-truth prefix followed by 20 self-forced student chunks, totaling 189 latent frames or approximately 31.4 seconds; the teacher and LoRA critic score the complete trajectory using a DMD-style loss, while student history is detached between chunks to bound backpropagation memory. The objective is augmented with a supervised warp-conditioning loss for camera adherence. The key design choices—external geometric retention, sparse teacher attention, and per-chunk conditioning—are motivated plausibly, but their relative necessity is only partially isolated by the experiments. Key Results: On the 158-case WBench navigation split, Evoke reports group averages of 82.79 for Video Quality, 83.76 for Setting, 78.63 for Interaction/Navigation, 86.87 for Consistency, and 72.06 for Physical, with an overall public-leaderboard average of 80.8. It is best among the listed systems on the first, second, and fifth group averages, but its Navigation score of 78.63 and Perspective score of 69.74 are weaker than several peers; its overall lead over the second-ranked WBench system is only 0.1 points and is not step-matched. It scores 66.77 on VBench-2.0, narrowly above the reported Veo 3 score of 66.72, and 85.11 on VBench-Long, ranking seventh of ten and below IPOW at 88.26; these comparisons use Evoke with three evaluations and no CFG against peers' many-step defaults. The authors report eight continuous 65.5-minute rollouts, each 2,619 chunks and 94,281 generated frames, with a 90-second geometry retention window. Photometric measures stabilize after an initial transient, and the opening-window content descriptor plateaus around cosine 0.523, comparable to real footage sampled 60 seconds apart; the authors correctly interpret this as evidence against runaway degradation, not proof of persistent scene identity. The long-horizon teacher comparison reports 74% versus 101% of opening brightness for short- versus long-horizon students, with seven of eight clips improving and Wilcoxon p = 0.016, but no significant content-descriptor improvement and no sharpness improvement. Geometric revisit tests show 20 of 21 comparisons following the predicted retention transition, with retention windows covering the time away yielding 2.3–3.2 dB higher revisit PSNR and a 15.4–17.8 dB plateau, which indicates recognizable but not pixel-faithful recall. In timed prompt tests, newly requested unanchored content is realized in 67% of cases versus 4% for requests that would overwrite geometry-supported content. Diffusion time is 2.11 seconds per 1.5-second chunk on one H200 at 384x640, while appendix measurements report approximately 4.01 seconds per chunk with shipped geometric memory and full decoding/I/O-related overhead; geometry adds 1.84 seconds and 38% of the denoiser cost. The results are strongest for bounded runtime, photometric stability, coarse spatial recall, and low-step interactive quality, not for indefinite identity preservation or dynamic physical consistency. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the coordinated separation of pose-addressed persistent geometry from the denoiser and teacher-side long-horizon/per-chunk supervision for a three-step student; sparse attention, geometric warping, self-forcing, DMD, and CFG-free sampling are established components combined in a new interactive-world setting rather than individually new techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides controlled comparisons for short- versus long-horizon teachers, retention-window effects, prompt anchoring, and geometric-path cost, and it reports one statistical test for the photometric comparison (Wilcoxon p = 0.016). It explicitly distinguishes supervision horizon from gradient horizon and acknowledges that the teacher ablation improves photometric stability but not measured content consistency. However, the strongest long-session claims rely on only eight rollouts, while one figure labels a 65.5-minute stability analysis as n = 1; error bars and seed aggregation are limited, and no broad significance analysis is given for benchmark differences. The WBench and VBench comparisons are not step-matched, VBench uses one sample per prompt rather than five and altered clip lengths/resolution, and the WBench overall margin is within the authors' own stated over-interpretation threshold. Training uses Sekai plus additional internal video data, so the complete training mixture is not reproducible from the paper. The paper links code at https://github.com/SII-YuanyangYin/Evoke and a project page at https://evoke-world.github.io/Evoke/, but it does not state whether all training data, teacher weights, critic weights, depth components, or released student weights are available. There is no direct controlled comparison against equally bounded learned retrieval, alternative geometric representations, or a no-memory baseline over the same trajectories, and the benchmark evaluation is partly entangled with authors' own released system and nonstandard protocols. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper builds and evaluates a runnable interactive video generation system with an external memory path and released code. - Practical: The model runs on commercially available hardware—a single H200 at 384x640—but the reported 2.11-second diffusion latency per 1.5-second chunk, or about 4.01 seconds including the shipped geometric path and full execution path, is not real-time at the demonstrated resolution. - Efficient: Per-step denoiser context, positional range, and retained geometry are bounded; however, geometric memory adds 1.84 seconds per chunk, 38% of denoiser cost and 93% relative to a step that skips the geometric path, while training requires a 14B teacher, critic, 60 student forward passes, and 6x8 GPUs for long distillation. - Effective: Evidence shows improved photometric stability, coarse revisit recall, timed prompt response, and competitive benchmark scores, but it does not establish fine-grained object identity, physical-world validity, or reliable overwriting/control of anchored content. - Scalable: The implementation bounds individual-step cost and demonstrates 65.5-minute and qualitative two-hour sessions, but it retains only 90 seconds of geometry, tests no 10x–100x scale, and does not measure performance or fidelity after repeated eviction and revisits over hours. The work delivers a code release and a trained student system; the paper does not establish that the complete training pipeline, all model components, or all data are publicly reproducible. Strengths: - The paper identifies a useful architectural decomposition: learned long-range temporal behavior and explicit spatial recall address different failure modes, rather than expecting one denoiser context to provide both. - The teacher is treated as a transferable capability specification, not merely a high-quality target generator; the matched teacher comparison provides causal evidence for improved photometric stability. - The recurrent interface has a concrete bounded-cost implementation, including fixed local history, bounded source-view retrieval, visibility-aware token pruning, and local positional layouts. - The evaluation is unusually candid about evidence boundaries: the authors state that the content descriptor is a stability proxy rather than a fidelity metric, quantify geometry recall as recognizable rather than pixel-faithful, and report that long-horizon supervision does not improve every consistency measure. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the geometric bank mainly preserves coarse scene structure and has limited fine-grained object identity, appearance, and local-detail consistency. They do not model persistent dynamic state such as object motion, state transitions, or long-term evolution. They also acknowledge that further inference acceleration is needed for truly real-time interaction, including faster video VAEs, more efficient few-step generators, and cheaper geometric conditioning. These limitations are confronted directly in the conclusion and partially reflected in the quantitative analysis rather than being presented as solved problems. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not provide a fair step- and compute-matched comparison against competing memory mechanisms or against an Evoke variant without external geometry on the same long trajectories. The 90-second retention budget is central to the claimed bounded-memory behavior, but the paper does not quantify how recall and scene identity degrade under repeated eviction, revisits after more than 90 seconds, or trajectories designed to maximize coverage conflicts. The geometry bank stores independently estimated depth rather than a globally consistent scene model, so scale drift, occlusion errors, and contradictory observations may accumulate; these failure modes receive little systematic evaluation. Prompt switching is measured on 48 schedules from one checkpoint, and the anchor-pause ablation is acknowledged as confounded because pausing the anchor also freezes the camera. The 67% unanchored realization rate and 4% anchored overwrite rate therefore do not isolate the causal contribution of per-chunk teacher conditioning. The long-horizon teacher experiment has only eight clips and shows no content-consistency or sharpness benefit, which weakens the broader claim that the method transfers long-term content consistency. The use of internal training data and nonstandard VBench protocols further limits independent verification. Finally, the reported two-hour examples are qualitative, while the quantitative tests stop at 65.5 minutes and do not assess user-perceived interaction latency, dynamic scenes, adversarial camera motion, or recovery after severe generation errors. Bottom Line: Evoke is a technically credible and useful systems paper for bounded-cost interactive video generation, with its strongest contribution being the combination of external pose-addressed geometry and long-horizon teacher design, but its evidence supports bounded stability and coarse recall—not an endless, high-fidelity, dynamically consistent world—and stronger matched baselines and eviction-scale evaluations are needed before treating it as a general solution.

#27 — Highly Innovative (77)

Macaron-V1: Towards Open Continual Learning with Self-Improvement and Mixture-of-LoRA (212 ▲ )

Mind Lab, :, Vin Bo, Asher Cai, Jingwei Cao, Song Cao, Vic Cao, Amelia Chen, Andrew Chen, Kaijie Chen, Cleon Cheng, Steven Chiang, Kaixuan Fan, Hera Feng, Huan Feng, Arthur Fu, Jun Gao, Pyke Han, Nolan Ho, Ori Hong, Hailee Hou, Piers Hua, Charles Huang, Miles Jiang, Nora Jiang, Yuyi Jiang, Qiuyu Jin, Fancy Kong, Kuss Koo, Jaron Lee, Andrew Lei, Alexy Li, Dawn Li, Lucian Li, Ray Li, Ricardo Li, Smith Li, Theo Li, Allen Lin, Elliot Lin, Fan Lin, Chen Ling, Kairus Liu, Kieran Liu, Logan Liu, Neo Liu, Xiang Liu, Yuxin Lu, Maeve Luo, Pony Ma, Verity Niu, Cole Qiao, Guian Qiu, Vince Qu, Sentry, Niko Song, Vincent Wang, Bo Wu, Rio Yang, Evelyn Ye, Fiona Ye, Ina Ye, Regis Ye, Josh Ying, Atlas Zeng, Danney Zeng, Salmon Zhan, Anya Zhang, Di Zhang, Mia Zhang, Sueky Zhang, Wei Zhao, Ada Zhou, Adrian Zhou, Yuhua Zhou, Juno Zhu, Murphy Zhuang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an open agent-model family that combines a frozen large language-model base with four routed LoRA specialists, a production-aligned model–harness revision loop, and infrastructure for adapter training and long-context serving. - Why it's important: Deployed agents face changing tools, users, tasks, and interaction histories, while monolithic post-trained checkpoints do not provide a demonstrated mechanism for systematic post-deployment improvement. - How it does it: A proxy routes each user turn through an L0 chat adapter, invokes one specialist adapter, summarizes the turn into shared context, and links versioned harness configurations with selected trajectories and future LoRA revisions. - The good: The released Venti system reaches 87.8 on UI4A-Bench, 87.6 on TerminalBench 2.1, 58.3 on ChatBench, and 64.0 on LivingBench, while the paper reports concrete routing, latency, memory-residency, and long-context operating measurements. - The missing: The paper does not demonstrate continual improvement across generations, causal gains from MoL or the harness, or collective-intelligence gains from independently trained specialists; most headline system claims lack controlled component ablations. - Read it or not: Systems and agent researchers should read it for its integrated open implementation and deployment lessons, but readers seeking evidence for continual learning or self-improvement should treat the central claims as an agenda and inspect the paper’s limitations closely.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (75) and Non-Obviousness (72) are meaningful because the paper treats the versioned model–harness pair and per-turn adapter-specific context as the unit of continual improvement, while co-designing serving, training, and execution infrastructure. Rigor (65) is reduced by missing component-isolated and budget-matched baselines, training-data routing evaluation, heterogeneous imported benchmark numbers, and the absence of generation-by-generation evidence for continual improvement, despite unusually detailed measurements and public artifacts. Completeness (78) and Resilience (68) are supported by explicit separation of demonstrated functionality from future claims and extensive acknowledgment of safety, generalization, and reproducibility gaps. Impact (90) is high because model artifacts, the serving harness, HCP tooling, and infrastructure interfaces are released, though the central RSI and collective-intelligence claims remain unproven.
