Scaling Inherently Interpretable Language Models (13 ▲ )

Guide Labs Team, Andreas Madsen, Aya Abdelsalam Ismail, Giang Nguyen, Isaac Plant, Muawiz Chaudhary, Nathaniel Monson, Saqib Azim, Zhichen Guo, Julius Adebayo · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a training-time recipe, concept-annotated corpus, causal-diffusion architecture, and 8B-parameter Steerling language model whose outputs can be decomposed into input-token, human-labeled concept, and similar-training-data attributions. - Why it's important: Reliable interpretability and intervention are usually added after training, but the paper targets models that can be inspected and modified without retraining while retaining useful language-model capability. - How it does it: It combines masked diffusion for an in-distribution absence baseline, block-causal attention for KV caching, a supervised-plus-unsupervised additive concept bottleneck, and auxiliary concept, reconstruction, and independence losses. - The good: Across three orders of magnitude of compute, the four reported interpretability metrics improve with scale, and Steerling-8B reaches a 51.6% average over seven benchmarks after 1.35T training tokens while exposing exact logit-level concept decompositions. - The missing: The central claim of human-faithful interpretability is evaluated mainly with self-defined metrics and LLM judges, while the training-data attribution is explicitly similarity retrieval rather than causal influence and the model retains a nontrivial residual pathway. - Read it or not: Interpretability, mechanistic transparency, and language-model systems researchers should read it for the large-scale integration and scaling study; readers seeking demonstrated causal explanations or production-quality capability should treat it as an ambitious preprint rather than a settled result.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (85) and Non-Obviousness (86) are high for integrating an additive concept bottleneck, causal diffusion, large-scale concept annotation, exact logit attribution, and steering into an 8B language-model system. Rigor (72) and Completeness (82) benefit from extensive ablations, scaling sweeps, human validation, and unusually candid failure analysis, but are reduced by reliance on self-defined and LLM-judged metrics, limited human studies, heterogeneous baselines, and no independent large-model seeds. Resilience (70) is constrained by the gap between algebraic faithfulness to the designed interface and human-faithful or causal interpretability, as well as missing deployment measurements. Impact (68) reflects a substantial trained system and attribution pipeline, but the lack of concrete artifact URLs and missing latency, memory, energy, and cost results limit deployability. Weighted composite: 0.15*85 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*86 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*70 + 0.30*68 = 75.35, rounded to 75.

Problem & Motivation: Current language models are trained primarily for prediction and then analyzed with probes, saliency methods, sparse autoencoders, perturbations, chain-of-thought, or influence approximations. The paper argues that these post-hoc methods need not provide variables that are causally used by the model, valid intervention baselines, semantically complete descriptions, or stable explanations across equally performing models. The target problem is therefore to construct language models whose explanation and intervention interfaces are part of the trained computation. The intended users include researchers and practitioners auditing, debugging, steering, or tracing outputs from large language models. The paper focuses on three queries: which input tokens mattered, which human-understandable concepts contributed, and which training examples are similar to the output. Key Idea: Make interpretability an architectural and training contract rather than a post-hoc estimator: train on concept-annotated data, route predictions through explicit concept variables, train on masked inputs so absence interventions are supported by the data distribution, and penalize concept leakage, residual domination, and dependence between known and unknown concept channels. The most important technical insight is the additive bottleneck: because the bottlenecked representation is a sum of concept contributions and a residual before a linear language-model head, every output logit has an exact algebraic decomposition. This is not wholly new—the authors explicitly connect it to concept bottleneck models, concept bottleneck generative models, masking-based attribution, and interpretable-by-design architectures—but the paper scales and combines these ideas for language-model pretraining. Methodology: Atlas first samples 6.6 million documents, chunks them into 44 million local spans, and uses an instruction model to generate roughly 500 million free-form tags. It embeds nearly 14 million unique tags with all-mpnet-base-v2, clusters them with GPU k-means, filters clusters using LLM-judged coherence thresholds, labels surviving clusters with Mistral-Small-3.1-24B-Instruct, and repeatedly merges near-duplicate concepts using an embedding graph and Louvain communities. The resulting 33,732-concept library is used to train a positive-unlabeled concept annotator based on Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, a shared MLP, dot products against concept embeddings, masked binary cross-entropy, and a non-negative PU loss. The annotator labels approximately 1.5T corpus tokens and provides embeddings for an approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval index. The model uses Causal Diffusion: sequences are divided into blocks, attention is bidirectional within a block and causal across blocks, and masked diffusion is trained on a single noisy sequence rather than the noisy/clean pair used by Block Diffusion. This preserves parallel denoising within blocks and KV caching across blocks. The concept module transforms a transformer state h into known concepts, unknown concepts, and a residual: h-bar equals k-hat plus u-hat plus epsilon. Known and unknown activations are sigmoid outputs over 33,732 and 101,196 concepts respectively; the unknown embedding matrix is factorized with rank 256. The language-modeling objective is masked diffusion loss on the bottlenecked representation. It is combined with chunk-level concept BCE, an MSE reconstruction loss for the unknown channel, and a normalized cross-covariance independence penalty: L = L-LM + lambda-concept L-concept + lambda-rec L-rec + lambda-indep L-indep. Teacher forcing initially substitutes ground-truth or analytically computed concept representations and is annealed toward model-predicted representations. Input attribution uses Integrated Gradients with [MASK] as baseline; concept attribution sums exact per-concept logit terms over a chunk; data attribution maps model chunk representations into a separate embedding space and performs IVFPQ retrieval over approximately 11 billion training chunks. Steering injects normalized concept embeddings into hidden states and applies a ReLU-gated logit subtraction for suppression. Key Results: The scaling study trains AR, causal-diffusion, AR-plus-concept, and causal-diffusion-plus-concept families across four IsoFLOP slices spanning roughly three orders of magnitude, with model sizes from 10M to 5B backbone parameters and 4,096-token sequences. The AR baseline has compute-optimal parameter exponent alpha-P = 0.528, while AR-plus-concept has 0.621; causal diffusion has 0.632, while causal-diffusion-plus-concept has 0.503. The authors interpret these as small fixed offsets rather than a growing interpretability penalty, although the concept-library overhead biases the smallest models. The 8B Steerling validation loss is 2.72, versus 2.61 predicted by a small-scale joint Chinchilla fit, an error of 0.11 nats. Three of four interpretability metrics extrapolate closely to 8B: causal-diffusion-plus-concept concept loss is predicted and measured at 0.002, concept contribution is predicted at 0.844 versus measured at 0.876, and known-concept alignment is predicted at 3.967 versus measured at 3.770 on a 1–5 LLM-judge scale. Concept independence is measured at 1.55 versus a joint-fit prediction of 0.624, so the claimed favorable extrapolation depends on the metric and fit choice. Atlas produces 33,732 concepts from 1.5T annotated tokens. On LLM-judged relevance, 98.0% of 12.2 million concept-chunk pairs score at least 2/5, although the Stage-3 annotator scores lower: 95.5% of held-out chunk averages reach at least 2/5 and predicted-concept ratings average 2.94. In a human study of 100 stratified concepts, lifted-word evidence receives a mean coherence score of 3.52/5; 55% of responses are judged recognizable and 17% incoherent. In blind comparison over 34 concepts and 1,025 ratings, Atlas labels score 3.98 versus 3.50 for independently generated human labels, receive a top-two rating 79% versus 63%, and beat a human label with probability 0.62 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.58, 0.66]). This validates aggregate label recoverability, not every concept. Steerling-8B is pretrained for 1.2T tokens on 320 A100 GPUs for approximately 21 days and 161,000 GPU-hours, then mid-trained for 150B tokens. Pretraining initially degrades MMLU and WinoGrande as the moving Gaussian masking schedule rises toward 80% masking; the final pretrained checkpoint scores MMLU 29.8%, GSM8K 14.0%, ARC-Challenge 48.4%, HellaSwag 67.3%, HumanEval 4.9%, MBPP 0.4%, and WinoGrande 59.6%. Mid-training with uniform masking, more math/code data, altered independence losses, increased residual dropout, sparsified heads, zero teacher-forcing floors, and interleaved steering raises these to 46.4%, 44.4%, 52.3%, 70.3%, 8.5%, 11.0%, and 64.2%, respectively, for a seven-benchmark mean of 51.6% versus 32.1% pretrained. Compared with reported open base models, Steerling is below Gemma 1 7B, LLaMA 3 8B, LLaDA 8B, and OLMo 2 7B on the listed average, but above LLaMA 2 7B and DeepSeek 7B; the peer models reportedly use 2–16 times more training compute. Steering improves after mid-training: concept score rises from 1.072 to 1.247, quality from 0.972 to 1.064, and harmonic mean from 1.020 to 1.148 on 72 sampled concepts, but these are LLM-judged scores on a 0–2 scale. The initial pretrained model demonstrates the practical failure mode: steering obtains a higher concept score than prompting but lower quality and lower harmonic mean than prompting. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The formal “inherent interpretability” contract and the three-axis interface are a useful synthesis, while the additive concept bottleneck and masking baseline extend established concept-bottleneck and diffusion ideas; the strongest genuine contributions are the 33,732-concept Atlas pipeline at trillion-token scale, the Causal Diffusion architecture, the full-scale Steerling system, and the empirical observation that the paper’s selected interpretability metrics improve across scale. The work does not introduce a fundamentally new concept-bottleneck principle, causal training-data attribution method, or universally valid theory of interpretability. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes extensive component ablations at approximately 1B scale: block size 32 versus 64, uniform versus moving-Gaussian masking, unknown capacity 3n versus 5n, dense versus rank-256 unknown embeddings, residual versus no residual, and teacher-forcing floors of 0.0 versus 0.5. These ablations support several design choices, including a roughly 15x reduction from factorizing the unknown embedding matrix with little capability loss, and show that removing the residual produces a large capability penalty despite forcing concept contribution to 1.0. Scaling fits use 90% residual-bootstrap intervals over 10,000 iterations, but the paper does not report multiple independent random seeds for the large model or a conventional statistical comparison across model-training runs. The primary interpretability evaluations rely heavily on LLM judges, including Atlas relevance, concept alignment, and steering quality; human validation is small relative to the 33,732-concept library and is based on lifted-word evidence rather than full documents or interventions. The concept and independence metrics are partly training-objective-aligned, so improvements may reflect optimization of the chosen proxy rather than general interpretability. Training-data attribution is explicitly nearest-neighbor similarity, not causal influence, and its 96.8% recall@10 estimate uses queries drawn from the indexed corpus, which is an easier setting than arbitrary generated outputs. The manuscript states that Steerling weights and attribution/steering artifacts were released, but no repository URL is provided in the text. The corpus, complete Atlas annotations, and 808GB retrieval index are not stated to be publicly released. Baseline comparisons use reported results from prior model papers with heterogeneous data, evaluation, and compute protocols; the main scaling comparison is stronger because it holds data and optimizer settings fixed within model-family pairs. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS with substantial EMPIRICAL evaluation, because the paper builds and evaluates a trained language-model system, annotation pipeline, retrieval index, and serving-oriented architecture. - Practical: The model trains on commercially available A100 GPUs and reports a 320-GPU run, while causal block attention and KV caching target practical inference; however, end-to-end serving latency, throughput, denoising-step counts, and memory usage are not quantitatively reported. - Efficient: Causal Diffusion is claimed to halve the training cost of Block Diffusion by removing its clean sequence and provides KV caching across blocks; factorizing unknown embeddings reduces that component by roughly 15x, but the full method still adds 33,732 known concepts, 101,196 unknown concepts, extra heads, concept annotation, and a large retrieval index. - Effective: The evidence shows competitive benchmark capability and improved LLM-judged steering after dedicated steering training, but it does not establish that explanations identify the model’s complete causal reasoning or that retrieved examples caused an output. - Scalable: The system is trained at 8B parameters and 1.35T tokens, and scaling sweeps reach 5B backbones and roughly 10^20 FLOPs, but there is no experiment at 10x–100x the deployed model scale; frontier-scale behavior is extrapolated from fits whose asymptotes are often weakly identified or pinned to metric bounds. The work delivers a trained Steerling model, Atlas concept-annotation pipeline, concept library, attribution and steering mechanisms, and a large approximate retrieval index; the text does not provide a concrete public URL for these artifacts. Strengths: - It presents a coherent end-to-end design in which data supervision, architecture, losses, inference interventions, and evaluation correspond to explicit interpretability requirements rather than treating interpretability as a visualization layer. - The exact additive logit decomposition is technically clear and operationally useful: concept contributions can be computed from the forward pass, and the same learned directions can support steering without retraining. - Atlas addresses a real bottleneck for concept-supervised language-model pretraining and validates the label-generation process with a blinded human comparison rather than relying only on LLM fluency judgments. - The paper reports failures and corrective experiments, including high-mask-rate capability degradation, late concept-head entanglement, insufficient math/code data, and out-of-distribution steering; the subsequent mid-training interventions improve both capability and steering scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the concept library is fixed before training, concepts mostly describe document-segment topics, supervision is chunk-level, the additive bottleneck is only one possible design, the model stops at supervised fine-tuning, and the current system is a first instantiation rather than a finished frontier model. They explicitly acknowledge that data attribution is similarity retrieval rather than causal influence, that a minority of Atlas concept-evidence lists are noisy, that the human study does not validate every concept, that the residual is uninterpreted, and that pretraining steering fails for roughly one third of less-frequent concepts. They also acknowledge that the moving masking curriculum was too aggressive at full scale and that the corpus contained only slightly over 100B math and code tokens out of 1.2T. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unsupported leap is from algebraic faithfulness of the concept pathway to human-faithful explanation: the decomposition is exact for the variables the architecture defines, but the semantic cards may be incomplete, concepts can remain entangled with residual or unknown channels, and the metrics do not test whether an informed human can predict or correct model behavior better than existing post-hoc methods. The residual pathway remains material: the final concept contribution is 0.876, leaving approximately 12% of the reported logit-magnitude attribution outside the concept module, and the unknown concepts are not human-labeled. The paper does not provide direct intervention-agreement curves, counterfactual prediction tests, concept-leakage audits, or comparisons against strong SAE, probe, activation-steering, or causal attribution baselines on the same model and tasks. It does not evaluate steering suppression and amplification broadly against prompt-based, contrastive, or SAE-vector baselines under matched quality constraints. The LLM-judge dependence creates evaluator-model contamination and circularity risks because the same model family helps create, validate, and score concepts. The human study samples only 100 concepts, uses sparse lifted-word evidence rather than model activations or generated behavior, and includes only 34 concepts in the direct label comparison. The scaling-law evidence has only four compute slices per family, heterogeneous concept-module overhead at small scale, no independent seed replication, and several asymptotes at natural bounds; this supports observed trends but not strong claims about frontier extrapolation. Benchmark comparisons are not compute- or data-matched, and the reported average advantage over some peers is modest while stronger peers remain substantially ahead. Finally, practical deployment claims omit latency, throughput, denoising iterations, memory, energy, and cost measurements, which are especially important for diffusion generation and concept-level attribution. Bottom Line: This is a substantial and unusually candid systems paper that makes training-time interpretability operational at language-model scale and is worth reading for its architecture, Atlas pipeline, scaling methodology, and failure analysis, but its evidence supports “exactly interpretable with respect to a designed concept interface” more strongly than “human-faithfully interpretable,” and stronger causal, human-centered, and efficiency evaluations are required before adopting its headline claims.

Ouroboros: A Self-Developing Frontier Coding Agent with Reviewed Core Evolution (66 ▲ )

Anton Razzhigaev, Andrei Gritsaev, Andrei Kaznacheev, Nikita Dragunov, Roman Yampolskiy, Andrei Kuznetsov · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Ouroboros, a version-controlled coding-agent harness that can modify its own tools, prompts, context assembly, workflows, and core implementation through reviewed commits that become the runtime for later tasks. - Why it's important: Long-horizon agent performance depends substantially on the harness surrounding the base model, while self-modification creates risks that ordinary fixed-harness architectures do not address. - How it does it: It separates a mutable agent repository from an independently supervised launcher and admits self-changes only through staged-diff fingerprinting, multi-model review, protected paths, rollback, external spending limits, and an operator emergency stop. - The good: The released system reports 86.74% audited accuracy on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 90.69% on OSWorld-Verified, and 0.2301 on CL-Bench, alongside detailed traces, manifests, and a 161-day deployment record. - The missing: The paper does not provide a controlled comparison showing that core evolution itself improves performance, because the benchmark campaigns disable evolution and the live study follows only one evolving lineage. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners building persistent or self-modifying agents should read it for its concrete architecture and operational lessons, but readers seeking causal evidence for self-improvement should treat the performance claims as largely unestablished.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (78) is substantial at the systems level because Ouroboros implements reviewed, versioned evolution of the core harness behind an independently supervised authority boundary. Rigor (61) is constrained by preprint status, single-lineage deployment, frozen benchmark campaigns with evolution disabled, limited independent replication, and external or vendor baseline comparisons. Completeness (75) and Resilience (67) are stronger because the paper documents protocol failures, audits, rollback mechanisms, and operational limitations rather than hiding them. Impact (85) is the major strength: the MIT-licensed system, traces, manifests, and long deployment record provide a concrete reusable artifact, although causal evidence that self-development improves capability is still missing.

Problem & Motivation Long-horizon coding and computer-use performance arises from the interaction of the base model, harness, tools, context construction, verification, recovery logic, and deployment environment rather than from the model alone. Existing harnesses generally freeze these components after design, making recurring failures, inefficient context assembly, tool-path problems, and user-discovered defects expensive to repair manually. The paper targets developers of persistent coding agents and autonomous software systems that need to improve during deployment while preserving operator authority. The central gap is an architecture for changing the harness's implementation—not merely its memory, prompts, skills, or task-specific plans—while retaining an auditable and reversible mutation boundary. Key Idea The core insight is to treat the agent harness as a continuously versioned software substrate and to make each accepted self-modification a reviewed commit that becomes the execution environment for subsequent work. Ouroboros combines two evolution modes: recursive free evolution, in which improvement is itself a task that can schedule another improvement cycle, and experience-driven core evolution, in which ordinary tasks, reflection, review failures, instrumentation, and social feedback produce durable error classes and candidate structural repairs. The distinctive systems idea is not simply self-editing, but self-editing behind an independently supervised commit gate whose authority is intended to survive changes to the agent's own code, prompts, tools, and model routes. Methodology Ouroboros uses a launcher and supervisor that own startup, process supervision, release bootstrapping, budgets, recovery, and panic-stop semantics, while a mutable repository contains the task loop, tools, prompts, memory projections, review logic, adapters, and interfaces. Self-repository changes pass through owner-selected light, advanced, or pro modes; each staged write invalidates previous review evidence, deterministic preflight checks run, the staged diff is fingerprinted, a multi-model diff-review panel must reach quorum, and the fingerprint is checked again before commit. Max context mode additionally performs whole-repository scope review, whereas low mode records that scope review was skipped. Tasks produce separate execution, objective, review, and artifact outcomes with revision-bound verification receipts. Planning scouts are read-only; acting subagents use isolated worktrees or external workspaces, and the parent verifies lineage, hashes, protected paths, and three-way patch integration before retaining commit authority. Free evolution loops through inspection, change selection, implementation, review, and optional rescheduling; experience-driven evolution records observed failures and opens maintenance work under the same gate. The paper does not state a formal optimization objective, training loss, or quantitative evolution-selection criterion; model decisions and review policies are described procedurally. The important design decisions—separating supervisor authority from mutable code, binding review evidence to an immutable staged snapshot, and disabling delegation/evolution in benchmark profiles—are operationally motivated, but the paper does not isolate their individual effects. Key Results The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.08311v2, 11 August 2026) and reports results across five benchmark families. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, five trials over 89 tasks yield 387/445, or 86.97%, and trajectory auditing removes one weak-verifier shortcut for 386/445, or 86.74%; this exceeds the named Claude Code + Fable 5 baseline at 83.8%, Codex CLI with GPT-5.5 at 83.1%, and Cursor with Grok 4.5 at 79.3%. The authors report approximately ±1.7 percentage points binomial standard error and estimate the audited score is roughly two standard errors above the strongest named baseline. On OSWorld-Verified, a single Opus 5 campaign scores 327.39/361, or 90.69%, versus Intelligence-Indeed at 90.19%, Claude Mythos Preview at 85.4%, and Pointer Agent with Opus 4.7 at 83.64%. On CL-Bench, five ordered stateful rollouts with Sonnet 4.6 achieve normalized reward 0.2301 versus 0.1960 for in-context learning with Sonnet 4.6, 0.1890 for ICL with GPT-5.4, and 0.1855 for Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6. On SWE-bench Pro, after symmetrically removing instances where either arm reached the reference solution, Ouroboros obtains 58.2% versus Codex at 59.4% on 655 paired tasks, with McNemar p=0.40; on GAIA it obtains 78.2% versus Claude Code at 78.8%. The benchmark tests are standard rather than toy-scale, but OSWorld and CL-Bench use single campaigns, and all benchmark profiles disable core evolution; therefore these numbers evaluate a frozen Ouroboros harness, not the causal benefit of ongoing self-development. The separate Hope deployment covers 161 continuous days, approximately 3,600 participants, 222,474 public messages, 3,166 voice calls, 5,507 emails, $110.6K in model spend, 79.7B tokens, 1,085 self-modification commits, 1,522 reviewed self-edit attempts, a 63.5% recent review-block rate, and 40 recurring error classes with 659 recurrences, but these are operational counts rather than controlled capability or safety outcomes. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is an implemented, deployed architecture that allows an agent to evolve its core harness through reviewed, versioned commits while retaining a separate supervisor and operator boundary; the underlying ingredients—self-editing agents, persistent memory, multi-agent review, rollback, and agent-computer interfaces—are established and are combined here in a more operationally integrated setting rather than replaced by a fundamentally new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper releases Ouroboros under the MIT license and gives the repository URL as https://github.com/razzant/ouroboros; it also links benchmark submissions, manifests, per-task traces, audits, and scrubbed evidence bundles, although model weights are not part of the contribution. It discloses model routes, effort settings, seed commits, task selection, memory state, delegation, web and vision settings, and evolution status. The Terminal-Bench campaign uses 445 trials and reports binomial standard errors, while CL-Bench provides per-task means with standard errors; OSWorld and CL-Bench headline results are single scored campaigns, and no multiple-seed comparison, confidence interval for paired benchmark differences beyond the stated tests, or broad statistical analysis of the live deployment is reported. The authors audit one Terminal-Bench shortcut, identify SWE-bench reference leakage, correct historical GAIA isolation problems, and document OSWorld remote-state drift and CL-Bench memory failures. However, there are no ablations comparing evolution modes, review gates, memory projections, context-atlas changes, or supervisor controls; no controlled before/after evaluation of the evolving lineage; and no independent replication. Several comparisons rely on published or vendor-reported baselines with potentially different infrastructure and evaluation conditions, while the strongest benchmark claims are based on narrow campaigns. Benchmark evaluation on frozen seeds with evolution disabled also prevents Goodhart-style contamination by self-modification but simultaneously leaves the paper's central self-development claim empirically unsupported. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, with substantial empirical benchmarking. Practical: The system runs through standard model APIs, terminal and GUI environments, repositories, remote workspaces, and communication surfaces, so it is technically deployable on commercially available infrastructure; however, the reported Hope deployment consumed $110.6K and 79.7B tokens over 161 days, making the demonstrated operating point expensive for most users. Efficient: The paper reports no end-to-end latency, throughput, memory, or cost-per-solved-task comparison against alternatives, and reviewed multi-model diffs, persistent projections, and long-running memory add overhead whose magnitude is not measured. Effective: The frozen harness matches or exceeds named systems on several benchmarks and reaches parity on SWE-bench Pro and GAIA, but the evidence demonstrates task performance of Ouroboros as configured, not that self-evolution caused the gains or reliably improves real deployment outcomes. Scalable: Hope demonstrates 161 days, seven interaction surfaces, 175,755 lines of code, and 227 MB of memory artifacts, but the paper does not test 10×–100× more users, tasks, repository size, concurrent agents, or evolution cycles; it reports no scaling law for review cost, context size, memory retrieval, or safety incidents. The work delivers a reusable open-source software artifact, benchmark adapters, traces, and deployment methodology. It does not deliver a formal proof technique or a trained model. Strengths - It makes self-modification concrete at the level of core implementation, model routing, review logic, and deployment state rather than restricting adaptation to prompts or memory. - The supervisor/mutable-repository split, staged-diff fingerprinting, protected paths, rollback, external spend cap, and pre-agent panic path provide a coherent authority model for a system that can change its own code. - The authors report and correct several protocol failures, including a Terminal-Bench shortcut, SWE-bench reference leakage, GAIA filesystem isolation problems, OSWorld endpoint drift, and CL-Bench schema drift; this improves the credibility of the evaluation discussion even though it does not eliminate the underlying threats. - The public Hope deployment supplies unusually detailed operational scale and change-history statistics, including 1,085 self-modification commits and 1,522 reviewed attempts, and gives concrete examples of social feedback and observed failures producing later structural fixes. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the deployment follows one evolving lineage rather than a controlled population of independently evolving agents; SWE-bench Pro suffers from public-reference leakage and task defects; LLM reviewers may share blind spots with the agent; and low context mode omits whole-repository scope review. They also acknowledge incomplete filesystem isolation, continual-memory failures under schema drift, and the dual-use nature of self-modifying and remote-workspace capabilities. These limitations are confronted directly through audits and proposed safeguards, although the paper does not quantify the residual risk after the fixes. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central causal claim is untested: benchmark runs disable core evolution, and the single Hope lineage lacks a frozen-control twin, randomized task assignment, pre/post capability measurements, or independent evolving replicas. - The paper does not quantify how much performance comes from the base model, prompt and context design, memory, review passes, benchmark-specific adapters, or the self-development mechanism itself. - The review gate is described as multi-model and quorum-based, but reviewer identities, model diversity, disagreement rates, false-accept/false-reject rates, and adversarial evaluation of reviewer collusion or shared blind spots are not reported. - Safety evidence is observational and anecdotal: no red-team campaign, mutation escape-rate measurement, privilege-escalation test, prompt-injection stress test, or quantitative emergency-stop latency/reliability result is provided. - The deployment statistics are self-reported from a redacted operational export, with no independent audit and no user-level measures of response quality, harmful behavior, uptime, cost efficiency, or regressions across successive versions. - Baseline comparability remains imperfect because several results use external published or vendor numbers, different provider routes and configurations, and single campaigns; the paper does not provide matched reruns of every baseline under the same infrastructure. - The paper claims resilience and scalability from a 161-day deployment, but it does not evaluate behavior at substantially larger repository, memory, interaction, concurrency, or review-panel scales. Bottom Line This is a valuable open systems report and a useful reference architecture for researchers building persistent self-modifying agents, but it should not be read as evidence that reviewed core evolution improves capability until controlled longitudinal ablations and independent safety evaluations are supplied.

Know It, Act on It: Investigating Memory Utilization in LLM Personalization

Z Feng, J Ma, E Chersoni · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces KnowAct, a paired evaluation benchmark and protocol that separately measures whether an LLM agent can recall a user preference (Know) and apply that same preference in an implicit behavioral scenario (Act). - Why it's important: Personalized agents can create safety and utility failures when they retrieve sensitive user information, such as allergies or emotional conditions, but fail to incorporate it into recommendations. - How it does it: The authors inject 1,000 preferences into 50 synthetic personas at explicit, incidental, or inferential expression levels, evaluate 16 systems across five memory architectures, and compute utilization as the fraction of correctly recalled preferences that also affect behavior. - The good: Across systems, the experiments provide consistent evidence of a Know–Act dissociation; for example, Mem0 raises GPT-4o-mini utilization from 16.3% to 54.6% on the aggregate metric, while the strongest long-context system, Claude 4.6 Sonnet, reaches 65.1%. - The missing: The benchmark is synthetic, relatively retrieval-friendly, and judged primarily by LLMs; the paper does not establish performance on real longitudinal histories, substantially noisier memory stores, or statistically replicated runs with error bars. - Read it or not: Researchers working on LLM memory, personalization, and agent evaluation should read it for the diagnostic distinction between recall and behavioral use, while practitioners should treat the absolute percentages as preliminary because the scenarios and evaluation are synthetic.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the failure of personalized LLM agents to use information about a user even when the information is stored or available in context. This affects persistent assistants and companion systems that must personalize recommendations, planning, advice, and tone across sessions. Existing evaluations generally measure factual memory, retrieval, or behavioral personalization separately, so a behavioral failure cannot be attributed to forgetting, retrieval, comprehension, or failure to apply known information. The paper targets this diagnostic gap by testing recall and behavior on the same preference, including preferences expressed indirectly during ordinary task-oriented interactions. The motivation is especially consequential for health, medical, and therapy-related information, although the benchmark does not use real user data. Key Idea: The central insight is to decouple remembering a preference from using it by pairing a direct Know question with an implicit Act scenario for the identical preference. The resulting conditional utilization rate, defined as the proportion of Know-pass cases that also pass the Act test, exposes failures that ordinary memory-recall benchmarks hide. A second insight is that expression strength changes the location of the bottleneck: explicit preferences often produce high recall but poor utilization, whereas incidental and inferential preferences more often fail during storage or comprehension. Methodology: The authors select 50 personas from PersonaMem-v2 across 11 cultural regions and sample 20 target preferences per persona, yielding 1,000 preferences distributed among stereotypical, anti-stereotypical, neutral, health/medical, and therapy/emotional categories. Each target preference is represented in three parallel incremental conversation histories: an explicit snippet where the preference is the central topic, an incidental snippet where it is embedded in a task request, and an inferential snippet where it must be inferred from behavioral cues. The histories contain 20 target and approximately 50–70 non-target chunks, totaling 11,955 chunks and 4.55 million tokens. The evaluation feeds chunks sequentially through each system’s native ingestion pipeline, then runs independent Know and Act sessions. Know asks a direct first-person recall question and scores the response against a ground truth. Act gives a natural request that does not mention the preference; an LLM judge compares the memory-enabled response with a zero-memory response and labels whether the former reflects the preference. The systems include four long-context models, BM25, three dense-retrieval systems, four structure-augmented systems, and four agentic-memory systems. All non-long-context systems use GPT-4o-mini as the generator, while long-context systems use their native backbones. The main design decisions—paired tests, controlled expression variants with shared non-target context, and incremental native memory ingestion—are well aligned with the stated diagnostic goal. However, the reliance on GPT-5 to generate snippets and tests, and the use of a binary judge for nuanced behavioral adaptation, remain important validity constraints. Key Results: Across 16 systems, Know and Act diverge substantially. Aggregate Know/Act/utilization rates include GPT-4o-mini at 34.7%/17.3%/16.3%, GPT-4o at 65.6%/29.3%/32.1%, Gemini 3.1 Flash at 78.8%/53.4%/57.0%, and Claude 4.6 Sonnet at 76.2%/61.5%/65.1%. Among memory architectures sharing GPT-4o-mini, Mem0 is the strongest overall non-long-context system at 60.3% Know, 46.0% Act, and 54.6% utilization; its utilization is approximately 3.4 times the GPT-4o-mini long-context baseline. Dense embedding RAG reaches at most 33.5% utilization on average, Self-RAG reaches 35.3%, and the remaining structure-augmented and agentic systems range from 16.7% to 33.2%, with Zep/Graphiti particularly weak at 16.7%. Explicit expression yields high Know accuracy but still limited utilization; incidental expression is the hardest for recall across all architecture categories, while inferential expression partially recovers because the relevant topic provides richer semantic cues. Health/medical preferences have the lowest category-level utilization among the memory-architecture groups, averaging 15.58% in the paper’s category plot, while therapy/emotional preferences are relatively easy to recall but difficult to use; even Claude’s health/medical utilization is only 71.3% on its category-specific average. In Mem0’s 722 Know-pass/Act-fail cases, the authors attribute 30.7% to retrieval, 53.0% to comprehension, and 16.2% to application failures. These results support the claim that memory systems improve actionable presentation more than simple recall, but they do not demonstrate behavior in real deployments or prove that an Act pass corresponds to safe, correct personalization. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and modestly NEW EVALUATION METHOD; the paired Know–Act formulation and conditional utilization metric are the main original contributions, whereas the evaluated memory mechanisms themselves are existing systems combined with a new diagnostic protocol rather than new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports a substantial controlled comparison with 1,000 preferences, three expression conditions, five architecture categories, and detailed prompts and implementation settings. It validates zero-memory Know performance below 3% for four generation models, reports human–GPT-5 agreement of κ=0.89 for Know and κ=0.82 for Act in one description, and separately reports human-majority agreement of κ=0.91 and κ=0.84; GPT-5–Claude agreement is reported as κ=0.91/0.88 in the main text and κ=0.87/0.81 in the appendix, an inconsistency that should be corrected. Blinded Act judging agrees with the non-blinded judge on 95% of 200 cases, with κ=0.87. The authors state that code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/KnowAct_Benchmark-5BEB/, and they document prompts, seeds, system versions, and validation procedures. However, there are no reported multiple-seed outcome intervals, standard errors, significance tests, or component ablations demonstrating which parts of individual memory systems drive the gains. The comparison is also not fully factorial: long-context models use stronger and different native generation backbones, while all retrieval and agentic systems use GPT-4o-mini, so architecture and model capability are not cleanly separated across the full comparison. The benchmark is built partly from GPT-generated data and evaluation items, and the Act criterion allows a judge to label any discernible difference from a baseline as preference use, which may not guarantee correctness or safety. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: The evaluated methods use commercially available LLM APIs, vector databases, embeddings, and open-source memory frameworks, so the basic pipelines can run on current hardware or through hosted services, although the cost and latency of 16-system evaluation are not reported. Efficient: The paper does not measure ingestion latency, query latency, token consumption, GPU/CPU memory, or dollar cost at inference; 1M-token long-context models outperform most memory systems but may incur substantially different serving costs. Effective: The evidence shows improved benchmarked preference recall and conditional behavioral adaptation, especially for Mem0, but only on synthetic, short, controlled scenarios and not on real user outcomes or safety-critical decisions. Scalable: The histories contain up to roughly 116 chunks per persona and about 27.5K–33.1K tokens per expression condition, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger histories, higher distractor density, topic drift, contradictions, concurrent users, or production throughput. The work delivers a benchmark, dataset, evaluation code, and experimental integrations rather than a new deployable memory library or trained model. Strengths: - The paired evaluation directly addresses a real ambiguity in personalization research: a failed personalized response may reflect forgetting, retrieval failure, comprehension failure, or failure to apply known information. - The expression-strength manipulation is conceptually useful and empirically revealing: incidental snippets are harder to recall than inferential snippets, while explicit snippets expose a utilization gap. - The 16-system comparison spans long-context, lexical RAG, dense RAG, structured memory, and agentic memory, making the diagnostic finding less dependent on one architecture family. - The Mem0 oracle study adds causal localization beyond aggregate scores, identifying comprehension as the dominant failure source in 53.0% of Know-pass/Act-fail cases and application as a residual failure even when the preference is explicitly supplied. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge dependence on LLM judges, possible judge biases such as verbosity preference and insensitivity to subtle cues, synthetic PersonaMem-v2 personas, lack of real longitudinal histories, and a retrieval setting with one target passage and limited distractors. They appropriately characterize the observed Know–Act gap as a conservative lower bound because real histories contain more noise, fragmentation, topic drift, and contradictions. The ethics statement notes that no real user data are used and highlights risks around health and medical preferences. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The benchmark’s synthetic generation process may make the target preference unusually coherent and may entangle expression condition with GPT-5 writing style, despite shared non-target chunks. The incidental and inferential conditions are not human-authored or independently calibrated for semantic difficulty, and the paper reports only structural validation plus manual inspection of 100 Act scenarios rather than item-level agreement or adjudication for all 1,000 pairs. The Act metric is conditional on Know passing and therefore can be unstable at low Know rates; the paper does not report confidence intervals or raw contingency counts for every system. The zero-memory comparison is useful for detecting personalization but does not establish that the memory response is objectively correct, safe, or preferable, particularly for medical and therapy scenarios where omission may be appropriate and personalized advice can be harmful. The use of different native backbones for long-context versus memory-augmented systems complicates claims about architecture superiority, and no compute-normalized comparison is provided. Finally, the paper does not test preference conflicts, updates, forget requests for target preferences, multiple simultaneously relevant constraints, multilingual interactions, adversarial memory content, privacy leakage, or whether memory systems incorrectly act on sensitive information when it should not influence behavior. Bottom Line: This is a useful and reasonably rigorous evaluation paper whose Know–Act distinction and failure attribution should influence future LLM-memory benchmarks, but its practical conclusions remain provisional until validated with real longitudinal interactions, objective behavioral criteria, stronger statistical reporting, and compute- and backbone-matched baselines.

Xiaohongshu Inc · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 12 Aug 2026

Problem & Motivation Everyday-life assistance requires an agent to manage a changing situation over a lifecycle rather than complete a clearly specified request in one interaction. Users need help with travel, finances, litigation, renovation, health and fitness, exams, rentals, shopping, careers, and team activities, where deadlines, bookings, prices, weather, policies, health information, and user preferences evolve independently of the agent. The specific gap is that existing benchmarks mostly focus on coding, office work, computer use, or isolated tool-use tasks in environments that change only in response to agent actions. They therefore under-measure whether an agent independently checks state, distinguishes when to act from when to remain silent, extracts implicit constraints and authorization boundaries, propagates changes into an existing plan, and preserves consistency across many stages. Key Idea The central insight is to make the task a clock-driven world rather than a prompt. In particular, silently applying background mutations without triggering an agent turn creates a direct test of proactive perception: the agent must periodically re-inspect relevant services, discover changes that were never announced, and update durable plans before downstream deadlines. The benchmark couples this mechanism with implicit constraints and cross-stage checks, so an agent cannot obtain a high score through locally plausible replies alone. Methodology Each task is represented as a tuple consisting of an initial world state, an ordered event timeline, enabled service capabilities, persona/workspace context, and weighted deterministic scoring predicates. The harness advances the task stage by stage. User messages, world observations, and notifications trigger turns; silent mutations directly alter backend state without producing a turn. The agent can query and modify 22 mock services, write workspace files and notes, send email, update calendars, and produce replies. At each stage, checkers inspect observable artifacts; final scoring is the weighted fraction of passed checks on a 0–100 scale. Checks cover per-stage timeliness, cross-stage invariants, and final state. Three critical design decisions are well motivated: silent mutations test proactive re-inspection; weighted checks make safety and hard constraints more consequential than cosmetic actions; and shared deterministic backends with task-specific seed data improve auditability and reproducibility. The paper does not provide an explicit optimization objective or train an agent; it evaluates existing policies. The task-authoring process deliberately embeds distractors, implicit constraints, unsafe shortcuts, and authorization rules, but the paper gives limited independent evidence that these authoring choices represent real user distributions rather than benchmark designer judgments. Key Results The evaluation covers 200 tasks, evenly distributed across 10 domains, with a median horizon of 29 simulated days, 24 stages, 36 events, seven services, and 58 checks per task. The suite contains 7,453 scripted events: 2,247 user messages (30.1%), 1,925 notifications (25.8%), 1,798 world observations (24.1%), and 1,483 silent mutations (19.9%); 17 tasks run longer than 60 days and the longest spans about 111 days. Across three runs per task, Claude Opus 5 obtains the highest avg@3 at 32.5, followed by GPT-5.5 at 30.1, Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8 at 27.5, GLM-5.2 at 25.4, Kimi-K2.6 at 22.6, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 21.1. Claude Opus 5 reaches max@3 41.2 and min@3 23.8; within-task standard deviation ranges from 3.7 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro to 10.0 for GPT-5.5. For Claude Opus 5, domain scores range from 21.8 on team building to 51.1 on shopping; travel scores 41.0 and renovation 45.7, while rental scores 25.4 and exam preparation 23.5. Across models, capability-axis pass rates remain low: proactivity ranges from 16.0 to 33.6, propagation and recovery from 18.5 to 32.0, persistence and bookkeeping from 18.9 to 28.0, safety and privacy from 23.0 to 31.1, and authorization boundary from 17.8 to 34.8. Every model's per-stage pass rate falls by 10–15 points from the first to the last third of the timeline. These results measure performance on the benchmark's observable checks; the paper's broader conclusion that models are not ready for real-life assistance remains an extrapolation from a simulated proxy. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM; NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the integrated benchmark formulation that combines everyday-life domains, autonomous clock-driven state changes, silent mutations, implicit constraints, and cross-stage artifact-based grading; the mock services, weighted checkers, and harness are substantial benchmark infrastructure, while the model evaluation supplies a new empirical finding about weak persistence and proactivity. The individual ingredients—tool-use evaluation, long-horizon trajectories, stateful environments, safety checks, and event-driven simulation—are established in related work, so the novelty lies primarily in their joint application to a life-assistance setting rather than in a new agent algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports three runs per task, avg@3/max@3/min@3, within-task standard deviation, per-domain results, per-tier and per-capability pass rates, interaction costs, and timeline-position analysis. Scoring reads backend state and durable artifacts rather than hidden reasoning or self-reported success, which reduces one class of evaluation leakage. However, the paper reports no confidence intervals across tasks, significance tests, seed analysis beyond three stochastic runs, scorer audits, human validation, inter-rater agreement, or ablations over mutation rate, task horizon, constraint density, scoring weights, and event composition. Capability axes are assigned by keyword matching over check names and are explicitly described as indicative, weakening the causal interpretation of those categories. The seven model comparisons use the same openclaw scaffold and strongest reasoning settings, but the paper does not establish that these settings are equivalent across vendors or provide detailed model versions, prompts, temperature settings, rate limits, or cost normalization. The paper states that all tasks, environments, and the evaluation framework will be open-sourced; it does not provide a VibeLifeBench release URL. It links the Terrarium infrastructure at https://github.com/evolvent-ai/Terrarium. The benchmark is entirely based on author-scripted mock services and may be vulnerable to task-authoring bias or future contamination once released. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a benchmark/system artifact rather than a deployed assistant. Practical: The offline simulator can run on ordinary commercially available compute, but evaluating a frontier model costs substantial interaction and token budgets; reported per-run usage ranges from 13.7M to 41.2M context tokens, 79k to 325k output tokens, and 203 to 332 tool calls. Efficient: The benchmark is deterministic and reuses 22 lightweight backends, but the agent-side evaluation is expensive, and the paper does not report wall-clock time, hardware, memory use, or cost per task. Effective: The checks directly measure observable state changes, timely actions, safety behavior, and cross-stage consistency within the simulated world, but evidence that these proxies predict successful assistance with real services and users is not provided. Scalable: The suite scales to 200 tasks and horizons up to approximately 111 days, but it does not test 10×–100× more tasks, substantially denser event streams, richer service state, concurrent users, real asynchronous latency, or horizons beyond the scripted range. The work delivers a promised benchmark dataset, deterministic environment, checker framework, and task harness; based on the paper, the VibeLifeBench release itself was not yet available, while Terrarium is linked as open-source infrastructure. Strengths - The benchmark targets a meaningful evaluation gap by jointly testing proactivity, autonomous environmental change, and long-horizon coherence instead of treating them as isolated properties. - Silent mutations provide a concrete, behaviorally testable mechanism for distinguishing a genuinely persistent agent from one that only reacts to incoming messages. - Observable-artifact scoring is stronger than grading free-form responses alone: backend state, calendars, notes, ledgers, sent messages, and cross-stage invariants expose whether the agent actually completed and maintained its work. - The evaluation reports useful failure structure, including 10–15-point late-horizon degradation, low cross-stage pass rates, and the finding that greater token or turn expenditure does not guarantee better scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper does not present a dedicated limitations section or explicitly discuss major validity threats. It does state scope boundaries: the environments are simulated, the services are mock backends, tasks are scripted and deterministic, and the benchmark is intended to measure life-domain agent behavior rather than operate real services. It also acknowledges that the capability-axis assignment is indicative because it uses keyword matching over check names. The authors promise to release the tasks, environments, and evaluation framework, but do not report an available release in the paper. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not validate whether the 10 domains, personas, implicit constraints, event frequencies, mutation patterns, or authorization rules reflect real user workloads; all tasks appear to be authored by the benchmark creators. - There is no human-agent comparison, expert judgment study, correlation with real-world task success, or test of whether benchmark rankings predict deployment reliability. - The scoring weights are described as deliberately uneven, but the paper does not show sensitivity analyses demonstrating that the model ranking and conclusions persist under alternative weights. - The benchmark may conflate persistence with compliance with a prescribed bookkeeping format, such as a specific journal and expense-log structure, rather than measuring whether equivalent durable state representations work. - The mutation mechanism tests whether agents poll, but the paper does not analyze the trade-off between proactive polling, unnecessary actions, user annoyance, tool cost, and missed changes; the claimed ideal of acting, asking, or staying silent is therefore only partially evaluated. - The comparison lacks strong non-LLM or engineered-agent baselines, memory/planning scaffolds, retrieval systems, polling policies, and ablations that would identify whether failures arise from model reasoning, harness design, memory management, or tool semantics. - Three runs per task provide limited evidence for stochastic reliability, and no confidence intervals or paired statistical tests are reported for model differences. - Several model names and cited benchmarks are future-dated relative to the August 11, 2026 arXiv v1 timestamp, and the paper provides vendor/model configuration details insufficient for independent replication or comparison. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically concrete benchmark paper for researchers studying persistent tool-using agents, but its innovation is primarily an important evaluation formulation and simulator rather than a validated measure of real-world life-assistant competence, so practitioners should treat the reported rankings as preliminary until the release, ablations, and external validity studies appear.

Problem & Motivation: Professional refactoring requires behavior-preserving changes that propagate across APIs, implementations, tests, build files, documentation, and configuration. Existing coding benchmarks primarily evaluate isolated functions, repository-level bug fixes, or feature additions, and the paper argues that many are either too easy or compromised by narrow tests, broad tests that enforce unstated requirements, ambiguous issue descriptions, and possible training-data contamination. The target users are researchers and practitioners evaluating AI coding agents, especially agents intended for long-horizon repository maintenance. The specific gap is a benchmark that combines genuine multi-file refactoring, multilingual repository coverage, and manually reviewed task specifications and test suites. Key Idea: The central insight is to use real, large refactoring commits as outcome-based benchmark tasks while separating the original developer patch from a newly rewritten specification and manually reviewed behavioral tests. This makes cross-file coordination and preservation of repository behavior the evaluation target rather than reproduction of a known gold patch or compliance with implementation-specific tests. The paper does not introduce a new agent-solving technique; its intellectual contribution is the benchmark design and curation protocol. Methodology: The benchmark-construction pipeline has three stages. First, the authors search repositories with at least 500 GitHub stars, approved open-source licenses, and at least 80% primary-language composition in one of seven target languages; they select commits after January 2025 whose messages contain “refactor,” exclude messages containing “bug fix,” and require changes to both test and non-test files. Second, they clone each repository at the pre-refactoring commit, install dependencies in an isolated Docker environment, apply the gold source and test patch, and retain only instances whose full test suite executes successfully. Third, human experts, assisted by LLMs, analyze the commit, discard single-file, low-complexity, or simplistic tasks, remove tests judged overly narrow or broad, rewrite the problem statement from scratch, and perform a final human consistency check. Each task contains the pre-refactoring repository, a natural-language issue description, a validation test suite, and the gold patch; an agent succeeds only if all tests pass. The evaluation runs six models with mini-swe-agent and OpenHands, with 300 interaction steps and a $10 per-instance limit, and reports Pass@1 resolve rate, per-language performance, steps, cost, and trajectory behavior. Critical design decisions are the aggressive scale filtering, the specification/test rewriting, and execution-based binary evaluation. The paper gives a rationale for each, but it does not quantify inter-annotator agreement or independently establish that the tests are both necessary and sufficient beyond the authors’ review process. Key Results: SWE-Bench ProMax retains 170 instances from 29,782 initial candidates, covering 70 repositories and seven languages. Gold source patches modify an average of 11.4 files and 261.6 LOC, with maxima of 182 source files and 4,503 LOC; including test changes, patches average 15.9 modified files. The language distribution is Python 29, Java 26, TypeScript 28, Go 23, C 20, C++ 22, and Rust 22 instances. Under OpenHands, GPT-5.2 obtains the highest overall resolve rate at 41.2%, followed by Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38.8%, GLM-5 and Qwen3.5 at 36.5%, Kimi-K2.5 at 32.9%, and Gemini-3-Pro at 19.4%. Under mini-swe-agent, the corresponding rates are 21.8%, 30.6%, 22.9%, 20.6%, 26.5%, and 26.5%, respectively. Open-weight models approach proprietary-model performance at lower reported API cost: GLM-5 resolves 36.5% at $0.24 per instance, compared with GPT-5.2 at 41.2% and $3.60 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38.8% and $4.77. OpenHands improves most models substantially, although Gemini-3-Pro falls from 26.5% to 19.4%. Performance varies by language: GPT-5.2 reaches 75.0% on C and 48.3% on Python, Claude reaches 53.6% on TypeScript and 63.6% on Rust, and Qwen3.5 reaches 54.5% on C++. The trajectory analysis of Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Kimi-K2.5 shows agents modifying fewer files than gold patches, especially for large changes, while failed attempts consume more interaction rounds. These results support the claim that incomplete cross-file propagation is a common failure mode, but the paper does not provide statistical tests or repeated runs establishing the robustness of these comparisons. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the combination of expert-rewritten specifications, manually reviewed tests, large multi-file refactoring, and seven-language repository coverage in one benchmark; the agent evaluation and binary test-based scoring use standard practices, and the trajectory and cost findings are empirical analyses enabled by the benchmark rather than new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a clear selection pipeline, repository list, commit URLs for representative examples, detailed dataset statistics, Docker-based environments, model/scaffold settings, and a public Hugging Face dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/swe-bench-promax/SWE-Bench-ProMax. It reports both overall and per-language results and compares two agent scaffolds, which improves diagnostic value. However, it reports no ablations of the filtering, rewriting, or test-review stages; no annotation agreement, reviewer counts, or adjudication protocol; no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests; and no controlled comparison against the same models on existing refactoring benchmarks. The benchmark is selected using commit-message keywords and repository popularity, which introduces selection bias, and the authors’ claim that tests are necessary and sufficient is not independently audited. TypeScript is heavily concentrated in Angular—25 of 28 TypeScript instances come from one repository—and language-level conclusions therefore cannot be interpreted as broad language effects. The evaluation also uses model versions and pricing that may change over time, and the binary “all tests pass” metric cannot detect behavior not covered by the curated tests. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper delivers an executable benchmark with Docker environments and evaluates deployed agent scaffolds, although it is primarily a dataset and evaluation artifact rather than production infrastructure. - Practical: The benchmark can run on commercially available hardware in principle because it uses Dockerized repositories and standard agent interfaces, but the paper does not state hardware requirements, total evaluation time, or whether every repository builds reliably outside the authors’ prepared environments. - Efficient: Per-instance reported API costs range from $0.10 to $4.77 and agents are capped at 300 steps and $10, but the paper does not report CPU, RAM, storage, container-build, or full-suite execution costs relative to existing benchmarks. - Effective: Execution-based resolution directly measures whether an agent produces a test-passing repository state, and the 41.2% best result demonstrates challenge value; it remains only a proxy for production-quality, behavior-preserving refactoring because test coverage and specification validity are not independently measured. - Scalable: The dataset scales to 170 tasks and patches up to 182 source files, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger datasets, repositories, or agent trajectories and provides no evidence that its curation pipeline scales beyond the retained 170 instances. The work delivers a reusable dataset and Dockerized benchmark artifact, not a general-purpose refactoring tool, trained model, or new agent algorithm. Strengths: - The benchmark targets a concrete capability gap—large-scale, behavior-preserving coordination across repository boundaries—that small issue-resolution tasks underrepresent. - The dataset is unusually large in patch scope: 30% of instances modify more than 10 files and 32% modify more than 200 LOC, compared with 86% single-file instances in SWE-bench Verified according to the paper’s comparison. - The construction process explicitly addresses known benchmark defects by rewriting specifications and reviewing tests rather than relying directly on commit messages and existing validation suites. - The two-scaffold, six-model evaluation exposes meaningful interactions between model choice, runtime tooling, cost, language, and failure mode; the observation that agents often stop after modifying only a subset of affected files is more actionable than a single aggregate score. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Not stated as a dedicated limitations section. The paper implicitly acknowledges that the benchmark is limited to 170 retained instances, seven languages, publicly available repositories, and the tested model/scaffold configurations. It also notes concentration differences across languages, including TypeScript’s reliance on two repositories, but does not frame this as a formal threat to validity. No explicit discussion is provided of annotation subjectivity, test coverage, repository selection bias, or benchmark contamination after publication. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest concern is that “expert curation” is asserted more strongly than it is measured: the paper gives no reviewer identities or expertise distribution, independent review protocol, agreement statistics, adjudication process, or post-release audit. The keyword-based mining rule and requirement that commits modify tests may exclude valid refactorings and favor projects whose developers use particular commit conventions. The benchmark mixes refactoring with new features and bug fixes—43.5% and 41.2% of instances, respectively—so resolve rates do not isolate refactoring capability. Gold-patch size is used as a proxy for difficulty, although large diffs can contain repetitive mechanical edits and small diffs can require substantial semantic reasoning. Per-language comparisons are underpowered and confounded by repository and task composition, especially for TypeScript. The paper does not compare evaluation outcomes before and after test curation, against a held-out human-authored set, or under alternative validation such as hidden tests, semantic checks, compilation-only checks, or human judgment. It also lacks repeated stochastic runs, making differences of a few percentage points difficult to interpret. Finally, the claim that incomplete file coverage is the dominant failure mode is based on two representative models and manual trajectory inspection rather than a quantified analysis over all model runs. Bottom Line: Practitioners and researchers building or evaluating long-horizon coding agents should read and use this benchmark, but the paper’s conclusions about evaluation validity and language-specific difficulty should be treated as provisional until curation reliability, task validity, contamination resistance, and repeated-run robustness are independently demonstrated.
