Problem & Motivation: The work addresses reliable AI-mediated customer support in an enterprise setting spanning many product lines and 36+ languages, where policies, product capabilities, retrieval indices, prompts, tools, and content continuously change. Static handcrafted prompts, fixed retrieval pipelines, and periodic human QA can become stale, induce hallucinations, break tool flows, and create inconsistent multilingual behavior. The specific gap is an operational feedback loop that can evaluate failures by dimension, attribute regressions to system components, adapt behavior without foundation-model retraining, and safely promote or roll back changes. The paper frames this as a production reliability and lifecycle-management problem rather than a conventional static chatbot-benchmark problem. Key Idea: Treat prompts, retrieval configuration, evaluation signals, and longer-lived operational knowledge as versioned artifacts in a closed-loop control system: an agent uses retrieval as an explicit action, evaluators produce decomposed fitness signals, and constrained evolutionary search updates prompt policies while immutable business rules and gated rollout limit behavioral drift. The central insight is operational co-evolution with auditable mutation boundaries, rather than unconstrained agent memory or model retraining. Methodology: At inference time, a user query and chat context enter an agent runtime whose system prompt is assembled from the Auto-Prompt Engine; the agent reasons and acts, optionally invoking a RAG tool. The RAG pipeline ingests help articles, learning content, and product documentation through ETL, chunks and embeds them, applies hybrid dense-sparse retrieval and semantic reranking, and returns top-k evidence with URL, locale, source, and snapshot provenance. A versioned content lake uses product, locale, and snapshot-date facets and retires old content through snapshot pointers. Responses and traces feed a modular evaluator composed of groundedness, relevance or intent alignment, completeness, tool-execution, translation, terminology, fluency, and style or policy checks, combining rules, XGLM perplexity, and LLM judgments; a consensus layer is periodically calibrated against human annotations. Offline fitness drives an outer evolutionary loop: an LLM initializes a population of prompts from business rules, top-K candidates are selected, parents are semantically blended, mutations are applied, and candidates are cached and iterated for G generations. Prompts violating immutable business rules are filtered or assigned zero fitness. Production changes pass regression tests and staged rollout before deployment, with versioned artifacts and rollback. The key design decisions—agent-controlled retrieval, constrained crossover and mutation, and decomposed evaluation—are motivated operationally, but the paper does not provide enough implementation detail to independently assess prompt operators, evaluator aggregation, retrieval hyperparameters, population sizes, or deployment thresholds. Key Results: In a 100-interaction anonymized human-validated RAG simulation, vanilla RAG scored 2.59/3.00 overall, hallucinated on 5.3% of responses, and achieved 78.7% completeness; ReAct-style RAG scored 2.56, 4.8%, and 79.0%; an OpenAI tool-agent RAG scored 2.48, 6.2%, and 75.0%; and the full Support AI Agent scored 2.78, under 0.1%, and 87.8%, respectively. The evaluation used multiple inference runs per interaction and GPT-4.1 as judge, with GPT-4o-mini as the production generator. On a routing-intent dataset of only N=30, average prompt accuracy increased from 62.6% at generation 0 to 68.0% after two generations when crossover and mutation were both enabled, with the best prompt reaching 73.3%; removing either operator produced only 64.0% or 63.3% average accuracy after two generations, although the table does not report variance or statistical tests. In evaluator ablations on 100 premium-tier chats, alignment with human labels was 87% for the full evaluation, 76% without groundedness, 82% without relevance, 86% without completeness, and 67% using only an overall score; three reviewers had 92% raw agreement before majority-vote resolution. On an English-Chinese translation set of N=300, reported evaluator accuracy was 49.7% for COMET, 76.5% for a single-agent LLM judge, and 84.8% for the modular multi-agent evaluator. The two-week production A/B test randomized users 50/50 against the original production agent: QA self-serve rose from 33.7% to 42.7% (+9.0 percentage points, 95% CI [8.4, 9.6]); cancellation self-serve rose from 61.9% to 66.6% (+4.8 points, 95% CI [3.8, 5.7]); and routing accuracy rose from 38.2% to 68.8% (+30.6 points, 95% CI [23.6, 37.6]). The first two metrics used tens of thousands of conversations and users, whereas routing used only 356 decisions per arm. All reported tests had p much less than 10^-4 and remained significant after Holm correction; user-clustered GEE/CR2 errors reportedly preserved significance. The online result is an integrated system effect, not a component-isolated effect, and the paper does not report absolute sample sizes for every monitored outcome, latency changes, or longer-term retention of the gains. Baselines are relevant production and agentic-RAG configurations, but the offline comparisons do not establish superiority over current prompt optimizers, stronger retrieval systems, fine-tuned support models, or alternative evaluator and rollout strategies. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper's genuine contribution is an enterprise production architecture and deployment workflow that combines known evolutionary prompt search, agentic RAG, LLM-as-judge evaluation, versioning, and safe rollout into a continuously operated closed loop, plus an empirical production report; the individual algorithmic components are largely standard combinations rather than a fundamentally new optimization method. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for crossover versus mutation, evaluator-signal removal, and alternative translation evaluators, plus a randomized two-week online experiment with fixed user assignment, confidence intervals, multiple-outcome correction, and a user-clustered robustness analysis. However, the offline RAG sample contains only 100 interactions, the prompt-evolution dataset contains 30 examples, the routing online set contains 356 decisions per arm, and no multiple-seed results, error bars for prompt evolution, search-budget sensitivity, or independent replication are reported. Human calibration is present, but evaluator dependence remains substantial: GPT-4.1 supplies the main fitness and response judgments, and the translation comparison labels a modular evaluator's agreement or accuracy without fully specifying the gold-label construction, confidence intervals, or evaluator prompts. The online experiment compares a bundled treatment against the prior production system and therefore cannot attribute gains to Auto-Prompt, agent-invoked RAG, evaluator-driven iteration, or their interactions. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.10224v1, dated 10 August 2026), not presented here as peer-reviewed. No code, data, model weights, or public repository URL is mentioned; the system depends on LinkedIn's proprietary traffic, content lake, search backend, and Azure-hosted GPT-4o-mini/GPT-4.1, making end-to-end reproduction unavailable. The routing result's very large effect also merits scrutiny because its evaluation set is small and the paper does not describe label generation, stratification, or confidence-interval methodology in enough detail. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper describes a deployed production tool and evaluates it online, while also containing empirical simulations. * Practical: The architecture runs on commercially available hosted LLM and search infrastructure, and the paper reports live LinkedIn deployment; however, the cost, latency, throughput, and required infrastructure for the full control plane are not quantified. * Efficient: Evolution requires repeated LLM inference over candidate populations and generations, with an end-to-end cycle taking hours to days; no comparison of compute, token, memory, or serving latency against the original agent is provided. * Effective: The production A/B test shows improvements on self-serve and routing proxies, with no reported regressions in escalation, feedback, latency, satisfaction, or moderation incidents, but it does not measure broader customer welfare, factual correctness independent of retrieved content, or long-term operational outcomes. * Scalable: The system is designed for 36+ languages, multiple product lines, changing content, and staged rollout, but direct controlled multilingual evidence is limited to English-Chinese and the study covers one enterprise surface for two weeks; behavior at 10x–100x traffic, larger prompt populations, more tools, or longer drift periods is not evaluated. The work delivers a proprietary production support-agent architecture, configuration and artifact-versioning workflow, evaluator framework, and evolutionary prompt engine, but no reusable public library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or open-source implementation. Strengths: - The paper identifies a real production failure mode—continual upstream change—and connects optimization, evaluation, versioning, rollback, and fallback into one operational design rather than treating prompt tuning as an isolated offline task. - The constrained evolutionary search explicitly separates immutable policy requirements from mutable quality optimization, a sensible safeguard against prompt drift that is more operationally relevant than unconstrained prompt maximization. - The decomposed evaluator provides actionable signals: removing groundedness reduces human-label alignment by 11 points, while collapsing all signals into one score reduces alignment by 20 points, supporting the value of failure-specific diagnostics. - The randomized production experiment reports large absolute improvements on three operational metrics with user-level assignment and clustered-error robustness checks, supplying stronger evidence than simulation-only agent papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge dependence on GPT-4.1 LLM judges, the inference cost and hours-to-days cadence of evolutionary search, evaluation on one enterprise deployment over two weeks, lack of online component attribution, retrieval coverage as a quality ceiling, limited controlled multilingual testing focused on English-Chinese, and closed-source model and search dependencies. They confront these limitations directly and propose larger human-label samples, open evaluators, faster adaptation, factorial deployments, broader language testing, and open-source reproduction as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central online claim is confounded by a bundled intervention; without factorial or sequential component ablations in production, the paper cannot show that self-evolution rather than the new RAG policy, prompt rewrite, retrieval changes, or ordinary engineering improvements caused the gains. - The prompt optimizer is evaluated on N=30 examples and appears vulnerable to overfitting, but the paper does not provide a held-out test set, prompt-search train/test separation, cross-product generalization, or protection against optimizing the same judge used for selection. - The evaluation framework may suffer from judge-model bias and circularity because LLM-generated fitness signals drive optimization and the same broad evaluator family is used to assess outcomes; cross-model, blinded, human-endpoint validation is insufficiently specified. - The headline routing improvement uses only 356 decisions per arm and lacks details about the labeled-set construction, class balance, confidence intervals beyond the aggregate result, and whether routing behavior was optimized directly against that set. - The paper does not report retrieval recall, citation precision, tool-call success, per-language and per-product breakdowns, latency and cost distributions, or failure cases, limiting diagnosis of whether gains arise from better retrieval, stricter abstention, or genuine answer quality. - Claims about continual adaptation and scalability exceed the evidence from a two-week single-tenant deployment; there is no long-horizon drift experiment, incident-rate analysis, or 10x–100x stress test. Bottom Line: This is a useful production engineering case study for teams operating enterprise support agents under knowledge and policy drift, with credible short-term online gains, but it is not a strong standalone algorithmic contribution and its causal attribution, small offline evaluations, proprietary dependencies, and limited durability evidence substantially constrain generality.

Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs (32 ▲ )

Alexander Panfilov, David Schmotz, Ilia Shumailov, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Joachim Schaeffer, Ameya Prabhu, Jonas Geiping, Maksym Andriushchenko · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper demonstrates a cross-session, cross-user, and cross-model attack that replays client-held reasoning signatures into weaker models from the same provider to reconstruct hidden reasoning traces in plaintext. - Why it's important: The attack undermines proprietary-model anti-distillation defenses and exposes private data, credentials, harmful intermediate content, and invisible prompt-injection payloads that users and monitoring systems cannot inspect. - How it does it: It treats a compatible weaker model as a model-mediated decryption oracle, coercing it to transcribe an authenticated reasoning block without directly bypassing the stronger source model. - The good: Across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google APIs, the extracted-token counts closely track provider-reported thinking-token counts, and a scan of 315,320 blocks recovered 62 API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens, 7 private keys, and other artifacts from genuine user sessions. - The missing: The paper lacks ground-truth plaintext traces, strong independent baselines, and a systematic ablation of prompt templates, sampling, model choice, and provider-side defenses; its main attacks were no longer reproducible after disclosure patches. - Read it or not: Security researchers, API designers, and operators of agentic systems should read it for the concrete architectural failure mode and mitigation design, but should treat claims about exact extraction fidelity and prevalence as provisional.

Problem & Motivation Proprietary reasoning-model APIs increasingly return opaque thinking blocks to clients so that multi-turn reasoning can continue without server-side storage while protecting model intellectual property and limiting disclosure of harmful or sensitive intermediate content. The paper addresses the security gap created when those blocks remain portable across sessions, users, and model versions. The affected parties include API providers seeking anti-distillation protection, developers storing or publishing agent trajectories, users whose private data enters model reasoning, and downstream agent workflows that replay opaque state. Prior work had shown replay or portability of encrypted reasoning blocks; the paper targets the stronger gap that a weaker, less safeguarded model in the same provider ecosystem can be used to decode a stronger model's block. Key Idea The central insight is that authenticated transport-level protection does not provide confidentiality against a compatible model that legitimately receives and processes the protected content. If a provider accepts the same reasoning envelope across model boundaries, an attacker can send a frontier-model signature to a cheaper sibling and prompt that sibling to transcribe the attached reasoning. The signature need not be cryptographically forged: portability and the decoder model's behavioral compliance provide the decryption channel. This extends earlier replay observations into a practical cross-model extraction attack. Methodology The paper defines first-party attackers who generate their own source traces and third-party attackers who obtain traces from other users or public repositories. It characterizes three compatibility levels: replay across turns or sessions, replay across users, and replay across models. The extraction pipeline obtains a signed or opaque reasoning block from a source model, injects it into a compatible decoder model, and uses provider-specific transcription prompts, assistant-turn prefilling, repeated injection, best-of-n sampling, reconciliation, or short continuation chunks. Claude extraction uses Haiku 4.5 as a fuzzy decoder with an assistant prefill; GPT extraction uses GPT-5.6 Luna, with up to 50 candidates, fallback to Terra, and chunks under approximately 50 tokens when output safeguards trigger; Gemini extraction uses Gemini Robotics ER-1.6 and optional reconciliation with Gemini 3.5 Flash. Fidelity is estimated mainly by comparing reconstructed-token counts with API-reported thinking-token counts, not by comparing against plaintext ground truth. Controlled source traces come from AIME 2025, Codeforces, and Humanity's Last Exam; public-trace analysis uses 6,708 trajectories from GitHub and Hugging Face. Additional experiments test distillation relevance, harmful-information exposure, prompt injection, privacy leakage, style drift, perplexity, and summary faithfulness. The main design choices—using weaker sibling models, provider-specific prefilling, and token-count matching—are operationally plausible, but the paper provides limited causal or statistical justification for why these measures establish verbatim recovery rather than high-level reconstruction. Key Results The attack is demonstrated against Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google APIs, with Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, and Gemini Robotics 1.6 serving as decoders. On 120 Codeforces problems, extracted and API-reported thinking-token counts generally track closely, but the paper does not provide a single aggregate fidelity percentage or exact error distribution in the main text. The authors report that decoding 10,000 traces at roughly 12,000 input and output tokens would cost approximately $720 using cited Claude Haiku pricing. In a public-data scan, 315,320 reasoning blocks from 6,708 sessions were reconstructed; 1,028 blocks, or 0.3%, were judged to contain at least one privacy leakage, and 328 sessions, or 4.9%, contained at least one real sensitive item. Across genuine non-benchmark sessions, the paper reports 62 API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens, 7 private keys, 30 personal emails, 6 non-localhost IP addresses, 130 names, and 36 postal addresses. Of 704 non-benchmark artifacts, 64 were absent from the visible chat history. The paper also shows proof-of-concept harmful-content recovery from a model whose visible answer rejected a vehicle-theft request, and hidden prompt injection that caused GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.7 workflows to upload files to an attacker-controlled server. In Appendix B, a 1% Opus reasoning prefill increased Kimi-K3's best-of-100 visible-answer n-gram overlap with Opus answers by 0.15 on STEM and 0.086 on non-STEM HLE problems, with paired-test p-values of 1.7e-5 and 6.3e-6; however, the authors explicitly state that these experiments do not establish proprietary-model distillation. Baselines are mostly behavioral controls, such as unprefilled and self-prefilled models, rather than strong end-to-end attack or defense baselines. Novelty Classification NEW SECURITY PROBLEM, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW ATTACK METHOD, and ENGINEERING/SYSTEMS ANALYSIS: the genuinely new contribution is the demonstrated use of cross-model compatibility and a weaker sibling model as a reasoning-transcription oracle across three proprietary API ecosystems; the underlying ingredients—AEAD envelopes, replay attacks, prompt prefilling, model extraction, and LLM-as-a-judge labeling—are established techniques combined in a new API-security setting. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes controlled experiments, provider-specific attack details, negative/control conditions for style-prefill experiments, cross-validation grouped by problem for style classifiers, statistical tests for selected n-gram comparisons, and extensive appendices. It spent approximately $30,000 in API credits. However, the core fidelity metric assumes provider-reported token counts are exact and treats matching length as evidence of content faithfulness; this cannot distinguish verbatim extraction from plausible or repetitive reconstruction. The authors acknowledge that no ground-truth plaintext is available. GPT extraction uses adaptive prompt search, candidate selection, fallbacks, chunking, and ad hoc refusal filtering, making success rates difficult to compare cleanly across providers. The privacy findings rely on two-stage LLM labeling rather than independent human annotation or secret-validation measurements, and the reported prevalence comes from a targeted, non-exhaustive corpus. No public code, dataset of recovered traces, model weights, or reusable attack implementation URL is stated; sensitive recovered material was deleted. The reproducibility statement says that providers mitigated the attack after disclosure, so the central experiments could not be rerun as of August 2026. The paper also does not report a systematic ablation of decoder capability, prompt variants, temperature, number of candidates, chunk size, signature age, or API rate limits. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: The attack uses ordinary API access and commercially available models, with no provider-infrastructure access or model weights required, although it depends on a compatible decoder endpoint and the precise provider implementation. - Efficient: The paper reports an estimated $720 to decode 10,000 traces with Haiku 4.5 under a stated workload; GPT extraction can require multiple candidates, fallbacks, and chunked calls, but a complete cost comparison against direct jailbreaking or output-only distillation is not evaluated. - Effective: The experiments demonstrate recovery of reasoning-like text, secrets, harmful intermediate content, and prompt-injection behavior, but exact verbatim fidelity and the downstream utility of recovered traces are only partially measured. - Scalable: The public scan reaches 315,320 blocks and the attack is demonstrated across three vendors, but the paper does not test 10x–100x larger corpora, provider-wide rate limits, long-term account detection, or post-patch robustness; scalability beyond the reported corpus is claimed rather than established. The work provides a security analysis, attack procedures, and a proposed context-bound envelope design, but no released software artifact or sanitized reusable attack package is stated. The proposed mitigation binds envelopes to user identity, session state, predecessor blocks, conversational position, model context, or server-side identifiers; it also recommends key rotation, cross-model isolation, replay detection, revocation, and model-level refusal training. Strengths - It identifies a consequential security asymmetry: a weaker model can defeat protections applied to a stronger model without directly extracting from the stronger endpoint. - It connects one architectural property—portable client-side reasoning envelopes—to four distinct attack surfaces: proprietary reasoning theft, secret extraction, hidden harmful content, and opaque prompt injection. - The public-trace audit gives the vulnerability concrete operational significance, including quantified leakage rates and separate treatment of benchmark versus genuine user sessions. - The mitigation discussion is more specific than a generic recommendation to “use encryption”: it distinguishes user binding, session hash chains, Merkle-root compaction, legacy-key rotation, cross-model isolation, and residual model-level defenses. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that evaluation covers only the API versions and reasoning models available from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google in early July 2026; proprietary cryptographic implementations may change without notice. They acknowledge that extracted text cannot be fully verified against ground-truth reasoning, that decoder generation is stochastic, and that token-count agreement is only an indirect fidelity signal. They also state that the public-trace scan is targeted rather than exhaustive, that the results may underestimate leakage in private or production traces, and that the attack was no longer reproducible after provider mitigations. Appendix B explicitly disclaims causal conclusions about whether open models were distilled from proprietary reasoning. Analyst-Identified Gaps The paper does not establish that the opaque payloads are actually decrypted in the cryptographic sense; the evidence shows that a model receiving a valid envelope can emit text consistent with the hidden content, which could involve model-side reconstruction, server-side disclosure, or other implementation behavior. It lacks an independent plaintext oracle, human verification of sampled reconstructions, or cryptographic protocol documentation from providers. The extraction pipeline is heavily tuned per vendor and uses adaptive filtering, so reported cross-provider breadth may overstate uniformity. The privacy scan's LLM judges may produce false positives and false negatives, and the paper does not validate whether recovered credentials were live, revoked, synthetic, duplicated, or attributable to the model's hidden state rather than the original session context. The prompt-injection demonstrations show capability transfer in selected workflows but do not measure attack success rates across diverse scaffolds, monitoring systems, or tool permissions. The work also omits a systematic comparison with simpler attacks such as direct prompting, visible-log scraping, model-specific jailbreaks, or provider-side server-state designs, and it does not evaluate the performance, storage, latency, or compatibility costs of the proposed cryptographic fixes. Bottom Line This is a high-impact security paper with a compelling architectural finding and unusually concrete privacy consequences; practitioners operating reasoning APIs or public agent traces should read it, while reviewers should discount claims of verbatim extraction and general prevalence until independent post-patch replication and stronger fidelity validation exist.

DistillCache: KL-Guided Adaptive KV-Cache Eviction for Memory-Efficient LLM Inference

A Althoubi · arxiv.org · inference optimize llm faster inference throughput - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DistillCache, a reinforcement-learning controller that selects token-level KV-cache entries to retain under a fixed memory budget. - Why it's important: KV-cache memory grows with context length and limits the number of long-context requests that can run concurrently on available hardware. - How it does it: A 200K-parameter MLP scores tokens using attention mass, value norms, attention variance, attention entropy, and position, while REINFORCE trains Gumbel-top-\( B \) selections to minimize the per-step KL divergence between full-cache and pruned-cache next-token distributions. - The good: At a 25% cache budget on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, it reaches 39.1% LongBench accuracy, or 94.2% of the 41.5% full-cache score, exceeding H2O by 2.7 points, SnapKV by 2.1 points, ForesightKV by 0.9 points, and RLKV by 1.4 points under the reported reimplementations. - The missing: The strongest learned baselines are reimplemented rather than evaluated from official code, and the study does not test the claimed long-context advantage at 32K–128K tokens, larger models, or multi-request serving scale. - Read it or not: Researchers working on KV-cache compression or learned inference control should read it for the distributional reward and ablations, while practitioners seeking immediately deployable serving gains should wait for released code and broader systems-level validation.

Problem & Motivation: Long-context autoregressive LLM inference stores keys and values for prior tokens, making KV-cache memory scale linearly with sequence length and reducing per-GPU concurrency and feasible context length. Existing methods such as H2O and SnapKV use cumulative attention, positional structure, or local clustering as token-importance proxies; these signals can discard tokens whose importance appears only through later generation, especially in long-range dependency and reasoning tasks. The paper targets memory-constrained inference for instruction-tuned LLMs, where the gap is to identify cache entries by their downstream effect on generation rather than by retrospective attention or fixed positional heuristics. Key Idea: Train cache eviction as a sequential decision problem whose reward is the negative KL divergence between the full-cache teacher distribution and the pruned-cache student distribution at every decoding step. The central insight is that preserving the model's next-token distribution provides a task-general, end-to-end signal for cache utility and can learn to retain less-attended but prediction-critical tokens such as negations and clause-governing words. Methodology: During decoding, each cached token receives a five-dimensional feature vector consisting of average attention mass across heads and layers, value-vector ℓ2 norm, cross-head attention variance, attention-weighted entropy over the most recent 64 queries, and normalized position. A two-layer 128-unit ReLU MLP with LayerNorm maps each feature vector to a scalar retention score. During training, Gumbel perturbations produce stochastic top-\( B \) subsets under a Plackett–Luce selection distribution; the student cache is pruned recursively while a separate teacher cache remains complete. The reward is \( R_t=-D_{KL}(P_t\|\hat P_t) \), where the distributions are the next-token outputs of the full and pruned branches. REINFORCE optimizes discounted returns with \(\gamma=0.99 \), entropy regularization \(\beta=0.01 \), leave-one-out and moving-average baselines, and exact dynamic-programming computation of the subset log partition function in \( O(LB) \) time during training. At inference, the teacher and reward branches disappear: the model performs one forward pass, the policy scores the resulting cache, deterministic top-\( B \) retention is applied for the next step, and the current token is selected from the current logits. The fixed budget uses \( B=\max(\lfloor rL_t\rfloor,32) \). The feature set is motivated but not individually derived from a principled causal model; the independent per-token MLP simplifies deployment but omits explicit token interactions; and the KL reward is well aligned with distributional fidelity but does not directly optimize task accuracy, latency, or energy. Key Results: On Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, the full-cache scores are 41.5% on LongBench and 52.0% on the average of GSM8K and BBH. At a 25% budget, DistillCache obtains 39.1±1.1% LongBench accuracy, compared with H2O 36.4±1.5%, SnapKV 37.0±1.3%, ForesightKV 38.2±1.2%, and RLKV 37.7±1.4%; on reasoning it obtains 45.0±1.2%, below RLKV's 45.7±1.4% but above H2O's 41.4±1.7% and SnapKV's 42.7±1.5%. At 12.5%, it reaches 36.6% LongBench and 39.9% reasoning, outperforming RLKV by 3.1 and 1.0 points respectively. With a fixed 25% budget, accuracy at 2K/4K/8K context lengths is 40.5/40.2/38.1%, compared with RLKV's 40.7/39.5/36.4%; the advantage grows at 8K. Perplexity increase at 25% is reported as +0.35 versus +0.62 for H2O, +0.55 for SnapKV, +0.44 for ForesightKV, and +0.47 for RLKV. On 2× RTX 4090, throughput is 38.0 tokens/s at 25% versus 18.0 tokens/s for full cache, approximately 2.1× faster, but below H2O's 42.8, SnapKV's 41.5, ForesightKV's 38.2, and RLKV's 39.5 tokens/s because of approximately 1.4 ms/token policy and feature overhead. A zero-shot policy trained on Mistral transfers to Llama-3-8B-Instruct with 38.4% LongBench and 46.2% reasoning at 25%, exceeding native H2O and SnapKV but trailing retrained ForesightKV and RLKV. The reward ablation reports 39.1% for per-step KL versus 36.8% for an approximated ForesightKV-style reward and 37.5% for holistic future-utility ranking. The hybrid with RLKV-style head gating reaches 39.8%, a 0.7-point gain. These results were measured on standard benchmarks and contexts up to 8K, not at the 32K–128K scales emphasized in the motivation. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper combines known policy-gradient and Gumbel-top-\( B \) selection machinery with a distinctive per-step full-cache/pruned-cache KL objective and a lightweight token-level controller, while the empirical evidence supports gains over heuristics and the reported reimplementations of concurrent RL methods rather than introducing a new benchmark or fundamental RL algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper specifies the model, feature definitions, reward, policy architecture, optimizer, learning rate, training length, prompt formats, maximum sequence length, cache budgets, hardware, and five random seeds; tables generally report mean ± standard deviation over five independent training runs. It includes reward, feature, supervised-ranking, entropy-regularization, context-length, transfer, error-mode, per-task, and hybrid ablations. The most important ablations support both feature diversity and RL optimization: at 25% LongBench, attention-only RL obtains 36.5%, attention-plus-entropy RL 37.4%, supervised full-feature ranking 37.8%, no-entropy RL 38.1%, and the full method 39.1%. However, statistical significance tests and confidence intervals are not reported, and the five runs appear to vary policy training rather than independently evaluating broad prompt or model variability. ForesightKV and RLKV are best-effort reimplementations from descriptions rather than official implementations, making the 0.9–1.4-point comparisons uncertain. The policy is trained on part of LongBench and GSM8K, although the paper says the 2wikimqa split is excluded from the test average and GSM8K exemplars are separated; this creates a benchmark-family exposure concern that deserves a clearly isolated unseen-dataset evaluation. Public datasets are available, but the source-code section says code will be released upon acceptance and provides no repository URL in the supplied paper, so current artifact availability is not established. The KL bound relies on bounded value norms, a projection-dependent constant, local softmax Lipschitz behavior, and a minimum softmax probability; these assumptions can be restrictive for large vocabularies, and the displayed argument is a motivation rather than a formal theorem with a practically quantified guarantee. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, with empirical evaluation of an inference-time cache-management controller. Practical: The method runs on commercially available GPUs—the reported experiments use 2× RTX 4090—and requires only a frozen LLM plus a roughly 200K-parameter policy, but integration requires access to per-token attention statistics and cache-management code. Efficient: A 25% cache budget gives 18.5 ms attention latency and 38.0 tokens/s end-to-end versus 42.1 ms and 18.0 tokens/s for full cache, but the controller adds about 1.4 ms/token and is slower than H2O and SnapKV at the same budget. Effective: The evidence shows improved LongBench accuracy and perplexity relative to the evaluated baselines, with the strongest gains on multi-document QA and summarization, but reasoning remains below RLKV at moderate compression and the reward is only an indirect proxy for benchmark correctness. Scalable: The method is tested only through 8K contexts, a 7B/8B model scale, and a 2×-4090 setup; behavior at 10×–100× longer contexts, larger models, larger batch sizes, and distributed or multi-tenant serving is not evaluated. The paper delivers an inference controller and training procedure, but no currently verifiable released software artifact or model-weight artifact is identified. Strengths: - The per-step KL teacher–student reward directly measures distributional distortion caused by recurrent eviction decisions, avoiding dependence on a single handcrafted attention score or final-answer reward. - The causal dual-cache training setup correctly exposes the policy to compounding effects of earlier eviction decisions rather than evaluating isolated one-step deletions. - The ablations separate feature richness from optimization strategy: the full-feature supervised ranker reaches 37.8% while full RL reaches 39.1% at 25%, providing evidence that the result is not only feature engineering. - The method shows useful cross-model transfer: a Mistral-trained policy reaches 89.7% of Llama-3's full-cache LongBench score without retraining, although it does not beat retrained learned baselines. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly report approximately 130 GPU-hours of training, doubled training memory from the teacher/student caches, REINFORCE variance, a 1.4 ms/token inference overhead, weaker reasoning results than RLKV at moderate budgets, independent token scoring without inter-token modeling, dependence on transformer attention features, and uncertainty from reimplemented concurrent baselines. They also state that serving-system benefits in distributed or multi-tenant environments, larger models, 32K–128K contexts, lower-cost optimization, and broader transfer remain future work. These limitations are confronted directly, although the conclusion still frames the method as deployment-oriented despite the substantial offline training cost. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The evaluation omits several system-level or training-free alternatives discussed in the paper, including RocketKV and SpeCache, so the practical memory/latency trade-off is not compared against the full relevant deployment landscape. - The central learned-baseline claims depend on non-official ForesightKV and RLKV reimplementations with potentially unequal tuning, and no implementation parity audit or sensitivity analysis is provided. - The paper does not report peak memory, maximum concurrent requests, batch-size scaling, energy, or actual serving throughput under realistic scheduling; tokens/s on 2× GPUs is insufficient to establish production-level capacity gains. - LongBench is used both as training material and evaluation context, creating possible task-family overfitting even though one split is excluded; evaluations on entirely unseen long-context datasets and domains would strengthen the claim of generality. - The controller uses the current forward pass's attention statistics and then prunes for the next step, but the computational and memory cost of extracting all five features across layers and heads at much longer contexts is not measured beyond the reported 0.9 ms feature component at the tested scale. - The paper's theoretical motivation does not establish that minimizing per-step KL reliably minimizes sequence-level task loss; no analysis quantifies error propagation over long generations or compares alternative KL directions and calibration-sensitive objectives. - Reported throughput is described once as using 2× RTX 4090 and later as limited to a single-GPU setting, an experimental-description inconsistency that should be resolved. Bottom Line: DistillCache is a credible and technically coherent contribution to learned KV-cache eviction, with useful ablations and measurable gains over the reported baselines, but its practical superiority remains unproven until official-baseline comparisons, unseen-dataset evaluation, larger-context tests, and real serving-scale memory measurements are provided.

DCAS: Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding to Internalize Planning across Scaffolds (12 ▲ )

Kishanthan Thangarajah, Boyuan Chen, Ahmed E. Hassan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DCAS, an API-interception and trajectory-logging layer, and uses it to train Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct on 576 planning-aware Claude Code trajectories for improved performance across CLI agent scaffolds. - Why it's important: Fine-tuned coding agents can perform well only under the scaffold used for training, limiting deployment choices driven by cost, latency, licensing, and privacy. - How it does it: DCAS substitutes backend models inside unmodified CLI scaffolds, separates explicit planning from execution, and fine-tunes on either planning-only or planning-plus-execution traces. - The good: A controlled plan-source intervention raises SWE-bench Verified Pass@1 from 42.8% to 57.8%, while Plan+Exec fine-tuning reaches 55.8% on the training scaffold and improves self-planning performance on OpenCode and mini-swe-agent. - The missing: The experiments do not isolate planning from other scaffold-specific factors such as tool schemas, parsers, context handling, and turn management, and they lack execution-only, token-matched, multi-seed, and model-scale controls. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners building open coding agents should read it for the cross-scaffold evaluation methodology and released artifacts, but should treat the claim that planning explains the deployment gap as suggestive rather than established.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses poor portability of fine-tuned CLI-based software-engineering agents across agent scaffolds. Open training datasets such as SWE-Gym, Nebius, SWE-Lego, and CoderForge are collected primarily under OpenHands, so models learn conventions associated with that environment. When deployed under Claude Code, OpenCode, or mini-swe-agent, these models can lose substantial performance despite their underlying base models showing smaller scaffold-to-scaffold variation. The practical problem affects developers who choose scaffolds for cost, licensing, latency, or privacy rather than for compatibility with the training environment. The paper focuses on planning as a candidate source of the mismatch, distinguishing explicit pre-execution plans from implicit conventions governing decomposition, tool sequencing, exploration, and recovery. However, tool-call formats, parsers, context limits, and turn management also vary across scaffolds, so the prior-work gap is only partially isolated by the study. Key Idea The central insight is to treat scaffold-specific planning structure as a behavioral capability that can be moved from the scaffold into the model. DCAS makes this testable by intercepting and translating API traffic so the same backend model can operate inside different unmodified scaffolds, while logging the resulting interactions as training trajectories. The PlanOnly versus Plan+Exec comparison further argues that implicit planning conventions can be learned from planning turns alone, whereas productive use of an explicit plan requires examples containing both planning and subsequent execution. Methodology DCAS sits between a CLI scaffold and a backend model, translating requests and responses between API formats and logging model interactions. The authors use Claude Code 2.0.76 as the main collection and evaluation scaffold, then evaluate Claude Code 2.1.73, OpenCode 0.0.55, and mini-swe-agent 2.2.8. In RQ1, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct executes SWE-bench Verified issues under no-plan, self-plan, and externally supplied plan conditions; external plans come from Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, or Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct. The plan is inserted as a user-prompt artifact, with a maximum of eight plan steps, and execution is capped at 100 turns; planning receives a separate 500-turn allowance. For RQ2, GLM-4.7 generates two-phase trajectories on approximately 5,000-task SWE-Lego Real Data, and rejection sampling retains 576 successful trajectories. PlanOnly contains 14,162 planning-phase per-turn samples, while Plan+Exec contains 36,259 samples from both planning and execution. The target model receives full-parameter SFT with LLaMA-Factory, learning rate 4.0e-6, cosine scheduling, BF16, 65,536-token context, Flash Attention 2, and ZeRO-3. The key design decisions—holding scaffold and executor fixed in RQ1, separating planning-only from planning-plus-execution data, and evaluating unseen scaffold versions—are logically motivated. Nevertheless, the plan injection intervention does not fully control for additional planner calls, routing behavior, plan length, or changes in context, and the SFT comparison lacks execution-only and compute/token-matched controls. Key Results On SWE-bench Verified, the cross-scaffold baseline study reports that fine-tuned models degrade outside their training environments: SWE-Lego-Qwen3-32B falls from 52.6% on OpenHands to 44.2% on Claude Code and 8.4% on OpenCode, while Nebius-SWE-Rebench-30B falls from 49.7% on OpenHands to 20.4% on mini-swe-agent. Untrained Qwen3-32B varies from 29.0% to 8.0% across the same scaffolds, suggesting—but not proving—that fine-tuning increases scaffold dependence. In RQ1, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct scores 42.8% with no plan, 48.2% with self-planning, 49.2% with Qwen3-480B plans, 54.2% with fixed-routing Opus 4.5 plans, 56.0% with default-routing Opus plans, and 57.8% with Sonnet 4.5 plans. Thus the largest reported plan-source improvement is 15.0 percentage points. In RQ2, PlanOnly reaches 53.8% without an inference-time plan and 53.2% with self-planning; Plan+Exec reaches 52.8% without a plan and 55.8% with self-planning, compared with the 42.8% base no-plan score. In RQ3, Plan+Exec reaches 54.6% without a plan and 57.2% with self-planning on Claude Code 2.1.73, 47.6% and 49.4% on OpenCode, and 39.2% and 42.4% on mini-swe-agent. The gains on unseen scaffolds are positive but smaller than on Claude Code, consistent with partial rather than complete portability. All primary evaluation uses the 500-instance SWE-bench Verified benchmark and Pass@1; no error bars, significance tests, trajectory-efficiency metrics, or direct plan-quality scores are reported. Codex CLI was attempted but excluded after the proxy interaction became unresponsive. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the systematic use of backend substitution and trace logging to study scaffold portability and collect planning-separated trajectories without modifying the scaffold; the planner-executor setup and SFT are combinations of established prompting and imitation-learning techniques, while the empirical claims about explicit versus implicit planning transfer are the paper's main scientific finding. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides useful controls within RQ1 and RQ2: the same executor, benchmark, scaffold version, and turn limit are used when comparing plan sources, and PlanOnly versus Plan+Exec provides a meaningful ablation of training content. It also reports base-model comparisons, a newer Claude Code version, and two unseen open scaffolds. However, it reports no random seeds, confidence intervals, repeated runs, statistical tests, or per-repository variance. The most important ablations are absent: execution-only SFT, token- or compute-matched training, degraded or independently scored plans, direct plan-quality/adherence measurements, and controls that hold tool schemas and context behavior fixed across scaffolds. Rejection sampling on successful trajectories creates an easier-task and success-only training distribution, and the authors do not quantify the rejected fraction or compare against non-rejected data. The authors acknowledge that planning co-varies with tool formats, parsers, turn management, and context handling, so the causal attribution remains incomplete. DCAS source code and reproduction scripts are reported as available in the Zenodo replication package (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19930073); model weights are reported at https://huggingface.co/kishanthan/models, and trajectories at https://huggingface.co/datasets/kishanthan/dcas_glm4.7_distill. The evaluation benchmark is decontaminated from the stated training source, but all primary results still rely on one benchmark and one target model family. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS and EMPIRICAL. Practical: DCAS and the evaluated open-weight models can run on commercially available accelerator infrastructure, although full-parameter fine-tuning of a 30B model and execution through frontier proprietary APIs impose substantial hardware and service costs. Efficient: The method uses only 576 retained trajectories and avoids an external planner at inference time for Plan+Exec, but the paper does not report wall-clock latency, token usage, memory consumption, collection cost, or comparison with alternative training regimes. Effective: The evidence shows measurable Pass@1 improvements on SWE-bench Verified, including 3.4 points on OpenCode and 7.0 points on mini-swe-agent under self-planning, but it does not establish that planning alone solves the full cross-scaffold problem because interface and execution variables remain confounded. Scalable: The study tests a 30B target model, 576 retained training instances, and three deployment environments, but it does not test 10x–100x more data, larger or smaller models, larger task suites, longer repositories, or additional major scaffolds; scalability beyond this setting is therefore not evaluated. The work delivers a software artifact, released training data, reproduction scripts, and fine-tuned model weights rather than stopping at a paper-only proposal. Strengths - DCAS enables a comparatively clean experimental capability—substituting the backend model while leaving the target scaffold unchanged—that is valuable for future multi-scaffold evaluation. - The explicit/implicit planning distinction is operationalized through PlanOnly and Plan+Exec datasets rather than remaining purely conceptual; the different no-plan and self-plan behaviors provide evidence that the two training signals are not identical. - The plan-source intervention produces a substantial 15.0-percentage-point Pass@1 difference under a fixed executor and scaffold, making planning a credible high-leverage variable even though it is not the only possible cause of scaffold mismatch. - The release of code, traces, dataset, and model weights improves reproducibility and makes the study more useful as infrastructure research than a result-only paper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that cross-scaffold attribution is incomplete because planning co-varies with tool-call schemas, parsers, turn management, and context-window handling. They acknowledge that the GLM-4.7 source model and successful-trajectory rejection sampling introduce confounds and bias toward easier instances, and that execution-only, token-matched, degraded-plan, and stronger-source-model controls remain future work. They also note that all experiments use SWE-bench Verified and one target model family, that only OpenCode and mini-swe-agent are evaluated as unseen scaffolds, that Codex CLI could not be evaluated, and that Pass@1 does not measure trajectory efficiency or direct plan quality. These limitations are discussed directly, which improves credibility, although the conclusion still uses stronger language than the causal evidence fully supports. Analyst-Identified Gaps The central causal claim is underdetermined: RQ1 establishes that an externally supplied plan changes performance, but not that planning explains most of the cross-scaffold degradation, since the plan condition also changes interaction length, context, model routing, and possibly hidden scaffold behavior. The PlanOnly result is also compatible with general exposure to successful trajectories or distributional adaptation, not uniquely implicit-planning acquisition; an execution-only dataset and token-matched controls are needed. Cross-scaffold transfer is compared mainly against the base model's no-plan condition, while matched base-versus-SFT self-plan comparisons show smaller gains and should be the primary portability comparison. The 576 trajectories are all successful and collected from a single scaffold using one source model, with no analysis of task composition, rejection rate, or whether gains concentrate on easy repositories. There is no direct measurement of plan quality, plan adherence, turn count, token cost, or failure modes, and no multi-seed uncertainty despite differences of only 1.4–3.8 points on some cross-scaffold conditions. Finally, the paper's claim that DCAS supports routing between any scaffold and backend is broader than the demonstrated evidence, since Codex failed and only a narrow set of API-compatible scaffolds was successfully evaluated. Bottom Line This is a useful and reproducible systems-and-empirical paper that should influence how coding-agent results are evaluated across scaffolds, but its strongest scientific claim should be narrowed from planning as the explanation of the deployment gap to planning as one demonstrably important and partially transferable component of that gap.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses dialogue systems that accept speech, text, and visual context but produce only text or speech, leaving the response visually disembodied. The target domain is interactive human-avatar dialogue, where visual behavior should reflect the current conversational state, vocal identity, and response semantics. Existing audio-driven avatar systems usually animate a reference identity from a completed or externally supplied waveform and optional manual prompt; joint audio-video generators generally condition on prompts, speech, or references without generating a response to a multimodal query. The specific data challenge is that large-scale samples pairing user query, response text, response speech, and target avatar video are unavailable, motivating a decomposition that can train dialogue, speech, and video pathways on heterogeneous datasets and reconnect them at inference time. Key Idea The central insight is to use two explicit interfaces between the response model and modality-specific renderers: a structured Visual Thought Plan (VTP) for response-dependent high-level visual intent, and native multi-codebook speech units for shared acoustic content and timing. The VTP exposes scene, emotion, movement style, and motion as an inspectable textual contract, while the speech units simultaneously drive waveform synthesis and frame-aligned avatar motion. For streaming, the key additional idea is to place the preceding chunk's clean terminal latent directly into each causal denoising window as a one-slot prefix, rather than relying only on cached history. Methodology The input consists of text and/or speech query x, reference image, and reference audio. Text and speech are embedded into a common Qwen3-8B dialogue-model space; the reference image is encoded by Qwen3-VL-2B for dialogue conditioning and independently by the Wan 3D VAE for video appearance, while reference audio is converted to a speaker embedding for Qwen3-TTS-0.6B. The dialogue model autoregressively emits a constrained five-field VTP inside a non-user-facing thinking span, followed by the response text. The Speech Generator then predicts a sequence U of 16-codebook acoustic units from response hidden states, response tokens, and reference-speaker embedding. Units are generated at 12.5 Hz, aggregated through a lightweight adapter, repeated two times per unit, and supplied at the 25-FPS video timeline; a codec decoder produces speech from the same units. The full-sequence Video Teacher is a Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B model initialized with OmniAvatar LoRA weights. It applies flow matching to VAE video latents, conditioned on the reference appearance latent, VTP text embedding, and aligned acoustic features injected into DiT blocks 2–15. The training objective is an autoregressive language loss over VTP and response, a 16-codebook speech cross-entropy loss, and a video flow-matching loss predicting epsilon minus the clean latent; the losses are activated only where corresponding supervision exists. Training uses approximately 800K ASR examples and 1M TTS examples in Stage 1, InstructS2S-200K and OmniCharacter in Stage 2, and approximately 140K filtered SpeakerVid clips with automatically generated VTP annotations in Stage 3. The Streaming Student is distilled from the frozen Teacher using AnyFlow-style flow-map and on-policy distribution-matching objectives. It performs bidirectional attention within four-latent windows and causal attention across windows; the first window contains the reference latent plus three new latents, and later windows contain a detached preceding clean latent plus three new latents. Every six speech units, representing 0.48 seconds, trigger 12 video frames. The VTP schema is directly supervised but its use of the shared autoregressive channel is only partially justified because it measurably reduces language QA performance. Key Results The main audio-video evaluation uses 200 CommonEval speech queries with fixed reference conditions sampled from the held-out SpeakerVid split. The Ex-Omni-2D Teacher reports PQ 7.53, CU 7.06, speaker similarity 0.417, subject consistency 94.62, image quality 67.31, dynamic degree 72.00, and SyncNet confidence 4.95. It does not dominate standalone renderers: echomimic reaches SC 97.87 and DD 74.00, OmniAvatar reaches Sync-C 5.64, and UniAVGen reaches IQ 68.02. The Teacher's value is therefore the combined dialogue, speech, personalized voice, VTP, and video interface rather than superior isolated rendering metrics. Student quality increases with denoising steps: the two-, four-, and eight-step variants obtain SC/IQ/DD/Sync-C of 93.33/52.70/9.50/3.51, 93.65/57.40/32.00/3.90, and 93.91/61.15/48.00/4.00, respectively. On four GPUs at 400x720 or 720x400, the four-step Student renders at 26.512 FPS with E2E RTF 1.293; the two-step Student reaches 39.546 FPS and RTF 1.201, while the eight-step Student reaches 15.622 FPS and RTF 1.932. These are incremental-generation measurements, not end-to-end real-time interaction. On VoiceBench speech QA, Ex-Omni-2D scores 4.28 on AlpacaEval, 3.71 on CommonEval, and 58.70 on BBH, below Qwen2.5-Omni's 4.49, 3.93, and 60.80 but above most listed alternatives. VTP supervision itself lowers CommonEval from 3.82 to 3.71 and BBH from 61.10 to 58.70 relative to response-only training. On the 400-dialogue OmniCharacter benchmark, Ex-Omni-2D improves the average of Fluency, Coherency, and Consistency over Qwen3-8B from 3.537 to 3.938, but its twelve-dimension average is only 3.283 versus 3.264, indicating a selective rather than uniform gain. The 16-codebook interface obtains Sync-C 4.95 with 0.011 seconds of conditioning latency, versus 5.83 and 0.051 seconds for waveform plus wav2vec and 2.07 and 0.003 seconds for a single-codebook interface. Prefix Streaming improves late-horizon behavior on the 200-video comparison: mean chunk consistency rises from 0.9251 to 0.9319, the consistency-error slope falls from 0.00783 to 0.00599 per chunk, and last-minus-first consistency error falls from 0.1005 to 0.0790. However, the first-frame VTP grounding score is only 43.00%, while the observational alignment scores for the other fields average 85.38%; these latter scores measure consistency of co-generated plan and video, not independent controllability. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the formulation of dialogue-native, reference-conditioned visual responses and the explicit VTP/acoustic-unit interfaces are the main conceptual contributions, while Prefix Streaming is a targeted streaming-state method built by adapting existing flow-map and on-policy distillation techniques to avatars. The individual components—LLM dialogue modeling, codec-based speech synthesis, audio-driven avatar diffusion, and teacher-student distillation—are largely established technologies combined in a new response-generation setting; the strongest genuinely new empirical claim concerns reduced cumulative late-chunk degradation from the clean-latent prefix. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes component ablations for VTP planning, personalized speech, speech-conditioning representation, denoising-step count, dialogue history, and Prefix Streaming. Prefix versus no-prefix comparisons use 200 paired CommonEval videos, bootstrap uncertainty, and report confidence intervals excluding zero for the later-chunk comparison; the paper also reports facial-detection, acceleration, and jerk confidence intervals. It uses deterministic decoding and fixed seeds for the main comparisons, but the supplied text does not state the number of independent training seeds or provide conventional statistical tests for all headline metrics. The main evaluation is narrow: 200 CommonEval requests, 400 OmniCharacter dialogues, and one filtered avatar-video source. The authors explicitly note that the main cross-paradigm table is capability-oriented rather than a strict same-interface ranking, and they control cascaded baselines with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, but several comparisons use different supported interfaces and output-length constraints. VTP annotations are generated by Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct, and evaluation includes GPT-4o-mini and Gemini 3.1 Pro judges, creating dependence on proprietary evaluators. The project page is https://logo-cuhksz.github.io/Ex-Omni-2D, but code, data, and model-weight release status are not stated in the provided paper text. The use of filtered SpeakerVid clips and teacher-forced speech units for video training creates a distribution gap from generated speech units and dialogue-derived VTPs at inference; the paper measures some interface ablations but does not fully quantify this train-test mismatch. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The system runs on commercially available CUDA GPUs, but the reported complete pipeline uses four GPUs with 141 GB of memory per GPU, which limits ordinary deployment. Efficient: Prefix Streaming reduces video denoising from the Teacher's 50 steps to 2–8 steps and reaches 39.546 FPS at two steps or 26.512 FPS at four steps, but full four-GPU end-to-end RTF remains 1.201–1.932 and the Teacher reaches 26.917. Effective: The evidence demonstrates synchronized, reference-conditioned avatar responses and improved streaming stability, but it does not show that generated visual plans independently control semantics, and the Teacher trails specialized renderers on several video metrics. Scalable: The paper tests one-, four-, and eight-GPU configurations and videos up to 16 streaming chunks, but it does not evaluate 10x–100x longer conversations, larger concurrent workloads beyond the reported two-replica eight-GPU setup, or scaling to larger video backbones. The work delivers a research system with a project page and trained model components; a reusable library, CLI, dataset, or publicly downloadable weights are not stated. Strengths - The interface-based decomposition addresses a real supervision bottleneck: dialogue and speech data train the response pathway, while avatar-video data train realization, without requiring large-scale query–response–speech–video tuples. - The 16-codebook speech interface is technically motivated by both codec fidelity and timing; the comparison shows a measurable synchronization-latency trade-off rather than assuming that direct units are automatically superior. - Prefix Streaming targets a specific causal diffusion failure mode—late-chunk subject drift—and supports the claim with paired full-set curves, chunk-level consistency statistics, and facial-dynamics analysis. - The paper is unusually candid about trade-offs: VTP supervision lowers speech QA and reasoning scores, the Student loses visual quality relative to the Teacher, speaker similarity remains limited, and the reported pipeline is not end-to-end real-time. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly identify weak reference-speaker similarity, incomplete independent VTP control, sensitivity to the balance between text and audio classifier-free guidance, a language and reasoning trade-off from VTP generation, limited long-horizon analysis, the computational cost of the bidirectional Teacher, lower Student quality, 3.142-second first-video latency, and E2E RTF above 1. They frame the Student as an incremental-output path rather than a replacement for the Teacher and propose planner isolation, adaptive guidance, larger causal video backbones, and more efficient distillation. These limitations are confronted with measurements rather than omitted, although the proposed deployment setting remains substantially constrained. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central claim of dialogue-derived visual intent is not tested with a strong independent controllability protocol. The VTP/video judge measures whether naturally co-generated plans match generated videos, so it cannot distinguish causal VTP control from correlated speech or video-generator priors. - The video pathway is trained on teacher-forced, automatically annotated VTPs and speech units from non-dialogue SpeakerVid clips, but the paper does not quantify degradation when conditioning on model-generated units and plans under realistic dialogue distribution shift. - Baselines are not fully interface-matched: some renderers receive completed audio, UniAVGen's joint mode is limited to five seconds, and the main table uses different capabilities across paradigms. This is acknowledged, but it limits conclusions about end-to-end superiority. - The work does not report human evaluations of naturalness, semantic appropriateness, perceived responsiveness, or avatar identity beyond automatic metrics. Dynamic Degree in particular measures motion incidence rather than motion quality, and the paper itself notes that higher DD is not necessarily better. - The paper does not provide a full cost analysis of training or memory, nor does it establish performance under long multi-turn conversations, concurrent users, diverse languages, non-human references, or substantial changes in reference image and voice conditions. Bottom Line Practitioners and researchers building embodied spoken dialogue systems should read this work for its explicit VTP/acoustic interface decomposition and evidence-backed prefix-state streaming design, but it is not yet a convincing replacement for specialized avatar renderers or a demonstrated real-time deployment solution.

Does More Retrieved Evidence Help Visual Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Diffusion Language Models?

J Wang, Y Gao, Z Zhang, X Fu, J Bai, C Gao · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Entropy-Based Candidate Filter (ECF), a training-free evidence-admission framework that combines layout-aware visual slicing with DLM-native, entropy-based selection of at most one additional retrieved visual candidate. - Why it's important: In visual RAG, expanding retrieval improves the chance of finding the answer-bearing page but can lower answer accuracy when conflicting pages enter the generator's context. - How it does it: ECF compares first-step answer-block entropy for a real candidate versus a geometry-matched blank candidate, then uses the entropy gain together with retrieval rank to decide whether and which candidate to admit. - The good: Across five visual QA benchmarks and three multimodal diffusion language models, ECF improves accuracy by an average of 2.62 percentage points over the strongest fixed top-k input and remains stable as the screened pool grows from 3 to 5 candidates. - The missing: The evaluation uses one run per fixed 2,500-example subset and reports no conventional multiple-seed error bars or significance tests, leaving the statistical reliability of several modest gains unclear. - Read it or not: Researchers working on diffusion language models, multimodal RAG, or evidence selection should read it for its source-conflict diagnosis and practical filtering rule; practitioners using autoregressive VLMs can likely skip it unless they are investigating DLM-specific context interference.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (82) are the main strengths: the paper identifies a specific DLM source-conflict mechanism and turns it into a geometry-controlled, entropy-based evidence-admission rule. Rigor (68) is reasonably strong because the work includes multiple model backends, five benchmarks, mechanism-oriented ablations, restricted theoretical analysis, controls, and released code, though the single fixed subset per configuration and lack of statistical testing are important weaknesses. Completeness (72) and Resilience (70) reflect careful scoping of the theory and explicit limitations, but broader candidate policies, long-form tasks, stronger autoregressive baselines, and sensitivity analyses are missing; Impact (65) is supported by a practical training-free method but limited to DLM-specific experimental code.
