Problem & Motivation: Numerical-relativity simulations of compact-binary mergers require solutions of the Einstein constraint equations whose residual violations and orbital artifacts do not contaminate subsequent evolutions. Existing multidomain spectral methods provide high accuracy but globally coupled Jacobians and uniform resolution become expensive for unequal masses, high mass ratios, matter surfaces, and generic spin orientations. The target users are researchers generating BNS and BHNS simulation suites for gravitational-wave modeling, particularly in precessing and high-mass-ratio regimes. The paper addresses the gap between methods that support generic spins but may incur substantial computational cost and methods such as FUKA that provide efficient Kadath-based construction but are restricted in physical or numerical scope. Key Idea: The central insight is to retain the exact current Newton Jacobian for matrix-free Newton–Krylov iterations while constructing only its structurally nonzero entries at selected refresh steps, factoring that sparse approximation with MUMPS and reusing the factors as a quasi-Newton right preconditioner. This is combined with exploiting reflection-parity sectors when available and refining only domain-coordinate pairs whose spectral tails remain unresolved. The contribution is therefore an integrated numerical strategy rather than a new formulation of the XCTS equations. Methodology: Celephaïs solves the conformally flat, maximal-slicing XCTS/Isenberg–Wilson–Mathews system for the fields $(\Psi,\alpha\Psi,\beta^i)$, coupled to neutron-star hydrostatic equations, irrotational or spinning-fluid prescriptions, black-hole excision boundary conditions, surface/interface conditions, and global mass, momentum, force-balance, and spin constraints. Each Newton state contains spectral coefficients, stellar-surface shapes, and scalar orbital or object parameters; residuals contain volume equations, boundary and matching conditions, and global constraints. A symbolic dependency graph traces each residual through intermediate definitions to field-domain leaves, excluding structural-zero Jacobian entries before differentiation. Batched forward-mode automatic differentiation evaluates compatible Jacobian columns together. When the binary has the specified reflection symmetry, unknowns and residuals are partitioned into even and odd sectors and factored separately; for nonzero radial approach speed, the parity mask is used only in the preconditioner while the matrix-free operator retains cross-sector coupling. MUMPS factors the sparse Jacobian at the first Newton step and at refresh events, and GMRES solves the current Jacobian system with the cached factors as a right preconditioner; the forcing tolerance follows Eisenstat–Walker choice 2, bounded between $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-3}$ with a 48-iteration cap. Adaptive refinement evaluates directional $L_2$ and $L_\infty$ spectral-tail ratios against tolerances $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-7}$, respectively; it inserts radial shells for suitable h moves or adds two points in selected coordinate directions for p moves, subject to domain-conformity, growth, and order-cap rules. For eccentricity initialization, post-Newtonian spin-orbit and spin-spin accelerations determine the orbital frequency, while the radial approach speed still uses an aligned-spin projection approximation; short evolutions then calibrate both parameters. Key Results: The representative equal-mass $1.35+1.35\,M_\odot$ precessing BNS Jacobian has 81,035 unknowns at spectral order $N=11$ and only 2.1% nonzero entries in the illustrated low-resolution sparse matrix; batched differentiation reduces residual traversals from 18,355 scalar sweeps to 2,980 grouped sweeps. On an Apple M4 Max, Jacobian assembly for this BNS takes 26.81 s at two MPI ranks and 8.85 s at eight ranks, with assembly speedups of 1.78x, 3.21x, and 5.40x for two, four, and eight ranks; the corresponding efficiencies are 89.1%, 80.2%, and 67.5%. At $N=13$ and two ranks, the case requires 120,168 degrees of freedom, 69.15 s for Jacobian assembly, 43.40 s for MUMPS factorization, and 13.873 GB resident memory. At $N=15$, in-core factorization is infeasible within the stated memory budget, although out-of-core factorization completes. The full production precessing BNS job reportedly uses under 17 GB and runs on a MacBook Pro with an Apple M4 Max. For a DD2 mass-ratio-20 BHNS at separation $240\,M_\odot$, one h move reduces the Hamiltonian-constraint norm by about a factor of 8 and achieves roughly 2.4 times lower norm than an equal-cost first p move; subsequent hp refinement reaches the finest uniform-grid accuracy with approximately three times fewer unknowns. For a mass-ratio-10 BHNS, p refinement reaches the uniform $N=15$ accuracy with about 1.6 times fewer unknowns. Binding-energy sequences for a nonspinning $q=2$ BNS, nonspinning $q=10$ BHNS, and spinning $q=7$, $\chi_{BH}=0.5$ BHNS follow the corresponding 4PN or spin-extended PN trends, but no tabulated numerical deviations are supplied. A precessing BNS initialized with the PN prescription has measured eccentricity below $10^{-2}$; one evolution-based correction removes most visible orbital-frequency oscillation and the binary completes more than seven orbits before merger. In the full evolution, the waveform-reconstructed radiation axis tracks a 3.5PN simple-precession model through most of the inspiral, departing near merger when the two leading radiation-axis eigenvalues become nearly degenerate. The waveform-based spin-tilt inversion estimates approximately $60^\circ$ versus the input $81^\circ$, while an ADM angular-momentum balance gives approximately $82^\circ$. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper delivers a new Celephaïs implementation that combines sparse dependency-aware Jacobian construction, refreshed sparse direct preconditioning, parity-sector handling, and spectral-tail-driven hp refinement for arbitrary-spin BNS/BHNS data; the XCTS equations, Newton–Krylov methods, automatic differentiation, MUMPS, parity decomposition, PN eccentricity control, and hp indicators are individually established techniques rather than newly formulated mathematics. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component-level benchmarks for sparsity, batched differentiation, strong scaling, memory, factorization, and refinement efficiency, plus cross-code compatibility with FUKA, PN binding-energy comparisons, an eccentricity-reduction evolution, and one full precessing BNS evolution. It does not report ablations isolating the contributions of dependency filtering, batching, parity separation, factor refresh frequency, or h versus p policy beyond selected refinement trajectories. Timing values are medians of three runs for the main linear-algebra table, but nonlinear iteration counts, failure rates, multiple-seed effects, statistical uncertainties, and solver-robustness distributions are not reported. The authors explicitly state that their measurements assess only the preconditioned implementation and do not compare against an unpreconditioned method. Comparisons with FUKA are limited to importing aligned-spin data because tilted-spin configurations have no overlapping reference solution; there is no matched comparison with SGRID, Elliptica, SpECTRE, NRPyElliptic, or other strong alternatives. Celephaïs is stated to be released under the GNU GPL upon article acceptance, with reproduction parameters and Matlab analysis scripts, but no repository URL or currently available release is provided. The paper is an arXiv preprint, version 1 dated August 7, 2026, and the manuscript is dated August 11, 2026; the results should therefore be treated as pre-publication claims. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper builds and benchmarks a reusable initial-data code and also evaluates one downstream evolution. * Practical: The demonstrated precessing BNS case runs on commercially available Apple M4 Max hardware with under 17 GB of memory, although BHNS factorization at $N=15$ already requires out-of-core storage and portability across architectures is not established. * Efficient: Sparse assembly, batching, parity splitting, factor reuse, and hp refinement reduce measured work or unknown count substantially, including approximately 3x fewer unknowns for the mass-ratio-20 BHNS and 1.6x for the mass-ratio-10 case, but matched end-to-end comparisons against alternative codes are absent. * Effective: Constraint residuals, PN binding-energy trends, low eccentricity, stable inspiral through merger, and agreement of the precession axis with a PN model show that the generated data are usable for the tested cases, but they do not establish waveform-phase accuracy or broad physical validity. * Scalable: The tests cover approximately $4.2\times10^4$–$1.9\times10^5$ unknowns, MPI ranks up to eight, and BHNS mass ratios 10 and 20; behavior at 10x–100x larger problem sizes, much larger surveys, higher spins, more extreme tilts, or strongly noncircular configurations is not evaluated. The work delivers a software artifact in planned form: a GPL release of Celephaïs with configuration parameters and Matlab analysis scripts is promised upon article acceptance, but the paper does not provide a public repository URL or an already released version. Strengths: - The sparse-Jacobian pipeline is technically specific and well matched to the Kadath residual representation: symbolic dependency filtering removes structural zeros before automatic differentiation, while batching reduces repeated expression traversal. - Reusing a refreshed sparse MUMPS factorization as a right preconditioner preserves the current Jacobian in the matrix-free Newton operator while avoiding dense storage; this is a credible compromise between direct-solve robustness and matrix-free memory use. - The hp-refinement policy responds to directional spectral tails and respects the unusual multidomain conformity constraints, producing measured reductions in unknown count rather than only claiming faster convergence. - The validation connects solver accuracy to physical usability through PN energy trends, eccentricity reduction, a stable merger evolution, and waveform-based precession diagnostics, including explicit discussion of the ill-conditioned spin-tilt inversion. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the full evolution does not establish waveform-phase convergence and defer multi-resolution phase-error studies. They acknowledge that black holes use excision rather than a puncture formulation, limiting direct matching to moving-puncture evolutions. For precessing configurations, the initial radial approach-speed estimate still uses an aligned-spin approximation. They also state that one eccentricity-correction iteration is demonstrated only for one precessing BNS and is not guaranteed across parameter space. The waveform-axis reconstruction becomes unreliable near merger as the leading eigenvalues approach degeneracy, and the simple-precession model is only controlled in the PN slow-motion inspiral regime. Planned extensions to puncture data and modified-gravity theories are not part of the current artifact. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper does not quantify end-to-end speed, memory, convergence robustness, or failure rates against FUKA, SGRID, Elliptica, SpECTRE, NRPyElliptic, or a baseline Kadath solver under matched accuracy and hardware conditions. - The central preconditioner design lacks ablations for refresh frequency, parity masking, batching, dependency filtering, and stale-factor effects, so the measured gains cannot be attributed to individual components. - Validation is narrow: the principal generic-spin evidence comes from one precessing BNS with one spinning star, tilt $81^\circ$, and $\chi=0.3$; the BHNS demonstrations are mostly nonspinning and use only mass ratios 10 and 20. - The paper uses constraint norms and PN trends as proxies for physical accuracy but does not measure waveform phase or amplitude convergence, constraint propagation during evolution, or sensitivity of merger observables to initial-data resolution. - The claimed practical scalability is extrapolated from laptop-scale systems and at most eight MPI ranks; no stress test demonstrates operation at the much larger unknown counts implied by survey production. - Code availability is conditional on article acceptance, with no current repository or executable version, which limits immediate reproducibility. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for numerical-relativity developers because it contributes a plausible and measurably effective sparse/adaptive initial-data implementation, but practitioners should not treat it as evidence of production-scale waveform accuracy until the missing baselines, ablations, broad parameter study, and phase-convergence analysis are supplied.

Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus (17 ▲ )

Zunhai Su, Bohan Sun, Xialie Zhuang, Shuibai Zhang, He Xiao, Jing Xiong, Hengyuan Zhang, Zhongzhu Zhou, Tiantian Zhang, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 14 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper characterizes two architecture-aligned massive-activation morphologies in layer-interleaved hybrid linear-attention language models: pre-attention spikes (PAS) and inter-spike plateaus (ISP), and relates them to a shared write–sink–cancel lifecycle. - Why it's important: Understanding these outliers matters for interpreting hybrid LLM computation and for managing numerical-range problems that can affect quantization, stability, and deployment of efficient long-context models. - How it does it: It identifies attention-sink tokens, traces their maximum hidden-state magnitudes across layers, varies linear-attention backbones and full-attention density, and validates the patterns with controlled pretraining, gating interventions, and signed residual-update decompositions. - The good: PAS localization reaches approximately 99.4–100.0% across five architectures and two scales, while ISP retention rises consistently as full-attention density increases, with statistically supported trends across 500 inputs from five domains. - The missing: The study does not establish that PAS or ISP cause downstream behavior, nor does it evaluate their impact on actual quantization error, inference robustness, latency, memory, or long-context performance. - Read it or not: Researchers studying mechanistic interpretability, linear-attention hybrids, or activation outliers should read it for the measurements and terminology; practitioners seeking an optimization or deployment method can largely skip it.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (80) are strong because PAS/ISP provide a new architecture-aligned empirical formulation and a plausible write–sink–cancel interpretation across many hybrid architectures. Rigor (82) benefits from broad controlled comparisons, bootstrap analysis, interventions, and released code/checkpoints, but is reduced by the preprint status, lack of multiple training seeds, and observational rather than causal mechanism tests. Completeness (68) and Resilience (65) are pulled down by the absence of quantization, numerical-stability, long-context, and downstream-impact evidence; Impact (35) is limited because the work releases diagnostics rather than a demonstrated optimization or deployment method. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*82 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*35 = 71.55, rounded to 72.

Problem & Motivation: Hybrid linear-attention LLMs seek to retain the efficiency of recurrent or state-space sequence mixing while recovering the expressive interactions of occasional full-attention layers. Their internal activation dynamics are poorly understood, particularly massive activations: sparse hidden-state entries with magnitudes far above typical values and strong associations with attention-sink tokens. Prior massive-activation work focuses mainly on full-attention Transformers, where magnitude-ranked outliers often remain aligned with attention sinks. Hybrid models weaken that alignment and can cause the maximally activated token to change between adjacent layers, making conventional magnitude-only tracing unreliable. The paper addresses the descriptive and mechanistic gap of how interleaving full and linear-time mixers reorganizes these outliers across depth. Key Idea: Full-attention placement acts as an architectural clock for massive activations. A sink-associated outlier typically peaks in the linear-attention layer immediately before a full-attention layer, producing a pre-attention spike; when full-attention layers are denser, the outlier survives across the intervening linear layers, producing an inter-spike plateau. The paper interprets both as different cancellation-timing regimes of one write–sink–cancel lifecycle rather than as separate phenomena. Methodology: The study first defines an HLA residual-block framework in which each mixer is either full attention or a linear recurrent/state-space mixer, with hybridization ratio \(\rho=L/L_{FA}\). Because layerwise magnitude ranking does not reliably preserve token identity in HLA models, it computes a consensus attention-sink token by averaging received attention over full-attention layers and heads, then tracks that fixed token's maximum absolute feature magnitude \(m^{(\ell)}_{x,t}=\|X^{(\ell)}_{x,t,:}\|_\infty\). It introduces sink–spike alignment, the fraction of full-attention boundaries where the immediately preceding linear layer is the blockwise maximum, and inter-spike retention (ISR), which averages activation between adjacent PAS normalized by the weaker neighboring spike. The main inference study uses 52 checkpoints from the public M-A-P suite: RetNet, HGRN, GLA, DeltaNet, and GDN; 340M and 1.3B parameters; 24-layer models; pure linear, 24:1, 12:1, 6:1, 3:1, and full-attention configurations; and 500 inputs spanning WikiText-103, Scientific Papers, GSM8K, CodeSearchNet, and FLORES-200. It then analyzes 12 public checkpoints from Kimi Linear, Qwen3.5, Nemotron-H, and Zamba2, spanning 1.2B–397B total parameters, different mixer families, schedules, and base/instruction variants. Finally, it trains controlled 24-layer GDN hybrids from scratch at 340M and 1.3B parameters on FineWeb-Edu, varying full-attention placement, density, and output gating; signed residual, attention, MLP, and block updates are decomposed at dominant coordinates. The sink-tracking procedure and the alignment/ISR metrics are well motivated for the descriptive goal, although the decision to focus most headline visualizations on the first token is only partially mitigated by appendix token controls. The write–sink–cancel analysis is supported by one fixed token–feature coordinate in a representative model and broader layerwise decompositions, but it remains observational rather than an intervention that tests causal mechanism. Key Results: In the M-A-P suite under 12:1 hybridization, sink–spike alignment is 99.4–100.0% across all ten architecture–scale pairs; macro-averages are 99.9/100.0% for RetNet, 100.0/100.0% for HGRN, 100.0/99.6% for GLA, 100.0/99.4% for DeltaNet, and 100.0/100.0% for GDN at 1.3B/340M. Relative to non-sink tokens, alignment gaps range from 6.5 to 58.6 percentage points and peak-excess gaps from 0.97 to 4.42 log2 units; all paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero. ISR increases monotonically as full attention becomes denser: at 1.3B/340M, RetNet rises from 18.8/36.8% at 12:1 to 85.4/87.2% at 3:1, HGRN from 7.2/5.0% to 92.5/81.2%, GLA from 27.3/31.9% to 88.0/88.1%, DeltaNet from 23.1/46.5% to 84.4/99.8%, and GDN from 18.4/39.7% to 77.8/86.7%. All 20 adjacent-ratio comparisons increase, with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero; absolute inter-spike activation increases in 19 of 20 comparisons. The morphology recurs qualitatively in 12 public checkpoints from 1.2B to 397B across Kimi Linear, Qwen3.5, Nemotron-H, and Zamba2, including state-space hybrids and output-gated full attention. In controlled pretraining, PAS is visible after 1B tokens in the 340M model and by 10B tokens in the 1.3B model; final alignment is 100% for the layer-12 configurations. A single full-attention layer placed at layer 4, 12, or 20 yields comparable modeling and commonsense results but different retrieval performance: for example, 340M FDA accuracy is 8.02%, 60.43%, and 53.71%, while NIAH-1 is 57.40%, 61.80%, and 90.60%, respectively. Under 3:1 hybridization, ISR is 90.56% at 340M and 94.47% at 1.3B. Adding full-attention output gates substantially reduces absolute PAS/ISP magnitudes but preserves organization; removing GDN output gates produces a smaller magnitude increase. The paper does not report standard end-to-end baselines for the downstream tasks beyond its controlled variants, and the central results are activation statistics rather than task improvements. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS: the paper introduces the PAS and ISP terminology and associated alignment/retention metrics, and reports their recurrence across hybrid architectures, densities, scales, domains, and state-space mixers; the underlying ingredients—activation tracing, attention-sink analysis, residual decomposition, and output gating—are established techniques combined for this setting rather than a new model or learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper uses controlled comparisons across five backbones, two scales, fixed 24-layer depth, shared pretraining recipes, six hybridization limits, five input domains, and 500 inputs for the main quantitative analyses. It includes non-sink, first-token, and random-layer controls, 10,000 stratified bootstrap resamples, paired comparisons across hybridization ratios, training-time trajectories, model-placement comparisons, and gating interventions. However, it does not report multiple training seeds, conventional error bars for the training runs, or formal causal tests of the proposed cancellation mechanism. The controlled suite and public checkpoints are available through the cited M-A-P Hugging Face collection; controlled trained checkpoints are stated to be available at https://huggingface.co/startlux-models/Massive-Activations-HLA; analysis code is stated to be available at https://github.com/StartluxLabs/Massive-Activations-HLA. The evaluation is heavily based on the authors' activation metrics and representative inputs, including the repeated example “Summer is warm. Winter is cold.” Although domain-level samples and large public models broaden coverage, no independent replication, adversarial prompt suite, sequence-length sweep, or comparison to alternative outlier definitions is reported. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.12149v1, dated 12 August 2026), so its results have not received peer-review confidence in the supplied document. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The analysis can run on commercially available hardware for the 340M–1.3B controlled models, but reproducing analysis of 397B checkpoints requires substantial multi-GPU infrastructure and the paper gives no end-to-end resource accounting. Efficient: The method is an offline diagnostic that adds attention extraction, activation tracing, and signed-update decomposition; it does not provide measured latency, memory, throughput, or cost comparisons against ordinary inference and is not itself an efficiency optimization. Effective: The evidence strongly establishes recurrence of PAS/ISP as activation morphology, but it does not show that detecting or modifying them improves task accuracy, quantization quality, numerical stability, or deployment reliability; the limited controlled task results are observational and mixed. Scalable: The phenomenon is measured from 1.2B to 397B total parameters, but the controlled causal studies stop at 1.3B and sequence lengths are evaluated at 2,048 or 4,096 tokens for downstream tasks; behavior at 10×–100× longer contexts, larger training budgets, or substantially deeper models is not tested. The work delivers analysis code, configuration files, and trained checkpoints, but no production library, inference-time mitigation, dataset, or trained model intended as a new end-user system. Strengths: - It identifies a clear and reusable architectural pattern—activation maxima immediately before full-attention layers—and names two measurable regimes, PAS and ISP, that organize prior qualitative observations. - The controlled M-A-P study separates mixer choice, full-attention density, model scale, and input domain more carefully than a single-model case study; the 99.4–100.0% alignment rates and monotonic ISR trends provide strong descriptive evidence. - The study checks external validity on 12 public checkpoints spanning 1.2B–397B, linear-attention and state-space mixers, periodic and nonuniform schedules, and base/instruction variants. - The fixed-coordinate signed-update analysis goes beyond plots of absolute magnitudes and provides a plausible mechanism linking outlier writing, attention-sink behavior, and later cancellation; the gating intervention also reveals an asymmetric relationship between full-attention and GDN gates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the factors regulating cancellation timing and the possible computational roles of PAS versus ISP remain unresolved. They also frame the systematic-outlier lifecycle as an account that is “consistent with” delayed cancellation rather than a complete causal explanation. Beyond these open questions, a dedicated limitations section is not stated; the paper does not explicitly discuss the first-token-heavy analysis, absence of long-context stress tests, lack of deployment measurements, or the limited scale of controlled pretraining as limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central mechanistic claim is not causally established: observing a pre-attention write and later opposite-signed update does not show that cancellation timing generates PAS/ISP or that attention sinks require the outlier. - The study largely measures maximum absolute activation at sink tokens, so it does not establish how many features, heads, tokens, or layers participate, nor whether the reported morphology depends on the \(\ell_\infty\) statistic. - The large-model evidence is mostly visual and uses representative inputs; it lacks reported alignment/ISR statistics, confidence intervals, and systematic token-position metrics for the 1.2B–397B checkpoints. - The paper does not evaluate activation or KV-cache quantization error, overflow, calibration, numerical instability, generation degradation, or any concrete mitigation, despite motivating relevance to deployment. - Downstream results use small controlled models and no strong external baselines; several retrieval scores vary substantially with attention placement, but the paper does not determine whether this variation is mediated by PAS/ISP or by ordinary architectural capacity and optimization effects. - No multiple-seed study, sequence-length scaling study, training-data ablation, normalization/activation-function ablation, or comparison against other outlier-tracking definitions tests the robustness of the findings. Bottom Line: This is a useful and reasonably well-controlled descriptive preprint for researchers investigating activation outliers and hybrid LLM internals, but it is not yet evidence that PAS/ISP explain model behavior or yield a practical intervention, so its innovation value is primarily in empirical characterization and terminology rather than a deployable advance.

SimWAM: A Simple World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving (22 ▲ )

Zongchuang Zhao, Xin Zhou, Tianyang Xu, Zhengyang Sun, Kaixuan Zhou, Honglin Li, Dingkang Liang, Xiang Bai · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SimWAM, a world-action driving planner that uses future-video generation for training-time supervision but directly predicts trajectories without generating future frames at inference. - Why it's important: Removing future-frame synthesis from the planning loop targets the latency and deployment cost that limit existing video-based world-action planners. - How it does it: It jointly trains a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer and a 1.02B-parameter action Diffusion Transformer with flow matching, using an isolated attention mask that blocks action tokens from accessing future-frame tokens, followed by LoRA-based GRPO reinforcement learning. - The good: On NAVSIM navtest, SimWAM reaches 91.5 PDMS using only one front camera, exceeding the reported WAM baselines DriveLaW and DriveWAM by 2.4 and 1.4 points, respectively, while reporting roughly 518 ms inference latency. - The missing: The paper does not report multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, or a fully controlled latency comparison against equally optimized and identically implemented baselines. - Read it or not: Researchers working on video world models, diffusion planners, or efficient autonomous-driving policies should read it for its clean training/inference decoupling; readers seeking real-vehicle or closed-loop evidence can skip it because the evaluation is benchmark-based and largely non-reactive.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (75) and Non-Obviousness (74) are solid because training-only future-video supervision with isolated attention cleanly separates world-model learning from inference-time planning, but the components are largely established. Rigor (72), Completeness (68), and Resilience (67) are reduced by single-benchmark optimization, mixed and uncontrolled baselines, absent seeds and uncertainty estimates, incomplete latency protocols, and no closed-loop vehicle evidence. Impact (78) benefits from released code and weights and a meaningful reduction in inference complexity, but deployment remains benchmark-level. Problem & Motivation: End-to-end autonomous-driving planners must predict safe, compliant, and progressive trajectories from visual observations while modeling how surrounding traffic and the scene will evolve. Conventional imitation policies encode temporal dynamics only indirectly through logged trajectories, while recent world-action models improve temporal reasoning by generating future observations but commonly require expensive imagine-then-act inference. The central gap is therefore how to transfer the dynamics information available in a video generator into trajectory prediction without retaining future-video synthesis in the real-time control loop. The target domain is camera-based autonomous driving, particularly single-front-camera planning under the NAVSIM benchmark. Key Idea: Future-video generation is treated as a training-only representation-learning signal rather than an inference-time latent variable. A causal-style isolated attention mask lets future-frame tokens and action tokens both attend to the current observation while preventing action tokens from reading future-frame tokens, so the action expert can benefit from jointly learned dynamics-aware representations without depending on future-frame rollout. The idea is conceptually close to distilling a video model's temporal prior into a direct planner, with the additional architectural consequence that the video and action experts can be replaced or scaled independently. Methodology: The input consists of a front-camera observation, ego state containing velocity, acceleration, and yaw rate, and a navigation command. The video branch uses a Wan2.2-5B video Diffusion Transformer, VAE, and T5 encoder; the current frame is kept clean, while eight future frames over four seconds are represented as noisy latent tokens and trained with rectified-flow matching. The action branch is a lightweight DiT with hidden size 1024 that encodes the current visual representation, ego state, and command and predicts eight future waypoints, each containing position and heading, using the flow-matching loss \(L_{FM}^{act}\). Joint training minimizes \(L=L_{FM}^{act}+\lambda L_{FM}^{vid}\), with \(\lambda=1\), AdamW, an initial learning rate of \(10^{-4}\), cosine scheduling, and 100 epochs. During inference, only the action branch is sampled through the flow ODE; the video decoder and future-frame generation are removed. For post-training optimization, the deterministic ODE is converted to a marginal-preserving SDE so that eight candidate trajectories per scenario have tractable transition likelihoods; GRPO then updates rank-32 LoRA adapters on action attention projections using the NAVSIM compositional PDM reward, focusing on navtrain scenes whose imitation PDMS is below 90. Critical design decisions are the isolated mask, the equal-weight joint video/action objective, and hard-scenario LoRA reinforcement learning. The paper provides empirical ablations for the mask and training stages, but does not deeply justify the choice of \(\lambda=1\), LoRA rank, SDE noise scale, or reward construction. Key Results: On NAVSIM, SimWAM is trained on 103,288 navtrain scenes and evaluated on 12,146 navtest scenes using one front camera at 384×672 resolution. It reports 98.4 NC, 98.7 DAC, 86.4 EP, 95.5 TTC, and 91.5 PDMS. The strongest listed learned comparator is SGDrive at 91.1 PDMS, while ReCogDrive reaches 90.8, ExploreVLA 90.4, DriveVLA-W0 90.2, DriveWAM 90.1, and DriveLaW 89.1; these comparisons mix published conference papers, preprints, and methods with different sensors, inputs, and training setups, so they are informative but not fully controlled. The action-only baseline obtains 86.6 PDMS, video co-training raises it to 90.3, and RL raises it to 91.5. Replacing Wan2.2-5B with LTX-Video, Wan2.1-1.3B, or Cosmos2.5 yields 88.7, 90.2, and 90.4 PDMS before RL, showing sensitivity to the video prior. Scaling the action expert from 0.21B to 1.02B raises PDMS from 89.9 to 90.3. Five action-flow steps achieve 90.1 PDMS at 297 ms, while ten steps achieve 90.3 at 518 ms and twenty steps achieve 90.2 at 968 ms. At 768×1344, PDMS reaches 90.6 with 573 ms latency in the reported resolution study. On zero-shot nuScenes open-loop planning, SimWAM reports 0.96 m average L2 error and 0.04% average collision rate, compared with DriveWAM's 0.96 m and 0.06%; this is cross-dataset evidence but not closed-loop deployment evidence. The surprising result is that isolated attention slightly outperforms bidirectional or action-to-video attention on PDMS while eliminating future-frame inference dependencies. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely distinct contribution is the isolated-attention, training-only future-video supervision design for a directly sampled action DiT, while flow matching, video DiTs, LoRA, and GRPO are established components combined in a new autonomous-driving architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component, attention-mask, video-backbone, action-scale, exploration-sampler, future-horizon, input-resolution, sampling-step, and RL-training-data ablations. These establish that video co-training contributes 3.7 PDMS over the action-only model and RL contributes a further 1.2 points, and they test several claimed flexibility properties. However, no random-seed variation, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The paper does not state the total trainable parameter count after co-training, training compute, wall-clock training time, memory use, or detailed latency measurement protocol beyond using one NVIDIA A100 for ablations. Latency comparisons in the main figure are not accompanied by equivalent hardware, batch-size, implementation, or sampling-step details for every baseline. The evaluation relies primarily on NAVSIM, which also supplies the PDM reward used for RL; optimizing a benchmark-derived reward and evaluating on the same benchmark creates a potential Goodhart concern. nuScenes provides useful zero-shot transfer evidence, but only in an open-loop setting. Code and model weights are reported as available at https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/SimWAM/; the paper does not state dataset-release details beyond using public benchmarks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. * Practical: The inference-time action model runs on commercially available NVIDIA hardware, and the reported 384×672 configuration produces trajectories in approximately 518 ms on an A100, but the paper does not establish real-vehicle compatibility, sensor timing, or operation on embedded automotive hardware. * Efficient: Removing future-video generation reduces inference to action-flow sampling, with reported latency of 297 ms at five steps and 518 ms at ten steps, but the approach still requires a large 5B video expert during training and the paper does not quantify end-to-end training or memory cost relative to alternatives. * Effective: The method improves NAVSIM PDMS from 86.6 for action-only to 91.5 after video co-training and RL and achieves 0.04% average collision rate on zero-shot nuScenes, but the evidence measures benchmark planning proxies rather than deployed closed-loop driving safety. * Scalable: The method supports action-expert scaling from 0.21B to 1.02B and several video backbones, while input-resolution and sampling studies cover limited local trade-offs; it does not test 10×–100× scene, dataset, fleet, horizon, or hardware scale, so broader scalability remains a claim. The work delivers a reproducible software and model artifact through the linked GitHub repository, including code and weights according to the paper; it does not deliver a deployed vehicle system or a new dataset. Strengths: - The isolated attention mask yields a concrete architectural separation between training-time world modeling and inference-time planning, directly addressing the dominant latency cost in imagine-then-act WAMs. - The ablations support the paper's causal story at the component level: action-only, video co-training, and RL produce 86.6, 90.3, and 91.5 PDMS, respectively, while alternative attention masks do not improve over isolation. - The design exposes two independent scaling axes—video-prior selection and action-expert capacity—and experiments with four video backbones and three action-model sizes rather than presenting only one fixed configuration. - Zero-shot transfer from NAVSIM to nuScenes without fine-tuning or auxiliary supervision provides evidence that the learned representation is not entirely tied to one benchmark, although the target evaluation remains open-loop. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors frame SimWAM as a simple baseline rather than claiming fundamental algorithmic superiority. They explicitly acknowledge that video-prior quality matters, as LTX-Video reaches 88.7 PDMS while Cosmos2.5 reaches 90.4, and they report diminishing returns from prolonged RL and from increasing sampling steps beyond ten. They do not state limitations concerning non-reactive evaluation, lack of real-vehicle testing, training cost, seed variability, or possible reward overfitting. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main evidence gap is the absence of a controlled latency and quality comparison against reimplemented baselines under identical hardware, input resolution, sampling budgets, and preprocessing. The paper also does not isolate whether gains attributed to future-video supervision arise from extra optimization, shared-attention capacity, or the pretrained video backbone; a matched auxiliary-loss or frozen-backbone comparison would help. RL uses the NAVSIM PDM reward and selects hard scenes using imitation PDMS, but the paper does not test reward transfer, held-out reward functions, or whether improvements come from exploiting benchmark scoring quirks. The zero-shot nuScenes result is limited to open-loop trajectory matching and collision-rate simulation, not interactive closed-loop driving. Missing seeds and uncertainty estimates make small differences such as 91.5 versus 91.1 difficult to assess. Finally, the claimed deployability is incomplete because training cost, memory footprint, embedded-device latency, temporal robustness, adverse weather, sensor corruption, and long-horizon closed-loop failure modes are not evaluated. Bottom Line: SimWAM is worth reading as a clean and reproducible baseline showing that future-video supervision can improve direct diffusion trajectory planning without future-video inference, but its ranking-level claims should be discounted until controlled latency studies, multi-seed evaluation, reward-independent tests, and closed-loop deployment experiments are provided.

Mendel Gödel Machine: Recursive Self-Improving Coding Agents via Comparative Evolution (22 ▲ )

Changzhi Liu, Yilun Liu, Sikuan Yan, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 12 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mendel Gödel Machine (MGM), an archive-based framework that recursively edits coding-agent scaffolds using comparative evidence across tasks and agent lineages. - Why it's important: Self-improving coding agents spend substantial evaluation budget making edits from noisy single-task failures, so better diagnosis could improve quality without additional task executions. - How it does it: MGM augments single-trajectory clonal mutation with reaction-norm mutation over multiple tasks from one agent and cross-lineage hybridization over different agents on the same task, while retaining HGM-style archive search and Thompson sampling. - The good: Under a matched 200-evaluation budget, MGM raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 50.8% to 93.2% on Polyglot-60 and from 68.3% to 78.3% on SWE-bench Verified-60, outperforming HGM at 77.9% and 73.3%, respectively. - The missing: The empirical conclusions rely primarily on one backbone, fixed 60-task subsets, a single reported evolution run per setting, and comparison mainly against HGM rather than a broad set of strong self-improvement or scaffold-search baselines. - Read it or not: Researchers working on self-evolving agents, automated agent design, or coding-agent evaluation should read it for the comparative-evidence mechanism and empirical transfer results, but should treat the magnitude and generality of the gains as provisional.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (82) are strong: comparative same-agent and cross-lineage evidence is a non-obvious refinement of archive-based self-improvement, with substantial transfer results. Problem & Motivation: Self-improving coding agents must modify executable prompts, tools, and control flow after observing task trajectories, but prior archive-based approaches such as DGM and HGM generally condition each edit on one agent's single failure trajectory. That evidence may mix task-specific accidents with persistent scaffold defects and does not exploit comparisons already stored in the archive. The target problem is therefore more informative, compute-efficient diagnosis for recursive coding-agent improvement, particularly in repository-level and multilingual software engineering. The claimed gap concerns the self-modification operator rather than archive selection: existing methods improve which agent to expand, while leaving the evidence supplied to the editor largely single-trajectory. Key Idea: Treat archived task outcomes as controlled comparative experiments that isolate heritable scaffold effects. Reaction-norm mutation compares the same agent across environments, using recurring or contrastive behavior to identify genotype-level weaknesses; cross-lineage hybridization compares different agents on the same task, using a successful or complementary reference trajectory as a behavioral donor. The core insight is diagnostic compression: narrowing the candidate causes of a failure should make an LLM editor more likely to repair a genuine scaffold defect without requiring another task evaluation. Methodology: MGM maintains a lineage tree in which each node stores an executable agent scaffold, evaluated tasks, trajectories, and binary outcomes. At each budgeted step, HGM-style policies choose either an evaluation or an expansion using node- and clade-level Beta posteriors with Thompson sampling. Evaluations run an agent on an unattempted task, record its trajectory and outcome, and add failed tasks to a global failed-task pool; tasks in that pool receive a configurable sampling boost to create overlap across lineages. During expansion, MGM forms an eligible operator set. Clonal mutation edits a selected agent using one failed trajectory. Reaction-norm mutation requires at least two evaluated tasks, selects a failed target trajectory plus another trajectory from the same agent, and asks the LLM editor to extract a recurring or contrastive weakness. Cross-lineage hybridization requires two agents from different lineages to have attempted the same task; it edits the failing agent using the other trajectory, or uses the higher-utility lineage as the target when both fail. Operator probabilities use fixed weights λCM=0.10, λRM=0.45, and λCH=0.45, with mRM=2 and failed-pool boost βfail=1.0. The formal surrogate represents an agent as a binary genotype with L loci, tasks as subsets of k loci, and success as all required loci being correct; edits select candidate loci and repair them probabilistically. The proof and simulation assume sparse causal defects, informative task overlap, sound comparative evidence, and an editor capable of exploiting it. These assumptions are central rather than derived from real trajectories, so the theoretical justification establishes superiority only within its stylized diagnostic model. Key Results: On SWE-bench Verified-60 with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the initial scaffold scores 68.3%, HGM reaches 73.3% (+5.0 percentage points), and MGM reaches 78.3% (+10.0), using 200 task evaluations and 24 expansions. On Polyglot-60, the corresponding scores are 50.8%, 77.9% (+27.1), and 93.2% (+42.4); wall-clock time is 93.02 hours for HGM and 96.11 hours for MGM on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs for SWE-bench, and 44.20 versus 40.14 hours on Polyglot. The full Polyglot evaluation reports 210/225 solved, or 93.3%, with per-language results of 25/26 C++, 36/39 Go, 43/47 Java, 46/49 JavaScript, 33/34 Python, and 27/30 Rust. When scaffolds evolved on Polyglot-60 are transferred zero-shot to held-out 60-task subsets, MGM scores 26.7% on SWE-bench Pro versus 16.7% initially and 13.3% for HGM, and 55.0% on SWE-bench Multilingual versus 41.7% initially and 43.3% for HGM. Scaffolds evolved on SWE-bench Verified-60 transfer across backbones: on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MGM scores 66.7% versus 60.0% for HGM and 50.0% for the initial scaffold; on DeepSeek-V4-Pro, it scores 75.0% versus 70.0% and 45.0%. A Polyglot-evolved Qwen scaffold paired with DeepSeek-V4-Pro reaches 96.89% on the full benchmark. Removing reaction-norm mutation lowers Polyglot-60 performance from 93.2% to 79.7%; removing cross-lineage hybridization lowers it to 74.6%. The surrogate simulation uses 100 seeds and reports 95% confidence intervals, but the primary empirical tables do not report multiple-seed variance or statistical tests. Baselines are matched HGM/DGM-style self-improvement systems, not a broad comparison against current automated agent-design, test-time adaptation, or training-based agent optimization methods. Some claims compare against external leaderboard or vendor-model numbers whose evaluation protocols and parameter estimates are not controlled by this paper. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the explicit use of same-agent multi-task comparisons and cross-lineage same-task comparisons as self-modification evidence within an archive-based coding-agent evolution loop; the surrounding archive search, Thompson sampling, LLM-based editing, and scaffold evolution are inherited or adapted from prior DGM/HGM and agent-design methods. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a formal model, a proposition with appendix derivation, Monte Carlo sweeps over initial difficulty and diagnostic advantage, matched evaluation and expansion budgets, component ablations, cross-benchmark checks, cross-model transfer, qualitative scaffold diffs, and detailed hardware and hyperparameter settings. Code is linked at https://github.com/RealLcz/MGM and a project page is provided at https://reallcz.github.io/MGM/. However, the proof assumes the comparative evidence is sound and effectively encodes the intended defect; the simulations directly parameterize the comparative advantage through ρ rather than measuring it from LLM edits. Primary experiments use fixed 60-task subsets, with the SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual subsets separately selected by ChatGPT, and the report does not state the number of independent evolution seeds for the main tables. It reports no real-experiment confidence intervals, significance tests, or systematic edit-success rates. The ablations remove one operator but do not isolate failed-task pooling, operator weights, overlap frequency, selection policy, or best-belief selection. Evaluation on public coding benchmarks may also be affected by benchmark contamination, and the use of the same archive trajectories for both evolution and node selection creates a potential adaptive-evaluation/selection bias even though private test cases are not exposed. Deployability (4-property check): SYSTEMS profile, because the paper implements and runs an archive-based self-improving coding-agent system, while also including empirical and theoretical analyses. Practical: The system runs on commercially available hardware, but the reported experiments require clusters with eight 80 GB NVIDIA H100 GPUs and approximately 2 TB host memory, so practical access is limited. Efficient: MGM uses the same 200 evaluations and 24 expansions as HGM, has similar per-operation token distributions, and is faster than HGM on Polyglot (40.14 versus 44.20 hours) but slightly slower on SWE-bench (96.11 versus 93.02 hours); it does not establish lower total cost than non-evolutionary alternatives or quantify LLM/API monetary cost. Effective: The evidence shows substantial benchmark accuracy improvements and transfer across the tested benchmarks and backbones, but it measures pass rates on curated public tasks rather than reliability, maintainability, security, or real production software maintenance. Scalable: The largest reported evolution uses 200 evaluations and 24 expansions, with post-evolution evaluation on 225 Polyglot tasks; behavior at 10×–100× this archive, task, lineage, or model scale is not evaluated, and the authors explicitly leave broader scalability as a claim. The work delivers a reproducible software implementation and evolved coding-agent scaffolds, not a standalone trained model or general-purpose self-improvement guarantee. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete bottleneck inside recursive agent evolution—diagnostic evidence quality—rather than only proposing another archive-selection heuristic. - Reaction-norm mutation and cross-lineage hybridization are operationally distinct, use data already generated by routine evaluation, and admit clear eligibility conditions and pseudocode. - The controlled surrogate model connects comparative evidence to an explicit candidate-set density and fix-probability mechanism, while the null case ρ=1 tests whether gains disappear when comparative evidence has no advantage. - The strongest empirical result is not only in-domain improvement but transfer: MGM-evolved scaffolds improve zero-shot performance on SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual and remain beneficial when paired with DeepSeek backbones. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly note the high wall-clock and GPU cost, limited independent seeds and hyperparameter sweeps, dependence on archive history and task overlap, reliance on an LLM editor that can make incorrect or unmaintainable edits, dependence on the backbone's reasoning and diagnosis ability, the stylized additive fitness model, fixed 60-task primary subsets, limited seed diversity, and uncertainty about transfer beyond coding-agent scaffolds and public software-engineering benchmarks. They also acknowledge sandboxing and dual-use risks, benchmark/model bias, lack of dedicated safety audits, and possible benchmark overlap with pretraining data. These limitations are confronted directly, although the conclusion still uses the results to motivate a potentially scalable path beyond the tested regime. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main empirical comparison is narrow: HGM is the primary baseline, while stronger automated scaffold-search, self-refinement, runtime adaptation, population-based, or learning-based methods are not evaluated under the same budget. The paper does not report independent-run variance for the headline numbers, making it difficult to distinguish robust gains from archive stochasticity and best-node selection. The externally selected 60-task subsets and adaptive reuse of failed tasks may make the measured improvement sensitive to task overlap and selection policy; no evaluation on independently sampled or fully held-out evolution runs addresses this. The formal proposition assumes precisely the informative recurring-defect and successful-reference conditions that make comparative evidence useful, and the simulations impose the advantage ratio rather than validating those assumptions against real trajectories. The ablations do not separate the effects of comparative prompting from increased context length, more reasoning tokens, or different editor behavior. Finally, the claimed generality of evolved skills is supported partly by qualitative examples and t-SNE visualization rather than a controlled study of skill transfer, maintainability, regression rates, or unseen real-world repositories. Bottom Line: MGM is a technically interesting and empirically promising improvement to archive-based self-evolving coding agents, worth reading for its comparative-diagnosis operators and transfer results, but its headline gains require confirmation across independent seeds, stronger baselines, unbiased task sampling, and substantially larger evaluation budgets.

Problem & Motivation Interactive video world models must respond to user controls while maintaining a coherent environment over long horizons. Existing benchmarks commonly replay fixed low-level camera or movement trajectories, which can unfairly penalize models whose action granularity or response speed differs from the benchmark’s assumed timing. These protocols also provide limited coverage of long-horizon revisitation, physically plausible interaction, hidden-state evolution after occlusion, and continuously observed processes. The affected users are researchers and practitioners comparing general-purpose interactive world models for exploration, simulation, games, robotics, and related embodied applications. The paper targets the evaluation gap between frame-level visual quality or short-horizon controllability and human judgments of whether a world remains spatially and causally coherent during purposeful interaction. Key Idea The central insight is to evaluate a model against a shared high-level objective rather than a rigid action trajectory, while retaining a basic action sequence as an initial reference for comparability. A multimodal Agent Player observes generated frames and action history and adjusts the timing or choice of actions only as needed to reach the same objective across models. This separates failure to execute a prescribed control schedule from failure to produce the intended world behavior. The idea is primarily a benchmark and protocol contribution rather than a new learning algorithm. Methodology PlayWorld constructs each case from an initial image/world, a scene-grounded long-horizon objective, a human-written basic action sequence, and a sample-specific VQA rubric. The initial images are collected from Pexels and Google Images, captioned initially with Gemini 3.1 Pro, then verified and revised by annotators. Cases cover four dimensions: geometry consistency, interaction fidelity, out-of-sight evolution, and insight evolution. During execution, the Agent Player receives the objective, scene description, remaining reference actions, recent actions, and generated observations. It selects Keep, Stop, Extend, Correct, or End; the interface translates the decision into model-native controls, captures the next frame, and repeats for up to 40 interaction steps or approximately 10–60 seconds. The reported benchmark uses Claude Haiku 4.5 as the Agent Player. A Gemini 3.1 Pro verifier evaluates binary, weighted rubric questions after dimension-specific trajectory validation; the case score is S_d = 1 + 4R_d, where R_d is the weighted fraction of satisfied applicable questions. Invalid trajectories receive the minimum score of 1 for geometry, interaction, or out-of-sight dimensions. Basic ability metrics include seven video-quality measures from VBench, Omni-WorldBench, MemoBench, and HyDRA, plus translation and rotation pass rates estimated with VGGT. The three key design decisions are the shared reference sequence plus online adaptation, the validation gate before semantic scoring, and sample-specific rubric questions. The paper empirically supports the first decision using a 25-case comparison, but provides less justification for the exact rubric weighting, threshold choices, or verifier architecture beyond practical considerations. Key Results PlayWorld contains 171 scenarios, 50 action patterns, more than 820 rubric questions, and over 1,400 generated interactive videos across nine models. On the 1–5 rubric score, Genie 3 ranks first overall at 2.12, followed by HappyOyster at 1.92, LingBot-World at 1.78, LingBot-World2 at 1.82, HY-World2 at 1.61, SANA-WM at 1.48, Hunyuan-GameCraft-2 at 1.42, HY-WorldPlay at 1.21, and Matrix-Game-3.0 at 1.14; Genie 3 leads geometry consistency at 2.74, interaction fidelity at 2.40, and out-of-sight evolution at 1.81, while LingBot-World2 leads insight evolution at 1.95. Trajectory-validation pass rates show Genie 3 at 87.1% overall, HappyOyster at 79.6%, LingBot-World2 at 78.8%, SANA-WM at 80.4%, and HY-WorldPlay at 41.6%; these rates do not consistently predict semantic rubric performance. In the 25-case Agent Player ablation, Preset + Agent obtains trajectory scores of 1.08 for Genie 3 and 1.12 for HappyOyster, versus 0.92 and 1.00 for Preset Only and 0.88 and 0.68 for Agent Only; human preference favors Preset + Agent at 65.6% and 67.4%, respectively. Claude Haiku has the lowest reported decision latency at 3.83 seconds per call, compared with 4.36 for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 6.21 for Claude Sonnet, although Sonnet obtains the highest trajectory score of 1.24. In basic ability, HappyOyster has the highest rank-based score at 76.4%, despite ranking second on the long-horizon rubric. Human validation uses 600 pairwise judgments and reports correlations of ρ = 0.983 for geometry, 0.933 for interaction, 0.812 for out-of-sight evolution, 0.745 for insight evolution, and 0.933 overall. The evaluated scale is standard for a benchmark study but modest for long-horizon generalization: 171 curated cases, nine models, and rollouts capped at 60 seconds; no 10×–100× stress test is reported. Baselines include several recent open-source and closed-source systems, but most comparisons are benchmark-internal rather than direct numerical comparisons with results from competing benchmarks. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: the genuinely new contribution is the combination of objective-conditioned, closed-loop Agent Player interaction with a four-dimensional rubric benchmark for long-horizon world-model behavior; the Agent Player itself uses standard multimodal language models and the automatic metrics combine existing VBench, geometry, depth, subject-consistency, and control measures. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes useful ablations of Preset Only, Agent Only, and Preset + Agent, as well as a comparison among Claude Haiku, Claude Sonnet, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. It reports five-rater pairwise human judgments, majority agreement, Fleiss’ κ, and a two-pass verifier variance analysis; overall majority agreement is 95.8% and Fleiss’ κ is 0.434. However, the main benchmark scores do not include confidence intervals, per-scenario variance, multiple-generation seeds, or statistical tests across model scores. The VQA verifier, caption generator, and part of the evaluation process rely on proprietary Gemini models, creating a potential evaluator bias and limiting exact reproducibility. The benchmark construction uses public images and model-generated captions, but the paper does not assess training-data overlap or contamination. The authors state that code and data are available at https://kxding.github.io/project/PlayWorld/; the parsed text does not provide a separate repository URL or model weights. HY-World2 cases that do not meet its input-image requirement are skipped, and Hunyuan-GameCraft-2 cannot always evaluate passive insight-evolution cases, so the effective sample composition may differ by model. The verifier robustness result is based on only two passes and the authors explicitly note that it is not a precise estimate of scoring uncertainty. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a benchmark/interface artifact rather than a deployed production system. Practical: The pipeline can interact with web-based models through browser automation and can run local model adapters, but hardware requirements, cloud costs, authentication constraints, and end-to-end evaluation time are not reported. Efficient: Agent decisions add approximately 3.83–6.21 seconds per call in the reported comparison, and each rollout can require up to 40 interaction steps; total compute and cost relative to fixed-trajectory evaluation are not quantified. Effective: The human-alignment study supports the claim that the rubric preserves human model rankings, with overall Spearman correlation 0.933, but it validates ranking agreement rather than whether the benchmark predicts downstream usefulness or real user satisfaction at deployment. Scalable: The paper evaluates 171 curated cases and rollouts up to 60 seconds but does not test 10×–100× more scenarios, longer horizons, more concurrent evaluations, or robustness to changing agent/verifier models. The work delivers a benchmark dataset, scoring pipeline, and browser/local interaction interface; it does not deliver a trained world model or learning algorithm. Strengths - It identifies a substantive evaluation mismatch: fixed low-level controls can measure trajectory execution rather than the intended world-model capability, and the closed-loop protocol addresses this with a concrete mechanism. - The four-way taxonomy separates global geometry, immediate interaction, hidden-state evolution, and visible process evolution, exposing failure modes that standard video-quality scores miss. - The benchmark reports a meaningful divergence between controllability and world-model quality; for example, SANA-WM achieves an 80.4% trajectory-validation pass rate but only a 1.48 overall rubric score. - The human-alignment study is a valuable sanity check, particularly because it reports dimension-specific correlations and agreement rather than relying only on automatic scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors acknowledge that proprietary VQA outputs can vary, that their two-pass robustness analysis is not a precise uncertainty estimate, and that multiple scoring passes increase evaluation cost. The implementation appendix also states that HY-World2 excludes cases whose initial images fail its input requirement and that Hunyuan-GameCraft-2 cannot always support insight-evolution cases requiring prolonged passive observation. They do not present a dedicated limitations section or quantify the resulting per-model coverage imbalance in the main results. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The benchmark’s automatic judge is not independent of benchmark construction: Gemini generates initial captions and also performs the main VQA verification, so systematic model-family preferences or shared visual-language biases remain possible. - Human validation uses only 120 video-pair items and nine model-level points per correlation plot; this is sufficient for a ranking sanity check but weak evidence for calibrated per-case validity, especially for the lower correlations of insight and out-of-sight evolution. - The paper does not report per-scenario counts, confidence intervals, or statistical comparisons for the headline model scores, making it difficult to determine whether close rankings such as HappyOyster versus LingBot-World2 are reliable. - Model coverage is not fully balanced because HY-World2 and Hunyuan-GameCraft-2 have protocol-specific exclusions, yet the overall score is an unweighted mean across dimensions and does not show whether every model receives the same case distribution. - The use of public images, generated captions, and hand-authored rubrics creates possible benchmark-specific familiarity or data contamination risks that are not investigated. - The protocol assumes that an external Agent Player can reliably recognize objective completion; errors in the agent’s visual reasoning may be attributed to the evaluated world model, and the paper does not quantify this source of error against human-controlled trajectories. - The results support ranking current systems on curated 10–60-second scenarios, but the conclusion that PlayWorld provides a general basis for long-horizon evaluation is broader than the tested domains, horizon, and scenario diversity establish. Bottom Line Practitioners evaluating interactive video world models should read this preprint because its objective-conditioned closed-loop protocol and failure taxonomy address a real weakness in fixed-trajectory benchmarks, but its conclusions should be treated as provisional until evaluator independence, balanced coverage, statistical uncertainty, and longer-horizon scalability are established.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses multi-hop logical query answering over incomplete knowledge graphs, where users may ask conjunction-, intersection-, and union-structured queries such as finding universities from which Canadian Turing Award winners graduated. Conventional relational query execution only returns entities supported by observed edges; it cannot infer plausible answers whose proof requires missing edges. Prior point-based query embeddings, particularly GQE, provide a compositional framework for conjunctive queries but do not naturally represent the interior of a set or handle arbitrary disjunctions in a closed, low-dimensional representation. The target users are researchers and applications that need approximate logical retrieval from noisy or incomplete relational graphs. Key Idea: Represent a query's answer set as a closed axis-aligned hyper-rectangle rather than as a single vector point. Relation projection translates the box and expands its offset, conjunction is modeled by producing a smaller box through attention-weighted center aggregation and coordinatewise offset reduction, and disjunction is handled by rewriting the query into DNF and taking the minimum distance to the resulting conjunctive-query boxes. The central insight is that box interiors naturally encode multiple valid answers and answer-set uncertainty, while DNF preserves closure without requiring a geometric union operator. Methodology: Each entity has a vector embedding in R^d, and a query box p is parameterized by a center Cen(p) and nonnegative offset Off(p), representing all vectors between Cen(p) - Off(p) and Cen(p) + Off(p). Anchor entities start as zero-offset boxes. For a relation r, projection applies p + r: centers are translated by the relation center and offsets are enlarged by the relation offset. For intersection, the center is an attention-weighted sum of input box centers, with attention weights generated by an MLP; the output offset is the elementwise minimum of input offsets multiplied by a sigmoid-transformed DeepSets function of the input boxes. Candidate entities are ranked with an entity-to-box distance consisting of an outside-box L1 distance plus alpha times an inside-box distance, where 0 < alpha < 1 discounts the position of points already inside the box. Training uses a margin-based negative-sampling loss that drives positive entity distances below a fixed margin gamma and negative distances above it. EPFO queries are converted to DNF by moving union operations to the final stage; each conjunctive branch is embedded independently and candidate distance is the minimum across branches. The projection rule is simple and interpretable but only loosely justified geometrically; the attention intersection is motivated by the need for a weighted center and supported by ablation, while the DNF transformation is logically exact but can incur substantial branch expansion that is not empirically characterized. Key Results: On H@3, Query2Box obtains average scores of 0.484 on FB15K, 0.268 on FB15K-237, and 0.306 on NELL995, compared with 0.386, 0.228, and 0.247 for GQE and 0.384, 0.230, and 0.248 for GQE-DOUBLE. The reported absolute gains over the best listed baseline are 9.8, 3.8, and 5.9 percentage points, corresponding to relative improvements of approximately 25%, 15%, and 24%. Query2Box's per-structure H@3 includes 0.786/0.413/0.303 for 1p/2p/3p and 0.593/0.712 for 2i/3i on FB15K; 0.467/0.240/0.186 and 0.324/0.453 on FB15K-237; and 0.555/0.266/0.233 and 0.343/0.480 on NELL995. It also evaluates unseen conjunctive structures ip and pi and union structures 2u and up, with FB15K scores of 0.211, 0.397, 0.608, and 0.330, respectively. Training uses five query structures and evaluation covers all nine structures, including structures unseen during training. The datasets are FB15K with 14,951 entities and 1,345 relations, FB15K-237 with 14,505 entities and 237 relations, and NELL995 with 63,361 entities and 200 relations. Queries are generated from sampled graph structures with at least one edge held out, and evaluation ranks answers in the test-minus-validation answer set. The baselines shown are relevant earlier neural query-embedding models but are limited to GQE variants; no newer or non-embedding baselines are reported in the supplied document. The experiments are standard-scale rather than stress-scale, and no latency, throughput, memory, or parameter-count results are given. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the genuinely distinctive contribution is the compositional box representation with learned intersection and DNF-based disjunction handling, while negative-sampling training, relation translation, attention, DeepSets, and ranking evaluation are established components applied in a new logical-query embedding formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation uses three established knowledge-graph datasets, explicit edge-based train/validation/test construction, filtered ranking over nontrivial answers, nine query structures, and ablations for attention versus averaging or DeepSets, training only on 1p queries, and shared versus adaptive box offsets. The ablations show that attention and adaptive offsets improve average H@3, and that training on complex queries is important: for example, on FB15K average H@3 falls from 0.484 for Query2Box to 0.385 when the variant is trained only on 1p queries and to 0.372 with shared offsets. However, the supplied document reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, sensitivity analysis for embedding dimension, alpha, negative-sampling count, or DNF branch count. It does not mention a code, data, or model-weight release URL. Query generation and evaluation are based on the same benchmark graphs, and the missing-edge protocol measures link-prediction-style recovery rather than validity against independently collected facts. The baseline set is narrow and does not establish performance against stronger contemporary methods or exact/approximate database systems. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: The model consists of vector operations, MLPs, and ranking over entity embeddings, but the document does not report a runnable implementation, hardware requirements, or deployment results. - Efficient: Projection and intersection are inexpensive per query, but DNF answering requires evaluating all N conjunctive branches; no measured latency, memory footprint, parameter count, or comparison with alternatives is provided. - Effective: The method improves H@3 on three benchmark graphs and unseen query structures, demonstrating effectiveness for the paper's missing-edge retrieval proxy, but not for downstream application accuracy or factual correctness outside those graphs. - Scalable: The paper argues that DNF branches can be parallelized, yet it does not test 10x–100x larger graphs, longer queries, larger intersections, or high-branching disjunctions; DNF expansion may become the dominant cost. The work delivers a technical model and query-answering framework, but the supplied document does not state that it releases a library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or other software artifact. Strengths: - The box representation directly addresses a structural weakness of point embeddings: a query can denote a set with nonzero interior, and adaptive offsets can reflect varying answer-set sizes. - The DNF/minimum-distance construction provides a simple, compositional way to support disjunction without forcing a non-rectangular union into a single box; the paper also gives a VC-dimension argument explaining why a direct low-dimensional geometric union is problematic. - The evaluation tests both familiar and unseen query structures, rather than restricting results to the structures used for training, and the gains persist across FB15K, FB15K-237, and NELL995. - The ablations isolate meaningful design choices: attention improves over averaging and DeepSets, complex-query training matters, and shared offsets are inferior to query-adaptive offsets. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The supplied document does not state explicit limitations or failure modes. It does acknowledge a computational issue with direct geometric union and notes that DNF evaluation costs the equivalent of evaluating all conjunctive branches, although it emphasizes parallelization rather than quantifying the resulting overhead. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The evaluation omits runtime, memory, parameter-size, and branch-expansion measurements, leaving the practical cost of the DNF strategy unknown. It tests only three relatively small benchmark families and does not evaluate robustness to noisy, contradictory, or adversarial graph edges, relation sparsity, longer paths, larger intersections, or high-cardinality unions. The query generator samples structures and edges from the same graphs used for evaluation, so its distribution may not represent naturally occurring user queries. The missing-edge split treats held-out graph edges as ground truth and does not establish that predicted edges are factually correct in the real world. The supplied material reports only GQE and GQE-DOUBLE as baselines, without stronger contemporary query-embedding, tensor-factorization, graph-neural, or symbolic approximate-query methods. The theorem concerns representational complexity of a class of distance functions, but the presentation does not provide enough proof detail to independently assess all assumptions or the claimed relationship between VC dimension and embedding dimension. No seed variation or statistical testing is reported, and no study examines whether the gains come primarily from additional model capacity, query-specific offsets, or differences in training data and optimization. Bottom Line: This is a consequential and technically useful formulation for neural logical query answering, worth reading for its box-based compositional representation and disjunction treatment, but its practical and scientific claims should be limited to benchmark ranking improvements until scalability, stronger baselines, reproducibility, and real-world factual validation are demonstrated.
