Problem & Motivation: Semantic query systems apply LLM-backed filters, maps, joins, classifications, and transformations to tables containing unstructured data such as clinical notes, contracts, biomedical articles, and claims. Existing systems such as Lotus and Palimpzest understand query operators but commonly execute them operator-at-a-time, while request-centric LLM engines such as vLLM see independent inference requests and cannot exploit dependencies in the query plan. When downstream operators process the same tuple context as upstream operators, their prompts share a prefix whose KV-cache state could be reused; under bounded GPU memory, however, materialization and concurrent upstream execution can evict that state before downstream processing. The gap is therefore serving-layer optimization that uses semantic query structure to coordinate pipelining, GPU admission, and cache retention without changing query semantics or relying on accuracy–latency approximations. Key Idea: Treat a semantic query plan as a memory-aware pipeline rather than a sequence of independent LLM requests: launch downstream tasks promptly after their parent task completes, while dynamically allocating enough memory across stages to retain reusable prefixes but not so much upstream work that downstream stages starve or the KV cache saturates. The central insight is that query-dependent selectivity and join fanout make fixed stage-memory allocations unreliable, so queue pressure can serve as an online signal for shifting memory between stages. Methodology: Kalypso places a query parser, scheduler, executor, memory estimator, KV-memory monitor, and deadlock monitor between a semantic-query client and an LLM engine, implemented on top of vLLM. Operators are registered as user-defined functions with an execution contract specifying whether they can be pipelined, whether they are predicates that prune tuples, and whether they form a Cartesian product. The parser groups nonblocking operators into pipelines and divides pipelines into stages at Cartesian-product boundaries; one stage invocation on one tuple becomes a schedulable task. Completed tasks enqueue dependent downstream tasks without materializing intermediate tuples, allowing vLLM prefix caching to reuse shared system-prompt and tuple-context KV entries. The scheduler maintains per-stage waiting queues and running tasks, admits work only when the stage’s current memory budget can accommodate the task, tracks parent–child dependencies, releases memory after predicates or final-stage completion, and rebalances budgets using low/high queue thresholds. A stage is considered starving when its queue is below a threshold and saturated when it exceeds one; budget is moved toward upstream stages under starvation and toward later stages when upstream work saturates memory. Each task receives a maximum output-token bound; for adaptive estimation, Kalypso uses the calibrated 99th percentile of the observed output-to-input token ratio and retries requests that exceed their bound. It supports virtual pinning through admission control under an LRU assumption and explicit pinning through approximately 200 lines of vLLM modifications, with deadlock detection that falls back from explicit to virtual pinning. These design choices are plausible and supported by ablations, but the queue-threshold policy, fixed alpha/beta settings (1 and 0.5), LRU assumption, and token-bound estimator receive limited theoretical or cross-workload justification. Key Results: The paper is an arXiv preprint (v1, dated July 26, 2026) and evaluates four workloads on four NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 GPUs using Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct across GPUs, vLLM v0.13.0rc4, and three runs per measurement. Against Lotus, Kalypso reduces FEVER latency from 258.1 s to 172.6 s (1.49×), MEDEC from 714.6 s to 464.3 s (1.54×), BioDEX from 910.3 s to 703.4 s (1.29×), and ContractNLI from 4,854 s to 1,062.4 s (4.57×). Against Palimpzest, it improves MEDEC from 808.2 s to 464.3 s (1.74×) and ContractNLI from 2,373.4 s to 1,062.4 s (2.23×); Palimpzest is not evaluated on FEVER or BioDEX because of unsupported operators. Oracle LLM-call counts are similar rather than substantially reduced: for example, FEVER uses 1,183 Lotus calls and 1,243 Kalypso calls, BioDEX uses 6,881 and 7,016, and ContractNLI uses 17,445 and 17,342; Kalypso reports 0, 21, 0, and 167 retries respectively for these workloads. Relative to a blocking Kalypso variant, pipelining improves latency by 1.20× on FEVER, 1.30× on MEDEC, 1.34× on BioDEX, and 1.83× on ContractNLI. Adaptive budgeting beats all tested fixed two-stage splits on BioDEX and ContractNLI at both 90% and 60% vLLM-memory settings. Virtual and explicit pinning have similar latency, with explicit pinning slightly faster on FEVER, BioDEX, and ContractNLI but slower on MEDEC. When vLLM KV-cache capacity falls from approximately 190.6 GB to 38.6 GB, MEDEC latency rises only 9% for Kalypso, compared with 44% for Lotus and 29% for Palimpzest; ContractNLI remains below 1,348.3 s for Kalypso, while Lotus remains above 4,854.0 s and Palimpzest above 2,296.5 s. These results establish latency and memory-robustness gains, but not semantic accuracy preservation: output quality, correctness, cache-hit rates, GPU utilization, energy, and cost are not quantitatively reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION—the paper formulates online scheduling of dependent semantic operators under bounded KV-cache capacity and implements an adaptive pipeline scheduler, while the underlying prefix caching, LLM inference engine, semantic operators, and query optimization techniques are standard components applied in a new serving-layer architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study includes useful ablations for blocking versus pipelined execution, adaptive versus fixed memory allocation, virtual versus explicit pinning, token-budget sensitivity, and reduced-memory operation. It uses three runs per experiment and reports averages, but no error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or per-run variance are provided. The baselines use the same manually optimized plans, operator implementations, oracle model, hardware, and vLLM engine where possible, which isolates serving effects, but the comparison is not against end-to-end combinations of Kalypso with the strongest plan optimization or proxy strategies. Fairness is also imperfect: Lotus uses proxy cascades on some workloads while Kalypso uses oracle-only implementations on MEDEC and ContractNLI because the proxy behavior was nondeterministic; this makes the latency comparison informative but not a clean measure of equal-quality execution. FEVER and BioDEX exclude Palimpzest due to unsupported operators, and the workloads are small in input-row count, although some contain long documents or large join expansions. The paper does not mention a public code repository, dataset release, model-weight release, or reproducibility package; release status is Not stated. A potentially important methodological issue is that the paper claims semantic preservation but does not measure accuracy or verify that retries, prompt formatting, proxy differences, and execution order leave outputs unchanged. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS—the paper builds and evaluates a serving system layered over vLLM, although the evaluation is primarily offline rather than a production deployment. * Practical: The system runs on commercially available NVIDIA GPUs and uses vLLM, but the demonstrated configuration requires four high-memory RTX Pro 6000 GPUs for the 70B model and explicit pinning requires vLLM modifications. * Efficient: It reduces latency without materially reducing LLM-call counts, primarily by avoiding repeated prefill and improving KV-cache reuse; memory reservations, retries, scheduler overhead, and the cost of the 70B model are not compared against alternative serving configurations in isolation. * Effective: The evidence shows lower completion time for four semantic-query workloads and robustness under lower KV-cache capacity, but it evaluates latency rather than whether the returned semantic results remain equivalent or accurate. * Scalable: The paper tests memory capacities from approximately 38.6 GB to 190.6 GB and workloads up to 17,445 oracle calls, but it does not test 10×–100× larger datasets, multiple simultaneous queries, distributed query execution, multiple model architectures, or multi-tenant serving; scalability beyond the tested setup is therefore a claim rather than an established result. The work delivers a software-system artifact and an API design, plus a scheduler implementation and an optional approximately 200-line vLLM pinning modification. A public repository, CLI, dataset package, or trained model artifact is Not stated. Strengths: - Identifies a concrete systems bottleneck—cross-operator KV-prefix eviction—that request-centric LLM serving cannot address, and separates it from semantic approximation and call-reduction techniques. - Gives a clear online scheduling formulation in which operator dependencies, queue pressure, token-dependent memory demand, and cache retention interact; the starvation/saturation analysis motivates adaptive rather than fixed stage budgets. - Provides an API abstraction that accommodates filters, maps, joins, cascades, vector indexes, and blocking operators instead of hard-coding one query workload. - The evaluation includes component-level ablations and memory-pressure sweeps, with the strongest gains appearing on long-context ContractNLI, where prefix reuse is plausibly most valuable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly notes that blocking operators such as aggregation and top-k are materialized rather than pipelined; Cartesian-product support is restricted to static right-side tables and left-deep plans; token bounds can be inaccurate and cause retries; explicit pinning can deadlock; virtual pinning depends on an LRU-style eviction policy; and some workloads require unsupported operators in Palimpzest. It also acknowledges nondeterministic proxy behavior and disables cascading for Kalypso on MEDEC and ContractNLI to make the experiments reproducible. These limitations are discussed directly, although the paper does not frame the resulting quality and generalization limitations as major threats to validity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper does not measure semantic-output accuracy, agreement with blocking execution, or the effect of prompt-prefix formatting and retries on results, despite claiming preserved query semantics and output accuracy. - The evaluation is narrow: four workloads, one model family, one serving engine, one server topology, manually optimized plans, and no concurrent-query or multi-tenant experiments. - Baseline coverage is incomplete. Palimpzest cannot run two workloads, and the study does not compare against modern query-aware batching, operator fusion, prefill scheduling, SGLang-style structured execution, or combinations with the best proxy/cascade and query-optimization methods. - The reported speedups combine pipeline overlap and prefix reuse; cache-hit rates, prefill/decode breakdowns, GPU utilization, scheduler overhead, and memory traffic are not reported, so the causal contribution of each mechanism remains only partially isolated. - Adaptive rebalancing uses fixed alpha/beta thresholds and a relatively simple starvation/saturation heuristic, but sensitivity to these parameters, adversarial selectivity/fanout patterns, workload phase changes, and estimation drift is not evaluated. - The system accepts only static left-deep plans and has restricted join support, leaving unclear how it handles bushy plans, dynamic plan changes, multiple input streams, or concurrent queries sharing the KV cache. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile systems paper for its query-aware KV-cache scheduling formulation and credible latency gains, but its practical significance should be discounted until semantic equivalence, broader serving baselines, public artifacts, and multi-query production-scale behavior are evaluated.

Cheng Qian, Wenting Zhao, Liangwei Yang, Heng Wang, Jielin Qiu, Heng Ji, Silvio Savarese, Huan Wang, Shelby Heinecke · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an inference-time scaffold-building framework in which a strong builder model writes and iteratively refines executable harnesses that improve a fixed weaker target model without changing its parameters. - Why it's important: The approach offers a possible alternative to retraining or deploying a larger model by moving capability into reusable routing, prompting, verification, and deterministic code, potentially lowering downstream model cost. - How it does it: The builder receives task instructions, a target-model calling interface, and labeled validation examples; it constructs a scaffold, evaluates it on validation data, diagnoses errors, and exports the final executable harness for hidden-test evaluation. - The good: Across 57 GPT-5.4-mini-target runs, the mean macro accuracy increases from 0.488 to 0.763, every run beats the vanilla baseline, and the best GPT-5.5/GPT Codex scaffold reaches 0.912 while fixing 1,717 baseline errors and breaking 105. - The missing: The central mechanism is supported mainly by observational correlations and a narrow Theory-of-Mind evaluation; there are no controlled component ablations, end-to-end deployment-cost measurements, or experiments outside four potentially shortcut-prone benchmarks. - Read it or not: Read it for empirical evidence and design lessons about automatically generated LLM harnesses, but treat claims about general capability transfer and practical cost savings as unvalidated beyond this benchmark setting.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses unreliable performance from smaller language models when tasks impose substantial burdens for state tracking, perspective shifts, nested beliefs, format compliance, and structured inference. This matters to practitioners deploying cheaper models inside agentic pipelines, where external routing, tools, verification, and preprocessing can change the difficulty of the inference problem without modifying model weights. Prior distillation methods generally update the student through supervised, rationale, preference, or on-policy training; inference-time prompting and tool-use methods generally optimize a procedure for the same model rather than asking a strong model to construct a reusable procedure for another model. The paper targets this gap in the context of four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, whose procedural regularities may permit deterministic or hybrid solutions but whose higher-order belief and Bayesian goal-inference cases remain difficult. Key Idea: A strong model can act as a compiler of task competence: it spends a one-time construction budget inspecting validation examples and converts recurring reasoning structure into routing rules, parsers, deterministic solvers, constrained prompts, and format controls that a weaker model can execute at test time. The paper’s most important insight is that gains appear to come primarily from externalizing predictable reasoning and reducing avoidable execution errors, rather than from eliciting longer target-model chains of thought or more sampling. This is a meaningful framing of cross-model harness construction, although the implemented mechanisms themselves largely combine established prompting, programmatic reasoning, routing, and output-control techniques. Methodology: For each benchmark, the authors reserve a labeled validation subset and keep the remaining examples hidden until final evaluation. A builder model operates in an agentic coding environment with a rule file, target-model demonstration/interface, and validation data. It repeatedly inspects resources, proposes or revises an unconstrained scaffold, calls the fixed target model on validation examples, records accuracy and errors, and exports an entry point that is run once on the hidden set. Scaffolds may contain prompt templates, benchmark routing, greedy decoding, forced chain-of-thought, deterministic preprocessing or postprocessing, polarity/negation logic, structured state extraction, few-shot examples, verification, hybrid fallbacks, and direct symbolic solvers. The primary metric is the unweighted macro-average of accuracy over BigToM (1,200 items), Hi-ToM (1,200), MMToM-QA (600), and MuMA-ToM (900), totaling 3,900 hidden items; validation usage is treated as a secondary efficiency metric. The study varies builder model, builder reasoning effort, builder platform, target model, and repeat, reporting 72 runs overall and three repeats per setting. Critical design choices are (1) allowing an open-ended scaffold space, which maximizes builder expressivity but complicates causal attribution; (2) using validation performance as the selection signal, which is practical but exposes the study to benchmark-specific optimization; and (3) evaluating both GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-3.5-flash targets, which tests headroom dependence but covers only two target models. The paper states that the validation split is 5% in the main methodology and setup, but an appendix instruction says 2%, an unresolved protocol inconsistency. Key Results: With GPT-5.4-mini as target, the vanilla macro-average is 0.488. Across 57 scaffolded runs, the mean is 0.763, an absolute uplift of 0.275, and 100% of runs exceed vanilla. The best run, GPT-5.5 as builder on GPT Codex, reaches 0.912, an uplift of 0.423 or 86.7% relative to baseline. Averaged by builder, GPT-5.5 reaches 0.875, Opus-4.7 extra-high 0.856, Gemini-3.5-flash 0.813, Sonnet-4.6 0.810, and Grok-0.1 0.563. The best scaffold’s per-benchmark accuracies are 1.00 on BigToM, 0.80 on Hi-ToM, 0.84 on MMToM-QA, and 0.88 on MuMA-ToM, compared with 0.95, 0.87, 0.98, and 0.96 for the human-designed UserHarness reference; thus automatic scaffolding wins on BigToM but remains below the human harness overall. The best scaffold also exceeds the reported unscaffolded GPT-5.4 and GPT-OSS-120B references on every benchmark shown. Run-to-run standard deviation averages 0.036, although the widest repeat range is 0.201. Builders use a median of five validation evaluations; best validation accuracy correlates with full-set accuracy at Pearson r=0.96, while the number of refinement iterations correlates only at r=0.17. Technique prevalence is high for format enforcement (57/57), greedy decoding (56/57), routing (54/57), forced chain-of-thought and polarity logic (45/57 each), and deterministic solvers (31/57). Technique-level associations are largest for polarity/negation logic (+0.090), structured extraction (+0.055), few-shot examples (+0.042), hybrid fallback (+0.040), and deterministic solving (+0.026), but these are explicitly associational because techniques co-occur. Deterministic workload fraction correlates with accuracy at r=0.72 across 18 tagged runs; mean offloadability is approximately 0.94 for BigToM, 0.51 for Hi-ToM, 0.44 for MMToM-QA, and 0.36 for MuMA-ToM. Increasing Opus-4.7 reasoning effort raises pooled accuracy from 0.711 at low effort to 0.793, 0.807, and 0.856 at medium, high, and extra-high effort, with Spearman rho=0.77 and reported permutation-test p-values of 0.013 versus high and 0.002 versus low for extra-high. Platform effects are small: native-platform advantage averages +0.013, with paired permutation p=0.484. For Gemini-3.5-flash as target, average performance rises from 0.761 to 0.871 (+0.110), compared with +0.262 for GPT-5.4-mini; Gemini gains almost entirely on BigToM (+0.42) and regresses on average on Hi-ToM (-0.04) and MuMA-ToM (-0.02). Residual errors for top scaffolds concentrate at Hi-ToM recursion order 4 (0.700 accuracy), deception cases, MMToM-QA Bayesian goal-inference subtypes (as low as 0.680), and MuMA social-goal/belief-of-goal questions. The reported best-scaffold McNemar tests are significant at p<10^-4, but statistical significance is unsurprising with 3,900 paired items and does not establish that any particular scaffold component causes the gain. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION—the genuinely new contribution is the explicit strong-builder/weak-target, validation-only, hidden-test formulation and its empirical analysis, while the scaffold mechanisms themselves are mostly established prompting, routing, deterministic execution, and output-control techniques recombined in a cross-model harness-construction setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study has a substantial factorial evaluation with 72 runs, three repeats per setting, per-benchmark results, held-out full-set testing, validation/full-set comparisons, an item-level fix/break analysis, and explicit acknowledgment that technique comparisons are associational rather than causal. It reports standard deviations, correlations, a paired permutation test for platform comparisons, permutation tests for reasoning effort, and McNemar tests for the best-scaffold comparison. However, there are no randomized component ablations that independently remove routing, deterministic code, format enforcement, greedy decoding, or structured extraction; the technique attribution therefore cannot support the claimed causal mechanism. Several contrast groups are extremely small, including 1 run without greedy decoding, 3 without routing, and 7 with verification, and the authors note that these comparisons are unreliable. The benchmarks are procedurally structured and the builders are explicitly encouraged to exploit them, so the results may measure benchmark compilation more than general reasoning transfer. The paper is an arXiv preprint (v1, dated 12 August 2026), and no code, scaffold repository, dataset release, model weights, or public reproducibility URL is stated. The appendix conflicts with the main text over whether validation contains 5% or 2% of the data. The use of commercial model APIs and proprietary coding platforms also limits independent replication unless equivalent access is available. Deployability: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS profile. Practical: The exported harnesses are described as executable Python-style artifacts using commercial model interfaces and can in principle run on available cloud infrastructure, but the paper does not report a released implementation or deployment requirements. Efficient: The paper reports a one-time builder process, a median of five validation passes, and scaffold sizes of roughly 510–650 lines at low effort versus 1,000–1,300 at extra-high effort, but it does not measure target inference latency, token usage, API cost, memory, or cost relative to using a larger model or the UserHarness. Effective: On these four ToM benchmarks, the evidence shows large accuracy improvements over direct calls and broad correction of baseline errors, but it does not establish performance on real applications or unstructured tasks. Scalable: The hidden test contains 3,900 items and the final instructions mention up to 16 parallel workers, but there is no 10×–100× scale experiment, no stress test for larger contexts or task distributions, and no evidence that hand-coded rules remain robust under distribution shift. The work delivers an executable scaffold as a per-run system artifact in the experimental setting, but no reusable public library, CLI, dataset, or trained model is released. Strengths: - It isolates a clear and practically relevant transfer regime in which the target model remains frozen and capability is externalized into an inference-time harness. - The evaluation varies builder identity, reasoning effort, platform, target strength, repeats, and validation usage, producing a more informative account than a single prompt comparison. - The mechanism analysis connects performance to deterministic offloading, structured extraction, routing, and format control, and the residual-error analysis identifies concrete limits at higher-order recursion and Bayesian goal inference. - The item-level fix/break analysis is stronger than aggregate accuracy alone: the best GPT-5.4-mini scaffold fixes 1,717 baseline errors and breaks 105, while top scaffold unions reportedly cover 97% of baseline errors, indicating complementary failure repairs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict the main evaluation to four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks and state that broader benchmark families are needed. They acknowledge that automated scaffolding remains below the human-designed UserHarness on Hi-ToM, MMToM-QA, and MuMA-ToM; that deterministic-solver strategies can be unstable because one rule error can affect many items; that deeper recursion, deception, and Bayesian goal inference remain difficult; and that scaffolding can backfire on already strong targets. They also acknowledge that technique-level comparisons are associational rather than causal and that platform averages confound platform identity with builder composition. These limitations are discussed directly, although the generalization and benchmark-shortcut implications remain underexplored. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The main causal claim about cognitive-load reduction is not isolated from confounders: builders that write more deterministic code may also be stronger, use more reasoning, route more effectively, or exploit benchmark-specific artifacts. - There is no controlled ablation matrix or matched scaffold comparison quantifying the marginal effect of format enforcement, routing, greedy decoding, forced chain-of-thought, deterministic solvers, or structured extraction. - The evaluation lacks non-ToM tasks, natural-language or open-ended outputs, distribution-shifted test sets, adversarial perturbations, and independently authored benchmarks, so “capability transfer” may overstate what is demonstrated. - The human-inspired UserHarness is a strong reference but not a fair cost-controlled baseline unless its construction effort, inference cost, and access to task-specific human insight are reported alongside the automatically built harnesses. - The paper does not report target-model token counts, number of calls per item, latency, dollar cost, builder construction cost, code execution failures, or maintenance cost; consequently, the claim that scaffolding enables cheaper deployment is not measured. - Validation selection and final scaffold selection are insufficiently specified, and the 5% versus 2% discrepancy in the appendix creates uncertainty about the exact protocol. - The top-scaffold union covering 97% of baseline errors is an oracle-style retrospective statistic; the paper does not provide a deployable, validation-only procedure for selecting or combining multiple scaffolds without hidden-test knowledge. - The benchmarks may contain exploitable templates and label/format regularities, especially BigToM, where the best scaffold reaches 1.00; the paper argues this is legitimate structure discovery but does not test robustness to template changes or semantically equivalent perturbations. Bottom Line: This is a strong and useful preprint for researchers studying LLM harness optimization and test-time systems, with convincing benchmark-level gains and a plausible compiler/offloading interpretation, but its novelty is primarily the evaluation formulation and empirical characterization rather than a new algorithm, and its practical and general reasoning-transfer claims remain unproven.

Zero-Mem

Yilin Xiao, Zhehan Zhu, Yujing Zhang, Jin Chen, Zijin Hong, Luyao Zhuang, Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Xiaocao Ouyang, Lingfei Ren, Xiao Huang · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Zero-Mem, a provenance-preserving agent-memory system that performs memory construction, routing, retrieval, evidence closure, and calibration without LLM calls or LLM input/output tokens, reserving the LLM for final question answering. - Why it's important: Removing recurring generative memory operations can reduce latency, token expenditure, and information loss in agents that maintain long, multi-session histories. - How it does it: It combines an entity–context graph for relational retrieval with a temporal hierarchy for local and session-aware retrieval, fuses both views using deterministic query routing, and applies rule-based evidence and answer calibration. - The good: On LoCoMo, it reaches 59.15 F1 and 52.96 BLEU-1 with GPT-4o-mini, exceeding the strongest reported baseline GAM by 5.40 and 5.45 points, while reducing memory-operation latency by 57.6% versus LightMem under the unified efficiency setup. - The missing: The paper does not sufficiently specify or independently validate key deterministic components, such as query-profile construction, episode segmentation, calibration rules, and the full encoder/indexing cost at substantially larger or more realistic agent workloads. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners working on long-term LLM-agent memory should read it for its clear zero-generative-memory design and empirical trade-off study, but should treat deployment claims as provisional until the promised implementation and broader stress tests are available.

Rigor (68) is supported by two readers, multiple benchmarks, relevant recent baselines, and ablations, but is reduced by absent uncertainty estimates, underspecified deterministic heuristics, conditional code release, and incomplete efficiency accounting. Completeness (68) and Resilience (65) are moderate-to-strong because the paper clearly separates memory-operation cost from reader inference and acknowledges that zero tokens is not zero computation, although deployment-scale updates and natural histories are untested. Problem & Motivation: Long-running LLM agents must recover entity-specific, temporally valid, and distributed evidence from accumulated user messages, actions, tool observations, and session histories. Existing systems often invoke an LLM to summarize, consolidate, update, route, or retrieve memories, creating recurring token and latency costs and potentially losing provenance through omission, merging, or temporal blurring. Direct lexical or dense retrieval preserves raw evidence but can confuse similar entities or sessions and miss evidence spread across multiple interactions. The target problem is therefore structured, provenance-preserving evidence selection over long conversational and document histories without making memory management itself a generative workload. Key Idea: The central insight is to replace generated memory abstractions with two complementary, non-generative views over the original traces: an entity–context graph that connects recurring entities and adjacent context units, and a temporal hierarchy that preserves session, episode, window, turn, and local-span structure. A deterministic query profile chooses which view receives greater weight, while closure adds relational bridges and neighboring context. This is more than raw retrieval but largely combines established graph propagation, PageRank, hierarchical indexing, lexical retrieval, dense embeddings, and rule-based filtering under the explicitly defined zero-token operating regime. Methodology: Given an interaction history H and query q, Zero-Mem first retains each source trace with text, provenance identifiers, timestamps, session boundaries, and metadata. It applies non-generative NER, such as spaCy, to construct an entity–context graph with entity–context co-occurrence edges weighted by normalized entity frequency and adjacency edges between neighboring context units. In parallel, it builds a hierarchy of turns, windows, episodes, and local spans; the paper states that episodes use semantic continuity and available temporal or session boundaries, but does not give a sufficiently detailed segmentation algorithm. It indexes units with BM25 and BGE-M3 embeddings. For each query, a deterministic profile contains subject, keywords, answer type, temporal cues, and boundary information. Relational queries prioritize the graph and local queries prioritize the hierarchy using a globally shared coefficient rho = 0.6, although both views run. Graph retrieval aligns query entities by dense similarity, propagates activation through co-occurrence evidence using query-relevant sentence similarity, combines these signals into a reset vector, and applies personalized PageRank, followed by lexical refinement. Hierarchical retrieval proceeds coarse-to-fine from episodes to windows to turns to local spans using semantic relevance and structural compatibility. Min–max-normalized scores from both views are fused, then evidence closure adds bounded graph neighbors and hierarchical neighbors. Deterministic calibration filters provenance- or boundary-incompatible candidates and ranks them by subject, temporal, and answer-type compatibility. The final reader LLM generates an answer from the selected evidence; post-reader calibration performs support checks, type and format checks, extractive shortening, and list pruning. The two-view architecture is motivated and ablated, but the paper gives limited justification for the fixed rho, the exact routing rules, graph propagation depth, segmentation choices, and calibration implementation. Key Results: On LoCoMo, using GPT-4o-mini, Zero-Mem obtains 59.15 average F1 and 52.96 BLEU-1, compared with 53.75 and 47.51 for GAM, the strongest listed baseline; the gains are 5.40 and 5.45 absolute points. Using Qwen2.5-14B, it obtains 57.57 F1 and 51.41 BLEU-1 versus GAM's 52.70 and 46.55. With GPT-4o-mini, Zero-Mem leads on single-hop, temporal, and open-domain LoCoMo questions and is below GAM on multi-hop F1 and BLEU-1; with Qwen2.5-14B, it leads every reported category. On the curated HotpotQA memory variant, it achieves F1 scores of 72.07, 66.43, and 65.04 at 56K, 224K, and 448K context lengths with GPT-4o-mini, and 68.58, 65.47, and 61.02 with Qwen2.5-14B, leading all listed baselines at every length. In the unified efficiency comparison with GPT-4o-mini, it uses zero memory-operation LLM tokens and reports 334.77 seconds total or 0.22 seconds per query, versus LightMem's 877,086 tokens, 788.76 seconds total, and 0.51 seconds per query; this is a reported 57.6% latency reduction. The setup uses four concurrent threads, an NVIDIA RTX 4090 environment, a maximum of five retrieved items, and identical final readers/context budgets. In the HotpotQA 56K ablation, full Zero-Mem scores 72.07 F1, versus 62.50 for graph-only and 54.88 for hierarchy-only; removing closure gives 67.90 and removing calibration gives 70.13. Increasing the LoCoMo primary retrieval budget from 5 to 10 raises average F1 from 59.15 to 59.80, showing modest sensitivity and diminishing returns. The baselines include recent systems such as GAM, SimpleMem, LightMem, and CompassMem, but the paper does not establish that every comparison uses independently reproduced, equally optimized implementations. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the explicit zero-token memory-operation regime together with a provenance-preserving dual-view retrieval pipeline; its individual mechanisms—NER graphs, PageRank, BM25, dense retrieval, hierarchical chunking, score fusion, and deterministic filtering—are standard or familiar components combined for this setting rather than newly invented algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation uses two readers, two benchmarks, multiple LoCoMo question types, three HotpotQA context lengths, recent memory baselines, an efficiency comparison on common hardware, component ablations, and retrieval-budget sensitivity. The ablations support the utility of both views, closure, and calibration, although they are concentrated on HotpotQA at one context length and one reader. The paper reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. It fixes gamma and rho at 0.6 but does not report tuning procedures, validation splits, sensitivity to these values, or whether query-profile rules were designed using the evaluation benchmarks. The code and implementation details are promised at https://github.com/TheMoon0815/Zero-mem after peer review; the paper does not state that code, data, model weights, or a runnable release are currently available. The efficiency accounting explicitly excludes LLM tokens but includes some non-generative processing; the reported tables do not fully decompose encoder inference, graph construction, indexing, storage, preprocessing, and update costs. The use of a curated HotpotQA memory variant with gold supporting documents plus distractors may not represent naturally accumulated agent histories, and the paper does not report memory construction/update quality or retrieval recall independently of final-answer quality. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL — the paper implements and evaluates a retrieval system, but does not present a production deployment. - Practical: The system uses commercially available components and hardware, including BGE-M3, BM25, NER, and an RTX 4090-class GPU, so the retrieval pipeline is plausibly runnable, although memory footprint, indexing throughput, update behavior, and production integration costs are not stated. - Efficient: It consumes zero LLM input/output tokens during memory operations and reports 0.22 seconds per query versus LightMem's 0.51 seconds, but the comparison does not provide a complete accounting of encoder, preprocessing, storage, graph-maintenance, and indexing costs. - Effective: Results on LoCoMo and the curated 56K–448K HotpotQA variant show higher answer F1 than the listed baselines under shared final readers, but they evaluate QA proxies rather than reliability in interactive agents, online memory updates, hallucination rates, privacy, or adversarially conflicting histories. - Scalable: Testing reaches 448K-token contexts and shows performance declining from 72.07 to 65.04 F1 with GPT-4o-mini, but there is no experiment at 10×–100× larger histories, many users, sustained online updates, graph growth, or distributed deployment; scalability beyond the tested benchmark is therefore a claim rather than evidence. The work delivers a research system design and an intended software artifact, but the release is not yet documented as available in the paper. Strengths: - It identifies and operationalizes a meaningful systems trade-off—eliminating generative memory operations rather than merely reducing their token count—while clearly separating memory-operation cost from final-reader inference. - The dual-view representation addresses two distinct retrieval failure modes: graph connectivity supports distributed relational evidence, while temporal hierarchy preserves locality, order, session boundaries, and state. - Provenance preservation is a technically useful design constraint: retrieved units resolve to original traces rather than opaque generated summaries, improving traceability and reducing one class of abstraction-induced information loss. - The empirical pattern is consistent across readers and task families: Zero-Mem leads the listed baselines on both LoCoMo averages and all reported HotpotQA context lengths, while the ablations show that the full system materially outperforms either single view. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that zero-token operation does not mean zero computation and that encoder inference, organization, retrieval, and deterministic calibration still incur cost. It also reports that top-10 retrieval performs slightly better than the top-5 configuration used for main comparisons, and explains the choice as matching the baselines' retrieval budget. Beyond these points, explicit limitations and failure modes are not substantially discussed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not quantify graph and hierarchy construction cost during online ingestion, storage/memory overhead, update latency, or performance as histories accumulate; this weakens the practical interpretation of the latency result. Query-profile extraction, routing rules, episode segmentation, evidence-conflict detection, answer-type extraction, and calibration are described at a high level, making the method difficult to reproduce and leaving open whether benchmark-specific heuristics or hidden supervision influence results. The fixed global rho = 0.6 is not sensitivity-tested, and the paper does not compare against simpler strong variants such as a carefully tuned hybrid BM25+dense retriever with temporal/session filtering and neighboring-span expansion. It does not report retrieval recall, evidence precision, answer faithfulness, or calibration accuracy separately, so improvements could arise from answer post-processing rather than better memory selection. The HotpotQA setup supplies gold supporting documents and synthetic distractor scaling, which may favor structured retrieval and does not establish performance on organically noisy, continuously updated agent histories. There are no multi-seed results or uncertainty estimates, and no evaluation of entity-linking errors, aliases, coreference, contradictory updates, privacy-sensitive traces, multilingual data, or histories far beyond 448K tokens. Finally, the promised code release is conditional on peer review, so current reproducibility is limited. Bottom Line: This is a useful and empirically credible systems paper for long-context and long-term agent-memory research, with a strong cost/provenance design point, but its deployment claims should remain tentative until the underspecified heuristics, full preprocessing costs, online-update behavior, and broader baselines are made reproducible.

LiveAnimate: Stable Long-Form Streaming Human Animation in Real-Time (10 ▲ )

Yuxuan Zhang, Haozhong Xiong, Yubo Huang, Jiayi Song, Jinpeng Yu, Haofan Wang, Jiaming Liu, Ruihua Huang, Liwei Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 14 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LiveAnimate, a 14B-parameter pose-driven human-animation system that generates open-ended video streams causally at approximately 19.63 FPS while preserving identity and appearance over three-minute rollouts. - Why it's important: Interactive applications such as live streaming, telepresence, and virtual avatars cannot use existing diffusion animation systems that require minutes to hours to render a clip or degrade over long horizons. - How it does it: It converts a bidirectional video Diffusion Transformer into a block-causal generator, distills it to three denoising steps, and uses Pose-Retrieval Sink Attention to retain a bounded set of identity- and pose-relevant KV-cache context. - The good: On 24 three-minute sequences, IQA changes only from 4.047 in the initial segment to 4.026 in the final segment, while throughput reaches 19.63 FPS on two NVIDIA H100 GPUs. - The missing: The real-time claim excludes VAE encoding/decoding and conditioning costs, and the evaluation does not establish end-to-end latency, performance beyond three minutes, or robustness on higher-resolution, multi-person, or camera-motion scenarios. - Read it or not: Researchers and engineers working on streaming video diffusion, human animation, or long-horizon autoregressive generation should read it for its cache design and systems trade-offs; readers seeking a broadly deployable animation model can defer until code, end-to-end benchmarks, and wider evaluations are available.

Problem & Motivation: Pose-driven human animation must synthesize a target person from one reference image while following a stream of body and facial controls. The application domains include virtual avatars, live streaming, telepresence, virtual try-on, and digital-human creation. Existing diffusion systems provide strong short-clip quality, and recent methods extend generation to minute-scale videos, but they generally operate offline, require minutes to hours per clip, use fixed temporal windows, or accumulate identity, background, and appearance drift during autoregressive rollout. The specific unresolved problem is to combine causal open-ended streaming, interactive latency, and stable long-form identity preservation in a billion-parameter video diffusion model. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat long-horizon consistency as selective retrieval of historical attention states rather than retaining the entire generated sequence. Pose-Retrieval Sink Attention combines a permanent first-block Static Sink for global appearance anchoring, a Dynamic Sink populated with a pose-matched historical block, and a three-block Rolling Window for local continuity. The method therefore preserves both time-invariant identity context and pose-specific evidence while keeping cache size and attention cost bounded. The training contribution complements this cache mechanism by exposing a bidirectional DiT to causal histories and then training it on its own autoregressive trajectories. Methodology: LiveAnimate starts from the Wan2.2-Animate-14B checkpoint and fine-tunes LoRA parameters in two stages. In Stage 1, Reference-Anchored Teacher-Forcing Adaptation partitions training videos into blocks of three latent frames, or 12 RGB frames, and denoises each block with block-causal attention to ground-truth clean history. A global Ref Sink stores key-value states from the reference image and remains visible to every block; the causal attention reads the reference KV states, preceding clean-history KV states, and the current noisy block. At inference, each generated block receives three denoising steps and undergoes an additional clean-timestep forward pass to write its KV states into the historical cache. Stage 2 applies Block-wise Self-Forcing Distillation based on distribution-matching distillation. A no-gradient rollout first generates a complete student trajectory using the student’s own predictions as context. The training procedure then replays one block at a time, detaches all other trajectory and KV states, recomputes only the selected block with gradients, and evaluates a DMD loss on the complete detached-plus-recomputed trajectory; the block index slides across the rollout. This avoids retaining the full rollout computation graph and supports distillation of the 14B model with LoRA on one 8×80GB GPU node. PR-Sink computes a 558-dimensional fingerprint from three pose frames, using 62 body and hand landmarks with coordinates and confidence values. A five-entry memory bank is updated during the first 20 blocks using a diversity objective that favors low average pairwise cosine similarity. Before each block, the most similar stored pose is retrieved, excluding the immediately preceding block, and its pre-RoPE keys and values are re-rotated into the current cache positions. The cache contains the reference-image Ref Sink, first generated block, retrieved historical block, and three recent blocks. Ulysses sequence parallelism distributes attention across GPUs, while torch.compile and operator/kernel fusion reduce execution overhead. The three most consequential design choices—teacher-forced causal adaptation, block-wise self-forcing distillation, and the Static/Dynamic Sink decomposition—are motivated by exposure bias, memory constraints, and complementary identity-versus-pose context, although the paper does not provide a formal analysis of their operating conditions. Key Results: The evaluation uses 24 three-minute reference/driver pairs: 12 in-the-wild web videos and 12 sequences derived from X-Dance by playing motion forward, backward, and forward again to induce pose recurrence. At 480×480 resolution, the full model obtains ASE 2.823 and IQA 4.047 on the initial 0–30-second segment. From the initial segment to 120–180 seconds, IQA changes from 4.047 to 4.026, ASE from 2.823 to 2.824, and DINO-S from 0.833 to 0.818. One-to-All declines over the same horizon from IQA 3.402 to 1.786 and DINO-S 0.769 to 0.328, while its FID increases from 146.29 to 386.33. Removing the Dynamic Sink reduces final-segment DINO-S from 0.818 to 0.805 and raises FID from 100.90 to 106.52; removing the Static Sink lowers final DINO-S to 0.693 while retaining moderate frame-level scores of ASE 2.726 and IQA 3.833. Replacing DMD self-forcing with conventional teacher forcing causes IQA to fall from 3.849 to 3.438 and DINO-S from 0.780 to 0.679 across the rollout. Four sampling steps produce the strongest frame-level metrics, whereas two steps reduce final DINO-S to 0.783; three steps are selected as the efficiency-quality compromise. Generation of one 12-RGB-frame block takes 0.611276 seconds on two H100 GPUs, corresponding to 19.63 FPS; denoising accounts for 75.07% of this time and the clean KV update for 24.388%. One H100 achieves 12.41 FPS, two achieve 19.63 FPS with 79.1% parallel efficiency, and four achieve 22.13 FPS with 44.6% efficiency. The paper reports approximately four minutes to generate a three-minute sequence, compared with approximately two to five hours for the evaluated baselines. The baselines include EverAnimate, One-to-All, SCAIL, UniAnimate-DiT, and Wan2.2-Animate. SCAIL and UniAnimate-DiT sometimes obtain higher DINO-S, but the authors report more inter-frame flickering; the comparison is not fully latency-matched because several baselines are offline systems extended using a training-free sliding-window protocol. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the principal technical novelty is the pose-conditioned Static/Dynamic Sink cache with position-consistent RoPE reuse, while causal adaptation, self-forcing distillation, DMD, Ulysses parallelism, and attention sinks are adapted or combined from existing work for real-time pose-driven animation rather than introduced from first principles. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for the Dynamic Sink, Static Sink, RoPE re-indexing, and DMD-based self-forcing, plus a two-, three-, and four-step sampling comparison. These ablations support the claimed complementary roles of the sinks and the importance of self-forcing, although they are reported primarily as metric trajectories and qualitative samples rather than confidence intervals or statistical tests. The evaluation spans 24 sequences, but the controlled long-horizon portion reuses motion by playing sequences forward, backward, and forward again, which directly tests recurrence but may not represent natural three-minute motion. No multiple-seed results or error bars are stated. The training data comprise 40,000 talking videos and 20,000 human-motion videos, but their exact composition, licensing, preprocessing, train/test separation, and availability are not stated. The paper links to https://liveanimate.github.io/, but it does not explicitly state that source code, weights, training data, or a runnable model are released. The latency protocol measures only the DiT generation loop and excludes pose/reference encoding and VAE encoding/decoding; this is clearly disclosed but weakens direct claims about end-to-end real-time deployment. Comparisons against fixed-window baselines rely on author-designed sliding-window extensions rather than uniformly native implementations, and the paper does not report a complete end-to-end latency or memory table. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, with substantial empirical evaluation. Practical: The DiT loop runs on commercially available NVIDIA H100 GPUs, but the reported operating point requires two 80GB accelerators and excludes some preprocessing and decoding costs, so practical deployment on consumer or lower-memory hardware is not established. Efficient: The system delivers 19.63 FPS at 480×480 on two H100s, with 0.611 seconds per 12-frame block and constant cache size, but four-GPU scaling reaches only 22.13 FPS and the clean KV update consumes 24.388% of block time. Effective: On the reported 24-sequence, three-minute benchmark, the method preserves perceptual quality and identity substantially better than several offline or extended baselines, but its evidence is based on proxy metrics and qualitative inspection rather than user studies, pose-accuracy metrics, or end-to-end application performance. Scalable: Cache storage and attention cost are designed to remain constant with stream duration, but the paper tests only three-minute rollouts and does not measure 10×–100× longer streams, larger pose-memory banks, higher resolutions, multi-person scenes, or dynamic cameras. The work delivers a trained animation system and an online project page, but a publicly downloadable software artifact, model checkpoint, or dataset is not explicitly confirmed. Strengths: - It addresses a concrete systems bottleneck—interactive, open-ended human animation—rather than optimizing only short-clip perceptual quality. - The Static Sink and pose-retrieved Dynamic Sink separate global identity anchoring from pose-specific historical retrieval; the ablation shows that removing the Static Sink reduces final DINO-S to 0.693 and that removing the Dynamic Sink causes a smaller but measurable degradation. - Block-wise self-forcing replay is a practical training construction for a 14B autoregressive diffusion model: it exposes the student to its own history without retaining the full rollout graph and is reported to fit on one 8×80GB GPU node. - The evaluation measures quality as a function of elapsed rollout time and reports a useful inference breakdown, revealing both the approximately 19.63 FPS operating point and the substantial 24.388% cost of clean KV updates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the current system operates at 480×480 with three denoising steps, limiting visual fidelity and resolution. They also state that it does not support multi-person scenes or large camera motion. They leave higher-resolution streaming, multi-person animation, and camera-dynamic scenes for future work. These limitations are acknowledged directly, but the paper does not discuss the excluded VAE and conditioning costs as limitations to the end-to-end real-time claim, likely because those exclusions are presented in the measurement protocol rather than the conclusion. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest concern is that 19.63 FPS is a DiT-loop throughput number rather than an end-to-end streaming latency number; pose extraction with ViTPose, face processing, VAE decoding, data movement, compilation warm-up, and pipeline synchronization are excluded or assumed to overlap. The system’s core retrieval mechanism is evaluated on a benchmark deliberately constructed with repeated poses, but the paper does not test whether retrieval remains beneficial under genuinely novel, non-repeating motion, detector noise, occlusion, fast motion, or incorrect pose estimates. The five-entry memory bank is updated only during the first 20 blocks, so the claim of long-duration robustness is not supported beyond three minutes or beyond the initial coverage phase. The comparison omits recent causal real-time video-generation methods cited in related work, including Causal Forcing and Rolling Forcing, and does not establish whether a generic long-video causal baseline can achieve a better quality-latency trade-off. The paper reports no direct pose-following accuracy, temporal flicker metric, human preference study, failure-rate analysis, or per-sequence variance. It also does not quantify quality at resolutions other than 480×480 despite supporting aspect-ratio buckets, and it does not report peak GPU memory, total training compute, or energy cost. Finally, the reliance on a 14B proprietary starting checkpoint, undisclosed training-data details, and an unconfirmed code/weight release limits independent reproduction. Bottom Line: LiveAnimate is a technically credible and practically relevant systems contribution whose bounded pose-retrieval cache and self-forcing distillation offer a meaningful operating point for 480×480 single-person animation, but its strongest real-time and scalability claims remain narrower than the headline because end-to-end cost, longer streams, broader motion conditions, and reproducibility are not established.

Learning Globally Reusable Skills for Coding Agents

C Yang, J Tian, Z Wang, X Liu, M Ye, J Chen · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GSE, a skill-evolution framework that maintains a Skill Relation Graph and consolidates execution-derived updates into replay-validated, reusable skills for coding agents. - Why it's important: Coding agents can accumulate local, project-specific fixes that conflict with existing guidance, overfit observed failures, and cause regressions without model retraining. - How it does it: GSE diagnoses failures, propagates updates through inter-skill dependency/co-usage/conflict relations, clusters related proposals, abstracts them into generalized skills, and accepts only candidate skill banks that pass replay on historical cases. - The good: Across OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent, GSE improves F1 over the strongest compared evolution baseline from 0.22 to 0.31 and from 0.29 to 0.38 for test generation, and from 0.43 to 0.70 and from 0.39 to 0.46 for false-positive filtering. - The missing: The paper does not report multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, detailed held-out project results, or evaluation at substantially larger skill-bank and task scales. - Read it or not: Researchers working on self-evolving LLM agents or software-engineering agents should read it for the relation-aware and replay-based design, while practitioners should wait for evidence beyond two tasks, one proprietary industrial setting, and undisclosed implementation artifacts.

Problem & Motivation: Coding agents for repository exploration, test generation, and bug analysis rely on explicit skills, prompts, and tool-use procedures that can become inadequate as projects, languages, conventions, and failure modes change. Existing skill-evolution methods derive updates from individual execution traces and merge them locally; this can produce skills that are overly specific to observed projects or bugs, conflict with assumptions made by other skills, and regress performance on future tasks. The target problem is therefore continual improvement of a skill bank without retraining the underlying LLM while preserving compatibility among skills and generalizing local experience across projects. The application domains evaluated are bug-revealing Java test generation and Go false-positive bug-report filtering. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat the skill bank as an interconnected object whose nodes and relationships must evolve together, rather than as an unordered collection of independent textual updates. GSE combines a Skill Relation Graph, which represents dependency, co-usage, and conflict relations, with consolidation and replay validation that turn multiple locally successful updates into higher-level capability abstractions. The most non-obvious design move is the use of historical cases activated by affected skills as a regression filter for generalized updates; however, the paper does not establish formally that the graph or its clustering criteria recover true causal skill relationships. Methodology: GSE first records agent reasoning blocks, tool calls, command parameters, environment feedback, and outcomes, then simplifies traces by removing verbose search results, raw file contents, and low-value logs while retaining commands, paths, errors, warnings, and reasoning. An update agent diagnoses each failure as primarily a navigation, reasoning, or execution deficiency and categorizes the resulting update as a general capability or reusable problem-pattern skill. It emits a structured DSL proposal containing the target skill, operation, content, rationale, expected behavior, and relation changes. The SRG is a directed graph over skills with dependency, co-usage, and conflict edges; the update agent examines graph neighbors and semantically retrieves additional potentially related skills, then generates auxiliary proposals when assumptions or interactions change. Each proposal is applied to a temporary skill bank and locally verified by replaying its originating failure. Locally successful proposals modifying existing skills are clustered by affected skill set; proposals introducing new skills are clustered by semantic similarity of their rationales and expected effects. A merge agent extracts shared capability patterns, removes case-specific details, resolves redundancy or conflicts, and creates candidate skill banks. Candidate banks are replayed on historical cases that previously activated affected skills, or on the proposal-generating cases for new skills, and are accepted only if they preserve or improve replay performance. The objective is described conceptually as maximizing expected task success over the task distribution, but GSE does not provide an explicit trainable loss or formal optimization procedure. Critical design decisions include graph-based propagation, LLM-mediated clustering/generalization, and replay-based acceptance; the ablations support their usefulness, but the paper gives limited details about graph construction, retrieval thresholds, clustering prompts, merge-agent behavior, and acceptance criteria. Key Results: On 108 triggerable buggy Java focal methods from 9 open-source projects derived from Multi-SWE-Bench, GSE reaches precision/recall/F1 of 0.35/0.28/0.31 with OpenHands, versus the strongest baseline values of 0.33/0.17/0.22, and 0.55/0.29/0.38 with mini-SWE-agent, versus 0.43/0.22/0.29. On IndustrialBugs, a proprietary Go dataset of 500 reports from 8 production repositories containing 132 confirmed bugs and 368 false alarms, GSE reaches 0.55/0.95/0.70 with OpenHands versus the strongest baseline's 0.29/0.84/0.43, and 0.30/0.97/0.46 with mini-SWE-agent versus 0.26/0.84/0.39. The ablations on OpenHands reduce F1 from 0.31 to 0.27 for test generation and from 0.70 to 0.59 for filtering without the SRG; removing generalization reduces them to 0.27 and 0.54. Evolution consumes 401.55K tokens per case versus 357.64K for Trace2Skill, a 12.28% increase, while downstream execution consumes 593.21K tokens per case versus 489.31K for the base agent and 619.65K for Trace2Skill. On the partner's internal agent, GSE increases filtering F1 from 0.43 to 0.71, with precision rising from 0.29 to 0.56 and recall from 0.83 to 0.97. The held-out-project protocol is a meaningful generalization test, but the reported aggregate tables do not show per-project dispersion or sample counts. The baselines include vanilla agents, manually authored skills from six senior engineers, Live-SWE-agent, and Trace2Skill under a shared LLM, harness, environment, and budget; the compared evolution methods are recent, although their adaptation to these tasks may affect fairness. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper's genuine contribution is the combination of relation-aware co-evolution of a textual skill bank with cluster-based abstraction and replay-gated integration, whereas trace collection, LLM reflection, skill extraction, semantic clustering, and replay are individually established patterns applied here to globalized coding-agent skill evolution. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations, a one-project-held-out protocol, matched base LLMs and execution budgets, a token-cost analysis, and an industrial deployment evaluation. It reports deterministic temperature-zero runs but does not report multiple seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or per-project results, so the reliability of the gains—especially on 108 Java cases and 132 positive industrial examples—is difficult to assess. The graph, proposal DSL, consolidation, and replay mechanisms are not evaluated with independent human annotations or controlled diagnostic accuracy tests, and the ablations combine several changes when removing the SRG or generalization. The authors state that released artifacts were reused for baselines, but no public GSE code, dataset, model weights, or repository URL is stated; IndustrialBugs is proprietary. The held-out protocol reduces direct benchmark leakage, and the authors report that generated tests did not match reference tests, but the evolution and evaluation distributions remain limited to two task types and the internal dataset may favor the partner's domain. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The system runs on commercially available hardware—a 128-core CPU machine with 128 GB RAM—and uses API-hosted DeepSeek-V4-Flash, although the paper does not report wall-clock latency, monetary API cost, or the hardware requirements of replay at deployment scale. Efficient: GSE adds 12.28% token cost to evolution relative to Trace2Skill and 21.2% downstream tokens relative to the vanilla agent, but uses 4.3% fewer downstream tokens than Trace2Skill; memory, CPU time, number of replays, and total end-to-end cost are not reported. Effective: The evidence shows improved precision, recall, and F1 on two held-out-project tasks and a proprietary-agent deployment, but it measures benchmark classification and bug-triggering proxies rather than downstream developer time, defect-remediation cost, or production safety. Scalable: The paper tests 108 Java focal methods, 500 Go reports, and skill evolution per case, but does not test 10x–100x larger skill banks, repositories, historical replay sets, concurrent evolution, or long-term continual operation; scalability is therefore claimed rather than demonstrated. The work delivers an implemented Python framework using LangChain, SQLite trace/state storage, and Git-worktree skill versioning, but public release of the GSE software is not stated. Strengths: - The paper identifies a substantive failure mode in continual skill evolution—interactions among accumulated skills—and operationalizes it with explicit dependency, co-usage, and conflict relations rather than treating skills as independent prompts. - The separation between local validation and cross-case replay validation directly targets overfitting and behavioral regressions; the generalization ablation shows a large F1 drop for filtering, from 0.70 to 0.54, when this mechanism is removed. - The evaluation controls the base LLM, harness, tools, environment, and task budget across methods and evaluates both open-source agents and a stronger internal industrial agent. - The gains are particularly relevant on false-positive filtering, where OpenHands precision increases from 0.29 for the strongest baseline to 0.55 while recall increases from 0.84 to 0.95, indicating a change in the precision–recall tradeoff rather than recall-only improvement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge threats to generalization across coding agents, programming languages, and software-engineering tasks; possible implementation errors; LLM randomness; and data leakage. They mitigate these with two open-source agents, Java and Go tasks, an industrial agent, official/released baseline implementations, temperature-zero execution, held-out projects, and checks against reference tests. They do not explicitly acknowledge the absence of statistical uncertainty reporting, the limited number of tasks and projects, the proprietary nature of IndustrialBugs, or the lack of large-scale and long-term evolution experiments. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main concern is that the paper attributes large improvements to global skill evolution without quantifying how many proposals, clusters, graph edges, replays, accepted updates, or regressions occurred, making the mechanism difficult to audit or reproduce. No multi-seed evaluation or statistical testing leaves open whether some gains reflect deterministic but benchmark-specific LLM behavior. The replay set for new skills consists of the cases that generated the proposals, which is not an independent generalization test; even for existing skills, historical cases selected by skill activation may miss unobserved failure modes. The study lacks stronger alternative controls such as consolidation without an SRG, an SRG with fixed relations, random or embedding-based clustering, replay on a temporally later stream, and equal-token or equal-API-budget comparisons. IndustrialBugs cannot be independently inspected, and the class imbalance and task-specific decision costs are not analyzed. The reported test-generation recall definition includes false-positive bug-revealing tests in the denominator, which differs from conventional case-level recall and should be justified more carefully. Finally, the framework relies heavily on opaque LLM agents for diagnosis, relation inference, clustering, and merging, but does not measure their error rates or sensitivity to prompts and model choice. Bottom Line: This is a useful and empirically promising framework paper for researchers studying self-evolving coding agents, but its strong aggregate gains are not yet sufficient to establish robust, general-purpose global skill evolution without variance analysis, independent replay tests, broader baselines, and public artifacts.

Walkable to Whom? Capturing Subjective Variability in Walkability Perception Using Multimodal Deep Learning

M Damandeh, M Saberi · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a sidewalk-view walkability perception dataset and a user-conditioned multimodal ordinal model that predicts five-point ratings from panoramic imagery and respondent attributes. - Why it's important: Aggregated walkability scores can conceal systematic differences across users, potentially producing pedestrian assessments and routes that underserve people with different backgrounds, habits, ages, or mobility needs. - How it does it: It encodes sidewalk panoramas with Swin-Tiny, respondent attributes with FT-Transformer, fuses both representations with a Transformer, and predicts ordinal thresholds using CORAL. - The good: On a rating-completion test split, user conditioning raises quadratic weighted kappa from 0.285 ± 0.023 to 0.469 ± 0.026, a 65% relative improvement over the image-only baseline. - The missing: The main evaluation allows the same images and respondents to occur in both training and test partitions, so it does not establish generalization to unseen streets, locations, or users; stronger image- and respondent-disjoint evaluations are absent. - Read it or not: Urban-computing and transportation researchers studying subjective perception should read it for the dataset and formulation, while practitioners seeking deployment-ready personalized routing evidence can stop because routing is only proposed, not evaluated.
