Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the difficulty of measuring perceived walkability when people evaluate the same pedestrian environment differently. This matters to urban planners, transportation researchers, accessibility analysts, and potentially routing systems that need user-specific assessments. Existing visual models generally use vehicle-mounted street-view imagery and predict one aggregate score per location, treating observer variation as noise; planning approaches that consider heterogeneity often use manually defined user groups rather than learning differences from individual ratings. The paper also targets the unresolved question of whether sidewalk-view imagery changes perceived walkability relative to matched vehicle-based imagery. Its motivating gap is therefore both representational—observer-independent prediction—and observational—insufficient pedestrian-perspective, respondent-linked data. Key Idea: The central insight is to model walkability as an interaction between an environment and the person judging it, rather than as an image-only property. The paper combines a visual representation of the sidewalk with a structured representation of the respondent and learns their joint effect on an ordinal rating. This is a meaningful formulation for walkability, but the underlying multimodal fusion and ordinal-regression components are established techniques adapted to a new transportation-perception setting. Methodology: The dataset begins with high-resolution 360-degree sidewalk imagery from footpath.ai across nine Australian locations and urban, suburban, and regional settings. Threshold-Constrained Stratified Sampling selects 974 images while keeping each sampled walkability-related attribute within 5% of its source-pool marginal distribution. An online survey asks 1,196 respondents to rate 25 panoramic images each on a five-point Likert scale, producing 29,870 valid image–respondent ratings; respondents report age, gender, current and childhood residential context, upbringing country, walking frequency, and walking-related disability or health condition. Quality controls include repeated-image consistency checks, speed thresholds, straightlining detection, and duplicate/automated-response controls. A separate matched-viewpoint survey compares sidewalk and Google street-view images at 100 locations. For prediction, a pretrained ImageNet-1K Swin-Tiny processes a centered 224 × 224 crop from each 2:1 equirectangular panorama, retaining approximately the central 180 degrees; an FT-Transformer encodes categorical respondent attributes; modality representations are projected into a common 768-dimensional space and passed through three Transformer fusion blocks. CORAL converts the five-class target into four cumulative threshold tasks, with binary cross-entropy loss summed across thresholds and predictions recovered by counting threshold probabilities above 0.5. Critical design choices include direct Likert ratings, which preserve respondent-level labels; CORAL, which respects ordinal structure; and Transformer-based tabular and cross-modal encoders, which are justified mainly through sequential validation-set ablations rather than independent theoretical analysis. The image preprocessing is a notable limitation because it applies a standard perspective crop to panoramic data without geometric correction and discards much of the 360-degree view. Key Results: The dataset’s ratings are concentrated in the middle: ratings 3 and 4 account for 61.1% of responses, while rating 1 accounts for 5.8%. Mean pairwise quadratic weighted kappa among respondents is 0.17, above a shuffled null of approximately 0.000 (SD 0.026, p < 0.001), indicating limited but nonzero shared agreement. In the viewpoint study, sidewalk-view images receive mean ratings of 3.48 versus 3.16 for matched street-view images; the location-aggregated Wilcoxon test reports W = 207.5, Z = 4.385, p < 0.001, rank-biserial effect size r = 0.61, and median ratings of 3.50 versus 3.00. However, 48 of 100 locations have identical median ratings, and at the individual-pair level 40.1% favor sidewalk view, 41.4% are tied, and 18.6% favor street view. The principal 70/10/20 rating-completion evaluation compares an image-only Swin-based baseline with the multimodal model: QWK improves from 0.285 ± 0.023 to 0.469 ± 0.026, MAE from 0.885 ± 0.014 to 0.785 ± 0.029, exact accuracy from 0.344 ± 0.005 to 0.410 ± 0.018, and within-one accuracy from 0.802 ± 0.007 to 0.835 ± 0.011 over five seeds. User conditioning particularly improves recall for ratings 1, 2, and 5—0.106 to 0.271, 0.124 to 0.324, and 0.224 to 0.402, respectively—while rating-3 recall decreases from 0.478 to 0.437. Validation ablations select Swin-Tiny over ConvNeXt-Tiny and CaFormer, FT-Transformer over an MLP, Transformer fusion over an MLP head, and CORAL over CORN and cross-entropy; the selected validation QWK is 0.490 ± 0.015. Age has the largest reported permutation importance (QWK decrease 0.204), followed by residence type (0.166) and walking frequency (0.164), but these values are not additive contributions. Novelty Classification: The contribution is best classified as NEW FORMULATION, NEW DATASET/ BENCHMARK, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper newly frames walkability prediction as respondent-conditioned ordinal perception, releases a respondent-linked Australian sidewalk-view dataset, and measures a viewpoint effect, while the neural encoders, Transformer fusion, and CORAL objective are standard components combined for this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study reports five random-seed runs with mean and standard deviation, validation ablations across image backbones, tabular encoders, fusion modules, and losses, class-level results, permutation-based attribute analysis, and a paired nonparametric viewpoint test. Code and data are stated to be available at https://github.com/Moloudd/user-conditioned-walkability-assessment, although the paper text does not clarify the exact licensing, completeness of the image source, or whether redistribution restrictions apply to footpath.ai and Google imagery. The main methodological concern is the split protocol: images and respondents may recur across training and test sets, with only individual image–respondent ratings held out. Consequently, the model can exploit image-specific visual memorization and respondent-profile regularities, and QWK = 0.469 measures completion of missing ratings within the sampled pool rather than prediction for unseen streets or unseen people. The sole image-only baseline is useful but insufficiently strong as a general benchmark; comparisons with aggregate-score models, respondent-only models, feature-engineered statistical mixed-effects models, and image encoders designed for panoramas are missing. No confidence intervals or significance tests compare model variants directly, and the permutation importance analysis is acknowledged to be distorted by correlated attributes and unrealistic shuffled profiles. Potential panel-selection, self-report, order, and survey-interface effects are not fully quantified. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The model uses commercially available GPU hardware and conventional pretrained components, but the paper does not report inference latency, hardware requirements, or the operational cost of acquiring sidewalk-view imagery and respondent profiles. Efficient: No parameter counts, training duration, memory footprint, inference throughput, or cost comparison with a simpler CNN/MLP or statistical mixed-effects model is provided, so efficiency relative to alternatives is Not evaluated. Effective: The evidence shows improved agreement with held-out ratings under an image- and respondent-reusing completion protocol and a statistically significant viewpoint difference, but it does not show improved real-world pedestrian accessibility, route choice, safety, mobility outcomes, or planner decisions. Scalable: The experiment covers 974 images, 1,196 respondents, and nine Australian locations; performance at 10×–100× more streets, cities, cultures, or users is not tested, and claims about personalized routing and inclusive assessment remain prospective. The work delivers a code repository and a stated dataset artifact, but no deployed routing system, production API, or trained-model release details are specified. Strengths: - It identifies a substantive modeling target—observer-conditioned walkability—that is usually collapsed into an image-level aggregate, and supports the formulation with low inter-rater agreement and significant respondent–environment interactions. - It contributes a relatively large respondent-linked dataset of 29,870 ratings across 974 sidewalk panoramas and urban, suburban, and regional contexts, addressing a genuine data gap for individual-level pedestrian perception. - The viewpoint comparison is more informative than a purely architectural contribution: matched locations show a measurable 0.32-point mean difference between sidewalk and street views, warning that imagery source can alter survey conclusions. - The ordinal objective and component ablations are technically appropriate, and the gains are not confined to exact accuracy; the model reduces MAE and improves recognition of the underrepresented rating extremes. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the dataset and respondent pool are predominantly Australian, leaving transferability to other cultural and infrastructural contexts unestablished. They acknowledge that group-level attributes cannot capture fully individual preferences despite modest inter-rater agreement. They also characterize the viewpoint comparison as supplementary rather than a systematic study and leave broader imagery and participant evaluations for future work. The authors further note that permutation importance is not additive and can be inflated by correlated respondent attributes. They directly disclose the rating-completion split and frame generalization beyond the sampled image pool as future work, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most important unaddressed issue is that the headline model result does not test the deployment scenario implied by the paper: with image overlap across partitions, it does not establish generalization to unseen locations, streets, or visual environments, and with respondent overlap it does not establish generalization to new users. A location-disjoint, image-disjoint, respondent-disjoint, and cross-city evaluation is needed. The paper does not compare against a mixed-effects ordinal model, respondent-only predictor, image-plus-simple-demographics model, aggregate-rating predictor, or modern multimodal baselines, so the marginal value of the elaborate Transformer architecture is unclear. It also does not test whether the viewpoint effect persists after matching field of view, time, weather, camera height, image quality, and image orientation; the two viewpoints may differ in more than pedestrian versus vehicle perspective. The dataset’s commercial image provenance, sampling from nine locations, self-selection through an online panel, and underrepresentation of disability and non-Australian backgrounds limit claims about inclusive assessment. Finally, the proposed use in personalized routing is not evaluated for route quality, calibration, fairness, safety, or behavioral validity, and the model’s predictions are not assessed for calibration or uncertainty despite substantial human disagreement. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile dataset-and-formulation paper for researchers studying personalized urban perception, but its strongest model claim should be treated as within-dataset completion evidence rather than evidence of deployable walkability prediction until disjoint-location and cross-population tests are provided.

Rehearse

Jiazhen Ji, Shouhong Ding · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Rehearse, a Propose–Predict–Execute controller that ranks several machine-learning code modifications before training and retrieves similar past attempts with their measured outcomes. - Why it's important: Autoresearch spends a full training run on every rejected modification, while late-stage improvements become rarer and smaller, making pre-run selection a direct compute-efficiency bottleneck. - How it does it: Rehearse uses pairwise strict-consensus LLM judging over multiple proposals and supplies the judge with candidate-relevant outcome records retrieved by cosine similarity from the same task. - The good: On a 366-pair benchmark from 39 AutoSOTA tasks, focused outcome memory raises late-stage selective accuracy from 56.9% without memory to 83.5%, and the live system improves final results across nanochat, CIFAR-10, and ETTh1 under 100 training experiments. - The missing: The live comparison excludes proposal and judge-inference costs from its equal-budget accounting and evaluates only five seeds per configuration, so the claimed end-to-end compute advantage and robustness remain incompletely established. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-driven ML experimentation or agent memory and want a concrete depth-dependent failure analysis; skip it if you need evidence at large-scale training budgets or against strong non-LLM experiment-selection methods.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses compute-waste in measurable-objective autoresearch systems, where an LLM proposes a code modification, launches a full training job, and retains the change only if the validation metric improves. This problem affects researchers and engineering teams using autonomous ML experimentation, particularly after several accepted improvements have reduced remaining headroom. The paper reports from public AutoSOTA logs that the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in iterations 1–2 to 43% by iteration 6+, while the mean gain among successful changes falls from 3.6% to 0.3%. The specific prior-work gap is not merely candidate generation or post-execution memory: it is whether an agent can reliably decide which incremental proposal deserves execution as the accepted baseline evolves. The paper claims a late-stage “confidence cliff,” in which the judge becomes more willing to decide while becoming less accurate, but the depth relationship is observational rather than causally randomized. Key Idea: The central insight is that raw or summarized trajectory memory is less useful than a small, candidate-conditioned set of prior modifications annotated only with whether they worked. Rehearse treats prior outcomes as local precedents rather than global blacklists: a new proposal can resemble a failed attempt yet still be a useful correction in the opposite direction. This focused retrieval is combined with explicit comparison among several proposals before paying for one training run. Methodology: Rehearse wraps an existing autoresearch loop without changing model weights or target training code. At each step, the proposer reads the current code and log and emits five candidates containing a description, outcome-blind hypothesis, implementation plan, and coarse type. A pairwise LLM judge receives the shared task context and two candidates, plus retrieved prior attempts from the same task whose 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding has cosine similarity at least 0.40; each retrieved record contains only the attempted change and a binary worked/did-not-work label. Every pair is judged in both presentation orders, and only agreeing judgments count under strict consensus; candidates are ranked by vote count and the top one is executed. The resulting attempt is recorded, and successful changes update the accepted baseline while failures are discarded. The explicit live objective is not a new loss function: it is the original training metric, with a modification labeled successful only when it strictly improves the current accepted baseline; crashes, timeouts, invalid patches, and non-improvements count as failures. Critical design choices are the five-candidate pool, pairwise strict-consensus tournament, and fixed similarity-threshold retrieval. The paper supports the retrieval representation with ablations and a threshold sweep, but live candidate counts, alternative retrievers, and the total-cost trade-off are not comprehensively justified. Key Results: The single-turn benchmark contains 366 outcome-labeled pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks: 296 same-baseline pairs with one successful and one unsuccessful modification, plus 70 auxiliary pairs in which both modifications worked and the larger gain was the target. Across three judge models, the memoryless judge achieves 77.6% overall selective accuracy and 56.9% selective accuracy in the deep bucket with at least three successful baseline changes; Rehearse reaches 82.3% overall and 83.5% in the deep bucket, compared with 80.9% for an LLM history-summary baseline, 74.1% for a self-reflection buffer, and 70.8% for a full-history dump. The memoryless judge’s deep-bucket coverage rises from 76% at shallow depth to 85% at depth at least three, whereas Rehearse has 77% deep coverage, indicating that the gain is partly from declining unreliable decisions. On type-1 classification pairs, selective accuracy increases from 79.5% without memory to 84.2% with Rehearse; on the auxiliary worked-versus-worked ranking pairs it increases from 67.4% to 74.1%. In live nanochat experiments with 100 thirty-minute training runs and five seeds, vanilla achieves 7.1% mean improvement, propose-many without selection 6.9%, selection without memory 8.4%, and Rehearse 10.7%; Rehearse reaches 8.9% improvement by experiment 30 versus 3.3% for vanilla. On CIFAR-10, Rehearse improves accuracy by 2.85% over baseline versus 2.10% for vanilla; on ETTh1 it reduces MSE by 54.0% versus 40.1%. It reaches vanilla’s final level after 54 CIFAR-10 experiments and 63 ETTh1 experiments versus 100 for vanilla, and finishes ahead on 9 of 10 additional-loop seeds. These results are promising but modest in breadth: the baseline is primarily the authors’ vanilla loop, and the pairwise-to-pool calibration is a Monte Carlo approximation rather than a live evaluation of larger selection budgets. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and an incremental NEW METHOD: the depth-indexed confidence-cliff analysis and same-baseline modification benchmark are the strongest original contributions, while the operational method combines standard LLM judging, pairwise selection, embeddings, and experience retrieval in a new autoresearch controller. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations, three judge models for single-turn results, a fixed outcome-blind benchmark construction, both-order judging to mitigate position bias, a length-balanced candidate variant, a retrieval-threshold sensitivity sweep, a non-LLM heuristic baseline, five seeds per live configuration, and per-seed outcomes for the two additional tasks. The ablations identify meaningful dependencies: removing candidate rationale lowers deep selective accuracy to 70.2%, replacing focused retrieval with a full dump lowers it to 70.8%, removing outcome labels lowers it to 77.5%, and adding failure reasons lowers it to 80.6%. However, the benchmark is derived from modifications proposed by the same general class of LLM-driven optimizer that the method targets, so it measures prediction on a selected proposal distribution rather than arbitrary ML engineering changes. The depth effect is confounded by headroom, modification family, and difficulty, as the authors acknowledge. Live experiments pair each serving model with one task—hy3-preview with nanochat, glm-5.1 with CIFAR-10, and deepseek-v4 with ETTh1—so model and task effects are not separated. The paper reports standard deviations but no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or more than five seeds. The skill and benchmark are stated to be released, but no repository URL or already-available artifact is specified; the current implementation uses plain files and proprietary or alias-based CodeBuddy model endpoints, limiting exact replication. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper builds and evaluates a controller skill around live ML training loops and also reports controlled benchmark experiments. * Practical: The controller can run on commercially available hardware and existing ML repositories, but each selected experiment uses a thirty-minute training budget and the live evaluation depends on external LLM serving endpoints. * Efficient: It preserves the number of training runs but adds five-proposal generation and 20 pairwise judge calls per step for a five-candidate tournament; because inference and proposal costs are excluded from the reported budget, total compute efficiency relative to vanilla is not established. * Effective: Evidence shows higher final metric improvement than the vanilla loop on three tasks—10.7% versus 7.1% on nanochat, 2.85% versus 2.10% accuracy gain on CIFAR-10, and 54.0% versus 40.1% MSE reduction on ETTh1—but this demonstrates effectiveness on three controlled proxies rather than general ML research productivity. * Scalable: The paper tests 100 experiments per run, five candidates, and 39 source tasks for the offline benchmark; it does not test 10×–100× longer trajectories, larger candidate pools, larger training jobs, or the latency and context costs of maintaining selection at scale. The work delivers a lightweight autoresearch skill/controller and an intended benchmark, backed by a focused outcome store implemented with plain files. It does not introduce a new trained model, training loss, or target-code modification. The release status and a concrete public repository are not stated. Strengths: - The confidence-cliff observation is a useful reframing of late-stage autoresearch failure: it separates declining proposal success rates from declining pre-execution discrimination and measures coverage jointly with selective accuracy. - The same-accepted-baseline construction for 296 primary pairs reduces a major source of label ambiguity and makes the pairwise outcome comparison more interpretable than comparisons across unrelated search states. - The focused-memory ablations are unusually diagnostic for an agent-memory intervention: they show that candidate text, both positive and negative outcomes, and selective retrieval each contribute, while extra failure explanations and full-history context hurt. - The live ablation separates proposal breadth, selection, and memory on nanochat, then tests the complete controller on two unrelated tasks; Rehearse beats vanilla on 9 of 10 additional-loop seeds, although the sample remains small. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the evidence to three measurable-outcome loops and exclude paper-scored or novelty-oriented systems and larger-scale seed studies. They state that live aggregates use five seeds, that the depth variable is observational rather than causal, that the benchmark is a controlled proxy, that proposal and judge inference costs are excluded from the training-run budget, and that candidate counts and memory forms are incompletely tested. They also note that longer runs and other pool sizes remain untested. These limitations are confronted directly in the limitations section rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most important unaddressed issue is whether Rehearse improves total wall-clock or monetary efficiency after accounting for the additional proposal call and up to 20 judge calls per training step; preserving training-run count is not equivalent to preserving compute. The paper lacks comparisons with strong experiment-selection baselines such as Bayesian optimization, bandit or surrogate-based selection, calibrated uncertainty models, and a reproduced ForeAgent-style selector under the same live budget. The offline benchmark may contain leakage or distributional alignment because candidate rationales are generated after log collection by an LLM and the evaluation source consists of LLM-proposed changes; the paper does not test human-authored proposals or held-out tasks separated from benchmark construction. The live model-task pairing prevents attribution of gains to the controller rather than particular serving models or task-model compatibility. Five seeds and 100-step runs provide limited evidence for the reported variance and late-stage benefits, and no statistical tests quantify whether the endpoint gaps are reliable. Finally, the strict-consensus protocol may trade away useful decisions through abstention, but the paper does not report the net latency and cost impact of abstentions or compare against calibrated single-call judges. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile empirical systems paper for researchers building LLM-driven ML experimentation loops because it identifies and measures a plausible late-stage failure mode and provides a simple, ablated intervention, but its practical compute advantage and generality remain unproven until inference costs, stronger selection baselines, held-out proposal distributions, and larger-scale repetitions are evaluated.

Prefix sliding for efficient test-time scaling

N Muennighoff, Z Wang, Z Chen, W Shi, B Hui, J Yang… · openreview.net · Percy Liang - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Prefix Sliding, an inference and reinforcement-learning mechanism that retains a fixed task prefix plus a recency window while evicting intermediate reasoning tokens. - Why it's important: It targets the growing memory, latency, and throughput costs of long-horizon reasoning, where full attention becomes increasingly expensive as every generated token extends the KV cache. - How it does it: It combines global attention to the prompt/instruction prefix with local sliding-window attention over recent reasoning tokens and implements the resulting sparse pattern in a FlashAttention-compatible kernel. - The good: On Qwen3-1.7B, a 4,096-token window produces comparable benchmark accuracy to full attention while increasing throughput from 1,477 to 5,479 tokens/s at 32K sequences and from 448 to 5,224 tokens/s at 128K sequences. - The missing: The evaluation is concentrated on one 1.7B pretrained model and mostly mathematical reasoning, while the claimed generality, very-long-horizon robustness, and superiority to stronger adaptive KV-cache and alternative-architecture baselines remain insufficiently tested. - Read it or not: Systems researchers and practitioners building long-running reasoning or agentic inference should read it for the simple cache policy and kernel design, while readers seeking a broadly validated solution to long-context reasoning can treat it as promising but preliminary.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the cost of sequential test-time scaling for decoder-only language models, particularly mathematical reasoning, coding, scientific question answering, and potentially agentic tasks that require generations lasting tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens. With full attention, each newly generated token attends to the complete prompt and reasoning trace, causing the KV cache and per-token computation to grow with sequence length. The paper argues that intermediate reasoning tokens often become less useful after their local computation is complete, whereas the initial instructions/task specification and the most recent reasoning tokens remain important. The relevant prior-work gap is a method that can be applied to existing full-attention models without retraining, maintains bounded per-token cost and memory for arbitrarily long generations, and avoids the reprocessing and irregular latency of periodically deleting or summarizing context. Key Idea: Preserve the entire initial prefix as global context while retaining only a fixed-size suffix of recent reasoning tokens. The core insight is that this asymmetric retention policy should preserve task identity, tool instructions, and current local reasoning while discarding stale intermediate tokens. The mechanism is not architecturally novel in the broad sense: the authors explicitly characterize it as equivalent to sliding-window attention with global tokens, using multiple consecutive prefix tokens and applying it to decoder-only reasoning models. Its contribution is the targeted application, training procedure, and hardware implementation for long-horizon test-time scaling. Methodology: During generation, the system partitions the sequence into a fixed prefix and a sliding window of size W. The prefix is retained permanently; as new tokens arrive, the window advances and older non-prefix tokens are removed. The maximum active context is therefore approximately prefix length plus W, and the asymptotic attention cost per new token becomes constant after the warm-up phase. For rotary position embeddings, the authors compare resetting positions after eviction with continuing the original positions; they use Continue PE because it permits KV reuse and report similar performance to Reset PE. For reinforcement learning, they use GRPO with synchronous TRL or asynchronous prime-rl infrastructure, construct a filtered math dataset from public sources, and train with Prefix Sliding rollouts. To avoid trainer memory exhaustion, they use truncated backpropagation: with window size W, they pass 4W preceding tokens to the trainer but compute the RL loss only on the final W tokens. They also describe chunked backpropagation as a closer approximation to full backpropagation for longer traces. The custom Hopper kernel uses intra-tile masking for partially valid attention blocks and inter-tile skipping for blocks outside the prefix-or-window region; this preserves exactness for the prescribed sparse pattern while approximating regular sliding-window kernel efficiency. The fixed prefix is well motivated by task and attention-sink considerations, and the 4x trainer-context multiplier is supported by a KL-mismatch ablation, but the assumptions that stale intermediate tokens can be discarded and that a fixed prefix is sufficient are only partially justified by attention visualizations and task-specific experiments. Key Results: The primary experiments use Qwen3-1.7B, vLLM, FlashAttention, Nvidia H100 GPUs, window sizes from 512 to 16,384, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, budget forcing, and 64-run averages on GPQA, MATH500, and AIME25. In the main table, Prefix Sliding with W=4,096 obtains AIME25 avg@64 of 33.9 versus 34.2 for full attention, GPQA of 37.0 versus 37.6, and MATH500 of 91.5 versus 91.7. At W=8,192, it obtains 35.8, 38.0, and 91.4 respectively, while average generated lengths are 19,373, 13,605, and 6,229 tokens. Throughput at 32K-sequence length is 5,479 tokens/s for W=4,096 versus 1,477 for full attention, and at 128K it is 5,224 versus 448 tokens/s; the corresponding speedups are approximately 3.7x and 11.7x. Throughput stabilizes at roughly 5,000 tokens/s for Prefix Sliding and regular sliding-window attention after the warm-up phase, whereas full attention continues degrading through 520K-token sequences. On the AIME25 time-accuracy curves, the method reaches comparable or better accuracy at lower wall-clock thinking time because it can generate more tokens, not because each token is shown to be intrinsically more accurate. In the alternative comparison, Prefix Sliding exceeds 30% AIME25 accuracy, while vanilla sliding window remains near 6%, and the reported H2O result is 7% under a budget-matched 4,096-token setup. LiveCodeBench exposes a failure mode: a window of at least 16,384 is needed to match full attention, with smaller windows losing code and comments needed later. On HealthBench, where the model averages only 2,086 generated tokens, gains are minor. RL experiments claim higher reward and traces beyond 100,000 tokens under equal memory, and a short 7B validation reports comparable performance to full attention, but the paper provides limited numerical detail and statistical analysis for these training results. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the underlying attention pattern is a known global-token/sliding-window combination, while the genuinely new contribution is its simple prefix-preserving policy for reasoning rollouts, its truncated-backpropagation recipe, and its FlashAttention-compatible implementation and evaluation for test-time scaling. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful ablations over window sizes, Continue versus Reset positional embeddings, the amount of context passed to the trainer, and comparisons with vanilla sliding window, Last-k deletion, summarization, and H2O. The KL-mismatch study shows that passing only the final 2,048 tokens gives KL above 0.1, while passing 4x the window substantially reduces mismatch and is close to passing 8x; this supports the chosen trainer context. However, the paper does not report conventional multi-seed error bars or significance tests for most benchmark comparisons, despite averaging 64 sampled runs per evaluation point. The main empirical study uses one model family and size, Qwen3-1.7B, with only a short DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B RL validation. The training data is a filtered, partly author-constructed mixture of public math sources, and the filtering criteria may bias training toward verifiable mathematical tasks. Comparisons omit many adaptive KV-cache eviction methods, mixed full/local-attention models, subquadratic attention methods, RNN/SSM alternatives, and methods requiring retraining; the authors acknowledge this restriction. The code, kernels, dataset, models, and scripts are not yet released; the paper only states that the authors aim to release them. The custom-kernel speed results are hardware- and implementation-dependent, and the comparison emphasizes tokens/s and wall-clock thinking time without reporting total GPU-hours, memory occupancy, energy, cost per solved problem, or end-to-end serving utilization. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper delivers a custom inference kernel and evaluates both inference and RL-training procedures. Practical: The method runs on commercially available Nvidia H100 hardware and is applied to an existing pretrained model without additional training, although the reported kernel targets Hopper and portability to other accelerators is not evaluated. Efficient: It bounds active generation context to prefix plus W and delivers roughly 3.7x throughput at 32K sequences and 11.7x at 128K for W=4,096, but it retains the full prefix and does not reduce prefix prefill cost, which can dominate for long prompts. Effective: On GPQA, MATH500, and AIME25, accuracy is close to full attention for suitable windows, but effectiveness degrades on tasks such as LiveCodeBench when essential information lies thousands of tokens outside the window, and short generations receive little benefit. Scalable: The authors report experiments exceeding one million thinking tokens and sequences up to 520K in throughput tests, but they do not establish behavior at 10x–100x larger model or workload scales, and the long-horizon evidence is narrow in task and model diversity. The work delivers a custom attention kernel, inference/training implementation, filtered training dataset, and intended model/scripts release, but no public artifact is available in the paper. Strengths: - The prefix-plus-window policy directly addresses a concrete failure mode of ordinary sliding windows: forgetting the task definition, tools, or system instructions after the prefix falls out of context. - The kernel design maps the sparse attention region onto FlashAttention-style tiling, avoiding the obvious implementation weakness of many cache-eviction methods that cannot use optimized serving kernels. - The paper evaluates wall-clock throughput rather than only token counts and demonstrates a clear asymptotic advantage over full attention at 32K–520K sequence lengths. - The authors explicitly test and document important failure cases, including LiveCodeBench information loss, limited benefit for short generations, and prefix prefill costs, rather than presenting the method as universally reliable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge limited comparisons against alternative architectures, subquadratic methods, and mixed sliding-window models because those approaches often require retraining or do not satisfy the paper's bounded-cost criterion. They report information loss when a task requires intermediate reasoning content beyond the retained window, with LiveCodeBench requiring W at least 16,384 to match full attention. They also acknowledge limited gains for short generations, inability to handle oversized system outputs or read-in contents when the window is too small, the unchanged prefill cost for long prefixes, and the need for more experiments at larger scales. These limitations are confronted directly, although the paper generally frames the omitted baselines as outside scope rather than quantifying their practical tradeoffs. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central claim that attention maps identify discardable reasoning tokens is not rigorously validated: attention probability is used as motivation, but the paper does not compare eviction policies based on causal token importance, measure information retention directly, or test whether low-attention tokens can be safely removed across diverse reasoning trajectories. - The evaluation is narrow, relying mainly on Qwen3-1.7B and math benchmarks; it lacks broad tests across model families, larger models, multilingual tasks, retrieval-heavy tasks, tool use, multi-turn agents, and long-context question answering. - The comparisons do not include strong adaptive KV-cache compression or eviction baselines under matched kernels, memory, quality, and wall-clock budgets, making the claim of superiority over efficient alternatives less conclusive. - The RL evidence is underreported: the paper does not provide detailed reward curves, final benchmark tables, run counts, seeds, compute budgets, or a controlled comparison separating the effects of longer rollouts, altered context dynamics, and truncated gradients. - The fixed-prefix assumption can be problematic when the prompt contains long documents, retrieved evidence, tool outputs, or changing state; the paper discusses this issue but does not evaluate a mechanism for promoting important intermediate tokens into the prefix or external memory. - The stated constant cost applies after the prefix and window are populated, not to prefill, and the paper does not provide a complete end-to-end latency or cost model covering prompt processing, batching, memory fragmentation, kernel launch overhead, and heterogeneous request lengths. Bottom Line: Prefix Sliding is a useful and plausibly deployable systems contribution that provides substantial long-sequence throughput gains with near-baseline accuracy on selected reasoning benchmarks, but its novelty is incremental relative to global-token sliding attention and its broad claims require stronger baselines, model diversity, RL evidence, and agentic long-context evaluation before it supports a top-tier general conclusion.

Governing the KV Cache: Preventing Timing Side-Channel Leakage in Multi-Tenant LLM Inference

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces KVGov, a per-principal HMAC-salted namespace mechanism for isolating shared prefix, radix-tree, and exact-response KV caches, supplemented by an audit scheduler and cache-scope analysis. - Why it's important: Shared KV caches can reveal private prompts or sensitive template fields to another legitimate tenant through measurable time-to-first-token differences in production LLM serving. - How it does it: It derives a secret salt from the authenticated principal and injects that salt into the cache-key hash chain, preventing cross-principal cache collisions while preserving intra-principal reuse. - The good: The paper validates the underlying timing channel on Qwen2.5/vLLM/A100 hardware with cached-to-cold TTFT ratios of 0.22 and 0.37, and shows that HMAC salting reduces simulated PROMPTPEEK and InputSnatch ASR from 100.0% to 0.0%. - The missing: The central defense is not evaluated in a real multi-tenant serving deployment, and the claimed boundary-salting efficiency retention of 92.8% is extrapolated rather than measured end to end. - Read it or not: Security and serving-systems researchers should read it for the namespace-isolation formulation and threat taxonomy, but practitioners should treat the deployment claims as preliminary until cache-hit-rate, throughput, and attack results are measured on real workloads.

Problem & Motivation: Multi-tenant LLM serving engines reuse KV states for shared token prefixes to reduce prefill latency and improve throughput, but cache keys commonly depend only on token content rather than the authenticated tenant. This lets an adversarial tenant issue probes and infer whether another tenant's prompt or prompt prefix is resident from TTFT differences. The affected domain includes vLLM, SGLang, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, LMCache, and related prefix-cache deployments, particularly those with long shared system prompts, RAG templates, tool schemas, code-assistant contexts, or structured fields. Prior attacks pursue different goals—token reconstruction, candidate identification, or membership confirmation—and defenses such as larger cache blocks, flushing, noise, and admission control address only some attack cells. The paper argues that the common missing primitive is cryptographic binding of cache resolution to the requesting principal. Key Idea: The core insight is to remove the cross-tenant cache oracle rather than merely make its timing signal noisier or its reconstruction search space larger. KVGov derives a server-secret HMAC salt from the principal identity and incorporates it into the first block hash, causing the chained cache-key namespace to become principal-specific. The paper additionally observes that isolation need only begin at the first block where principals diverge: shared preamble blocks expose no identifying information, while salting the divergence boundary protects the private suffix. This boundary-salting proposal is conceptually useful but remains an unmeasured design extrapolation, and it requires serving-layer support for an authenticated boundary offset. Methodology: The framework has four main elements. First, for principal p it computes \(\sigma_p=\mathrm{HMAC}_K(p)\), uses \(h_0=H(\sigma_p\mathbin{\|}\mathrm{tokens}_0)\), and continues the existing chained block-hash computation; the same idea is mapped to radix-tree root partitioning and exact-response cache keys, but not semantic nearest-neighbor caches. Second, it classifies cache oracles and adversary goals, distinguishing reconstruction, identification, confirmation, and enumeration, and evaluates PROMPTPEEK with Pearson correlation, InputSnatch with exact token overlap, and EarlyBird with token recovery rate. Third, ORIGAMI solves a Stackelberg allocation problem, minimizing \(\max_i v_i(1-p_i)\) subject to an audit budget, yielding \(p_i^*=\max(0,1-\lambda/v_i)\). Fourth, a replicator-dynamics model compares global and ephemeral caching and derives a prevalence threshold. Critical design choices—HMAC salting, boundary rather than root salting, and deterministic attack judges—are reasonably motivated; however, boundary salting is not implemented or measured, and the audit-load experiment uses a different adversary heuristic from the theorem's payoff objective. Key Results: In a deterministic simulation with 1,000 trials and seed 2026, no defense produces 100.0% ASR for PROMPTPEEK, EarlyBird, and InputSnatch, whereas KVGov produces 0.0% for all three; HMAC-salt alone also produces 0.0% for PROMPTPEEK and InputSnatch. Session flushing leaves 19.5% PROMPTPEEK and 9.8% InputSnatch ASR, while 20-ms Gaussian noise reduces PROMPTPEEK to 0.3% but leaves InputSnatch at 100.0%. These 0% and 100% endpoint results are analytic controls under the simulation model rather than empirical attack measurements. ORIGAMI reduces adversary expected utility by 12.6% over random auditing at Gini 0.63 with 10 tenants and 50% audit coverage; under a separate 50-tenant, 500-round heuristic load simulation, it reports 58.4–66.5% breach reduction and 66.0–72.2% damage reduction, but the paper explicitly states that this does not validate the theorem's optimality. The hardware channel measurement uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, vLLM 0.26.0, and an NVIDIA A100: for 2,119 shared-prefix tokens, cold TTFT is 149.6 ms and cached TTFT is 32.8 ms, ratio 0.22; for 1,447 tokens, the values are 104.1 ms and 38.7 ms, ratio 0.37. An independent llama.cpp/Ollama/Qwen2.5-3B/Apple M4 setup reports 1,861 ms cold versus 173 ms cached, ratio 0.093. HMAC derivation adds 1.33 microseconds per lookup in a Python laptop microbenchmark. The baselines are relevant for the attack comparisons, but there is no end-to-end comparison against production isolation mechanisms, tenant-partitioned caches, or a measured boundary-salting implementation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the main novelty is the unified formulation of KV-cache timing attacks as cross-principal cache-oracle exposure and the straightforward but appropriate HMAC namespace-isolation defense, while ORIGAMI adapts standard Stackelberg water-filling and the evolutionary analysis applies standard replicator dynamics with paper-specified parameters. The hardware confirmation across two inference stacks is a useful empirical validation of the channel, but the cryptographic salting primitive itself is closely related to existing cache-salt support in vLLM and is not demonstrated as a complete production system. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides attack-specific deterministic judges, fixed seeds, an ablation isolating HMAC-salt, preregistered gates for the hardware timing experiment, server-side verification that the cold arm had only 0.7% cache hits, two independent hardware blocks, and replication on a different engine and accelerator. It claims that scripts and data reproduce Tables 3 and 4, but no repository URL or model-weight release is given in the paper. The main ASR evaluation is a discrete-event simulation with fixed 5-ms hit and 50-ms miss latencies; it does not model GPU contention, scheduling variance, network effects, concurrent tenants, or adaptive probing against a deployed defense. The paper correctly labels endpoint ASRs as analytic controls and acknowledges the mismatch between the ORIGAMI theorem and the adversarial-load heuristic. Nevertheless, the central zero-leakage result is not tested with real attacks against an instrumented multi-tenant KVGov deployment, and the semantic-cache attack path is explicitly not evaluated. Confidence is therefore high for the cryptographic collision argument under the stated threat model, moderate for the existence of the timing channel, and low-to-moderate for the full operational system claims. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper proposes an infrastructure-layer governance mechanism, performs hardware measurements, and claims a deployable serving-layer artifact, although it does not present a released library or integrated production implementation. Practical: Root salting can run on commercial hardware and is compatible in principle with existing hash-keyed prefix caches, but boundary salting requires an authenticated principal and an offset-aware cache implementation that current engines do not expose. Efficient: HMAC adds only 1.33 microseconds per lookup in the reported microbenchmark, but root namespace partitioning can eliminate cross-tenant prefix reuse; the paper does not measure the resulting throughput, memory, hit-rate, or latency impact on representative workloads, and its 92.8% boundary-salting benefit is estimated rather than measured. Effective: The cryptographic construction should prevent cross-principal equality-based cache hits under the stated secret-key and authentication assumptions, and simulation shows 0.0% ASR, but real adversarial attack success against the deployed defense is not evaluated and semantic-cache leakage remains outside the mechanism. Scalable: The key derivation cost is constant per request and the construction scales conceptually with tenant count, but the paper tests neither 10x–100x tenant concurrency nor large production workloads, and it provides no measured behavior under cache pressure, eviction, batching, autoscaling, or distributed cache coordination. The work stops short of delivering a clearly identified software artifact: it claims released scripts and data, but gives no URL, and it does not report a complete KVGov library, CLI, serving-engine patch, or trained model. Strengths: - It identifies a common security invariant—principal binding of cache resolution—that covers several apparently different prefix-cache attacks and is stronger than timing noise or block-size hardening. - It separates cache mechanisms from adversary goals, making clear why free-text reconstruction, candidate identification, and O(1) structured-field confirmation have radically different costs on the same cache. - It validates the existence of the timing channel with careful server-side cache-counter checks, internal TTFT instrumentation, multiple prefix lengths, and an independent llama.cpp/Apple-Metal stack. - The ablation is informative: noise and admission control fail against at least one attack family, whereas HMAC salting is the only evaluated component that removes both simulated equality-based attack paths. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that EarlyBird is evaluated in a block-size-1 reference simulation because vLLM 0.26.0 removed that configuration; that root-salting cache-efficiency costs are workload-dependent; that boundary-salting efficiency is extrapolated and requires unsupported engine functionality; that semantic caches require per-principal retrieval-index partitioning rather than salting; and that ASR experiments are simulations rather than production adversarial trials. They also acknowledge that the adversarial-load benchmark uses a heuristic inconsistent with the ORIGAMI theorem's payoff function. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, which improves the credibility of the narrower claims. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline 0.0% ASR result is tautological for the simulated equality oracle: once namespaces are disjoint, the simulated probe cannot hit the victim, so it does not establish robustness against timing leakage from shared scheduling, memory contention, batching, eviction, metadata, or implementation mistakes. - The paper does not evaluate KVGov in a real multi-tenant serving stack with concurrent victim and attacker requests, adaptive attackers, realistic latency distributions, cache eviction, request batching, or distributed workers. - The main practical trade-off—lost cross-tenant reuse—is not quantified with cache hit rate, GPU utilization, throughput, memory footprint, or cost across real workloads, despite shared system prompts being identified as a major exposure and performance case. - There is no measured implementation of boundary salting, even though the paper presents its estimated 92.8% retained benefit as a major practical advantage. - Semantic-cache leakage is outside the evaluation, so the claim of a unified defense is limited to prefix-cache paths; the taxonomy covers semantic caches but the proposed system does not protect them. - The ORIGAMI load benchmark's adversary objective differs from the theorem's objective, so its 58–67% breach reductions cannot be interpreted as evidence of optimal Stackelberg allocation. - The security model assumes millisecond-precision TTFT observation and known vocabularies/templates but does not analyze authentication failures, salt-key rotation, principal aliasing, cache sharing within organizational groups, or side channels in the boundary-detection/admission scan. Bottom Line: The paper offers a clear and likely correct infrastructure-level fix for equality-based cross-tenant KV-cache collisions and a careful demonstration that the timing channel exists, but practitioners should not accept its broader performance and system-security claims until the defense is implemented and evaluated under real concurrent workloads, with semantic caches and cache-efficiency costs included.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses inference-state migration for users moving between edge nodes that already host the same LLM weights. A handover must move the user's KV cache, whose size grows linearly with context length; for Qwen3-8B in BF16, the paper reports approximately 1.2 GB for an 8K-token context. Concurrent migrations share a constrained backhaul and may not complete before a 500 ms transfer window. Full KV-cache transfer preserves exact state but can be too slow, while raw-token transfer requires target-side re-prefill. Existing KV-cache eviction methods identify valuable entries for reducing memory, but do not determine how a shared backhaul should be divided among multiple migrating users. The gap is therefore joint semantic cache selection and multi-user bandwidth scheduling under an anytime-inference requirement. Key Idea: The central insight is to shape the utility curve before optimizing resource allocation. Sending KV entries in descending query-agnostic importance makes early cache prefixes disproportionately useful, moving the accuracy inflection point to approximately 6.4–6.7% of the cache and leaving most of the usable range concave. This transforms an otherwise nonconvex sigmoidal network-utility problem into a convex allocation problem after an admission rule raises each served user above its concavity anchor. The paper then allocates bytes according to equal marginal accuracy gain per transmitted bit, not equal bandwidth, progress, or user count. Methodology: During a session, the source assigns per-entry importance scores using Fast KVzip's gating-network scores and maintains a descending order over layer-head-token KV entries. Each entry is transmitted with coordinate metadata, so the target can reconstruct the received partial cache and resume decoding from the delivered prefix. For user i, the cache size is modeled as \(L_i=2n_Ln_Hd_hqT_i\) bits, and the scheduler tracks the received fraction \(x_i\), chooses a normalized delivery rate \(b_i\), and obtains \(y_i=x_i+b_i\Delta t\). The objective maximizes \(\sum_i[A_i(y_i)-A_i(x_i)]\) subject to \(\sum_iL_ib_i\le B\), nonnegative rates, and \(y_i\in[\tau_i,1]\). The measured utility is fit with an algebraic sigmoid, \(A_i(y)=\frac{M_i}{2}(1+\frac{k_i(y-\tau_i)}{\sqrt{1+k_i^2(y-\tau_i)^2}})\), whose inverse derivative enables closed-form water levels. If the budget exceeds \(B_{min}=\Delta t^{-1}\sum_iL_i[\tau_i-x_i]^+\), the algorithm finds a common dual price by bisection and assigns each user a cache-size-weighted water level; otherwise, it applies equalized-bytes admission among users below \(\tau_i\), redistributing capacity when users finish. The ordering choice is well motivated by prior KVzip results and the measured curves; the sigmoid choice is supported by fit quality and computational tractability; the one-slot objective is mathematically justified, but the fallback policy is heuristic and the horizon-myopic design is only empirically bounded. Key Results: On RULER, using Qwen3-8B as the primary model and additionally Qwen3-14B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the algebraic sigmoid achieves \(R^2>0.999\) for Qwen3-8B at 4K, 8K, and 16K contexts, with 8K RMSE 0.936, and \(R^2>0.99\) across the additional models and ordering schemes. Fast KVzip ordering places the fitted inflection point near 6.5% of the cache, whereas random ordering requires much more cache. In simulations with Qwen3-8B, BF16, 20 Gbps backhaul, 100 ms slots, 500 ms transfer windows, Poisson arrivals, and context lengths uniformly sampled from 4K, 8K, and 16K, ImpactHO reaches 93.7% average accuracy at 4 users/s versus a 94.1% full-cache ceiling. It outperforms equal allocation, winner-take-all, and proportional fairness over 1–8 users/s and 10–30 Gbps. Under random ordering, accuracy falls from 56.7% at 2 users/s to 20.2% at 8 users/s, while importance ordering remains above 90% in the plotted range. At 12 users/s, equalized-bytes admission reduces sub-threshold starvation to 0.65%, compared with 20.8% without admission and 15.5% for the WTA fallback. In an idealized latency comparison with unlimited transfer windows and no compute contention, the proposed method reaches 99% of full-cache accuracy in 229 ms, 353 ms, and 590 ms for 4K, 8K, and 16K contexts, respectively, versus 300/676/1,566 ms for re-prefill and 211/396/694 ms for the hybrid baseline. The paper also reports 98.2–99.5% of a clairvoyant global upper bound, with the gap increasing under heavier load. Baselines cover simple allocation heuristics and compute-based alternatives, but the strongest direct handover comparison is adapted from prior work and is not demonstrated as a complete deployed system. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a systems-oriented ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component: the genuinely new element is applying query-agnostic KV-eviction rankings to transmission ordering and coupling the resulting empirically shaped accuracy utility to a multi-user handover allocator with a weighted water-filling solution, while sigmoid fitting, KV importance scoring, and network utility maximization are individually established techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes a formal feasibility lemma, KKT-based proof of the water-filling theorem, sensitivity studies over handover rate, bandwidth, slot duration, and transfer window, and ablations for random versus importance ordering and for equalized-bytes versus WTA admission. It averages simulations over 100 seconds and 100 Monte Carlo runs, and reports 95% confidence intervals over RULER samples for end-to-end measurements. However, the main scheduler results rely heavily on algebraic utilities fitted from RULER and then evaluated through the same fitted task characterization; the end-to-end validation is described but not broken down by task, model, context, or seed. The main experiments use one model, one precision, one importance scorer, synthetic Poisson arrivals, and uniformly sampled context lengths. No code, dataset release, model-weight release, or repository URL is mentioned. The comparison to ctHO is largely structural, while the quantitative compute baselines use favorable assumptions such as sufficient independent GPUs and an infinite transfer window; stronger online scheduling and cache-transfer baselines are not fully evaluated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a proposed systems algorithm evaluated in simulation and partial end-to-end inference experiments. Practical: The method can in principle run on commercially available hardware—the authors use an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 and a 20 Gbps link—but deployment requires source-side Fast KVzip scoring, index sorting, partial-cache reconstruction, metadata handling, and compatible target-side inference support. Efficient: The allocator is near-linear in the number of active users per slot, using bisection over a scalar dual price; the paper estimates 3-byte coordinate metadata against 0.5 KB entries as under 1% wire overhead and describes scoring as one-time, but does not quantify scoring latency, GPU memory overhead, sorting time in absolute terms, or total system cost. Effective: Evidence shows higher average RULER accuracy and lower time to 99% full-cache accuracy than the selected baselines under the tested workloads, but it measures a benchmark accuracy proxy rather than user-level task success, conversational quality, or production handover continuity. Scalable: The experiments reach 8–12 handovers/s, 30 Gbps, 16K contexts, and 4,000-user traces, but do not test 10×–100× larger user populations, contexts, model sizes, backhaul topologies, or non-Poisson mobility; scalability beyond these settings is claimed through allocator complexity rather than demonstrated system measurements. The work delivers an algorithmic framework and simulator-style evaluation, not a released library, CLI, deployed service, or public dataset. Strengths: - It identifies a non-obvious interface between KV-cache eviction and communication scheduling: importance scores are used not merely to discard entries but to create a valuable anytime transmission prefix. - The weighted water-filling derivation is technically appropriate for the stated concave operating region, explicitly accounts for heterogeneous cache sizes, and provides a low-overhead online implementation with a formal optimality argument. - The paper separates the feasible and infeasible regimes and introduces an admission fallback that directly targets the observed starvation problem; the reported 0.65% versus 20.8% starvation result supports this design choice. - The experiments isolate the contributions of ordering and admission control and compare against both allocation heuristics and compute-based re-prefill strategies, rather than reporting only one aggregate comparison. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that importance ordering adds source-side scoring and O(n log n) sorting costs, requires per-entry coordinate metadata, and that the allocator optimizes each slot rather than the full transfer horizon. They report a widening gap from the clairvoyant upper bound at higher load and identify horizon-aware scheduling as future work. They also state that the framework can use other fixed orderings only when their induced utility is monotone and concave over the operating region. The paper does not substantially discuss limitations involving scorer generalization, task distribution shift, exact partial-KV semantics across model implementations, or real mobility traces. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The fitted sigmoid is calibrated on RULER and is then used as the core utility for the scheduler; stronger evidence would fit on one task/context split and evaluate on held-out tasks, prompts, and workloads to rule out benchmark-specific utility shaping. - The experimental evaluation is narrow: Qwen3-8B drives the system study, while the other models appear primarily in curve-fitting experiments; no larger model, quantization mode, serving engine, multi-GPU deployment, or production handover trace is tested. - The comparison set omits a direct adaptive baseline that combines the same importance ordering with an alternative online optimizer, making it difficult to separate the benefit of the water-filling policy from the benefit of ordering and admission control. - The method assumes the target can decode correctly from arbitrary top-ranked per-layer/head/token KV subsets and that the importance ordering remains valid for future queries; the paper does not evaluate query or conversation distribution shift, degradation on generation quality beyond RULER accuracy, or correctness across decoding settings. - The reported latency comparison gives the proposed method an anytime 99%-accuracy stopping criterion while baselines must fully restore context, and assumes compute contention-free re-prefill/hybrid baselines; this is informative for the stated use case but not an apples-to-apples end-to-end service comparison. Bottom Line: This is a technically coherent and potentially useful formulation for importance-aware edge-LLM handover, with convincing within-benchmark evidence and a clean allocator derivation, but its practical impact remains provisional until broader held-out task evaluation, stronger adaptive baselines, real traces, and a released implementation validate that partial KV-cache decoding behaves reliably outside the authors' fitted RULER setting.

AdvFD: Boosting Visual Generation via Adversarial Fr'echet Distance Loss (23 ▲ )

Mingju Gao, Jingkai Zhou, Kun Gai, Changqian Yu, Hao Tang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 12 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Adversarial Fréchet Distance (AdvFD), a post-training objective that augments frozen feature-space Fréchet matching with an adversarially adapted visual representation for one-step image generators. - Why it's important: Static feature objectives can improve their own scores while allowing visible artifacts and mismatches in other feature spaces, undermining reliable distribution-level training. - How it does it: AdvFD alternates generator minimization and representation maximization of a Fréchet discrepancy, using real-feature whitening to remove trivial feature-scale inflation. - The good: On ImageNet 256×256, AdvFD improves the FD-loss baseline across JiT and pMF backbones and scales, including a JiT-L held-out FD-r3 reduction from 5.46 to 3.20 and FD-r6 reduction from 3.24 to 2.01. - The missing: The evidence covers only class-conditional ImageNet at 256×256 and relies mainly on Fréchet metrics and qualitative examples, without human judgments, text-conditioned settings, higher resolutions, or video evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on fast image-generation post-training or objective hacking; skip it if you need evidence for broad generative-model deployment beyond ImageNet or a demonstrated inference-time improvement.
Why this rank
Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (80) are substantial: adaptive adversarial feature geometry plus whitening directly targets Fréchet hacking, and the held-out encoder gains are more informative than optimizing a single fixed metric. Rigor (62) is limited by the preprint status, absence of seeds and uncertainty estimates, encoder-dependent metrics, and confounding among adaptive-backbone initialization and capacity choices. Completeness (72) and Resilience (65) are moderate because the authors bound the scope honestly, but human perceptual quality, convergence or game stability, higher resolutions, and broader domains remain untested. Impact (58) reflects unchanged one-step inference and promising post-training improvements, but the added training complexity and lack of a confirmed code or model release weaken practical adoption. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*58 = 69.
empirical Novelty 78 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 80 Completeness 72 Resilience 65 Impact 58
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation The work addresses unreliable post-training of one-step visual generators using distribution-level losses. FD-loss matches real and generated samples through first- and second-order statistics in fixed pretrained feature spaces such as Inception, SigLIP, and MAE, but those spaces provide incomplete and static supervision. The paper documents a failure mode it calls “Fréchet hacking”: a generator can reduce the feature-space objective while retaining or introducing perceptually relevant artifacts and worsening alignment under an encoder not used for training. In one diagnostic, a universal perturbation lowers Inception FID from 3.31 to 2.56 despite visible high-frequency noise; during JiT-B training, FD-r-Inception decreases by 29.4% while FD-r-CLIP increases by 8.5%. The intended gap is therefore adaptive, distribution-level supervision that exposes residual mismatches without simply adding a larger fixed encoder ensemble. Key Idea The core insight is to learn the comparison geometry rather than only optimize a fixed comparison space: a trainable visual encoder maximizes the Fréchet discrepancy between real and generated distributions, and the generator then minimizes that discrepancy in the currently adapted feature space. Real-feature whitening is the essential calibration mechanism because raw Fréchet distance scales quadratically with feature magnitude, creating a trivial adversarial direction in which the encoder increases norms instead of revealing meaningful discrepancies. Methodology Let p be the real distribution and qθ the generator distribution. The static objective is Dstatic(p,qθ)=Σϕ λϕ DFDϕ(p,qθ), using frozen SigLIP, MAE, and Inception features. AdvFD adds a trainable representation ψω, initialized from a pretrained encoder, and computes Dadv as the squared Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussian distributions fitted to the mean and covariance of whitened real and generated features. In the G-step, ψω and the static encoders are frozen while θ minimizes Dstatic+λadvDadv; in the D-step, θ and generated samples are frozen while ω maximizes Dadv. The implementation uses AdamW, clipped representation gradients, separate exponential moving averages for feature statistics, a 50,000-sample feature queue, delayed activation at step 1,000, and a 4,000-step warm-up. Whitening centers real features and multiplies them by (Σp+εI)^−1/2, with ε=10−3; the paper provides an affine-invariance argument for exact whitening and discusses the approximation caused by minibatch statistics, ridge regularization, and detached EMA statistics. The three critical design decisions—retaining the static objective, initializing the adaptive branch from pretrained Inception, and applying whitening specifically to the adaptive branch—are supported by ablations, although the choice of pretrained Inception and the relative weighting remain empirical rather than theoretically derived. Key Results Experiments use class-conditional ImageNet-1K at 256×256, 50,000 generated evaluation samples, one-step sampling, and JiT and pixel MeanFlow (pMF) B/L/H models initialized from the same checkpoints as FD-loss. On JiT-B, AdvFD changes FID/FD-r6/held-out FD-r3 from 1.00/5.53/8.45 to 0.79/3.92/6.03, relative reductions of 21.0%, 29.1%, and 28.6%. On JiT-L, it changes 0.77/3.24/5.46 to 0.73/2.01/3.20, reductions of 5.2%, 38.0%, and 41.4%; on JiT-H, it changes 0.75/2.65/4.44 to 0.72/1.80/2.93, reductions of 4.0%, 32.1%, and 34.0%. On pMF-H, it changes 0.77/1.89/2.69 to 0.74/1.74/2.50, with smaller gains than on JiT. The held-out FD-r3 metric aggregates ConvNeXt, DINOv2, and CLIP, none of which are in the training SIM objective, so these results provide evidence of transfer beyond the optimized representations, though they remain proxy metrics. The strongest baseline is the corresponding FD-loss recipe under matched data, budget, sampling, and—in a separate experiment—wall-clock comparisons; the broader Table 1 comparison includes many multi-step and one-step models but is not a controlled comparison because architectures, spaces, and sampling budgets differ. PatchGAN and DMD-style alternatives do not match AdvFD on the reported metrics: for JiT-B, PatchGAN gives 0.90/5.57/8.90 and DMD gives 1.77/5.90/6.75 versus AdvFD's 0.79/3.92/6.03. Without whitening, performance collapses to FID 10.69, FD-r6 58.50, and FD-r3 40.54. No error bars, multiple-seed results, statistical tests, or human-study scores are reported. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The paper's main novelty is applying adversarially learned feature geometry to Fréchet-based generator post-training and combining it with real-feature whitening; the alternating min–max structure and moment matching draw on established GAN, Fréchet-distance, feature-matching, and distribution-distillation ideas rather than introducing a wholly new adversarial paradigm. The characterization of static-feature “Fréchet hacking” is a useful empirical finding, but the broader phenomenon is closely related to proxy and reward hacking. Rigor & Reproducibility The study includes useful component ablations: whitening location, alternative anti-hacking guidance, adversarial backbone and initialization, adversarial loss weight, frozen versus trainable adaptive representations, and wall-clock-matched FD-loss training. These isolate the contribution of adaptive representation learning reasonably well; in particular, freezing the added branch produces FID/FD-r6/FD-r3 of 1.62/11.02/8.71, while extra FD-loss steps matched to AdvFD wall-clock cost produce 1.71/7.70/8.63. However, the paper does not report seeds, variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, making the small FID gains on pMF-L and pMF-H difficult to assess. The evaluation is performed on the same ImageNet training distribution used for post-training, and all primary metrics are Fréchet statistics computed from pretrained encoders, so improvements may not fully establish human-perceived quality or true distributional fidelity. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.11205v1, dated 11 August 2026), and no code, dataset, or model-weight repository is explicitly stated; a project page is listed at https://gasaiyu.github.io/AdvFD-page, but the parsed paper does not confirm released implementation or checkpoints. Reproduction also depends on substantial implementation details such as EMA statistics, queue initialization, covariance eigendecomposition, CFG settings, and large global batches, which are documented but computationally demanding. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The method preserves the existing one-step inference architecture and runs on conventional GPU training infrastructure, but the paper does not provide a complete training-resource or wall-clock accounting beyond a matched-cost comparison. Efficient: Inference remains 1 NFE with unchanged generator parameter counts, while training adds a trainable visual encoder, whitening, feature-statistics maintenance, and extra forward/backward work; the exact overhead is not quantified. Effective: Metrics and qualitative samples show consistent improvements over FD-loss on ImageNet, especially in held-out representation spaces, but effectiveness for human preference, prompt adherence, safety, or real application quality is not evaluated. Scalable: Results cover JiT and pMF at B/L/H scales up to 953M generator parameters, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger models, higher resolutions, text conditioning, or video and explicitly leaves those settings unvalidated. The work delivers a research training method and an associated project page, but the paper does not explicitly confirm a released library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or code artifact. Strengths - It identifies and demonstrates a concrete failure mode of static Fréchet optimization using both a controlled universal-perturbation diagnostic and training trajectories in which the optimized and held-out metrics move in opposite directions. - The adaptive representation plus real-feature whitening targets a specific degeneracy of adversarial Fréchet optimization; the whitening ablation shows that omitting this component causes catastrophic feature-norm inflation and metric degradation. - The controlled comparisons are stronger than a single baseline experiment: improvements persist across two generator families and three scales, and the wall-clock experiment distinguishes adaptive representation learning from simply training the static objective longer. - The held-out FD-r3 evaluation excludes the three representations used in the SIM training objective, providing evidence that the method is not merely optimizing the exact reported training features. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet generation at 256×256 and that effectiveness on higher-resolution, text-conditioned, and video generation remains unvalidated. They also acknowledge extra training-time computation from adversarial representation updates and whitening, while noting that inference architecture and 1-NFE sampling cost remain unchanged. These boundaries are stated directly, but the paper does not discuss the absence of human evaluation, seed variability, or the dependence of results on pretrained visual encoders. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The principal evidence uses encoder-dependent Fréchet metrics, including a held-out set of other encoders, but no human preference study, perceptual artifact rating, task-based evaluation, or distributional metric independent of pretrained feature spaces tests whether the claimed visual improvements transfer beyond proxy metrics. - The paper does not report repeated runs, uncertainty, or statistical testing; this is particularly relevant for modest FID changes such as 0.78 to 0.77 on pMF-L. - The adaptive representation is initialized from pretrained Inception and fully fine-tuned, while SigLIP and MAE use rank-16 LoRA because of memory constraints; the comparison therefore confounds architecture, adaptation capacity, and initialization, and does not establish how performance changes with representation size or compute held constant. - The adversarial encoder is trained on the same ImageNet distribution and its statistics are updated through EMAs and minibatch estimates; sensitivity to batch size, queue size, EMA decay, covariance dimension, whitening ridge, clipping threshold, and critic update frequency is not systematically reported. - The theoretical discussion establishes scale-degeneracy removal and finite-horizon boundedness of the implemented optimizer, but it does not establish convergence, stability of the alternating game, or that maximizing second-order feature discrepancy reliably identifies perceptually important residual errors. - The reported comparisons against many external models in Table 1 mix one-step and multi-step systems, latent and pixel spaces, and different parameter and NFE budgets; they are useful context but should not be interpreted as controlled evidence that AdvFD is superior to those models. Bottom Line AdvFD is a technically coherent and empirically useful extension of Fréchet-loss post-training, with convincing controlled gains on ImageNet one-step generation, but its practical significance remains conditional on whether encoder-based improvements survive human evaluation and broader domains; practitioners working on fast image generation should read it, while broader claims should await stronger and more reproducible validation.
